The local girls taking on Liverpool and Manchester United

BBC News Fri, 31 Jul 2026 05:35:11 GMT

"Tough", "stronger" and "fitter" are probably not the words most footballers want to hear to describe their opposition.

For players from girls' teams in Northern Ireland, however, the standard of overseas opposition at the Girls' Super Cup NI is only a positive.

Now in its fifth season, the growing prestige and importance of the event has been highlighted by Liverpool making their debut this year.

The girls and their coaches say taking on big sides, including teams from countries such as the United States and Norway, is one of the best ways to improve and develop.

Games take place across Antrim and Newtownabbey council area, meaning sides like Manchester United and Chicago City are competing alongside the likes of Linfield, Glentoran and Crusaders on local pitches from Monkstown to Chimney Corner.

On Wednesday at The Diamond in Rathcoole, Crusaders took on American opponents Surf Select and went down to a 5-1 defeat.

But it was not a negative experience for the players involved.

Crusaders player Kelly, from Limavady, said a tough challenge also meant there was lots to learn.

"They're a lot stronger, quicker, fitter. It's just harder," she said.

"It's great for development, it's an elite competition so the competition is going to be good."

Erin from Lisburn also relished the challenge of foreign opposition.

"We learn loads of stuff by playing against American teams," she said.

"It just helps us develop as players."

"They're quick and strong, just running with them they'll outpace you," her teammate Daisy, from east Belfast, said.

Rachael from the west of the city agreed. "They're very fast and athletic," she said.

The girls' tournament - which is the counterpart of the long-running boys' event - started in 2022 with just six teams but now boasts 16 sides and this year's event saw English giants Liverpool take part for the first time.

Like the boys' event, the girls' tournament is now an established part of the calendar for many academy sides.

Crusaders coach Heather Mearns said it was a unique opportunity for teams to welcome top opposition from abroad and play them in their local communities.

"It's great because Northern Ireland's really small, it always feels like you're playing the same teams over and over again, the Super Cup's great because the girls all get to play teams that aren't from here," she said.

She added that the level of opposition and the growth of the tournament was only going to drive girls in Northern Ireland on.

"I don't think it's the most physical type of football over here, you have to play against the boys to get that kind of physicality, but when you play teams from down south or the Americans, they're all really athletic and really physical," she said.

"It shows our girls the levels in the other countries... it gives them something to aspire to."

One of the eye-catching fixtures on Wednesday, played in Monkstown not long after the Crusaders game finished, was Liverpool's debut in the Super Cup against Norwegian side IL Heming.

Despite taking the lead, Liverpool went down 3-1 against their opponents from Oslo.

Reds coach Zoey Shaw was full of praise for the Super Cup and the opportunities it gave her players.

"It's so welcoming to be here, all of the locals coming out to watch," she said.

"It's creating lots of different challenges for us, coming up against different opposition than normal.

"We're sharing a hotel with one of the American teams and the girls had a massive quiz night along with them," she said adding that it was good to connect with other countries off the pitch.

"Girls football is growing at a really good rate. It's still got a way to go, but to come to venues like this today and Ballyclare yesterday and see the crowds that come in, 700-plus coming to an under-16s game, they're the moments that I think all young girls want."

The Liverpool game was watched by a healthy crowd including Antrim and Newtownabbey Mayor Henry Cushinan and Deputy Mayor Alison Bennington.

Bennington is a former Northern Ireland international, with 24 caps for the women's side after making her debut in 1973.

"If Liverpool are coming here, if Manchester United are coming here, it's a big competition," she said.

"Fair play to the guys and the girls who have organised behind the scenes, bringing those teams here.

"It's taken a long time in Northern Ireland for football to develop, from how I played way back in the 70s, but how it's coming on now is absolutely fantastic.

"The young ones, and I see the young kiddies here watching the matches, taking part, wanting to be ball girls and how they're developing and they're the senior players playing, I'm very emotional about it."

Cushinan said the tournament had lots of benefits for the local area as well as for the teams taking part.

"It's great for the area to bring international guests in, it's a great benefit for hotels and local businesses.

"If people come and visit here for football they'll maybe come back and visit us again," he said.

What your summer reading list says about you

BBC News Fri, 31 Jul 2026 00:26:02 GMT

You've been dreaming about that summer break on the sun lounger, book in one hand and drink in the other, for months. Now the dash to the airport gate, train station or hours-long drive is all that stands in your way.

But what does the book you've just shoved in your suitcase say about you?

"It's definitely not a random choice," says Edgar Dubourg, a cognitive scientist at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris. "Your reading list is basically a map of your personality.

"When you pick a thriller or romance or horror or science fiction you're not escaping your psychology, in a way, you're really feeling very intuitive and very old parts of your brain.

"Fiction isn't inventing new emotions in you. It's pressing on those pre-existing motivations like instincts."

Studies have shown that our book choices can subconsciously reveal important parts of our personality - including what gives us pleasure and what makes us feel emotion.

Research by Dr Valerie van Mulukom, a senior lecturer in psychology at Oxford Brookes University, suggests that our inner anxieties (or what she calls existential insecurities) determine which book we pick from the shelf.

During her study, she used how often someone might engage with a certain genre to match it up with one of the following four clusters:

But what do they mean? And how do they match up with our own anxieties?

If, like me, you're big on crime novels, then this suggests you're concerned with - or intrigued by - threat and danger.

This isn't just limited to old-fashioned detective novels or psychological thrillers, but can be anything from true crime and spy stories to supernatural horrors like the works of Stephen King's books.

The UK bestseller lists have a range of titles that sit in the "threat and danger" category defined by the research, including:

Meanwhile, if lustful romance is more your thing (very much not mine), then your insecurities are more likely to be about your relationships, both romantic and platonic, and your thoughts on social status and reputation.

The UK bestseller lists have a range of titles that sit in the "everyday life and human relationships" category defined by the research, including:

At the opposite end, someone who likes science fiction or fantasy novels tends to be more concerned with the state of the world.

If you're spending your summer holiday finally reading the Game of Thrones novels, known for mixing political intrigue and medieval battles with tales of dragons and undead armies, then you're likely to be someone who worries about climate change or the threat of war.

The UK bestseller lists have a range of titles that sit in the "epic other-world adventures" category defined by the research, including:

For me, holiday reading is serious work. On my last trip abroad, I took eight books for a three-week holiday, ranging from Frank Herbert's sci-fi epic Dune to James Ellroy's noir throwback The Black Dahlia.

But not everyone likes disappearing off into fictional worlds. What if autobiographies or books about history are more your thing?

Dr Dubourg says it is narratives that are important, not necessarily whether they're fact or fiction.

"Everybody consumes narratives, be it in the form of actual news, of anecdotes, of stories that people tell in neighbourhoods."

The UK bestseller lists have a range of titles that sit in the "facts and history" category defined by the research, including:

So next time you pick up a book, what you think is just something vaguely interesting might actually make up an important part of your psychology.

Smallpox DNA in ancient Inca mummies shows virus came from Europe

New Scientist July 30, 2026

DNA samples collected from Inca mummies have confirmed the presence of a strain of smallpox that first emerged in Europe.

“We interpreted this as the first direct molecular evidence of smallpox introduction into the Americas through European colonisation,” says Shigeki Nakagome at Trinity College Dublin, Ireland.

Advertisement

The disease was particularly brutal in parts of the world colonised by Europeans, such as Australia and the Americas, where Indigenous populations had no natural immunity, resulting in millions of deaths.

Advertisement

At the same time, more houses have sprung up in forests outside cities like Barcelona, raising the risk of wildfires, which most often are ignited by humans.

Can cloud seeding save us from water bankruptcy?

Advertisement

Malaria, which caused an estimated 610,000 deaths in 80 countries in 2024, occurs when people get bitten by a mosquito infected by a Plasmodium parasite. Passing 1.5°C of global warming isn’t just a political disaster, it will have dire consequences for us all, as those living on the front line already know

Sadie Ryan at the University of Florida says this “really elegant study” pulls together various types of data to project the impacts of climate change. “Overall, it’s sad to see such stark evidence of climate-driven shifts”, especially given our capacity to mitigate this, she says.

Advertisement

In rodents, this acts on the brain, fat tissue and the liver to improve blood sugar levels and reduce the number of senescent cells. These cells, which accumulate with age, have stopped dividing and cause chronic inflammation.

Free newsletter

Restricting protein intake has also been shown to dampen the activity of a protein called mTORC1 in mice. mTORC1 ordinarily stimulates cell growth, but reducing its activity boosts cellular repair. “It essentially switches cells from a proliferative state, where they’re growing and engaging a lot of metabolism, to one where they’re dividing more slowly, if at all, and focusing on repair,” says Lamming. Studies suggest this cuts the risk of age-related conditions and extends lifespan in mice, he says.

Dudley says no studies were intentionally omitted. “We were focused on protein restriction, not the many studies looking at higher levels of protein intake,” he says. Beyond building muscle and preventing frailty, there’s mixed evidence on whether a higher protein intake helps with ageing, says Dudley.

Why have so many people become fixated on protein? Donald Layman is one of the people behind the research showing the benefits of getting more protein in your diet, but he thinks things have gone too far and wants to set the record straight

Where to watch the next total solar eclipse anywhere in the world

New Scientist July 31, 2026

On 12 August, a total solar eclipse will sweep a narrow path across parts of Europe and the Atlantic and Arctic oceans. Such an eclipse happens somewhere on Earth about once every 18 months as the moon and the sun line up just right so that the moon blocks out the entirety of the sun’s disc, darkening the sky and revealing the outermost layers of the sun that are usually hidden by the glare of its brighter surface.

For the most part, this August’s total eclipse will only be visible from the ocean and relatively remote areas of land: northern Russia, Greenland, the ocean, and then more inhabited regions as it passes through Iceland and Spain. A broader swathe will see a partial eclipse, but views of the total eclipse’s grandeur will be limited. If you aren’t able to spot this one, though, there will be other chances.

The next total eclipse will be on 2 August 2027. It will be visible in parts of northern Africa, and even though more than half of its path will be over ocean, for eclipse chasers, this will be the big one. That’s because totality – the period when the moon completely covers the sun’s disc, in this case 6 minutes and 23 seconds at its maximum – will last longer than it has for any other eclipse since 2009. A longer one won’t happen until the year 2114.

Advertisement

The length of totality varies because of the geometry of Earth’s orbit around the sun and the moon’s orbit around Earth. Neither of them are perfectly circular, so when the moon is a little bit closer to us or the sun further away, the moon takes longer to pass in front of the sun. If you are going to travel to see one solar eclipse, the one in 2027 is a good choice.

The next total eclipse after that, in July 2028, will be visible in New Zealand and Australia. In November 2030, one will pass through Australia again, as well as southern Africa. The eclipse in 2031 won’t be visible from land at all, and the one in 2033 will only briefly be visible from parts of Alaska and Siberia. In the following few years, two more total eclipses will pass over Australia, making it the best place to look for eclipses this decade.

Free newsletter

The next total eclipse to pass over a significant portion of the US will be in 2045. Parts of Asia will have total eclipses in 2034, 2035 and 2042, while South America will experience them in 2045, 2048 and 2059, and Africa will see total eclipses several times between now and 2060. Most of Europe won’t see one until 2081.

When planning for a solar eclipse, there are a few things to take into account, but the most important ones are the duration of totality and the expected weather. On weather, 2027 is a winner once again, thanks to the tendency for there to be relatively little cloud cover over northern Africa. Eclipses in more polar climes tend to be a riskier bet.

But if the clouds cooperate and you are at the right spot in the world, all you have to do is get to a sunny spot and look up – with appropriate eye protection, of course – to see one of the most astonishing shows in the cosmos.

How I wrote The Dog Stars, the novel behind Ridley Scott’s new film

The tiger left, the elephant, the apes, the baboon, the cheetah. The titmouse, the frigate bird, the pelican (gray), the whale (gray), the collared dove. Sad but. Didn’t cry until the last trout swam upriver looking for maybe cooler water.

Melissa, my wife, was an old hippy. Not that old. She looked good. In this story she might have been Eve, but I’m not Adam. I am more like Cain. They didn’t have a brother like me.

Did you ever read the Bible? I mean sit down and read it like it was a book? Check out Lamentations. That’s where we’re at, pretty much. Pretty much lamenting. Pretty much pouring our hearts out like water. They said at the end it would get colder after it gets warmer.

Way colder. Still waiting. She’s a surprise this old earth, one big surprise after another since before she separated from the moon who circles and circles like the mate of a shot goose.

No more geese. A few. Last October I heard the old bleating after dusk and saw them, five against the cold bloodwashed blue over the ridge. Five all fall, I think, next April none.

I hand pump the 100 low lead aviation gas out of the old airport tank when the sun is not shining, and I have the truck too that was making the fuel delivery. More fuel than the Beast can burn in my lifetime if I keep my sorties local, which I plan to, I have to. She’s a small plane, a 1956 Cessna 182, really a beaut. Cream and blue. I’m figuring I’m dead before the Beast gives up the final ghost. I will buy the farm. Eighty acres of bottomland hay and corn in a country where there is still a cold stream coming out of the purple mountains full of brookies and cuts.

Before that I will make my roundtrips. Out and back.

Only us for at least a radius of eight miles, which is the distance of open prairie to the first juniper woods on the skirt of the mountain. I just say, Hey. A lot of it standing dead now, just swaying like a thousand skeletons, sighing like a thousand ghosts, but not all. There are patches of green woods, and I am their biggest fan. I root for them out here on the plain. Go Go Go Grow Grow Grow! That’s our fight song. I yell it out the window as I fly low over. The green patches are_ spreading year by year. Life is tenacious if you give it one little bit of encouragement. I could swear they hear me. They wave back, wave their feathery arms back and forth down low by their sides, they remind me of women in kimonos. Tiny steps or no steps, wave wave hands at your sides.

I go up there on foot when I can. To the greener woods. Funny to say that: not like I have to clear my calendar. I go up to breathe. The different air. It’s dangerous, it’s an adrenalin rush I could do without. I have seen elk sign. Not so old. If there are still elk. Bangley says no way. Way, but. Never seen one. Seen plenty deer. I bring the .308 and I shoot a doe and I drag her back in the hull of a kayak which I sawed the deck off so it’s a sled. My green sled. The deer just stayed on with the rabbits and the rats. The cheat grass stayed on, I guess that’s enough.

Free newsletter

Before I go up there I fly it twice. One day, one night with the goggles. The goggles are pretty good at seeing down through trees if the trees aren’t too heavy. People make pulsing green shadows, even asleep. Better than not checking. Then I make a loop south and east, come back in from the north. Thirty miles out, at least a day for a traveler. That’s all open, all plains, sage and grass and rabbit brush and the old farms. The brown circles of fields like the footprint of a crutch fading into the prairie. Hedgerows and windbreaks, half the trees broken, blown over, a few still green by a seep or along a creek. Then I tell Bangley.

I cover the eight miles dragging the empty sled in two hours, then I am in cover. I can still move. It’s a long way back with a deer, though. Over open country. Bangley covers me from halfway out. We still have the handsets and they still recharge with the panels. Japanese built, good thing. Bangley has a .408 CheyTac sniper rifle set up on a platform he built. A rangefinder. My luck. A gun nut. A really mean gun nut. He says he can pot a man from a mile off. He has done. I’ve seen it more than once. Last summer he shot a girl who was chasing me across the open plain. A young girl, a scarecrow. I heard the shot, stopped, left the sled, went back. She was thrown back over a rock, a hole where her waist should have been, just about torn in half. Her chest was heaving, panting, her head twisted to the side, one black eye shiny and looking up at me, not fear, just like a question, burning, like of all things witnessed this one couldn’t be believed. Like that. Like fucking why?

That’s what I asked Bangley, fucking why.

She would have caught you.

So what? I had a gun, she had a little knife. To like protect her from me. She maybe wanted food.

Maybe. Maybe she’d slit your throat in the middle of the night.

I stared at him, his mind going that far, to the middle of the night, me and her. Jesus. My only neighbor. What can I say to Bangley? He has saved my bacon more times. Saving my bacon is his job. I have the plane, I am the eyes, he has the guns, he is the muscle. He knows I know he knows: he can’t fly, I don’t have the stomach for killing. Any other way probably just be one of us. Or none.

I also have Jasper, son of Daisy, which is the best last line of alarm.

So when we get sick of rabbits and sunfish from the pond, I get a deer. Mostly I just want to go up there. It feels like church, hallow and cool. The dead forest swaying and whispering, the green forest full of sighs. The musk smell of deer beds. The creeks where I always pray to see a trout. One fingerling. One big old survivor, his green shadow idling against the green shadows of the stones.

Eight miles of open ground to the mountain front, the first trees. That is our perimeter. Our safety zone. That is my job.

He can concentrate his firepower to the west that way. That’s how Bangley talks. Because it’s thirty miles out, high plains all other directions, more than a day’s walk, but just a couple of hours west to the first trees. The families are south ten miles but they don’t bother us. That’s what I call them. They are something like thirty Mennonites with a blood disease that hit after the flu. Like a plague but slow burning. Something like AIDS I think, maybe more contagious. The kids were born with it and it makes them all sick and weak and every year some die.

We have the perimeter. But if someone hid. In the old farmsteads. In the sage. The willows along a creek. Arroyos, too, with undercut banks. He asked me that once: how do I know. How do I know someone is not inside our perimeter, in all that empty country, hiding, waiting to attack us? But thing is I can see a lot. Not like the back of the hand, too simple, but like a book I have read and reread too many times to count, maybe like the Bible for some folks of old. I would know. A sentence out of place. A gap. Two periods where there should be one. I know.

I know, I think: if I am going to die – no If – it will be on one of these trips to the mountains. Crossing open ground with the full sled. Shot in the back with an arrow.

Bangley a long time ago gave me bulletproof, one of the vests in his arsenal. He has all kinds of shit. He said it’ll stop any handgun, an arrow, but with a rifle it depends, I better be lucky. I thought about that. We’re supposed to be the only two living souls but the families in at least hundreds of square miles, the only survivors, I better be lucky. So I wear the vest because it’s warm, but if it’s summer I mostly don’t. When I wear it, I feel like I’m waiting for something. Would I stand on a train platform and wait for a train that hasn’t come for months? Maybe. Sometimes this whole thing feels just like that.

How I wrote The Dog Stars, the novel behind Ridley Scott’s new film

New Scientist July 31, 2026

The Dog Stars was my first novel. It begins nine years after a super-flu pandemic kills off most of humanity. Hig lives with his old dog Jasper at a little country airport in Erie, north of Denver, Colorado, which he shares with a gun nut named Bangley who has been waiting for the apocalypse his whole life. Hig has lost his wife, who was pregnant with their first child, and all his friends, and he and Jasper fly a patrol every day in their 1956 Cessna searching for survivors.

When I sat down to write the book, I didn’t want to plot or outline. I had wanted to be a fiction writer since I was 11, but when I got out of college, I had to make a living and so I wrote for magazines. With every story I wrote I knew the ending, and I knew what was going to happen next, because it happened. It was journalism. Now, I didn’t want to know. I grew up as a kayaker and what I loved about running rivers was that if the stream had never been descended or described, you came around a tight bend in a canyon and there might be a waterfall, or a cougar drinking, or a flight of backlit swallows. I wanted the same thrill writing the novel. I wanted to launch onto a narrative current and follow it into wild new territory.

Read an extract from The Dog Stars by Peter Heller

Also, poetry was my first love. The novels I adored were the most lyrical. Conrad at the height of his power, in the grips of a typhoon. Faulkner following the cadence of the words into the mind of a smitten cow. Welty describing a slow stream. They seemed to be as much about the music of the language as any story. I knew that I would have to be enamoured first, of the sound of my own language, and follow the song into the narrative.

Advertisement

I went to the coffee shop in my neighborhood in Denver and I sat down and told myself, “Don’t think, don’t think, just listen.” I wrote, “I keep the Beast running. I keep the 100 low lead on tap. I foresee attacks…” A few lines later, “My name is Hig, one name. Big Hig if you need another. If I ever woke up crying in the middle of a dream, and I’m not saying I did, it’s because the trout are gone, every one.”

I sat up. “Speak,” I murmured. “You are a fisherman, just like me.” And then it was as if Hig were on the other side of a campfire on an October night, with the wind blowing the flames around, telling me what had happened to him a few years before. I wrote in a white heat. I was constantly surprised, awed, devastated by what happened. I’d have tears dripping off my chin onto the coffee shop table and I knew the other patrons were thinking, “That poor sonofabitch is going through a bad divorce. Or his dog died.” But really, I was completely transported, and more thrilled than I’d ever been in my life.

Hig’s plane, the Beast, is one of the most prominent characters in the novel. Hig and I had a few stories about it to help fill out the novel. Once on a trip to kayak a wilderness river in Montana with one of my oldest friends, we got a ride to the river on a single engine Cessna into a remote backcountry airstrip. This was before I wrote the book. The pilot flew so close to the ridges I could see the elk tracks zigzagging in the snow. I was fascinated. I said, “Hey, how fast could I learn to fly like this? Could I do it for an article?”

The pilot was a cowboy in every sense, had a handlebar moustache and a brash manner. He said, “Gimme five grand and three weeks of your time and we’ll get her done!”

He was fired two weeks later for drinking on the job. But the chief pilot of the little airport was one of the greatest bush pilots alive, and he gave the thumbs up. Dave Hoerner had 30,000 hours flying wildlife biologists into the mountains to track grizzly bears and wolves. The most dangerous kind of flying. I went back up to Kalispell and flew three times a day and studied aviation books at night. I got my pilot’s license in 20 days. I bought a 1956 Cessna 182 single engine plane. The engine was timed out, meaning it had run so many hours I was required to rebuild it, but I thought I could nurse it along. It’s the same plane Hig flies, same colour, same tail number: N6333A. And I kept it in Hig’s hangar at the Erie airport. Soon after I bought the Beast, the engine died, right over the Continental Divide, and we had just enough altitude to glide home. In The Dog Stars, Hig flies past his point of no return looking for human connection.

Free newsletter

Eight years after I published the novel, on a cool day in March of 2020, Denver shut down for the Covid pandemic. I went fishing that afternoon in a state park south of town. There was no ranger at the gate, I just drove in. Eerie. No other fishermen parked in the gravel lot by the river. I waded into a lovely stretch that bends through a grove of old cottonwoods and began to cast. Alone, the way Hig does in the book. And the only fish feeding were white suckers. There were no trout that night, as in the novel. The sun settled on the ridge and the evening chilled and I got goosebumps, and not just from the temperature. I drove home up a large boulevard, the only car, and every business on either side of the road was shut.

The hair stood up on the back of my neck. It was as if Hig had transported into my world, or I into his. Again.

Why full-fledged quantum computers might always be five years away

New Scientist July 31, 2026

What is a quantum computer? The question feels deceptively simple. It is a computer that uses quantum effects to run calculations – or at least, that is what I have been saying to friends and acquaintances for years. Because I report about the latest advances in quantum computing nearly constantly, I have felt confident in this answer. Recently, however, I have had to re-examine that confidence. A more detailed question makes clear why: though I can name many different components and functions of a quantum computer, could I identify exactly when they all become a quantum computer? One recent philosophical study suggests that this is at the root of the difficulty of forecasting the future of quantum computing.

Quantum computers are starting to become useful as scientific tools

For Christophe Jurczak at investment firm Quantonation, it all started at a conference that had nothing to do with quantum computing. Researchers were discussing a different emerging technology, and Jurczak realised that he had first heard about it 30 years ago. Back then, everyone was saying that it was only “five years away”. Déjà vu. Then, a worry set in – could quantum computers also be such a “perpetual five-year technology” (PFYT)? This drove him to do a year-long deep dive into philosophical literature. The paper I read was its outcome.

In it, he argues that, right now, quantum computers are firmly in the PFYT category. All attempts to forecast when quantum computers will truly arrive are misguided so long as they presuppose that we already know what quantum computers are, he writes. “If the identity of a quantum computer is still being settled as the machine develops, that presupposition fails.”

Advertisement

As someone who thinks about quantum computing an awful lot, I wanted to know what exactly brought Jurczak to this somewhat alarming conclusion. In the nearly five years that I have spent writing about quantum computers for New Scientist, they have certainly made measurable progress. Several firms have presented road maps for the future of their devices, including goals for their overall size and the performance of some of their components, and then they met those goals.

Quantum computers are also much closer to being useful devices than they were just a handful of years ago. Sure, they haven’t yet changed the world by aiding the discovery of some groundbreaking drug or battery redesign, but you could access a quantum computer through the cloud right now and use it as a scientific tool if you happen to be a chemist or a material scientist.

Jurczak doesn’t deny this. He even tells me that he recently ran an experiment remotely on a quantum computer made from extremely cold atoms that was housed in a lab in Canada while he was on his couch in Texas. But this doesn’t mean that the question of quantum computing is settled, he says. One way to see this is to note the diversity of approaches for building a quantum computer, as well as the many, many metrics that are important for capturing how well one might work.

The basic components of quantum computers are called qubits, and they can be built in many different ways, from using extremely cold atoms to tiny superconducting circuits or particles of light. Then, there are the things you may want to measure about your quantum computer: how many qubits it has, how well connected they are, how reliably they can be used for different parts of a computation, how quickly they can be controlled and so on. Perfecting one or even a few of these metrics typically doesn’t guarantee that all the others will become excellent too.

Having spoken to many researchers and executives within the field, I have come to recognise a certain mix of excitement and anxiety in how they often speak: celebrating all the components of a truly powerful machine having been proven to work by themselves, while trying to keep at bay the worry about what may happen when they are all put together.

Free newsletter

In his paper, Jurczak, together with Brooke Abeles at ENS Paris-Saclay in France, collected data about some of these metrics across the industry and inferred a clear trend – once a threshold is crossed for one metric, such as guaranteeing that a single qubit makes errors less often than once in a thousand times, the five-year horizon doesn’t collapse. Instead, it resets. This is a consequence of discovering what a quantum computer is as it is being built.

This was distinctly not the case during the development of conventional computers. Jurczak says sometimes researchers like to compare today’s quantum computers to ENIAC, the world’s first programmable general-purpose electronic computer, but building that room-sized digital behemoth was much more of an engineering challenge. “[Classical computing] was a very much more mature ecosystem at the time when it started,” says Jurczak. While he was digging through philosophical literature, he found that an idea more relevant for quantum computers from the philosopher of technology Gilbert Simondon.

His theory of “technical individuation” says a shifting assembly of elements becomes a coherent “individual” through a process that includes a whole ecosystem, which consists of infrastructure, knowledge and practices maturing through iterative steps of trial and error. A collection of qubits and the devices that control and house them, for example, becomes a quantum computer only through interconnected developments in, for instance, laser and cryogenics systems, the building of special chip foundries, the growth of a specialised quantum workforce and basic research in quantum physics and computer science. Really, the list goes on; the ecosystem is large and complex.

As we talked, I found myself increasingly won over to Jurczak’s view of what has happened with quantum computing. The fact that we don’t have a fully useful quantum computer yet isn’t a failure of prediction, nor a failure of the market, but rather reflects the groundbreaking, paradigm-shifting nature of trying to corral the denizens of the quantum world into doing computational work for us. The technology is still too close to scientific discovery to be easily wrangled, easily scaled, easily accelerated by the usual tricks of the economy. “Don’t despair,” Jurczak puts a positive spin on it, “this is highly nonlinear, it takes time.”

Currently, the quantum computing industry has its sights on reaching “fault tolerance”, or building a quantum computer that is so good at catching its own errors that it can reliably run unprecedentedly complex computations. Once this goal is reached – and many firms are projecting they will do so by the end of the decade – will quantum computers have arrived? Will we know which type of qubit won the quantum-computing race? And what will be the next milestone?

Though Jurczak says that his framework isn’t predictive, it does begin to unravel some of these questions. Almost certainly the horizon will shift again, and not all the machines will be fully individuated. He says he is excited about the possibility of a really heterogenous quantum-computing system – no specific qubit design will win, they will just, through their own process of individuation, find applications they are well suited for. The question of what a quantum computer is won’t be answered by just one device. “The people who will build and use these machines should have more of an open mind about what a quantum computer is as a technical individual and how it concretises and how it’s going to be used as well,” says Jurczak.

Quantum computers won’t remain PFYTs forever, but he speaks about them currently being in that category with excitement. When he says that the constantly resetting horizon represents possibility, I can’t help but find that compelling. But what should quantum-computing firms do with this philosophical insight, I asked him. Certainly, they will still have to put out road maps and announce their goals. It’s important to have strategies for the next five years, he conceded. “We all want that and that’s needed, but think beyond and have a little bit of imagination as well, would be my take,” says Jurczak.

Can video games help us better understand quantum mechanics?

One way to achieve that may be to start working with people outside physics, maybe even philosophers themselves. The ecosystem for a quantum computer ought to be interdisciplinary. AI companies are already hiring across not just the sciences, but also the humanities, and it ought to happen with quantum-computing firms as well, he says. Jurczak believes AI agents themselves may also help accelerate some of that interdisciplinary work, as they aren’t trained in the specialised ways that human researchers are. He and several researchers at quantum-computing company Pasqal, which he co-founded, have already tested several examples of how such agents could help quantum-computing novices run computations on real quantum hardware. “If you ask me in five years what failure would really be, [it would be] that we still have these silos,” he says.

My own physics education was definitely siloed, and I was never asked to take a class in philosophy or the history of technology. Because a reporter’s job is to take both the broad view and the long view, I have, at times, felt the lack of that training rather sharply. The sheer amount of research in quantum computing is both impressive and overwhelming, and making sense of it has required a different skill set than merely being literate in the mathematics of quantum theory and somewhat conversant in materials science.

To be fair, the next time someone asks me what a quantum computer is, I will almost definitely not be telling them that it is a technical individual in an ever-evolving state of becoming. For anyone who isn’t actively trying to shape the fast-growing quantum computing industry, that won’t be very helpful. But the next time a paper reporting some narrow yet impressive advance crosses my desk, I will file it away as part of this evolution, reset my personal expectations clock and get at least a little excited about the quantum-computing horizon having just shifted.

‘He was a dictator’ Mother of Marokopa children speaks out about her relationship with Tom Phillips

New Zealand Herald July 31, 2026

Cat Christey, the mother of the Marokopa children. Photo / MATA Reports, RNZ

By Mihingarangi Forbes and Annabelle Lee-Mather for Mata Reports

For most people, the Tom Phillips case began when he first disappeared with his children into the bush in 2021 and ended when he was shot dead by police last year.

But for the children’s mother, Cat Christey, the saga stretches back many more years, through a volatile and sometimes violent relationship - and the nightmare she’s experienced continues.

In her first interview since her children were recovered from the bush, Christey told Mata Reports: “I would like to see anybody else endure what I have endured for all these years”.

“People think that this started … when Thomas abducted the children the first time. This started long before that. This has been going on for a long, long time.”

As she still deals with agency meetings and the fallout from the dramatic end to Phillips’ time on the run, Christey has spoken out about the difficulties of her relationship with him and the toll it has taken.

“He was a good provider but very controlling. It was a very ... imbalanced relationship. His views on what a marriage should be were different to my own. We should have been a team. But there was no room for compromise, it was his way or the highway.

“And he liked to be in control, he was a dictator.”

Phillips first took the couple’s three children into the bush near Marokopa in the western Waikato in September 2021 without telling Christey where he was going. They were separated at the time.

He returned several weeks later, but then, in December 2021, he went bush with the children again.

Phillips remained a fugitive until he was killed in a shoot-out with police following a ram-raid in Piopio.

Christey says that during their relationship, Phillips “wasn’t extremely violent” although she described slaps and how he once strangled her.

But she was more concerned about his psychological abuse.

“He would control all the finances, he would take vehicle keys away from me … he would control who I saw and when I saw them.”

She says Phillips had a fascination with guns and that at one point, she twice rang 111 to tell the police about it.

However, she says, Phillips took the phone off her and hung up both times.

“I truly believed police would show up because it was a 111 call … but police did not come.”

Phillips ordered her out of the house after she called the police.

Although he later begged her to come back, Christey says she wouldn’t.

A few days later, he began proceedings against her and the situation spiralled over the next few years.

Christey found out about the shooting and the discovery of her children after police told a Netflix documentary crew - a documentary she says she told the officer in charge, Detective Inspector Andrew Saunders, that she objected to.

“I was dead set against it when they first told me. It was very blunt and I said they do not have my permission.

“[Saunders] told me they didn’t need my permission, that they were just letting me know.”

It’s one way in which she says she feels like she has been disregarded by police throughout the case.

For instance she says that she only found out through the media that police had decided not to charge anyone with assisting Phillips while he was on the run and that the case was no longer being actively investigated.

Also, she says, she was declined support for counselling because she was not considered a victim of crime.

“I had reached out to Victim Support … in the hopes that they might be able to assist with some sessions with my psychologist.”

Cat says Victim Support spoke to the police about her situation but was told nothing could be done.

“Police refused to do a referral stating that we’re not victims of crime.”

This was because what had happened to her was not considered domestic violence, a point disputed by Auckland University associate professor of law Carrie Leonetti.

“This abduction, I think, was an act of child abuse, but it was also an act of domestic violence against these children’s mother,” says Leonetti.

“Taking children and saying, ‘You will not see them for three years, they will live or die depending on what I decide’ is an act of domestic violence.”

Even Police Minister Mark Mitchell, who would not comment specifically about police actions, said he believed Cat Christey was a victim.

“Any right-minded person would say that a mother, regardless of the circumstances, when they’re separated from their children, and they’ve been through the tragedy that we all saw unfold in front of the country, a lot of people would probably consider her as much a victim in terms of what has happened,” Mitchell told Mata.

“But I cannot talk to the police response other than saying, in my experience, police are very, very good at making sure they identify, communicate and support [victims] as much as they can.”

In response to questions from Mata Reports about Christey’s treatment and allegations, Detective Inspector Ross McKay said: “A number of the matters you are asking about are subject to the government inquiry into the disappearance of the Phillips children, and it would therefore be inappropriate for us to comment at this time”.

A spokesperson for Manaaki Tāngata Victim Support said the organisation could not comment on individual cases, but added: “The Victims Assistance Scheme, which Victim Support administers on behalf of the Ministry of Justice, has specific eligibility criteria”.

“Our support workers carefully consider each person’s circumstances and identify the support available to them.”

A public inquiry into the disappearance of Phillips and his children has been delivered to Attorney-General Chris Bishop.

The inquiry, led by the Honourable Simon Moore KC, was set up under the orders of the previous Attorney-General, Judith Collins, and tasked with considering whether government agencies took all practicable steps to protect the welfare and safety of the children.

Bishop says the report will be presented to Parliament once the Government has considered the recommendations and how to deal with suppression orders that are in place in the High Court and Family Court.

Magnitude 4.6 earthquake near Porirua felt across North Island and South Island

New Zealand Herald July 31, 2026

A late-night quake has rattled thousands across the middle of the country.

The 4.6 magnitude earthquake struck at 11.09pm and was centred offshore 30km northwest of Porirua, GeoNet said.

Email us

It was 38km deep and almost 9000 felt reports have been logged from people in the bottom half of the North Island, including in Wellington, Taranaki and Manawatū, and across the upper South Island.

Some as far north as Auckland and as far south as Christchurch reported feeling the shake.

A 5.9 tremor struck 5km south of Taumarunui at 4.51am last Saturday, and two weeks ago Southlanders were jolted by a late evening quake – also measuring 5.9 – 40km north of Te Anau.

Raumati woman Jenny Smith described last night’s quake as “a couple of real jolts”.

Others flocked to social media to share their experiences.

A Waikanae Beach resident wrote on Facebook that the quake delivered a “sharp jolt and rumble”.

Another person initially blamed their cat.

“I just hopped into bed. And then I felt shaking‚ the cat was on the bed. I thought he was itching and shaking the bed."

Many described hearing the quake before feeling it, with a Kāpiti man noting the “phone alert went off same time as I heard [the earthquake].”

“Started with an audible bang before the shaking started,” one woman wrote on Facebook.

“Heard that one coming,” wrote another on X.

A Paraparaumu resident felt a “sharp jolt ... and an alarm went off on my phone!”

“Wobble, wobble,” chipped in another.

A third opted for a stronger choice of words.

“F******g hell that one went boom!”

Further north, a Whanganui resident described hearing a rumble before feeling “the swaying”.

“Just a small one.”

Others further away from the epicentre also reported minor effects, with a person in Blenheim writing on Facebook that they felt it, but “only just”.

“Gentle sway felt in Riwaka, Motueka”, wrote another.

And despite being close to the epicentre, the end-of-week slumber proved too deep for some.

“Missed it- Porirua”, one wrote.

Civil Defence reminded Kiwis earthquakes were a “good reminder to stay prepared”.

“Another shake tonight — this one located near Wellington and widely felt across parts of the motu", it wrote on Facebook.

“Drop, Cover, and Hold remains the right action to take during an earthquake. If you’re in bed, remember to Stay, Cover, and Hold.

“Earthquakes are a good reminder to stay prepared — check your emergency supplies and talk with whānau or flatmates about what you’d do in a bigger event."

Weather: Snowboarders rescued after spending six hours lost near Treble Cone ski field

New Zealand Herald July 31, 2026

Wet and wintry conditions are set to ease today, but much of the country is in for a frosty weekend. Photo / MetService

Two snowboarders have been rescued after becoming lost for about six hours in the Treble Cone back country during heavy snowfall, strong winds and near-zero visibility.

Police have warned it should serve as a timely reminder of the dangers of venturing beyond ski field boundaries, especially during adverse weather conditions.

The snowboarding pair ventured beyond the ski field boundary about 1.45pm on Thursday before becoming lost in extremely challenging conditions.

They were found about an hour before nightfall after a complex search involving the Wānaka Alpine Cliff Rescue Team, ski patrols, an aerial search team and Aspiring Helicopters.

Sergeant Darren Cranfield said the operation highlighted how quickly a trip into the back country could become life-threatening and urged anyone planning to enter alpine terrain to have the necessary experience, check weather and avalanche conditions, carry appropriate emergency equipment and know how to use it.

Much of New Zealand is set to enjoy a brighter but still frosty weekend after a blast of snow, rain and bitter southerlies.

A surge of Antarctic air yesterday prompted road snowfall warnings on several alpine routes overnight.

A warning is still in place for the Desert Rd (SH1) until 8am today, with snow showers expected to develop on higher parts of the route.

MetService meteorologist Vivien Whyte told the Herald snow showers across the South Island are forecast to ease today, with conditions improving as the burst of wet and wild weather moved away.

“Things are looking fine by this afternoon and it’s kind of looking like a nice bright weekend for the South Island, maybe with the exception of a few showers lingering on the West Coast.

“It’s kind of a case of snow at first and then easing throughout the day and then we’re kind of looking at more of a fine afternoon and then a very fine Sunday for the South Island.”

The band of rain affecting the South Island will move north before clearing today.

“That showery weather that’s kind of affecting the South Island is going to make its way up to the North Island today.”

While Saturday is expected to be wetter for parts of the North Island as the system tracks north, the unsettled conditions are expected to clear, with skies clearing from the south later in the day before a settled Sunday.

“By the time Sunday comes around, the whole country is looking pretty good,” she said.

While skies will brighten, Whyte said temperatures would remain typical for this time of year.

“We’re left with some pretty stock standard winter temperatures. It’s still chilly, so I can’t really say it’s warming because it doesn’t feel warm.”

Overnight lows are forecast to sit around 0C or just below in parts of the South Island, while day-time highs would reach the mid-teens.

The clearer skies are set to bring widespread frosts, particularly in inland areas.

“We’re looking at most of the country being pretty frosty over the weekend, but at least frosty and bright by Sunday.”

Hawke’s Bay farm Tarawera Station expands erosion-control planting

New Zealand Herald July 31, 2026

Hawke’s Bay Regional Council’s senior land management adviser Colin Stace (left) and Te Awahohonu Forest Trust general manager – farming at Tarawera Station.

Two hundred poplar and willow poles recently made their way from Napier to Tarawera Station, where they will be planted to help stabilise erosion-prone hill country.

The poles were grown at Hawke’s Bay Regional Council’s Allen Rd nursery, with the council also providing planting advice to support the station’s erosion-control efforts.

Tarawera Station is part of the Te Awahohonu Forest Trust’s 2650ha sheep and beef farm on the banks of the Mohaka River, about 60km from Napier on State Highway 5.

The station has bought poles from the council since 2020 to control erosion.

Te Awahohonu Forest Trust general manager – farming, Carl Read-Jones, said the trust first planted poplars and willows after Cyclone Bola in 1988, then restarted the work in 2020.

“The main reason is to protect the land from slipping,” he said.

“After seeing Cyclone Gabrielle, it definitely confirmed that it needed to be done.”

Cyclone Gabrielle caused slips across the property.

Early mapping suggested about 170ha had moved, although Read-Jones said the affected area was closer to 70ha once the land settled and grass returned.

Much of the vulnerable parts of the farm have shallow soil over solid rock, with slips typically shallow and gully erosion occurring near drainage lines.

Hawke’s Bay Regional Council’s senior land management adviser Colin Stace said it wasn’t just about planting more poles.

“It is about putting the right pole in the right place, so it has the best chance of doing its job.”

Since 2020, the farm has planted 1530 poplar and willow poles, all bought from the council’s Allen Rd nursery.

Stace said erosion-control planting was a long-term investment, taking about two years to establish and seven to eight years for the full benefits to be realised.

“You do not get the full benefit overnight, but once those root systems are well established, they become part of the farm’s long-term protection.”

The farm has missed two seasons because of Covid and Cyclone Gabrielle, but Read-Jones said the programme had become more targeted each year.

“We have learned a lot from the early years experimenting with the different varieties.”

Some varieties were not suited to windy or dry sites, and cattle damaged the lighter poles.

“We’ve learned from that, and now we use the varieties suitable for our farm conditions.”

About 252,000 hectares of Hawke’s Bay hill country is considered high risk, and pole planting can reduce erosion by up to 80%.

At Tarawera Station, the latest poles will be helicoptered into position on steep hill country – a cost covered by the farm – before being spread out for planting.

Read-Jones said dropping bundles close to planting sites meant contractors weren’t walking 600 or 700m with heavy poles and were more able to put them where planned.

He said the support from the council had been invaluable.

“Colin has helped us with a farm plan and advice on what varieties to use and where to plant them.

“That means I pass the right information to the contractors, and it has been of much help to us.”

Letters: Winston Peters and channels of accountability; science and sexual consent

New Zealand Herald July 31, 2026

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters could be held accountable outside of Parliament for his recent controversial comments, according to one reader. Photo / Sylvie Whinray

The Hon Winston Peters’ recent derogatory – and what I regard as racist – comments in Parliament have now been repeated in the public arena and parliamentary privilege no longer applies.

There is another area where he can be held to account. He is not hesitant to let people know he is a lawyer. To become a lawyer, you need to be admitted to the roll of barristers and solicitors of the High Court and need to be deemed to be “a fit and proper person”.

For those individuals whose names are on the High Court roll (and I believe that Peters remains on the roll) the Lawyers and Conveyancers Disciplinary Tribunal retains jurisdiction regardless of their current practising status. That would involve conduct that is deemed completely incompatible with the standards of the legal profession (such as comments regarded as racist, or hate speech).

No lawyer would be able to make the comments Peters did. The Standards Committee under section 130(c) has explicit statutory power “to investigate of its own motion any act, omission, allegation, practice, or other matter that may indicate misconduct”.

I have had 54 years as a practising lawyer and have been involved in Law Society affairs during that time. As a citizen and a retired lawyer, I am appalled at his attack on a fellow member of Parliament. As Winston Churchill said, “The price of greatness is responsibility”.

Gary Gotlieb, Central Auckland.

Winston Peters is right to be proud of New Zealand’s democracy, but pride doesn’t excuse using it as a cudgel against a fellow MP born overseas.

Telling someone to “go back where you’ve come from” isn’t defending democracy, it’s weaponising nationality to shut down debate. That’s not a proud tradition; it’s the opposite of the respectful discourse our system supposedly champions.

If Peters wants to compare political systems, he might pause before pointing fingers. New Zealand’s Westminster model closely mirrors the US and UK, both democracies currently struggling with deep polarisation, eroded trust, and foreign policy disasters that have cost countless lives.

Democracy isn’t a flawless virtue; it’s a fragile work in progress. Gloating about it while dismissing a Chinese-born Kiwi who’s been here since 1994 isn’t statesmanship, it’s cheap rhetoric. The real test of democracy isn’t boasting about it. It’s how we treat those who disagree with us, especially when they’re from different backgrounds. On that measure, Peters fell short.

James Gregory, Parnell.

In 2021, the Royal Society of New Zealand kindly published a comparison of Rutherford’s atomic model with current models of particle physics, one of which I had authored.

Rutherford is still well known today as the father of nuclear physics, but the status of today’s numerous models of particle physics remains murky. All assume the presence of unseen particles, and I for one am dubious of all of them as they currently stand.

One can only test available models as deeply as possible. The CERN laboratory in Geneva has tested electromagnetic models that Nobelist J. Schwinger and I proposed to no avail. I subsequently proposed a search at higher energies and smaller distances.

In the meantime, successful searches have been made for previously unseen planets near the centre of our galaxy. These results have buoyed our spirits. And negative searches for exotic “dark matter” have also been reported, which could be encouraging depending on which side of the fence you stand on. That’s the way of science today.

I hope that Science Minister Penny Simmonds’ recent funding plan won’t mean that fundamental research by New Zealand scientists, which has seen successful international collaborations, won’t fall by the wayside.

Phil Yock, Ōrākei.

Thursday’s coverage of AI and young people raises an urgent question. Why are we waiting?

Suicide, self-harm, sexual exploitation and humiliation are no longer simply theoretical risks. Families are already facing consequences. We need an urgent global response before the next tragedy.

Marie Frost, Freemans Bay.

I read with some trepidation the proposed construction of an AI centre in Southland. This large data centre will use huge amounts of electricity and water. Why come to New Zealand? NZ is already close to using our current power generation in winter so to supply this new enterprise we would have to generate a lot more.

The taxpayers are already subsidising the smelter. These huge AI companies are in business to make a profit and their only motive for proposing this centre for NZ is that it is in their interests to do so.

Bob Upperton, Whangārei.

Congratulations to Anoushka Bloem for her opinion piece on sexual consent (Herald, July 31). I would recommend readers to check her somewhat fuller account on the Herald’s website. At the heart of Bloem’s piece, in my view, lay her central thesis:

“Changing statutory language does not remove the central challenge facing every sexual offence trial: determining what happened when only two people were present.”

Those central challenges seem, in my view, irresolvable in legislation.

Nick Park, Ōrākei.

Like Simone Leung (Herald Letters, July 31), I too read Hannah McQueen’s article with interest.

The first thing I noticed was that I am in the minority. I’m male and an only child. Which brings me to the fact that being an only child is a double-edged sword. On the one hand, there is no support/relief from siblings. On the other hand, there is no second guessing/criticism on any decisions.

The second distinction I observed is that my mother was fully competent to live alone for several years after my father’s death.

At her request, we altered as many as possible of our accounts to being joint and the two of us had been handling my parents’ accounts for decades. My father had insisted on this. Therefore, there was no need for any awkward conversations.

Lastly, my mother was in her 90s and I was in my 60s before there was any need for my stepping in to help her handle day-to-day activities. I was therefore in a position to comfortably retire and move into the family home.

I have now become my mother’s primary caregiver and as such I have followed her desire to remain in the home she has known for over 25 years.

Thanks to my father’s planning and our various GPs, along with the health system’s Disability Support Link, we have all the basic aids we need to allow us to live comfortably and safely in a private residence as mother rapidly approaches her 105th birthday.

So, what I can recommend, from personal experience, is that Hannah McQueen is correct. It is vital that each of us actively plan as much as possible for our old age. That planning has to include involving any family members years before any needs arise. It makes your old age much easier for everyone and hopefully enjoyable.

Dunstan Sheldon, Hamilton.

A homeless person running away from an incipient move-on order would appear to be obeying the intention of the order with some alacrity. What is the appropriate speed at which they are expected to move on?

John O’Neill, Dargaville.

It is an appalling state of foreign affairs when its minister demeans a foreign-born New Zealand citizen for spurious political advantage. Winston Peters’ mature age is belied by his immature playground bully behaviour.

Michael Smythe, Northcote Point.

At the top of the list for why we are in the bottom 10% for getting value for our tax dollar is the richest New Zealanders pay less tax than our counterparts in nine other OECD countries, and from the first $500 we earn we begin paying tax. In Australia, the first $18,000 earned is tax-free.

Gary Hollis, Mellons Bay.

Of 20 issues, Labour was considered the most capable on 16 of them. Will it be 20 from 20 when they finally decide to release policy on any of these issues?

A Rotorua business leader told Prime Minister Christopher Luxon about the city’s struggling economy at a function yesterday, prompting the PM to tell business owners to “be adult”.

Luxon was in Rotorua this week with appointments including yesterday morning’s Business Chamber Westpac Smarts Breakfast.

Business Chamber chief executive Melanie Short said Rotorua had experienced the “sharpest fall” in business confidence in almost a decade.

“The affordability of doing business, it’s getting harder and harder ...

“How long can we hang on?”

Luxon told Short her view was “quite negative”.

New Zealand businesses needed to move away from a “parent-child mentality” of waiting to see what the Government would do, he said.

“Who cares what the Government will think or do?”

Productivity, technology and innovation to remain competitive amid global economic uncertainty were key discussion points at the event.

Short told Luxon of the Rotorua Business Chamber’s twice-yearly Business Pulse survey of 85 local businesses.

The survey revealed optimism about the economic outlook over the next 12 months dropped 62 percentage points for both New Zealand and Rotorua, while confidence in respondents’ own businesses fell 43 percentage points.

Short also noted inflation rates topping 4% – the worst in more than two years.

Businesses were absorbing rising costs rather than passing them on to customers as foot traffic continued to decline.

Luxon said if businesses were not “retooling and radically disrupting” their business – “you ain’t doing your job”.

He said he knew the “reality” of running a business.

“The last person I wanted to ever talk to as a CEO was the Government.”

He never wondered whether he could “get some grant money to do something”.

“No,” he said. “I was building a kick-arse business” like an “adult”.

He urged businesses to “go out there and smack it and go create the road”.

As Prime Minister, his job was to “set up the conditions for you to be able to go and create that growth”.

Some “big mistakes” were made during the Covid-19 pandemic when “the teenagers in charge [were] feeding the kids with sugar”.

“We’ve taken that lesson ... the economy’s on an upswing,” he said.

Luxon said his comments were “really blunt”, but he stood by them.

After a question-and-answer session, the Rotorua Daily Post asked Short what she made of his response.

Short said her concerns reflected the reality facing Rotorua businesses.

She regularly spoke with local businesses through the chamber, its board and as the owner of two businesses herself.

“Fundamentally I understand what he’s saying ... but it’s still hard ... it’s still tough,” she said.

“We do do it ourselves,” Short said.

She said the Government had a role in providing confidence and direction.

“It’s knowing the Government has a plan.”

The Rotorua Daily Post asked Luxon how the Government was helping those in the community facing financial hardship.

Luxon said the Government had focused on bringing inflation and interest rates down to get wages growing faster than prices.

He said that, in Rotorua, this would mean a “better quality of life”.

The community would benefit from the Government’s support through measures including more affordable housing, stable rents and help with early childcare costs, Luxon said.

The PM said he saw the “chaos that was ensuing” in Rotorua when he first came into office in 2023 and told the community they would “sort out Fenton St and emergency housing”.

He believed the Government had delivered on resolving housing issues.

Annabel Reid is a multimedia journalist for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post, based in Rotorua. Originally from Hawke’s Bay, she has a Bachelor of Communications from the University of Canterbury.

Tauranga woman Jess Payne diagnosed with cancer during IVF journey

New Zealand Herald July 31, 2026

Jess Payne had been going through in vitro fertilisation for almost two years when she found out she had cancer in her uterus.

The 30-year-old support worker was left “numb” and “shaking” after being diagnosed with endometrial endometrioid adenocarcinoma grade 1 stage 1A shortly before Christmas last year.

“I just didn’t expect it to be that bad … the whole room froze. I remember my partner, he had his hand on my shoulder, and I was just like, this can’t be right,” the Tauranga woman told the Bay of Plenty Times.

Payne and Max began their IVF journey when she was 28.

After miscarrying their first embryo, Payne said she was about to have another embryo transfer when the fertility doctor doing her scan noticed her uterus lining was “really thick”.

The doctor referred Payne for further testing.

Payne said a biopsy found she had pre-cancerous cells. She had a Mirena inserted (a hormonal intrauterine device), in the hope it would treat the condition.

However, a second biopsy six months later revealed it had progressed to stage 1 cancer.

She had no other symptoms.

“I actually owe my life to her because if she had not found that, then it could have been much, much worse and could have spread or been a higher stage.”

Payne had another round of egg retrievals before starting treatment.

In January, she began taking a progestogen medication called Provera, which “initially kills the cancer cells off”.

Her side effects included hair loss, headaches, body pain, irregular bleeding, restless legs and mood swings.

Payne said some side effects made working full time a struggle, but she had a supportive employer.

Payne said since January she had been constantly wondering if the treatment was working.

“I found out a couple of weeks ago that it’s working so I’m really, really stoked.”

The news gave her a sense of being able to “breathe”.

“My chest didn’t feel heavy anymore.”

Her other treatment option had been a hysterectomy, so she was really grateful the medication was working.

Payne said she would take Provera for another six months before having another check-up.

“If it’s all looking good, then hopefully be able to reduce some of that medication and maybe look at the fertility journey again.”

Payne has just done Dry July - an annual challenge where participants give up alcohol for a month and raise funds for non-medical cancer services, including the Cancer Rehabilitation Foundation, Pinc and Steel.

The charities delivered programmes and services nationally for people affected by cancer. This included rehabilitation to rebuild strength after treatment, exercise and recovery classes, counselling and support to help people regain confidence and independence.

While Payne was not a big drinker, she hoped to raise money for the services.

Payne said she approached the Cancer Rehabilitation Foundation but found out she had to self-fund her first few initial appointments because she had not had major surgery, radiation or chemotherapy.

She initially was not in the financial position to fund it, but later booked her first appointment.

After receiving her medication results, she decided to put it on hold.

“Obviously someone more important can use that funding for now and then if I need to, I can come back.

“Hopefully one day maybe if there’s enough funding, those initial costs could be wiped and maybe everybody could access it no matter their stage or treatment plan.”

Cancer Rehabilitation Foundation founder and chief executive Lou James, MNZM, said she recognised how difficult and frustrating it could be when someone needed rehabilitation support and could not afford it.

“We strongly believe cancer rehabilitation should be a standard part of cancer care and funded accordingly.

“We have been working hard to secure greater government and charitable investment, but demand continues to grow faster than the funding available.”

Medical referrals to its service had increased 58% in the past 12 months.

“Unfortunately, we are not currently able to fund every person referred.”

James said the charity had to prioritise its funding using clinical eligibility criteria. This meant some people may need to self-fund an initial individual appointment.

“Once assessed, they are able to access our fully funded group programmes, which are available both in person and online throughout New Zealand.”

James said its goal was “for rehabilitation to be available to everyone” and the charity would continue advocating for funding.

Dry July New Zealand Trust chief executive Gillian Odbert said donations remained open throughout August.

“We know it’s been a challenging year for many households, and we’re incredibly grateful to everyone who has taken part in Dry July or supported someone who has.”

More than $500,000 had been raised so far, with almost 5000 people taking up the challenge.

Odbert said the services funded by Dry July provided practical support “beyond medical treatment” and helped people navigate one of the most difficult times in their lives.

She said Dry July funding helped ensure the programmes remained free for the people who needed them.

“If you’re in a position to donate, we’d encourage you to do so.”

People can donate on the Dry July website.

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

The Years Ahead: How travel is helping older Hawke’s Bay residents redefine ageing

New Zealand Herald July 31, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

At 87, David Mitchell could have stayed home with his memories.

Instead, nearly three years after losing his wife, Patsy Mitchell, he packed his bags and boarded his first overseas trip alone.

It wasn’t an easy decision, as for more than 60 years, the Hawke’s Bay couple had been travelling around the world together before Patsy died of pancreatic cancer in July 2023, at 81.

“We used to travel for business. We were exporters,” David told Hawke’s Bay Today.

The pair have been to Europe, South America, Africa, China, Russia, and even to the Everest Base Camp.

“That was quite a highlight,” David said.

After Patsy died, David had to decide whether travel still would fit in his life.

“I thought about it a lot, and I know that she would have been telling me to do it,” he said.

“If it had been the other way around, I would have been saying to her that she’s got to live a life, and you have to carry on.

“I think it’s sort of to honour them, to be honest. I don’t think anybody wants somebody moping around.”

David recently returned from his first overseas trip alone since his wife’s death, a cruise to Singapore.

He had been anxious before leaving, particularly because his eyesight had declined and so much of modern travel now involves online systems, he said.

But the experience gave him confidence.

David now lives independently in Ahuriri after moving from the Pākōwhai area, where the couple’s property was flooded during Cyclone Gabrielle, just five months before Patsy died.

On that day, a neighbour rescued her by dinghy, and she was later winched from a shed roof by helicopter. David was also rescued by helicopter from the roof of the garage about seven hours later.

“It was one of the last major experiences we shared,” he said.

Now, David keeps himself busy through a local car club, friendships, and occasional trips around the country.

Some of those are with Bay Tours’ Senior Guided Tours programme, which offers about 80 trips a year, ranging from day trips, multi-day holidays and overseas tours.

Bay Tours owner Kerren Withington said most travellers were from Hawke’s Bay, and in their 70s and 80s.

“We pick everyone up from their home, take them out, and then, at the end of the day, we drive them back home,” she said.

Withington said the service was about making travel easier and helping older people stay connected while supporting local businesses.

While cost-of-living pressures were affecting travel decisions, she said demand remained strong with many repeat customers and a growing number of new members joining the programme.

Best Travel senior agent Jacqui Quilliam said the desire to make the most of retirement was something she had seen often in Hawke’s Bay.

Jacqui, 70, has worked in the travel industry since 1974 and said many clients in their 70s were now more “adventurous, fit” and determined to travel now, “while they’re healthy”.

She estimated at least 60% of her clients were aged 60-plus, and said many travel solo, often after losing a partner.

“If you lose a partner, you suddenly find yourself on your own, and you tend to lose confidence in yourself,” she said.

“But going away and getting out of your comfort zone and meeting other people just makes it so much easier.”

She said cruises and guided tours often created opportunities for solo travellers to connect, with some forming new friendships.

Jacqui also knows personally that later life can still hold unexpected chapters.

She married her husband, Bob, for the second time two years ago, 17 years after their divorce.

They had first married in 1983, separated after 20 years, then reconnected after Bob returned from Australia following retirement.

Their daughters were bridesmaids at the second wedding.

Jacqui has no plans to retire any time soon.

“I am still quite young,” she said.

For Jeanette and Paul Odell, retirement is all about having more time to travel.

The Havelock North couple, now aged 75 and 80, have spent much of their 43-year marriage packing suitcases, boarding planes and chasing their next adventure together.

They estimate they have done close to 30 cruises and visited more than 60 countries over the decades.

These days, retirement life usually includes two or three overseas trips a year, plus regular visits to one of their sons in Christchurch and flying over to Australia, where the other son lives on the Gold Coast.

“It’s a kind of excuse to go, really,” Jeanette laughed.

And they rarely need much convincing to pack their bags.

One Christmas was spent in Fiji with the whole family.

Another year, they stayed in Nevada with an American man whom they first met on a cruise ship.

He has since travelled to Hawke’s Bay and stayed with them too.

“Travel gives you great education,” Jeanette said.

“You meet people you would never otherwise meet.”

Jeanette, a former Air New Zealand flight attendant, says travel was always part of their lifestyle, but retirement brought something different: time.

Time to stay longer, book another cruise, say yes to one more trip, she said.

The pair already have their next trips booked, including a 35-day cruise in August, and another one booked for next year for 72 days.

They know not everyone can afford the kind of travel they’ve been lucky enough to experience.

But if there is one thing retirement has taught them, it is not to wait too long for the things you want to do.

“Don’t think, ‘I’ll do it tomorrow or next year,’” Paul said.

“Next year, you might have had a stroke or whatever. You’ve just got to do it while you can.”

Rafaella Melo has more than 10 years of experience as a journalist in Brazil. She has worn many hats, from radio and TV presenter and producer to magazine editor before joining the Hawke’s Bay Today team as a multimedia journalist.
