Carroll’s long run: Can the boy from Airport West outrun Andrews’ ghost?

Sydney Morning Herald August 01, 2026

Labor has turned to a “studious, serious” child of the west to save itself from electoral oblivion. But Ben Carroll has only a brief chance to right a rocking ship.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Bill Shorten spent much of his political life doing numbers. And the polling numbers coming out of Victoria’s Trades Hall a fortnight ago were scary.

Translated to the looming November election, the result would be a ruin deeper than that inflicted on Joan Kirner’s Labor government in 1992.

“Labor was heading off a cliff,” Shorten says. “In 1992, Joan Kirner got 27 seats and [Jeff] Kennett got 61. It [the 2026 election] was going to be worse than that.”

Shorten, a long-term powerbroker and former federal leader, argues the hostility confronting state Labor reflects a post-COVID frustration with all political parties, but especially Labor.

“In some ways, Ben’s two biggest rivals are not on the ballot paper: Dan Andrews is not on the ballot paper, and Pauline Hanson isn’t on the ballot paper, but that’s what people are voting on.”

That internal alarm explains why the Labor caucus executed its late-term change of leader, dumping Jacinta Allan after nearly three years in office to install her deputy, Ben Carroll.

Retiring Sydenham MP Natalie Hutchins makes no attempt to disguise the unsentimental calculation behind the move.

“Labor is in real danger in its seats in the west, and it’s time to have a premier willing to take on the hard issues affecting our residents,” she said.

Her outer-western electorate shares a boundary with Carroll’s seat of Niddrie. During four weeks of door-knocking, Hutchins encountered anger unprecedented in her political career.

Voters in the established estates of Taylors Lakes and Hillside cited crime, government inaction on CFMEU corruption, bad roads, and a sense that Melbourne’s east receives lavish infrastructure while the west misses out. For the first time, a disturbing number told her they intended to vote for One Nation.

“A lot of people, particularly in the outer west and newer suburbs, are pretty rattled about community safety,” Hutchins says. “And it’s not just the youth crime; it’s also the organised crime, the drug dealing, and also family violence that is all connected.”

Hutchins says Carroll has a strong sense of social justice and an understanding of the issues in Melbourne’s west, which she hopes will improve the party’s prospects.

Faced with $190 billion in state debt, ongoing revelations surrounding the $109 billion Big Build, and an electorate itching for change after 12 years of Labor rule, caucus concluded Allan could never separate herself from the era that created those problems.

Shorten sees Carroll as Labor’s only remaining path to a shifted conversation. “This state election was looming as a referendum on the question: ‘Are you dirty with the state of politics in Victoria?’ His promotion to leader provides a bit of a circuit-breaker to that.”

On his first afternoon as premier, Carroll stood at a media podium inside Parliament House and delivered a declaration explicitly designed to draw that line.

“I am not Daniel Andrews. I am not Jacinta Allan.”

The words were easy. Their political task is hard.

How hard? Don’t take our word for it. Read Carroll’s handwritten notes, captured during his first press conference as premier. “Not Daniel Andrews” was scrawled at the top of his talking points.

It’s easy to see why the 51-year-old Carroll was eager to press this point.

For three years, he served as Allan’s deputy, and for nine years before that, he sat around the cabinet table under Andrews, rising through government while two premiers came to define modern Victoria.

Now, just four months before the state election, Carroll confronts the defining challenge of his political career: can a long-serving Labor insider, groomed by party hard heads, persuade a sceptical electorate that his elevation represents genuine change rather than a cosmetic reshuffle?

Carroll is a more anonymous political figure than the leaders he follows.

Where Andrews centralised power with ruthless discipline, and Allan sought to weather scandal through endurance, Carroll belongs to a tradition of Labor pragmatism. His persona is suburban: a Catholic, straight-laced family man with a lifetime love of the Kangaroos who got a taste for marathon running in middle age.

But it will take more than pragmatism to solve the problems on his desk.

Carroll inherits a state carrying enormous debt and a government battered by two years of revelations surrounding the Big Build. The teachers he was responsible for until a few days ago are threatening to strike again.

The question confronting the ALP is whether the boy from Airport West has the time, the authority, and the independence from his two far better-known predecessors to drag his party back from the brink.

To understand Carroll’s politics, it helps to begin in Melbourne’s north-west.

Carroll lives in tree-lined Aberfeldie with wife Fiona Rothville – a lawyer who serves as director of Workplace Integrity at Deloitte – and their young daughter. Rothville’s father is a director of Nilsen, a major electrical contractor that has worked on state infrastructure projects; Carroll declares it in his register of interest.

Carroll’s roots in his electorate run deep. Raised in Airport West as the eldest of three children, he entered parliament in 2012. In his inaugural speech, he framed his story around the idea of opportunity, tracing his family’s journey from Irish labourer Michael Carroll from Tipperary, who arrived in Victoria in 1840, to his election more than 170 years later.

Opportunity, he told parliament, brought his parents, Greg and Kay Carroll, to Airport West, where they built the family home in 1974 and established a small electrical business. His mother Kay migrated from Texas and worked at Glenroy West Primary School. His father ran the family business until it collapsed during the recession of the early 1990s.

Carroll said his parents had “instilled in me the importance of family and the value of hard work”. As soon as he reached the legal working age of 14 years and nine months, he walked into Airport West Kmart looking for part-time work. “I soon found myself working on the cash registers as a checkout chick.”

He remained at the store for eight years while completing an arts degree with honours at La Trobe University in 2000. He joined the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association, later saying it gave him “a good understanding of the importance of unions in helping working people”. At times, he recalled, the union helped pay for his university textbooks.

On Wednesday morning, less than 24 hours after taking the top job, Carroll leaned into that retail origin story for his first public press conference as premier. Standing inside Kmart on Bourke Street in Melbourne’s CBD, he announced legislation for Workplace Protection Orders, giving courts powers to ban violent or abusive customers from retail, hospitality, and public transport workplaces for up to 12 months.

During his years behind a Kmart register, Carroll recalled being intimidated and threatened on the job, describing those checkout shifts as “crucible years”.

From the year 2000, Carroll advised premier Steve Bracks, then planning minister Justin Madden. After a stint as a trainee lawyer at the Victorian Government Solicitor’s Office, he moved to Canberra in 2011 to advise Right-faction powerbroker Stephen Conroy on the National Broadband Network.

Emma Dawson, executive director of Labor Party think tank the Chifley Research Centre, worked alongside Carroll in Conroy’s office, where he managed caucus relations.

She remembers an adviser distinct from typical Canberra political figures: “He’s a very studious, serious person.” Dawson recalls him parsing complex legislation before briefing MPs – a habit of constant note-taking highlighted by several people during the compilation of this story. “Ben is not afraid to ask questions and to listen to people. He takes notes – copious notes.”

Dawson says Carroll values evidence over factional orthodoxy, pointing to his decision as education minister to mandate synthetic phonics despite union pushback. “He’s interested in the evidence behind what works,” she says.

When former attorney-general Rob Hulls resigned from Niddrie in 2012, Carroll won the byelection, aged 36.

Standing in parliament after his victory, Carroll described representing Niddrie as his “greatest honour” because he would be serving “the community I was raised in, the people I am one of”.

Sebastian Agricola is a lawyer who has worked for more than 30 years in St Albans, just outside of Carroll’s electorate. The two met when they faced off as candidates for preselection in Niddrie.

Agricola recalls a younger man with similarly strong ties to the north-western suburbs, who engaged in the hand-to-hand combat of Labor preselection in a respectful and refreshingly down to earth way.

“He was competitive, in the sense of you have to be for that sort of a contest. But he played it straight down the line. He was fair, he never criticised me,” Agricola says. “People can let those preselections become very personal and vitriolic. Ben never did that.”

Agricola, veteran president of the St Albans Business Association, has remained plugged into community and political circles in Melbourne’s west, and says Carroll has been an approachable figure locally, who never gave in to cynicism.

“If people just accept that what you see is actually genuine, I think there’s a good chance that he’ll have a significant impact,” he says of the newly minted premier.

Carroll never hid his ambition. “I was always very keen to rise,” he told reporters at his first press conference after being made deputy premier.

That ambition fuelled years of quiet tension with Andrews who, after Labor’s 2022 election victory, installed Jacinta Allan as deputy, leaving Carroll in the corridor for an hour to receive his portfolio – a spot known as “Dan’s freezer”.

In 2023 when Andrews tried to hand-pick his successors – Allan as premier, treasurer Tim Pallas as deputy – Carroll threatened a membership ballot, which would have left Victoria without a permanent premier for a month. It triggered what colleagues described as a “nuclear meltdown” from Andrews. But Carroll was made deputy premier.

The political scar never healed. Later, Carroll was the only sitting Labor MP to publicly criticise Andrews after the former premier posed in a photograph in Beijing among a group of foreign officials and leaders that included Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong-un.

Shorten contrasts Carroll with his predecessors, pointing to his local focus and willingness to fight cabinet over the Airport Rail Link.

“He’s never been a schemer. He’s never tried to be a factional mini state warlord. He’s very different from someone like Dan Andrews. But he’s capable of being a very good state leader.”

Shorten says both he and Carroll advocated for an Airport Rail Link, putting Carroll at odds with colleagues focused on the Suburban Rail Loop.

“That made him not popular with the SRL zealots in the cabinet. He didn’t get the memo that he shouldn’t speak up about it,” says Shorten, who is now the University of Canberra vice-chancellor and who says he is no longer active in the Labor Party.

Carroll has held 14 separate ministerial portfolios. Danny Pearson, the retiring Labor MP for Essendon, says Carroll’s rise is the result of years of toil and ambition.

“To be the leader of a major political party, you’ve got to really want it, you’ve got to have ability and you’ve got to work hard,” he says. “You can’t be some sort of part-time dilettante who thinks, you know, swanning around in the members’ bar is the pathway to power.”

Former Andrews government minister Philip Dalidakis, a longtime friend who lured Carroll from a short career in law back into politics in Stephen Conroy’s office, describes him as “extraordinarily earnest” in his approach to both public policy and politics.

“He doesn’t yell, he doesn’t scream ‘Look at me!’, he just quietly goes about his policy work.”

Dalidakis sees Carroll’s style setting up a contest of substance against Liberal leader Jess Wilson, while signalling an end to the “command and control” cabinet model of Andrews and Allan.

“He doesn’t use policy to wield power for power’s sake, and I think that’s what we probably want in our leader. I think that’s probably why Jess Wilson has made a really good start in the last six months because she’s focused on good policy.”

Carroll needs to listen, he says, both to voters and to his cabinet colleagues. “The premier has said that he’s going to return to a proper cabinet consultative process … that can only be a good thing for Victoria.”

Carroll’s difficult task now is to speak to the big-spending legacy of the Andrews era without repudiating the government that elevated him.

His first major announcement was a state royal commission into corruption and organised crime infiltration across the Big Build, reversing the position Allan defended for two years.

Carroll promised sweeping terms of reference, a special prosecutor operating alongside the inquiry, and retrospective “follow-the-money” powers for IBAC.

The move illustrated how sharply he intends to distinguish himself from his predecessors.

Tim Read, the Greens MP who chairs parliament’s Integrity and Oversight Committee that monitors and reviews the performance of IBAC, says he’s reserving final judgment until the premier delivers deeper anti-corruption measures. “Without other powers, including removing the requirement that corrupt conduct [for IBAC] constitute a criminal offence, any new powers will be limited,” he says.

Carroll has moved quickly to distance himself from existing cabinet policy. He has put the SRL under review; one of his first phone calls as premier was to Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush; and he has previously publicly rejected the government’s push to phase out household gas connections.

Yet, the greatest obstacle confronting Carroll is not policy. It is credibility among voters.

Carroll is attempting to convince the electorate that someone who has spent years at the centre of power can embody a fresh start.

David Hayward, RMIT emeritus professor and an expert analyst of Victorian politics, says it was evident from his first speech as leader that Carroll is channelling his former boss Steve Bracks.

“I thought he handled it really well by coming out and using a Bracks-like phrasing of integrity, economy, and community safety as the leitmotif of his new government, and immediately saying, ‘I am not my predecessors’,” Hayward says.

Bracks pulled off a surprise heist when he defeated Kennett in 1999. Carroll will need to produce an even bigger upset if he is to deliver Labor a fourth term in government, unseen in Victorian politics since Henry Bolte and Rupert Hamer led the Liberals to nine straight election wins between 1955 and 1979.

To do so, Labor must treat the day that Carroll rolled Allan as day one of the election campaign, Hayward says.

“I think he had to distance himself from the malaise that had come to settle upon the government. It’s not like the Allan leadership was full of ideas and policy innovations. It really appeared to be very flat-footed.”

Anxious though he may be to separate himself from Andrews and Allan, Carroll cannot shrug off the state’s record debt.

Hayward says most voters were once unfazed about debt while it could be justified as delivering infrastructure assets, but that changed when the debt and the Big Build were linked with corruption, which was uncovered by a series of reports in The Age.

“Everything suddenly switched … this suddenly raised questions about the spend, about the infrastructure and [Allan] was never really able to respond.”

Carroll’s move to call a royal commission and establish a special prosecutor alongside it gives Labor one last chance to change the script.

“That’s another point about the change of leader. With somebody appearing to be so different to the previous premier, it gives a new energy,” Hayward says.

Time is working against him. Carroll has 119 days before Victorians go to the polls on the final Saturday in November.

He must also contend with the fatigue that follows 12 years of Labor rule, while confronting a surging One Nation vote, now polling at 22 per cent across Victoria and threatening Labor in outer-suburban seats.

By establishing a royal commission into the Big Build on his first day as premier, Carroll sought to isolate the scandal and cast it as part of Allan’s legacy rather than his own.

Whether voters accept that distinction – or regard Carroll as an equal participant in more than a decade of Labor government – could shape the outcome of November’s election.

Fourteen years after promising parliament he would “strive to work every day with that sort of passion and dedication”, Ben Carroll occupies the office he spent his political life pursuing.

For the marathon runner from Airport West, the final sprint has begun.

Dan Gorringe was a battling ruckman. He’s now a social media star and might even become an AFL rights holder

Sydney Morning Herald August 01, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

If you’re a football fan under the age of 35, chances are Dan Gorringe is everywhere when you pick up your phone.

Log on to Instagram, he’ll be there, over-celebrating a Carlton win or mourning a loss. You’ll find his mildly more serious football views on his Dan Does Footy YouTube channel. On TikTok, you’ll get his almost instant hot takes, delivered in his typically edgy style.

He’s labelled goalkicking great Matthew Lloyd a “dirty rat”, called prominent broadcaster Gerard Whateley a “muppet”, and told arguably the greatest player of all time Leigh Matthews to “f--- up”. He has had commercial partnerships with corporate bookies, sports drinks and alcohol brands.

It will come as a surprise, then, that Gorringe the footballer was the polar opposite in personality.

“He was as straight as six o’clock,” his first senior coach Guy McKenna said.

Former Carlton captain and one of Gorringe’s closest friends Sam Docherty, who was unwittingly embroiled in his stoush with Whateley, said his former teammate was rarely the centre of attention in the Blues locker room.

“He was fairly quiet, [but] still very funny,” Docherty said. “If you listen to him speak, he’s probably socially anxious and awkward through footy because he didn’t know where he stood or what he was doing. He always had that funny side to him.

“He joked around with a small group of mates as opposed to the whole locker room. Most people who played with him would have thought he was fairly reserved and didn’t speak very much.”

In many ways, Gorringe is the most unlikely of football personalities: polarising, unfiltered and contemptuous of traditional media.

But even the AFL wants him.

Traditionally, it has taken a long and distinguished on-field career for a retired player to make it in the media. Though a No.10 pick in 2010, his 26 games for Gold Coast and Carlton fall well short of the mark.

As a player, his most memorable moment came in retirement when he clattered into comedian Dave Hughes in a legends charity match. But the world of social media does not follow the same rules, and there are few in Australian sport better at playing this game than Gorringe, who has a team of more than 10 full-timers and additional casual and part-time staff behind the scenes managing content and his commercial partnerships. His success is no accident.

The former ruckman has a greater digital presence than some clubs. His 378,000 followers on Instagram is well over double that of Gold Coast, the club that drafted him. His 43,200 subscribers on YouTube is close to 50 per cent higher than another of his former teams, Carlton, and his TikTok following of 298,000 is more than the Blues and Suns combined.

His average of more than 300,000 views and 20,000-plus engagements per content item across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube makes him “one of Australia’s highest-performing independent sports creator brands”, Nathan Powell, the chief product and strategy officer at AI-powered creator technology platform Fabulate, said.

“Dan has managed to build something that’s much harder than simply accumulating followers,” Powell said.

“He’s built a highly concentrated Australian sporting audience that consistently chooses to engage with his content. The audience is also predominantly male and heavily concentrated in the 18-to-34 demographic, which is one of the most valuable audiences for sporting organisations and advertisers.

“That tells me people aren’t just following Dan because they know who he is – they’re following him because they genuinely value his perspective on sport and the content he creates.”

No wonder the AFL has Gorringe on its books as part of what its customer and commercial boss Bec Haagsma says is a “rapid transformation and evolution of our fan engagement and fan experience strategy”. They see Gorringe as pivotal to targeting the younger market – those under the age of 34.

In collaboration with the league’s broadcast partners, Gorringe appeared on The Ultimate Footy Watchalong for the Fremantle v Sydney and North Melbourne v Melbourne games, streamed live on the AFL’s YouTube channel, Kayo and 7plus.

“Watchalongs”, where fans stream themselves watching a game live and connect online in real time, are a new concept in Australia and, if experience overseas is any indication, here to stay.

“It goes back to the idea that media is changing, and social media is a massive part of the media industry,” Michael Neill, the head of Fox Footy, said. “It won’t get any smaller. We’d be foolish if we didn’t look at these new ideas and different ways to broadcast.

“The immediacy of his posts and how he gets his opinion out there really quick, it’s out there and it’s different.

“It comes from an ex-player’s perspective as well, and from someone who’s very smart when it comes to communication and how to get his message out there.”

For Seven, it gives the network another way to reach the younger market.

“Working with creators who love the game allows us to connect with audiences in authentic new ways,” Seven’s head of sport digital Kirsty Bradmore said. “We are continually exploring more ways to innovate our broadcast offering for viewers across Australia.”

This collaboration drew 250,000 live viewers across the league’s YouTube channel, Kayo, Foxtel and 7plus to watch while Gorringe and co-hosts – Seven reporter Xander McGuire and Collingwood AFLW captain and Kayo personality Ruby Schleicher – casually discussed the game, as opposed to the serious analysis on the main coverage. Socceroos goalkeeper Patrick Beach, a GWS fan, featured at half-time.

“Dan has been with us for a year now doing some hardcore engagement stuff,” Haagsma said. “He’s part of that strategy. For us, looking at how we attract, retain and engage with our avid fans is a different proposition to our younger fans.

“We knew we needed to engage a different strategy. We can’t put highlights on TikTok and go, ‘That will bring the kids in’. Dan has got a voice that we know speaks in a different way, and just resonates. He’s authentic in his point of view, and he loves the game.”

Gorringe’s channel markets itself as “unfiltered and unqualified”. The wider football community saw this side in March after he aired a voice memo left by Docherty of a candid and expletive-laden analysis of his former club’s failings in their thumping by Sydney on the opening night of the season.

Gorringe did not check with Docherty if the message was to be aired, as is the practice in mainstream media, drawing condemnation from Whateley – who slammed him for “reprehensible behaviour”.

His feud with Whateley, a highly respected veteran broadcaster, personified the clash between what Gorringe derides as “old-man media” and new media. Lloyd and Matthews became entangled after their discussion of Docherty’s comments on 3AW, prompting Gorringe to label the former as a “dirty rat” and telling the latter to “f--- up”.

There’s an element of lost in translation for the “dirty rat” reference. Rat is a term of endearment in the Dan Does Footy community. The moderator on his channel addressed his audience as “RATS” in a post this week.

Gorringe is social media’s answer to Port Adelaide great-turned-analyst Kane Cornes (a former columnist for this masthead) on traditional media. Both have found a gap in the market and filled it. Gorringe did not respond to interview requests, but his manager responded in writing to questions sent by this masthead, and happily shared a nude image of his client wearing only a strategically placed Sherrin.

“Dan set out to build something that reflected how most people actually experience sport,” Edward Deal, founder and head of talent at The Gifted Group, said.

“The vast majority of fans don’t sit around analysing defensive structures or selection strategy; they watch with their mates, they celebrate, they argue, they laugh and they overreact. Dan understood there was room for a platform that captured that experience authentically.

“Dan’s credibility doesn’t come from claiming to know more than everyone else. It comes from representing the experience of the supporter.

“He’s never pretended to be the smartest football mind in the room. His audience relates to him because he reacts to the game the same way they do. That’s always been his personality, and it’s what has made the platform resonate.”

That perhaps does not do full justice to Gorringe’s knowledge of the game. In the Dockers v Swans watchalong, the former ruckman observed the return of the leaping rucks – a subject discussed in football media this year – and seconds later foreshadowed Charlie Curnow playing on and kicking a trademark long goal from a mark outside 50. Dan Does Footy works, not least because Dan does the work.

“There’s no secret to why he’s successful in this space. If he put half as much effort into his footy he might have been a bloody good footballer in the end,” Docherty said with a laugh.

“I’ll be out for dinner with him and our partners, and he’ll have the game on in the background on his phone. He has to. This is his world. He lives it and breathes it.

“He’s found his niche in the market where he’s all over everything. He’s the first one to react and always got a video. With that comes a lot of pressure to be all over it and on top of everything.

“I watch about seven of the nine games, occasionally miss one with the kids, I don’t think he misses one – ever. It’s pretty crazy.”

Docherty is often at Gorringe’s South Melbourne home watching a game. It’s not uncommon for Gorringe to duck out at half-time to film himself and have a video posted online minutes later.

“He’ll pop into the backyard, do a one-take video, and it’s straight out to the public,” Docherty said. “It’s as raw as it comes, with no script. It’s just off the top of his head. It’s pretty crazy to watch.”

One of the main talking points from Collingwood’s upset win over Adelaide was their unlikely resurgence to again become a contender. Gorringe captured this point but delivered it in his trademark uncensored style.

“Now we’ll be terrified of the Pies again? How?” an incredulous Gorringe, a Carlton fan, posted to TikTok. “How are they doing this? They’re old. Pendles is 40. How? What is going on?”

The media rights landscape is constantly changing. UK YouTuber Mark Goldbridge, who hosts his own Manchester United fan channel, struck a deal with the Bundesliga to broadcast 20 games on one of his channels. Gorringe has similar aspirations.

“Absolutely. We’re constantly looking at what’s happening internationally,” Deal said. “Mark Goldbridge in Europe and Pat McAfee in the US have shown what’s possible when creators and rights holders work together.

“Australia has the opportunity to become a leader in that space as well. We think creator-led broadcasts are still in their infancy, and we’re excited about continuing to innovate alongside leagues and broadcasters.

“Official match vision has been something we’ve been working towards for a long time. We’d been speaking with the AFL for quite some time about what creator-led broadcasts could look like, and to their credit they were open-minded enough to explore it with us.

“The success of the watchalongs wasn’t just about the numbers. It demonstrated that creator broadcasts can sit alongside traditional coverage, enhance the fan experience and help grow engagement without taking anything away from the broadcast itself.”

The AFL is not ruling out Gorringe becoming a rights holder.

“You can never say never,” Haagsma said. “The future landscape is interesting. There’s different models. The model we’re running with watchalongs is the first creator-led AFL live stream to feature official AFL match vision. It’s a pretty big deal.

“How different people watch different games will change in time, and who holds the rights to those games may change as well. Who knows?”

Brash, colourful chaos agent ... or diligent, relentless leader in waiting?

Sydney Morning Herald August 01, 2026

Tim Wilson’s return to federal parliament was viewed by many as miraculous. But is he really the next Liberal messiah?

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Tim Wilson is in a boisterous, one might even say bumptious, mood. “Tigger’s got to do what Tiggers do!” the shadow treasurer blurts out suddenly, as he bustles around his parliament house office. “And what do Tiggers do best? They bounce!”

It’s late May, and the 46-year-old has just returned from the National Press Club, where he’s been hammering Labor’s controversial capital gains tax changes, unveiled in the budget a week earlier. Now in full flight, he’s telling me a story about once visiting Cambridge University and being invited to examine an early portfolio of Shakespeare’s works. To his hosts’ surprise, he was far more interested in an early edition of Winnie the Pooh, by British children’s author, A. A. Milne. Tigger, of course, is the most hyperactive of Pooh’s friends, a stripy, tigerish creature with boundless energy, and unshakeable self-confidence. A chaos agent.

Some days later, as we’re driving around Wilson’s Melbourne electorate in his bright blue campaign van, I ask if he identifies with this strange, fictional creature. “Exactly. I like Tigger, Tigger’s the best character,” he replies. “Energy, fun, [and] not to be too serious. There are too many people in these jobs that take themselves too seriously.”

Wilson is brash, colourful and determined to stand out. A man who wears eye-catching blue socks every day in parliament because every other male wears black. A man who, far from hiding his eccentricities, seems keen to highlight them. “I am idiosyncratic – I do accept that,” he says. “I openly accept I am unconventional.”

Wilson had been the Liberal MP for the well-heeled Melbourne electorate of Goldstein for six years before losing to independent Zoe Daniel in May 2022, succumbing to the “teal” tidal wave that swept the Liberals out of their most prized metropolitan seats. But in last year’s federal election, he wrenched the seat back on a wafer-thin margin of 175 votes, even as the party elsewhere endured its worst defeat on record. If former prime minister John Howard had once been “Lazarus with a triple bypass” (to quote Howard’s own words before reclaiming the Liberal leadership in 1995), Wilson’s return to parliament was seen, among colleagues, as an equally miraculous recovery. He dubbed it his “journey from oblivion to resurrection”.

It made him the only candidate to defeat a teal incumbent, the only Liberal to reclaim a metropolitan seat for the party last year, and the first Liberal in 100 or so years, he believes, to defeat an independent who’d been elected at a general election.

“Tim’s victory was just phenomenal, really the only bright spot … in a deeply depressing and dark election,” says Trent Zimmerman, the urbane former Liberal MP for North Sydney who, like Wilson, is gay, and for years campaigned alongside him in the federal parliament for marriage equality. “I think it made Tim a hero within the otherwise pretty depressed rank and file of the Liberal Party.”

In February this year, Angus Taylor – who’d rolled Sussan Ley for the party leadership – promoted him into the shadow treasurer’s post, arguably the second-most-critical job in opposition. “Tim was chosen as shadow treasurer because of his incredible drive, his energy, his great cut-through and because he has a very good grasp of economics,” says Liberal senator and shadow defence minister James Paterson. “He has serious thoughts to contribute to the future of tax and economic policy and he’s passionate – and I admire that about him.”

But Wilson can also be erratic, with a reputation for occasional errors and curious lapses of judgment. He’s now pitted against Labor’s most consequential, and polarising, budget in decades, while a resurgent One Nation tears at the Liberals’ right flank. Whether he can muster and maintain the political maturity to successfully navigate these challenges – at such a critical time – remains an open question along the parliamentary corridors. Sentiment among his colleagues is divided, with a number put off by his cockiness, his insistent self-promotion, and the ambition he takes little pains to hide.

His fellow Victorian federal Liberal MP and close friend from university days, Mary Aldred, acknowledges that Wilson’s brusque self-confidence “can irk some people, particularly some of his detractors, who are less sure of their own abilities”. But she insists that’s “different to arrogance. There’s an urbane manner about him, and an unflappability which annoys his opponents … because they can’t get under his skin.”

A harsher assessment comes from one party insider, who immediately opines that Wilson is “a figjam” (as in “f--- I’m good, just ask me”) who “grates people the wrong way” and indulges in “too much childish language and behaviour and stunts”. A senior banking executive says Wilson is intelligent and hard-working, but needs to remember he’s “meant to be the alternative economic brains of the country”, and to act accordingly.

Colleagues were startled earlier this year when Wilson burst into song on the floor of parliament, mangling a version of Billy Joel’s We Didn’t Start the Fire. His intent was to lampoon his opposite number, Treasurer Jim Chalmers, for tipping “petrol” onto the “inflation fire” but the tuneless performance fell flat. The next day Chalmers shot back: “Every three-ring circus needs a clown – and Tim is a clown.”

0:28

Tim Wilson attacks Jim Chalmers on inflation ... with some Billy Joel

The shadow treasurer butchered some lyrics from We Didn't Start The Fire to attack the government's economic management

In late May, Wilson had to apologise to the Speaker of the House, Milton Dick, for a snarky comment on X after he’d been booted from the chamber in question time. The incident triggered a scolding from The Australian’s national editor Dennis Shanahan in the usually Coalition-friendly broadsheet, urging the shadow treasurer to “grow up if he wants to be treated as a serious politician”.

Not long afterwards, Wilson got caught up in a fiery exchange on breakfast TV with Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth, when he told her to “get a breathalyser” after she raised the subject of his 2020 book, The New Social Contract.

Labor has used the book to mercilessly taunt Wilson because it presses the case for a fairer go for young people on housing, and more even-handed treatment of earnings from labour and capital – precisely the arguments, the government maintains, that support its tax changes. But an indignant Wilson argues that his position was to have all taxes come down, not for some to go up.

He defends his propensity for questionable stunts, maintaining that politics has become “very boring ... full of very conventional characters who were very scripted” and that “authenticity now is king”.

Even among detractors, there’s admiration for his campaigning skills. Wilson proved to be a devastatingly effective force in the lead-up to the 2019 federal election campaign, when he whipped pensioners into a panic over then Labor leader Bill Shorten’s plan to curb franking credit rebates.

Wilson rebranded it a “retiree tax” and leveraged his position as chair of the powerful parliamentary economics committee to amplify the attack, working in co-operation with his distant relative, fund manager Geoff Wilson, whose organisation at the time had $3 billion in funds under management. This use of the parliamentary committee system outraged Labor, and drew a strong rebuke from then speaker, Tony Smith. But it paid off for the Coalition. Former Liberal attorney-general George Brandis believes Wilson’s retiree tax campaign was “emphatically one of the main things that got [Scott] Morrison over the line”.

Wilson would later say that he applied tactics that “I learnt from the ACTU’s [anti] WorkChoices campaign that toppled John Howard”.

The contest with Chalmers, one of the government’s most effective communicators, will be key to Wilson’s future. Chalmers is now into his fifth year as treasurer, while Wilson has limited ministerial experience: seven months as assistant industry and energy minister in the dying days of the Morrison government. Apart from that, his economic credentials rest on his six years as an ardent free-marketeer at the right-wing Institute of Public Affairs, his time as chair of the parliament’s economics committee, a slew of articles and media appearances, and a post in the shadow ministry under Ley in the small business and industrial relations portfolios.

Wilson is being more forcefully targeted by Labor than his predecessor as shadow treasurer, Ted O’Brien, because, a colleague claims, “they know Tim could do damage if he finds his feet”. Privately, Labor scoffs at this, though a government insider adds, “we are careful not to write him off”.

Taylor, whose own performance as leader is now under scrutiny, praises Wilson as “serious, diligent and relentless”, telling Good Weekend: “Tim has brought energy to one of the hardest jobs in the opposition [and] has been like a dog with a bone in prosecuting the case against Labor’s toxic taxes.”

Brandis also comes to Wilson’s defence, saying: “There are no concerns about Tim Wilson being an intellectually serious person. He combines a technical understanding of policy with a capacity to deliver powerful political lines. That’s what Angus Taylor was looking for.”

“There would have been safer and greyer options to put up against Chalmers,” confides another senior Liberal colleague. “But I think Angus recognised that we just couldn’t persist with boring options. We needed to take a few risks.”

On a Saturday morning, under clear autumn skies, we’re on a brisk tour of Wilson’s electorate before heading to the first of seven local events he’s scheduled for the weekend. Servicing an ultra-marginal seat is relentless work, and Wilson is in constant campaigning mode, his electric blue Toyota HiAce (dubbed “Polly the Victory Van”) doubling as a mobile advertising board to “remove any doubt about where I am at any given time”.

Goldstein is an electorate cocooned in suburban comfort, more new Melbourne money than old, particularly along its western edge, which is bounded by Port Phillip Bay’s most picturesque stretches. Wilson points out the beach at Sandringham where Kylie Minogue shot a video to lure British tourists here. Over there lies Black Rock and Half Moon Bay, where the artists of the Heidelberg school sometimes came to paint. Further along the bay we’re at Brighton, where the famous brightly coloured bathing sheds have become a magnet for Chinese tourists, and the streets behind the beach are lined with generous suburban estates sheltering behind manicured hedges and ornate fences.

In Wilson’s view, Goldstein is awash with self-starting types, exactly his kind of people. “There’s a value set that runs along Port Phillip, which is very ‘live and let live’, and that’s my mindset,” he declares, jauntily. “I need to be with ‘live and let live’ people; I want to be surrounded by them, I want to represent them.”

At the monthly farmers’ market near the Sandringham Yacht Club, he’s on first-name terms with many of the stall-holders, stopping to chat with Caroline, a smartly groomed woman in her late 50s who makes perfumed soy wax candles, and Brad, an eager young entrepreneur who is developing a new soft drink from finger limes. (With constituents, Wilson is an attentive listener, though if you’re stuck on the receiving end of one of his monologues, it can be hard work getting a word in edgeways.)

Labor’s broken promises on negative gearing for property investors, coupled with sweeping changes to capital gains tax, have handed Wilson what should be a golden opportunity. He was quick to latch onto the viral social media campaign kickstarted by a group of entrepreneurs immediately after the budget, which mocked Prime Minister Anthony Albanese as the new silent partner in their businesses. (The government subsequently announced carve-outs for start-ups.)

“We needed to be the party of small business and self-starters and the biggest challenge was getting them to pay attention to the political process. Lo and behold! The government’s done that for us,” Wilson declares gleefully, accusing Labor of acting in a “deeply immoral” fashion. “They’ve driven a bulldozer through the economic structures of the nation without any sense of nuance.”

At the Bayside Community Sports Centre, his next stop, the air is alive with the shouts of hundreds of teenage girls playing netball across a dozen courts. He’s chatting courtside with coach Kristy Durston when I bring up the subject of that morning’s Redbridge poll, splashed across the front page of The Australian Financial Review. It’s the first of a series in coming weeks that will show One Nation surging ahead of the Coalition and, at one point, overtaking Labor as well. Wilson has taken to habitually referring to One Nation as “the orange paddock of despair” and, on this morning at least, seems almost blasé about the poll warning. “Two years out from an election ... you can’t draw massive conclusions,” he says. “In 2020, at this point in the electoral cycle we were going to win in a landslide and then of course it turned completely to poo.”

Nevertheless, he’s choosing his words carefully with constituents who raise the One Nation insurgency with him: “I don’t believe there’s hope or opportunity there – only resentment and despair and I’m not interested in that.” Australians, he asserts, “don’t want to be led through fear”.

Asked about vanquished arch-rival Zoe Daniel (who may or may not run again), he affects casual disinterest. I inquire whether it’s true, as rumoured, that he and Daniel privately loathe one another. “I don’t really think about the former member that much, so I’m afraid that’s a mischaracterisation from my part,” he responds coolly. (Daniel did not want to comment for this profile.)

Wilson was shattered when he lost his seat in 2022 and his old friend Mary Aldred recalls him going through “all the stages of grief”. Others urged him to seek psychological help. “It’s a devastating thing for a person to lose their seat,” observes Brandis, “particularly if they have had the possibility of a very big political career ahead of them.”

The day after the loss, Wilson broke down in front of the cameras, thanking his schoolteacher husband Ryan Bolger – a tall, strikingly handsome man four years his junior – for the sacrifices Bolger had made. Then Wilson flew to Canberra to pack up his office. “I wasn’t in a good place,” he recalls. “There’s a sense of purpose – then you just get smashed, and you stop.”

He describes taking comfort that day from the large, framed image hanging on the wall next to his desk, commemorating the historic vote for marriage equality in December 2017. The photo captures the landmark moment when the bill went to a final division, and an overwhelming majority of MPs sat shoulder-to-shoulder on one side of the house in support. That day was the culmination of “one of the four significant social movements in Australian political history”, he recalls, “and I wasn’t just in that, I was one of the leaders in it ... I [still] look up at that every day and go, ‘That was f---ing amazing.’ ”

“Twenty years ago it wasn’t necessarily easy to come out as a public figure,” reflects his friend Alex Greenwich, the progressive independent MP in the NSW parliament and former co-convenor of Australian Marriage Equality. In the early days, the campaign for same-sex marriage was driven by the Greens and the left, he points out, “but Tim really provided a leading voice on the conservative side of politics ... I respect his grit and his courage.”

He also praises Wilson’s later advocacy for LGBTQ people when Brandis appointed him to the Human Rights Commission in 2013. (Brandis had controversially placed him there to dilute the body’s anti-discrimination focus and steer it more towards individual rights, such as free speech. The appointment earned Wilson the satirical moniker “Freedom Boy” – plus a lucrative salary of $320,000 a year.)

After winning Goldstein at the 2016 federal election, Wilson, on December 4, 2017, tearfully proposed to Ryan Bolger from the floor of parliament during the final stages of the marriage equality debate. The theatrical gesture made international headlines and, three months later, Greenwich would sign the couple’s marriage certificate at a ceremony inside Melbourne’s botanic gardens. “I would not underestimate how important Ryan is to the whole operation,” reflects someone who knows the couple well. “It’s a genuinely loving marriage. But because Ryan is more flamboyant, people assume Tim is the more grounded one. In fact, it’s quite the opposite.”

Parliamentary proposal

During the same-sex marriage debate, Liberal MP Tim Wilson proposes to his long term partner Ryan Bolger.

Wilson attributes his determination – and his inherited “darkened, recessed eyes” – to his Armenian maternal grandfather, Ruthufus Adamyan, who arrived here as a merchant seaman. Soon afterwards, Ruthufus became Ronald and married Winifred. The couple ran a clothing factory in Gardenvale, in Wilson’s electorate. “They were an interracial couple in one of the most white-bread parts of Australia,” he recalls.

Wilson’s parents, Linda and Robert, pulled beers and ran pubs before splitting up when Wilson was seven. After the separation, Wilson moved to the Mornington Peninsula with his mother, older brother Simon and younger sister Carolyn. The siblings became self-reliant at an early age as Linda often worked “[late] at golf clubs and various things”, he remembers. (Linda later married one-time Victorian state Liberal MP David Morris.)

Wilson declined to make family members available for interview. When I press him for a childhood anecdote, he describes braving the brambles at a nearby estuary to collect blackberries and selling them to local caterers for extra cash. In the school holidays, he and his brother mowed lawns and did other jobs on worksites for his father’s small businesses.

Long-time friend Philip Starkins says he and Wilson were both outliers at high school, “neither in the cool-kid nor the alpha-male-type category – we played hockey. But Tim had this amazing creative streak, still does.” He recalls Wilson pouring intense effort into painting sets for the school production of Evita one year, and thinks he “found peace in it”.

Starkins sees another side to Wilson in private: “this warm, complicated, thoughtful man in there, that is also part of him”. Wilson had struggled silently with his sexuality all through his teenage years at a private school, then known as the Peninsula School (now Peninsula Grammar), at Mount Eliza on the picturesque Mornington Peninsula. He compares coming out at university to what the army used to call “resistance to interrogation” training.

“There was a series of moments where you have to push through fear,” Wilson explains. “You know when they train certain intelligence officers? They take them to the point of maximum fear because it teaches you to understand that feeling, so it’s not foreign. What I’m trying to express is, I’ve been taken to multiple points of fear in my life [when coming out] and pushed through it. I’m familiar with it.”

Wilson told The Age and Sydney Morning Herald’s Inside Politics podcast late last year that people find it “pretty off-putting … that I’m just not kind of afraid”. (One afternoon, he texts me a link to an article about himself that he’s pleased with. Tellingly, it carries the headline: “His superpower is shamelessness”.)

Soon after his loss to Zoe Daniel in 2022, Wilson went to London to console himself. He visited Winston Churchill’s residences. He planned to go dancing and drinking. But instead he found himself sitting under the trees in Hyde Park, reading Leadership in Turbulent Times by American historian Doris Kearns Goodwin. The book explored the journeys of four giants of US political history who overcame setbacks to ultimately gain the presidency, among them Teddy Roosevelt.

“There was a lot of the young Teddy Roosevelt that I recognised … before he went on to the presidency,” Wilson confesses. “It’s the character, his character I recognised in me.”

What did he recognise, I ask? There’s a long pause before Wilson replies. “I think, at the time, it was the extent of the abrasiveness,” he says. “I just recognised a lot of his behavioural traits and went, ‘That’s interesting.’ ” (Goodwin writes of Roosevelt that he had an “abrasive and manic energy”; Wilson says the book showed him the “necessity of failure”.)

By Christmas 2022, Wilson had resolved to attempt a parliamentary comeback, though feeling “terrified I was potentially at risk of throwing away a year of my life for an impossible task”. He discussed the prospect with Brandis, among others, who deemed it “very revealing of Tim’s character, that he ... threw everything at it for at least two years, despite a great deal of doubt about whether he would win the seat back”.

But first Wilson had to secure the formal endorsement of his party through another preselection, and raise funds to do it. “I approached it like a start-up,” he recalls. “I went to the donors and said, ‘I need you to provide start-up capital to get me into the race.’ ”

By the time of the preselection in March 2024, Wilson had amassed a war chest of $200,000, raised through a company called Bayside Forum Ltd, a local fundraising vehicle for the Liberal cause. At the time, it had a three-member board comprising Wilson, his husband and his former manager, Shaun Levin. This caused some consternation among those who felt other potential candidates for the preselection contest should also have access to the money and the research it funded, but Wilson says “it was not my right to allocate money raised for my campaign to go to another candidate without [donors’] permission. Anyone who wanted to raise funds and hold them in the Bayside Forum was welcome to do so. I did. Others did not.”

On the day of the contest, Wilson reminded Liberal preselectors of the “political earthquake” in 2022 that had delivered six of the party’s metropolitan seats to the teals. In a grandiloquent call to arms, he declared: “We are at a ‘Menziean’ moment. We are being called to break a cycle and make history.”

He prevailed over two female candidates, backed by a personal reference from then leader Peter Dutton, which he’d taken pains to secure months earlier. Long before the preselection, Wilson had decided to abandon the conventional Liberal Party playbook for a political campaign. He’d commissioned research to convince himself, and others, that gender would not be the deciding factor. He also abandoned the traditional dark blue colour for Liberal branding and selected his own, a kind of azure. “My conclusion was that we were fighting teals like we would fight Labor, and I realised that that wasn’t going to work.”

Instead, he would adopt teal-like tactics himself, branding himself a “community-backed” Liberal and building a local, T-shirt branded movement which ultimately grew, he claims, to more than 3000 people. “It was a show of force,” one of Daniel’s campaigners grumbled later. “He replicated our coffee swarms, our gatherings of people in T-shirts in cafes, he had a lot more fence signs – his visual presence in 2025, everything was larger.”

There had been, however, a damaging bump in the road early on, when Wilson became involved in a widely discussed local incident that soon became known as “wreathgate”. It was the Sunday before Anzac Day in 2023, when several hundred people had assembled for the annual Beaumaris commemoration, a major fixture in the local calendar. Zoe Daniel, by then the local MP, had a family commitment elsewhere and nominated a volunteer, Peter Newman, to lay a wreath (paid for by her office) on her behalf.

On the morning in question, VIPs were to collect their wreaths from an official table, as their names were read out. But when Daniel’s name was called, there was a delay before Newman could reach the marshalling point. Wilson, standing nearby, got there first and was handed the Daniel wreath by one of the women at the table. Newman recalls approaching Wilson, saying: “That’s our wreath.” But instead of relinquishing it, Wilson held on. What followed was the odd spectacle of both men laying it together.

Afterwards there was an acrimonious exchange between Newman and Wilson, recorded on a reporter’s phone. Wilson was irate when the story made headlines, and three years later is still arguing he was in the right. He insists he only heard the announcer say Daniel was absent, and nothing about Newman’s role as a stand-in. “I was just given it,” he states flatly. “At that point you have a choice, you can hand it back and say ‘No’ to the Beaumaris RSL in honouring lives, or you can do it. Of course, I did the honourable thing.” (He also claims Daniel “had a reputation for skipping events”, a claim contested by her office.)

What’s harder to understand is why he didn’t just hand the wreath over when requested, rather than risk an unedifying spectacle. Rather unconvincingly, he says he believed Newman might drop it. Newman told Good Weekend, “If it had been me, I would have turned around and said, ‘I’m sorry, I’ve made a mistake’ and just given it up.”

The atmosphere in Goldstein in the lead-up to the 2022 election campaign became increasingly poisonous. Claims of pressure tactics flew in both directions. Wilson says he and Bolger felt under such threat that they sought police protection and claimed this was why they later sold their Sandringham home in January 2024. (They now split time between a rented flat in the electorate and a two-bedder they own near the city centre; they also own an investment property on the Mornington Peninsula.)

By the time of the 2025 campaign, the atmosphere had grown even more toxic. Following the Hamas atrocities committed against Israelis in October 2023, the substantial Jewish vote in Goldstein had begun to fall in largely behind Wilson, who’d declared himself a “Proud Zionist” on the front page of the Australian Jewish News, while Daniel was formulating a more nuanced position.

Amy Bachrach, the Jewish liaison officer for Daniel’s campaign, would later tell a parliamentary inquiry that “the weaponisation of the Israel-Gaza issue by proxy groups and the opposition resulted in a fracturing of the Jewish community that is still having ramifications”. Wilson flatly denies any part in “weaponising” the Jewish vote against his opponent, insisting that “the former member weaponised that against herself” and that “my views on those issues have been long-standing and consistent”.

Corflute wars between the two sides intensified. Wilson says his campaign signs were vandalised and often stolen. On the other side, one of Daniel’s key organisers told Good Weekend that “the defacing of Zoe fence signs was next-level in 2025: eyes cut out, red paint symbolising blood, ‘Jew hunter’ [scrawled on them]. I began dreading going to the gate to see what had happened this time.”

Daniel was also dogged by mobile billboards being driven around the electorate advertising the fact that she had been referred to the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC). The complaint had been brought by Wilson’s close friend, Jason Falinski, a former Sydney federal Liberal MP who’d also lost to a teal in 2022 and who, by the time of the 2025 election, had become spokesman for Australians for Prosperity, one of the several third-party groups active against Daniel in Goldstein.

The gist of Falinski’s allegation was that a consultant to Daniel, while on the government payroll, had misused public funds by lobbying The Australian Financial Review on behalf of a client who was also one of her donors (climate campaigner Simon Holmes à Court). After investigating, the NACC concluded that the consultant, former ABC reporter Jim Middleton, was not on the taxpayers’ dollar at the time and curtly dismissed the matter. Yet the billboards publicising the NACC referral were still being wheeled out around Goldstein even after the complaint had been dismissed.

Wasn’t that unfair? I ask Wilson. “I had no knowledge of that billboard whatsoever until the first time I saw it when I was walking out of an event,” he shoots back tersely. “They [teal supporters] applied a win-at-all-cost approach in the 2022 election but they never seem to appreciate when anybody holds them to account.”

Wilson got his first taste of politics at university, twice becoming president of the Student Representative Council at Monash. He also started a degree in painting at the university’s Caulfield campus, but switched to policy studies (after an argument with a lecturer about the GST) and commenced part-time work for Victorian state Liberal MP David Davis.

Visual arts remained a passion, and he marks every major life event with a new acquisition. An original Norman Rockwell poster hangs in his electorate office and, for his 30th birthday, he tracked down a rare portrait of Ronald and Nancy Reagan, giving it pride of place over his bed.

He’s recently taken up linocut print-making and become quite adept, judging by two samples in his electorate office. A keen bushwalker, he’s also kept an economics PhD simmering on the backburner (through RMIT’s Blockchain Innovation Hub), and last September self-funded an AI fact-finding trip to the US. The doctorate, should he finish it, will join a CV already crammed with a bachelor of arts in public policy, a diploma of business, a masters in international trade and a certificate in carbon management.

Wilson’s career after university was just as eclectic, spanning consultancies in trade and communications, the Institute of Public Affairs, the Human Rights Commission, and even a stab at a media career on Melbourne talkback radio. When he walked away from his lucrative post on the commission to seek preselection in Goldstein in 2016, he had to stare down an anonymous homophobic smear sheet branding him a “danger” to families.

Brandis recalls writing the young Wilson a glowing endorsement, believing “this was an opportunity for the Victorian Liberal Party to choose another person who was going to be a significant thought leader”. (Wilson won by just two votes.)

Yet he continues to defy easy categorisation within the Liberal ecosystem. He’s long had a strong libertarian bent: witness, for instance, his violent dislike of plain packaging for cigarettes, his past opposition to section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act (which he said violated free speech) and his one-time support for pill-testing.

He also disavows media attempts to lump him in with the party’s fading moderate wing, stating “there is nothing moderate about my liberalism”. Once committed to net zero carbon emissions by 2050, he’s had to dance around the issue since Taylor scrapped it as Liberal policy. “The time frames for 2050 are now looking substantially more challenging than they initially did,” he proffers, carefully. “But I still absolutely support a commitment towards long-term decarbonisation through the use of technology.”

He’s never done much to hide his leadership ambitions (one Liberal insider says he “does himself damage by being so bloody obvious”). He insists he’s focused on doing his current job well. But he leaves the door ajar when asked if there’s a baton in his backpack. “If there’s a time where that’s what’s required of me,” he states, “then so be it.”

Inside the Canberra bubble, some speculate that if Taylor comes to grief, the next Liberal leadership contest could well be between Wilson and opposition industry minister Andrew Hastie, though Hastie is the likeliest next prospect. Zimmerman, for one, thinks Wilson could soar higher. “What Australians will care about is having a leader who can effectively manage the Australian economy, and if Tim can demonstrate that, then I think the sky’s the limit.”

Would Australians be ready for a gay married man as leader? Wilson brushes the question aside. “The country wants someone who has clarity and vision about where they want to build and take the country, and I think everything else is a completely secondary consideration.”

In the meantime, he intends to go on getting himself noticed. “I see a lot of people who are very good at being fakes,” he says. “I am not a fake, make whatever judgment you want.”

Field and French flourish for Wigan to boost title charge with victory at Leigh

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 21:08:49 GMT

Super League: Leigh 8-20 Wigan

Wigan move up to second within two points of Leeds

There are moments in Super League seasons, marathons as they are, which can often prove to be sliding doors occasions for both teams involved. And as the full-time hooter sounded in Leigh and Wigan celebrated another statement win with their travelling support, it was not difficult to imagine how one particular moment from this derby could swing the seasons of both teams.

For nearly 40 minutes, Leigh had done something no team had managed to do to Wigan for quite some time: make them appear second best. The Warriors, on a run of nine consecutive wins which began with their Challenge Cup triumph at Wembley in May, had been completely outplayed by their local rivals and even their own coach admitted they were lucky to be only 8-0 behind.

But great teams, and great players, find a way to win. Leigh’s first real mistake came two minutes before half-time, when they turned their backs on Jai Field after conceding a penalty, expecting Wigan to kick for touch. Instead, Field tapped the ball and raced 90m downfield to reduce the deficit to just two points by half-time. Just like that, it turned.

When Leigh produced another error three minutes after the restart, the Warriors’ other talisman, Bevan French, pounced to inexplicably move Wigan ahead in a game they had been dominated in to that point. Two more Leigh knock-ons followed in the proceeding minutes and once again, the visitors scored tries from both of them.

Nobody knows how this would have ended had Leigh led more convincingly at half-time. If the Leopards had won, they would have inserted themselves into the picture for the top two. Instead, they are now sitting sixth and looking nervously over their shoulders. Wigan, meanwhile, march on – they are now second and just two points behind the league leaders, Leeds.

Perhaps in a way it was a lesson as to the step Leigh still need to take to compete with a side like Wigan. But the Warriors, frustrated as they will be by the level of this performance, should take great heart from the fact that if they can be this below-par with the ball and still win against a playoff rival, imagine what they can do if it clicks in a playoff tie come autumn.

“We needed to improve because in that first half we were second best,” their coach, Matt Peet, said. “We’ve managed our way out of a situation there. There was nothing wrong with our effort but they were very good. You don’t want to win this way every week but it’s good to know it’s in the locker.”

Leigh deservedly led by eight points early on thanks to Innes Senior’s outstanding try and two goals from the boot of Adam Cook, but there was no doubting the big moment here – Field’s breakaway try – left a mark on them. The Leopards will hope it does not leave any long-lasting damage in their push to make the playoffs again in 2026.

“I went in and tried to lift them at half-time but it felt like that moment was a bit of an implosion,” Leigh’s coach, Adrian Lam, said. “It was hard to watch in the second half but we were awesome in that first half. It was unbelievably good, and we are very close to being very good. A bit of negativity crept in and our gameplan just fell apart.”

Field and French’s tries turned an eight-point deficit into a lead either side of half-time. When Leigh turned possession over cheaply again, Zach Eckersley was the third grateful recipient of a momentary lapse from the Leopards. Then as the hour mark struck, Noah Hodkinson was afforded the same opportunity to make it 20-8 and from there, Wigan were wise enough defensively to close out a crucial win.

But this was a captivating and engrossing derby overall. With the National Rugby League’s bid for control of Super League incoming over the next few days, this was an advert for everything that is great about the competition. A sold-out stadium, two local rivalries and star talent proving to be the difference when it mattered most.

Yet for all the change potentially Super League’s way off the field, one constant is that it would take a brave man to back against Wigan prevailing at Old Trafford again come October.

Georgia Hunter Bell outruns Odira to win Commonwealth Games 800m gold

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 21:01:31 GMT

Hunter Bell clocks 1min 59.51 to beat world champion

Win secures full set of major medals for English runner

There are late developers in sport, and then there is the brilliant Georgia Hunter Bell, who continues to defy sporting gravity at the age of 32.

And on Friday night under the Glasgow lights, she gave a tactical masterclass to outwit – and then outpace – the 800m world champion Lilian Odira and complete her set of global medals.

Incredibly it was only two years ago that she made her international debut here in Scotland’s biggest city. Back then she was a part-time runner working in tech. Now, staggeringly, she is one of Britain’s biggest sports stars and the proud owner of Olympic, World, European and now Commonwealth medals.

“There were some tears on the podium,” Hunter Bell said afterwards. “That showed me how much that meant.”

Hunter Bell’s story loses nothing in its retelling. As a teenager she was among the best runners in Britain. Then came a series of injuries, setbacks and heartaches. By her mid-20s she had retired. Then came a second act not even Hollywood would dare write.

It started with long cycle rides during lockdown, then a series of parkruns in Bushy Park. By November 2022 Hunter Bell had got in contact with her old coaches, Trevor Painter and Jenny Meadows, who guided Keely Hodgkinson to glory and had regarded Hunter Bell as “the one who got away”. Soon her injuries were long behind her – along with most of her opponents.

By March 2024 she was wearing her first GB vest in the world indoor championships in Glasgow. That August she won an Olympic 1500m bronze medal in a British record 3min 52.61sec. Since then she has given up her job and got even better. This medal, in an England vest, was her sixth time on a global podium.

“Lots of people reflect on being a kid and doing it for the kid version of yourself,” she said after. “But I ­actually think of the young woman version of myself, who was like 23, 24, and gave up and really didn’t know what she was doing with her life.

“I feel sorry for that girl, and then I feel proud of making it through that and coming back here,” she added. “That’s what makes me emotional.”

Going into the final, most thought that Odira, the Kenyan who had defied Hunter Bell and Hodgkinson to win gold at last year’s world championships, was the one to beat.

But Hunter Bell had other ideas, leading from tape to gun, to take an easy victory in 1min 59.51sec. Odira took silver, more than a second back, with the Australian Sarah Billings claiming bronze.

“I felt calm,” Hunter Bell said. “I really feel like I was composed. It didn’t go to plan as in the race. I did not think I would go gun-to-tape and lead it for the whole thing. I wanted to lead with 200m to go. But I found myself at the front, and so I thought ‘I’ll just control it, keep it relaxed, not too fast’, and then when I feel that pressure on me with the move being made, I’ll be ready to go.”

The thing is nobody came. They were through halfway in a slow 60.32sec, and the race had barely sped up when Hunter Bell finally powered clear with 200m to go. At this point Odira was five metres back and had no chance of closing.

“I’m really happy with that, it worked perfectly,” Hunter Bell said. “I really felt my legs were going in the last few steps and I couldn’t see where anyone was, but the crowd really pulled me home. It was great.”

There were also two silver medals for England on the night through Emily Newnham and Jake Minshull in the women’s and men’s 400m hurdles. But this was a night that belonged to Hunter Bell.

Elsewhere, Adaejah Hodge of the British Virgin Islands gave a small hint of her talent by storming to the women’s 200m title in 22.07.

The 20-year-old has already run 10.63 for the 100m this year, making her the fifth fastest woman in history. For good measure she has a personal best of 21.68 for the 200m, putting her joint-ninth of all time. But on a cold night in Glasgow, a more modest time was enough as she took gold ahead of Shaniqua Bascombe, of Trinidad and Tobago, with Jamaica’s Alana Reid picking up bronze.

In the men’s javelin Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Pathirage continued his annus mirabilis by winning gold with a huge throw of 89.75m, ahead of India’s Olympic champion, Neeraj Chopra.

Arsenal’s title defence: keeping tired players fit and the Vinícius question

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 19:00:31 GMT

Key players have piled up extra minutes at the World Cup and signing Vinícius Júnior would smash their wage structure

After beating MK Dons 3-0 in a training-ground friendly last weekend, Arsenal truly begin their pre-season programme against Girona on Saturday evening. It marks a return to action for the Premier League champions, who will want to show their success last season was not a one-off.

Retaining the English title is incredibly difficult if you are not Manchester City. No other club has done it since Manchester United won three in succession from 2007 to 2009. Chelsea have done it once, Liverpool have not managed it for more than 40 years, and it is the best part of a century since Arsenal retained the crown. Mikel Arteta faces a sizeable challenge.

Reaching a second successive Champions League final will not be simple either. Manchester City in 2021-22 are the only one of England’s previous five finalists who made it as far as the semi-finals the next season. With the Premier League stronger than ever, competing on two fronts has never been tougher. Transfer business may improve Arsenal’s chances, though their spending has been modest to this point. More than half of the £79m spent was on making Piero Hincapié’s loan permanent.

Elsewhere Arsenal have replaced Leandro Trossard with Christos Tzolis, a Greek winger, from Club Brugge. Seven years younger than the Belgian, his arrival is a logical move in future-proofing the squad. However, the left side of Arsenal’s attack would be elevated to truly elite level if they could secure reported target Vinícius Júnior. The on-field argument speaks for itself. Vinícius made 92 carries of at least five metres that ended with him either taking a shot (49) or creating a chance (43) last season, the most of anyone in Europe’s top five leagues. Open-play threat, for a side that has often relied on set pieces, would be considerably increased.

Those holding the purse strings at Arsenal may have pause for thought. Capology’s wage data estimates that Vinícius is the joint-third highest paid player in Europe’s top five leagues, earning in excess of £100,000 a week more than anyone at his potential new club. Would Arsenal be willing to rewrite their wage structure? They should expect calls from the agents of their current players if they are. In this sense, Bradley Barcola, with whom they have also been linked, makes a more plausible target. The issue there would be competition from Liverpool, who are in far greater need of wingers.

This is the test facing Andrea Berta, Arsenal’s sporting director. Improving a squad that is already one of the best around is not easy. When Berta’s arrived last year, the club’s primary targets were said to be Alexander Isak and Benjamin Sesko, both of whom joined rivals instead. The pool of players who could add something significant to Arteta’s options is drying up.

Keeping existing players fit may be more beneficial than enhancing the squad. Arsenal did well to win the league given only a handful of clubs had players that missed more games. Kai Havertz was reportedly their top earner before Bukayo Saka signed a contract extension in February, but he only started seven league games. The captain, Martin Ødegaard, was also unavailable for spells, meaning he and Saka started only 10 Premier League matches together in 2025-26. One of them coincided with the only game for which Declan Rice was injured (the 4-1 home win over Aston Villa), another (another home win, 2-1 against Brighton) when he started at right-back.

This meant Arteta was rarely able to give key men a breather. Arsenal have five of the Premier League’s top 20 players for club minutes in all competitions since the start of last season. Granted, the goalkeeper David Raya is one of them. But their outfield players with more than 4,200 minutes were Rice (4,456 minutes, the 11th most for a Premier League club), Martín Zubimendi (4,298, 15th), William Saliba (4,254, 17th) and Gabriel Magalhães (4,210, 19th), all vital components of the side’s spine.

Saliba also played 795 minutes for France, pushing him past 5,000 minutes before his World Cup was prematurely ended by a back injury that looks likely to sideline him for some time. It is remarkable Rice was able to play 1,026 minutes for England on top of his Arsenal commitments, not least as he has managed nerve pain in a hamstring throughout 2026.

This workload clearly impacted his ability to contribute at his best for Thomas Tuchel this summer, and that will be a concern for Arteta. With Viktor Gyökeres also clocking up plenty of playing time for Sweden, Arsenal have six players with at least 4,400 minutes for club and country since the start of last August.

This may have been a factor in Arsenal opting for a relatively low-key pre-season. They visited Asia last summer, but the trip to Catalonia to play Girona is the furthest they will travel this year. Arsenal also have games in Dublin (against Real Betis) and Cardiff (the Community Shield against City) sandwiching home friendlies against Borussia Dortmund and Como.

With players still recovering from their World Cup exertions, it may be some time before we see the true Arsenal. A combination of fatigue, injuries and potential squad additions means the process could take far longer than would be ideal.
