Infantino under huge pressure after plan for World Cup sell-off sparks resignation and rebuke

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 18:05:02 GMT

Cordeiro quits as senior adviser to Fifa president

Lamour: sell-off plan ‘defies belief and imagination’

The walls started closing in on Gianni Infantino after another dramatic day that saw one of his senior advisers resign and brought a scathing rebuke from Fifa’s own chief operating officer.

Infantino is under huge pressure after his plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors met a tide of opposition from around the globe. European countries have already promised to boycott Fifa competitions if he does not shelve the scheme but Friday’s developments, which led to two key members of his inner circle distancing themselves from him, may prove equally damaging to any prospects of salvaging his presidency.

Meanwhile Uefa and other confederations are actively seeking candidates to run against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, in which he had been expected to comfortably win a fourth term. The pressure that has built since this week’s revelations casts doubt on whether the previously unassailable Swiss, who has doubled down on the proposals, will be able to cling on for that long.

The resignation of Carlos Cordeiro, one of Infantino’s senior advisers since 2021, struck a fresh blow upon Infantino hours after Uefa’s 55 members had unanimously threatened a boycott. Cordeiro, a former US Soccer chief, said Infantino had proposed “a bad deal for Fifa’s member associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game”. He questioned the lack of transparency in Fifa’s process and pointed out that the governing body is sitting on vast debt-free reserves that could be used to fund development.

“Why this deal?” he asked. “Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?”

But an extraordinary statement later in the day by Kevin Lamour, Fifa’s current chief operating officer, may have inflicted a more serious wound. Lamour, a close associate of Infantino at Fifa and during their previous spells at Uefa, said staff and other stakeholders had been “deceived” by the president and said he would tolerate being sacked for expressing his views.

“What has been announced in recent days and what has been happening behind the scenes in recent months defies belief and imagination,” Lamour said. “To put it very clearly and directly: the project that has sparked so much controversy and debate is not a Fifa project. It is even less a project of Fifa’s administration. It is the project of one person.

“The Fifa vice-presidents, the members of the Fifa Council, the confederations, the federations, the players, the leagues, the clubs, and the fans were not the only ones who were ignored. Fifa’s own administration was also deceived.

“This lie by omission over many months and this unilateral exercise of power are not trivial. They are indicative of a lack of trust, a lack of transparency, a lack of discernment, a lack of good governance. And a serious lack of respect.”

Lamour said Fifa’s mission is “not to serve the personal interests of a person who, unfortunately, believes he embodies Fifa when he is supposed to be at its service”. He stated that his colleagues “deserve better than contempt and intimidation”, adding: “My feeling is that we all want to be proud to work for Fifa, and today, unfortunately, it seems that is no longer the case for many of us.”

Infantino appears to be shedding allies and there was no succour to be taken from a strongly worded statement from the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), which backed Uefa and Concacaf in their opposition to the privately funded Fifa Forward Enterprise plan. The AFC stopped short of matching Uefa’s boycott but was clear in saying the proposal should be scrapped.

“The fact that the situation has reached the point where the real possibility of a Fifa World Cup boycott has entered public discourse should concern everyone who cares about the future of our game,” it said. “The AFC believes that the proposed FFE cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward.”

It called upon Fifa to “undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework”, echoing its peers’ complaints about a lack of consultation regarding key decisions such as World Cup hosting arrangements.

A further revelation on Friday that Fifa has opened a tender for research companies to assess the economic benefits of expanding the World Cup to 64 teams, demanding a hugely accelerated timescale, has only increased such concerns in football’s corridors of power.

Uefa is minded to play a waiting game after securing a united front in opposing Infantino’s plan. It will assess how Fifa reacts, although early signs suggest little change of tack. Overnight Fifa had attempted to blame media reporting for such widespread opposition, claiming its commitment to “an open and democratic consultation”, although that intervention has cut no ice among its opponents.

It is unlikely any mechanism to depose Infantino will be triggered immediately although in theory an extraordinary Fifa Congress, and subsequent vote of confidence, could be convened if 43 countries make such a request. The priority around Uefa and beyond is to see off the FFE plan before taking further steps. Any Europe-backed candidate for the Fifa presidency election in March is likely to hail from a different continent, with the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, and AFC president, Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa, among possible contenders. The latter lost narrowly to Infantino in the 2016 election.

Fifa continues to lobby federations to accept their project and have stuck by the 19 September deadline originally given for those who wish to sign up.

Trump backtracks from promise to let Ukraine build Patriot missiles

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 17:58:56 GMT

US president tells reporters during Camp David cabinet meeting technology ‘a hard thing to give away’

Donald Trump has backed off a promise to let Ukraine manufacture its own Patriot air defense interceptors, telling reporters that handing over the underlying technology was “a hard thing to give away” during a cabinet meeting at Camp David.

The retreat, billed by the White House as “something different” for the cabinet to experience together, was the first such meeting at the presidential compound of Trump’s second term.

It also became the venue for the US president to unpick, in real time, a commitment he made to Volodymyr Zelenskyy just a few days earlier.

Asked whether he was ready to grant Kyiv a license to build Patriots domestically – something he had suggested at a Nato summit in Turkey just this month, and which the Ukrainian president described as a productive topic in their White House meeting on Tuesday – Trump was noncommittal.

“We have not agreed to that,” he said. “We’re talking about it, but it’s a hard thing to give away that kind of technology.”

Giving away the weapons carried its own risks, he added: “People that you give that technology, they can some day turn on you. You know that is possible.”

The interceptor travels at “8,600 miles an hour”, Trump explained, adding for context: “If you go 60, it gets to be a little fast.”

He went on to recall an occasion on which five missiles were fired “at Jordan” and were shot down in sequence – rendered by the president as “bing bing bing bing”.

“Nobody else has that capacity,” he said of the system, before concluding that Washington “will be building many plants” to produce Patriots and Tomahawk missiles domestically – just not, for now, in Ukraine.

The reversal is likely to unsettle Kyiv, which has spent the past year lobbying for both more interceptors and the means to produce its own, amid a global shortage that has been compounded by the volume of Patriot and Tomahawk stock expended in Washington’s confrontation with Iran.

Trump touched on that conflict too, telling reporters the US would be “hitting them very hard” if talks broke down, and dismissing Iran’s military as effectively hollowed out. “They have no navy … they have no anti-aircraft,” he complained, comparing the controversial five-month campaign favorably with US wars in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Korea, and arguing in each case that the war lasted “many years”, whereas his administration had achieved more, in less time. His stated goals for the campaign have repeatedly shifted.

An expert analysis of the Pentagon’s own arsenals tell a different story: the Center for Strategic and International Studies says two-thirds of the department’s Patriot interceptors have been used, perhaps prompting a $58.6bn army contract with Lockheed Martin to rebuild supplies, along with a recent White House request to Congress for tens of billions of dollars more in emergency funding.

The Camp David gathering came a day after Trump announced what he called a “historic” agreement for Hamas to disarm and for Israeli forces to withdraw from Gaza, a claim that has yet to be confirmed by Israel.

Pressed on the sequencing of the deal – whether disarmament or withdrawal would come first, the issue that has stalled negotiations for months – Trump declined to specify either way, saying only that Washington had “an understanding” with Israel and that the Israelis were “very happy about it”.

He was similarly light on detail when asked if the agreement would actually hold, despite a diplomatic backdrop that includes an outstanding international criminal court (ICC) arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, an unresolved international court of justice (ICJ) case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza, arms restrictions imposed by several governments over the conduct of the war, and a governing coalition at home that has repeatedly rejected anything short of Hamas’s total disarmament before any withdrawal.

“The people are very complex and difficult,” said Trump. “In many cases wonderful, in many cases not so wonderful.”

An Israeli official has said that no withdrawal from the so-called Yellow Line will happen before Hamas fully disarms, while members of Netanyahu’s own coalition have voiced opposition to the plan, details Trump did not address.

High court clears way for clinical trial giving puberty blockers to children

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 17:52:30 GMT

Legal challenge to King’s College London research study claimed it could harm participants but was rejected

A clinical trial of drugs that can delay puberty can go ahead after a high court judge threw out a legal challenge on Friday.

Campaigners had launched the attempt to halt the planned research into puberty blockers, to be run by researchers at King’s College London (KCL), on the grounds that they believed it could harm the children taking part.

But Mr Justice Chamberlain refused the application for a judicial review, saying none of their claims had a realistic chance of success in court. He said each patient involved in the Pathways trial would have been assessed over “many months” by specialist doctors who would have “formed the opinion that a child has a reasonable prospect of receiving a clinical benefit from the treatment”.

The university welcomed the court’s decision on Friday, saying particular care would be taken over the safety of participants of the trial, which will start recruiting more than 220 children aged between 11 and 16 years old from 1 August.

But opponents, including the psychotherapist James Esses and Keira Bell, who began taking puberty blockers as a teenager before later detransitioning, expressed sadness at the ruling.

Bell told the BBC: “It’s a tragedy that the court has refused permission for this challenge to proceed. The medical profession and morality do not always walk hand in hand. If they did, this trial would be out of the question.”

The Bayswater Group, which works with parents of gender-questioning children and was also part of the legal challenge, said: “We remain of the view that the Pathways trial does not meet the legal and ethical thresholds required for research on children.

“The design and scale of the study, the known and potential harms of the intervention, and the absence of a sufficient prior evidence base of benefit raise fundamental questions about whether the protective framework for minors has been properly implemented.”

A spokesperson for KCL said: “Pathways trial is a carefully designed study to give much needed evidence about the potential benefits and risks of puberty suppression to improve NHS care.

“A small number of young people with long-term gender incongruence, who have already received comprehensive psychological and social support through NHS gender services, will be eligible.”

The spokesperson added that the study would have “strict eligibility requirements” and that the trial’s design had been “carefully reviewed by independent researchers and has been approved by the UK’s health research regulators, the HRA and MHRA”.

The study was originally commissioned in response to a 2024 review of gender identity services by Dr Hilary Cass, which found that gender medicine was an “area of remarkably weak evidence” and “built on shaky foundations”. Initially used to treat early onset puberty, puberty blockers had been prescribed off-label to children with gender dysphoria until the NHS banned their use last year after the Cass review.

At least 57 people die as tens of thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 17:52:11 GMT

Pedro Sánchez decries ‘violation of territorial integrity’ as other EU countries criticise Madrid over incident

At least 57 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 50,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco in what Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”.

The huge influx, which took place over the course of just 24 hours, overwhelmed the city of 85,000 people, triggered a political crisis for Madrid and led to a mixed reaction from other EU countries, including calls for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.

Sánchez, who arrived in Ceuta on Friday morning, said he would use all the resources at his disposal to guarantee the safety of the city’s population.

He attributed the mass crossing to “human trafficking mafias” that had taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta, or Spain’s other north African enclave of Melilla, could not be summarily returned under special rules.

Sánchez said: “That has spread like wildfire during these last few hours through the networks of mafias that traffic in human beings and has produced an avalanche of the characteristics and dimension that we experienced yesterday.”

Sánchez said a temporary reception centre would be established to facilitate the documentation, registration, triage and “expedited” expulsion of people with no legal claim to be in Spain.

He also said the government would erect a visible barrier – a line of buoys – near the breakwater at Ceuta’s Tarajal beach to make it clear where the border was, and to legally comply with the court’s ruling.

Although the Spanish government said about 50,000 people had crossed the border on Thursday and in the early hours of Friday, the president of Ceuta put the figure at about 60,000.

Spain’s interior ministry, which has deployed additional police officers and soldiers to the enclave, said more than 48,300 people had voluntarily returned to Morocco by 6pm on Friday.

The Irish presidency of the EU has convened a meeting of member states on Saturday, under the Integrated Political Crisis Response mechanism.

EU sources said this will provide experts from member states with an opportunity “to discuss the movements into Ceuta over the last two days, the numbers of people who have returned to Morocco today, the supports being provided by the EU to Spain and diplomatic engagement with Morocco”.

A further meeting of EU ambassadors has been called in Brussels on Monday.

The latest incident dwarfs the last mass border crossing in May 2021, when Morocco loosened its border controls, allowing about 10,000 people to enter the territory over the course of two days.

That crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed over the territory to Morocco and Mauritania.

That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara – a move that had caused a diplomatic rift between Spain and Algeria, which had supported the Polisario group.

Sánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first such visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria.

Moroccan government sources told the Europa Press news agency that the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”.

Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich, was quoted by the Associated Press as saying that “we have always prioritized legal, orderly and safe migration for all” and indicated that the situation had developed against Rabat’s wishes.

Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers’ association representing officers of the Spanish Guardia Civil – which patrols Spain’s borders – described the situation as a “serious humanitarian crisis”.

Without shelter, thousands of people, including unaccompanied children, had been left sleeping in parks and on pavements, while others roamed the streets aimlessly. “It’s chaotic,” said Sbihi.

Among those who died, many drowned, but some were killed in a crush to cross the breakwater fence at Tarajal beach, Sbihi said.

Video footage on Thursday showed crowds of people walking around the breakwaters at Tarajal beach on to local roads. While most appeared to be young men, there were also families with women and small children.

Ceuta and Melilla have the E​U’s only land border with ​Africa. ‌Both cities ​periodically ​experience surges in attempted crossings by people seeking to reach Europe.

The events in Ceuta led some EU countries to issue strong threats or rebukes.

Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, summoned Italy’s ambassador to Madrid on Friday after Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.

Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now closed scheme to regularise the status of more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”.

Tajani’s remarks prompted a sharp response from Albares, who said the comments were “unbecoming” and accused Italy of “partisan demagoguery”.

Italy announced on Friday evening that it would be suspending its Schengen arrangements with Spain, but the practical impact of the move was not immediately clear.

Meloni said the measure would be kept in force only as long as needed, adding: “In parallel, Italy is ready to support every European initiative to assist Spanish institutions as needed to restore full control of the union’s external borders and to address the ongoing situation with determination.”

Responding to Italy’s unilateral decision, a European Commission spokesperson said a member state “may exceptionally and temporarily reintroduce internal border control as a matter of last resort, to address serious threats to public order or national security”. But they added that the member state would need to notify the commission and explain how the situation in Ceuta constituted such a threat.

The Guardian understands that Italy has not yet formally notified any of its EU partners of its decision.

The Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, urged Spain to “act swiftly to regain control of the situation and fulfil its commitments within Schengen cooperation”.

The Finnish interior minister, Mari Rantanen, said that as Spain had “completely failed to protect the Schengen area’s external border”, all EU countries should support Italy’s proposal to suspend its Schengen status.

However, in a statement later on Friday, the European Commission said Ceuta and Melilla were subject to special Schengen rules that prevented onward movement within the zone.

The EU’s migration commissioner, Magnus Brunner, called the situation in Ceuta “unacceptable” and said he was in close contact with the Spanish authorities. But he also confirmed there was no onward route from Ceuta given the enclave’s unique status under the Schengen rules.

He said: “The Schengen borders code provides for special rules that apply to Ceuta and Melilla. Border checks on persons departing from Ceuta and Melilla remain in force.”

But there were also shows of unity. The European Council president, António Costa, expressed his “solidarity with Spain in the current situation of illegal migration in Ceuta”.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had been in touch with the Spanish government to express his solidarity and to offer assistance to Spain. But, as a precautionary measure, Macron said he had asked the interior ministry to strengthen the French controls on its border with Spain with four mobile units and drones.

In Spain, the opposition People’s party (PP) called on Sánchez to come up with a tough response, saying the military and police reinforcements announced on Thursday night were insufficient.

In a post on X, the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, wrote: “People have continued to arrive in Ceuta throughout the night, and those on the ground describe an occupied city, with nothing sufficient being done to prevent it.” The far-right Vox party called the incident “an invasion”.

On Friday evening, hundreds attended an anti-migrant rally outside the Moroccan embassy in Madrid, with images showing some protesters performing Nazi salutes and waving flags with far-right insignia.

Burnham risks first revolt as PM over apparent support for North Sea drilling

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 17:38:28 GMT

Labour MPs fear No 10 team lack up-to-date energy insight and don’t fully recognise voters’ climate concerns

Andy Burnham was told he could face the first revolt of his premiership as Labour MPs and climate experts condemned his apparent support for renewed drilling for oil and gas.

As the UK suffers through drought, fires and heatwaves, the prime minister gave the strongest indication yet on Friday he was minded to allow new drilling. His comments came just hours before the UN secretary-general warned “every new fossil fuel project” made heatwaves more dangerous.

Speaking at a community centre in Sheffield on Friday, Burnham repeated he would be “pragmatic” about oil and gas and that decisions on new drilling would be made “in due course”. But he added: “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from.”

But many Labour MPs are increasingly worried about how support for expanded drilling will play with an electorate alarmed by the worst drought since 1976, soaring temperatures, wildfires, and climate-related food inflation and potential supply shortages.

They worry about losing more voters to the Greens: Zack Polanski’s party has stressed its opposition to further new licences for the North Sea, including the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea and the Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland. A decision to go ahead with the projects could trigger a new surge in defectors from Labour.

Rachael Maskell, the Labour MP for York Central, urged ministers to “keep carbon in the ground”, and watch the recent national emergency climate briefing. She added: “We’re seeing ice caps melting, seas warming up, hotter and hotter summers. This summer has been a warning that we have to go towards a sustainable future fast.”

Clive Lewis, the Labour MP for Norwich South, said there was “no legitimate reason” to press ahead with Jackdaw because it would make only a negligible difference to energy prices while sending the wrong signal internationally as Europe experienced record heat.

Lewis said approving the field would show Burnham was “not looking at the evidence” and that Labour risked adding “the stain of the climate crisis” to the party’s record, alongside Gaza.

Chris Murray, the Labour MP for Edinburgh East and Musselburgh, said the UK must stay the course on decarbonisation. “Britain was the first country to industrialise and we have a duty to lead the world on net zero. We must be wary of the self-interest from which oil and gas companies are arguing, while the future of the planet is at stake.”

António Guterres, the UN secretary-general, did not single out the UK but gave a pointed warning on Friday, as the World Meteorological Organisation forecast hotter temperatures from August to October. “Every new fossil fuel project approved today makes tomorrow’s heatwaves more dangerous, and our world less secure,” Guterres said.

“Yet some governments still plan to produce more than twice as much fossil fuel in 2030 as the 1.5-degree limit allows. More coal, oil and gas will lead to a more combustible future.”

These warnings are hitting home with voters, several Labour MPs told the Guardian. One source said “there will be a revolt” if there is a chance for Labour MPs to vote on new licences for the North Sea.

Jackdaw and Rosebank are already in the planning system, and so could be argued to fall outside Labour’s manifesto promise to halt new licensing.

Despite these loopholes, the source said Burnham would need “support from the Conservatives and possibly the SNP rather than Labour unity” if it came to a vote, though Burnham is likely to try to avoid this by taking any decisions as an administrative measure after consultations on the fields conclude in mid-August.

Concerns over the negative impact of allowing new North Sea drilling extend across the Labour party, transcending factions and “tribes”. The Guardian has contacted or been told of concerned MPs including ministers and junior members of government, longstanding senior backbench MPs and committee figures and new MPs from the 2024 general election intake.

A decision on Rosebank and Jackdaw will not come before the consultations end in mid-August, but the issue of whether further drilling could be allowed is likely to still be live when the budget comes on 28 October. In a video message on social media on Friday announcing the date, the chancellor, John Healey, said it would be “a budget that moves money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain”, and that it would be “built on fiscal discipline”.

Part of the North Sea problem, according to some insiders, is that Burnham has assembled an older economic team with traditional views on industry, lacking knowledge of the climate and the rapidly changing dynamics of energy around the world.

Several influential economists told the Guardian that increased drilling would not help the UK economy. Mariana Mazzucato, who worked closely with Burnham on the lauded transformation of transport in Manchester, and who has been a key influence on his thinking, said: “Drilling the North Sea won’t help people across the UK struggling with their energy bills – most of the oil and gas from these new sites would be sold to the highest bidder on international markets.

“But the bigger picture is that green industrial strategy requires coherent and credible policy signals, to give investors confidence that the ‘clean energy superpower’ mission of Labour’s manifesto is still the direction of travel – which this drilling would undermine.”

Daniela Gabor, a professor of economics at SOAS, added: “It’s a terrible idea. The Burnham government is caving to the fossil lobby just as we experience some of the most intense heatwaves of recent times.”

Nicholas Stern, the economist, said new drilling would not alleviate pressure on energy bills and dismissed arguments that UK North Sea oil would lead to fewer carbon emissions than imports. “Extra output leads to extra use and more greenhouse gases. Further, and importantly, it would send a dangerous signal to the world,” he said.

However, some backbench MPs are also wary of the “massive bear trap”, as one described it, of allowing the climate to become a wedge issue for voters, as the Tories and Reform party are seeking to do. They are prepared to keep the peace by accepting the go-ahead for the Jackdaw gasfield, and potentially even the more controversial Rosebank oilfield, if a line can then be drawn against any further licences and if Burnham reaffirms his commitment to pushing forward urgently with net zero.

That is still in question. “[There is] growing concern among MPs that No 10 don’t realise this [new drilling] won’t help with bills at all and will cause political damage,” said another Labour backbencher. “A pragmatic approach can help us navigate this but the fundamentals need to be understood.”

Tour de France Femmes under pressure to reroute Ventoux stage amid wildfire risk

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 17:13:37 GMT

Authorities want stage altered if risk is ‘extreme’

2025 champion Ferrand-Prévot faces sterner challenge

The Tour de France Femmes is facing pressure to reroute part of its key stage to the summit of Mont Ventoux next Friday because of the wildfires threat in Provence.

The women’s Tour, which begins in Lausanne on Saturday, is expected to keep the famous climb to the top of the “Giant of Provence”, but the current routing of the stage through the Ventoux’s foothills could be affected.

In a statement on its website, the Vaucluse prefecture said: “At a time when forest areas are at a peak risk of fire, the prefecture has asked the organisers of the Tour to consider an alternative route. Following a fire risk assessment on Tuesday 4 August, an alternative route will be implemented should the wildfire risk be considered extreme.”

Three stages of the men’s Tour de France, which finished in Paris last Sunday, were disrupted by wildfires, extreme heat and the deployment of French emergency services to assist with the wildfire crisis in the country’s south-west.

“We are in constant touch with the prefecture and we will adapt, just as the men’s Tour de France did,” said Marion Rousse, the Tour de France Femmes race director.

“We have to deal with the real world – this is a bike race and the real world always takes priority. There will still be a climb of the Ventoux, but we have several options. We are ready to work with the emergency services and the government.”

Few things demonstrate the fast‑track growth of women’s racing more than the inclusion of Mont Ventoux on the route for this year’s race. “There is no mountain that is too difficult for women,” Rousse said. “The level is now more and more consistent and they ride faster each time. Each year the progress is huge.”

The legendary climb is the standout stage in a race route that is bolder and bigger than it has been since the race was reintroduced in 2022 as a tentative bolt-on to the end of the men’s Tour de France.

Over nine stages, including an individual time trial and stages through the Jura, Massif Central and Provence Alps, 147 riders will wend their way to the Côte d’Azur for a testing finale in the hills inland from Nice.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, the defending champion, was a no-show at the top riders press conference on Friday afternoon, with her highly rated French teammate Marion Bunel, third overall in this year’s Vuelta Femenina, surprisingly taking her place.

Ferrand-Prévot was said to have already fulfilled plenty of media obligations, but her absence from a top table that included past winners and her main rivals, Demi Vollering and Kasia Niewiadoma, did not go unnoticed.

Ferrand-Prévot’s success last July was hailed in France, but she faces more rivals this year than she did 12 months ago, with the 23-year-old Spanish rider Paula Blasi, who sealed victory in the Vuelta on the brutal climb of the Angliru, a leading contender.

Elsewhere there are signs that others too, as Rousse suggested, have upped their game. The Swiss rider Marlen Reusser, who said she has had a “love-hate” relationship with the Tour Femmes in the past, is expected to shine in the individual time trial on stage four, while the long climb to the Ventoux is likely to feature the 2023 winner, Vollering, and the defending champion, Ferrand-Prévot, going head to head.

Reusser, the world time trial champion, has had a series of false starts in the French race. “This is the first year that I’m here and feel healthy and good,” she said. “It’s special to finally be here in that way.”

Ferrand-Prévot’s victory in last year’s race made her a household name in France and, after a long wait to see a home rider win the yellow jersey, drew crowds to the roadside in their thousands.

“Now women’s cycling in France is doing well and men’s cycling in France is also doing very well,” Rousse, said by way of tribute to Ferrand-Prévot’s success.

“We felt a real sense of patriotism with Pauline’s victory. Whether it was in the men’s or the women’s race, it’s been some time that we’ve been waiting for a French winner.

“Pauline gives a lot. To the public, her charisma has done cycling a lot of good. All those little girls who dream one day of becoming like Pauline. People are interested in her because she is so likable.”

Rousse is confident that Ferrand‑Prévot, despite a muted spring, will put up a staunch defence of her title. “There will be a great rivalry between her and Vollering,” she said. “I think that Pauline has increased her level in comparison to last year – she’s really gone up.”

Elsewhere, the upward trajectory of the race continues. The number of women riding the amateur Étape du Tour Femmes is higher than those who rode the Étape du Tour, on Alpe d’Huez, with 27% of all participants in the Étape Femmes being female.

“It shows that women put a lot less obstacles in their way than before, especially since the creation of the Tour de France Femmes,” Rousse said.

Saturday’s opening 138km stage in Switzerland features a hilly loop based on Lausanne, through the Cantons of Vaud and Fribourg, leading to a steep uphill finish on the Côte Saint-François, while on Sunday the peloton follows the northern shore of Lake Geneva before a lakeside finish, and a possible sprint, in Geneva.

I write as someone whose disabilities mean that I will be in receipt of social care support my whole life (Andy Burnham seeks cross-party agreement on future of social care, 27 July). For too long, people like me have been cannon fodder for politicians who routinely forget that their highest duty in providing social care is to protect those less able, or unable, to care for themselves. Investing in the right support for us unlocks our often-forgotten abilities. When we are successful, it is often because we have had opportunity to be because of that support, and when we aren’t, as so often happens, it is because society writes us off.

Andy Burnham’s intervention is welcome news as it shows that he considers us a priority. Reform of the social care system has to be taken hand in hand with disability groups and people with lived experience of being disabled. Too often the system traps people into dependency on temporary accommodation rather than providing them with the means to receive support in their own home.

Six years ago, this was the case for me, but not any more. I am now studying at university and have settled into a life that is light years better than what I had before.

The prime minister’s own experience of dealing with this issue is also helpful in this. In his first five years as the mayor of Greater Manchester, rough sleeping was reduced by two-thirds. If he wants to be bold, he only needs to look north and to his prior success in delivering this for Manchester. Robbie BentleyBristol

Despite economists saying that it is too hard to tax wealth rather than income, there is already a wealth tax in place paying for social care in this country. The trouble is that it’s only levied on those who have the misfortune to need it. As your explainer points out, disabled and elderly people in England with assets over £23,250 have to pay the full cost of their social care.

Why shouldn’t the super-rich be taxed on a similar basis – all assets over a threshold – and then they can pay for a functional and decent social care system for all the people who they made their money from by charging extortionate profits and paying sub-living wages?

If the working class isn’t allowed to pass down generational wealth, why should anyone else be?Rachel Powild Manchester

Rightwing politicians and newspapers screaming about inheritance grabs and new taxes to fund social care are missing the point, probably deliberately. Socialising the cost of social care does not increase the cost, but spreads it more fairly. At present it is a lottery: if you get a losing ticket and you or a family member needs long-term care for dementia, all your savings, and the capital tied up in your house, could disappear. If you are lucky and die quickly, your children get a windfall.

It is clearly fairer that everyone gives up a share of their wealth rather than some all and some none. Not only that, it removes the stress about whether a lifetime’s savings will suffice. A properly designed national care service will share risk, which is what a civilised society should value. Mike Cushman London

Any attempt to pay for the broken social care system should start with the abolition of the triple lock on pensions. I welcome the moves towards achieving a cross-party consensus, but fear that political point-scoring and manoeuvring will defeat them, as they have done in the past. Echoes of 1954 as Kerr, Wightman and rising star Myers face off in mile race

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 17:00:29 GMT

Roger Bannister’s ‘Miracle Mile’ race 72 years ago is set to gain a worthy successor as Scottish pair take on the prodigious Australian

They call it the Miracle Mile: the race still regarded as the greatest in Commonwealth Games history. And 72 years later in Glasgow, it finally has a worthy successor.

Rewind to 1954. In May Sir Roger Bannister had become the first man to run a mile in under four minutes. Six weeks later, the Australian John Landy lowered his mark by more than a second. Then came their epic clash in Vancouver.

“I felt it was a piece of unfinished business to be able to reproduce the performance of my sub-four-minute mile in a race,” Bannister later said. “However, at the half-mile … he was 15 yards ahead and I thought either he’s going to break a world record in 3min 56sec or he’s going to have to slow.”

Somehow Bannister dragged himself back into it by the bell, yet Landy was still leading as they turned into the home straight. But there was to be a dramatic late twist.

Because the roar of the crowd was so great, Landy was unable to hear his pursuer, so he looked over his left shoulder. At which point Bannister attacked and flew past his great rival on his right shoulder before storming to gold in 3:58.8.

On Saturday night the men’s mile should provide another contest for the ages, with Scotland’s Josh Kerr and Jake Wightman facing Australia’s new superstar Cameron Myers.

Everyone knows about Kerr. Since the 28-year-old ran an astonishing 3:42.66 to break the world mile record, there have been profiles in the New York Times and Wall Street Journal, and he has become joint favourite with Jude Bellingham to win the BBC’s Sports Personality of the Year.

Plenty of non-athletics fans will also be aware of Wightman, given that he won the world 1500m title in Eugene in 2022 while his dad, Geoff, was commentating in the stadium, and followed it up with a world silver in Tokyo in September 2025.

And while the 20-year-old Myers might be a new name to some, everyone in track and field is in awe of his talent. “I got beaten by him in 2024 in Australia,” says Wightman. “And I was like, ‘man, he’s going to be good.’ But he just kept getting better every year. He’s the future of the sport.”

How good might he be? “This is a crazy era,” says Wightman. “But we’re potentially racing against someone who’s going to be the best of all time – that’s the way I look at him.”

That is extraordinary praise given Myers was still a teenager at the start of June. But Wightman is just as effusive about Kerr’s mile world record. “It’s insane,” he says. “It’s like 54-second laps. The average person will get nowhere near running 100 metres at that pace, and I thought it was impossible to do that.

“The world record’s amazing and I’m sure that will stand for a long, long time. But the worst bit about it was I watching, thinking: ‘Christ, I’ve got to race him in a couple of weeks’ time.’”

The race tactics will be fascinating. Over 1500m this year, Kerr and Myers have run more than a second quicker than anyone else. But this is championship racing, with no pacemakers or wavelights. And that, as Kerr acknowledges, brings different challenges.

“It is very different to go from racing a clock to racing these guys,” he says. “They are some of the best milers in the world. But I thrive in a pressure environment. I’m here to show up and get a gold medal for Scotland.”

Most believe that Kerr will want a truly run race and will go to the front early if no one pushes the pace. But the slower the first two laps are, the more likely Wightman’s sprint finish will come into play.

“I pride myself on being good at champs,” says Wightman, who also ran the fifth fastest 1000m in history last month. “I know that I couldn’t do what Josh did in that world record. But I love the fact you come to champs and it becomes both a physical and mental battle. I’d love it to be cagey, others I’m sure wouldn’t.”

The great unknown is how much Kerr’s thrilling run in London has affected him. As Wightman says, it isn’t always easy to reset after a massive high. In 2022 he won the 1500m world title only to suffer a shock defeat to Olli Hoare in the Commonwealth Games 10 days later.

And while gold is surely between the big three, Kenya’s 2019 world champion, Timothy Cheruiyot, and Wales’ Jake Heyward, who is in the shape of his life, have medal chances too.

Wightman also points out another complicating factor. While much of Britain is enjoying a heatwave, the temperature when the race starts will be only 13C and gusty.

“It’s not the stillest track and the Glasgow weather’s not the kindest,” he says, smiling. “The potential is that if you go and take it out hard you might be ending up working a lot harder than you think you are. It’s going to be a battle.”

The echoes of 1954 will be heard loud and clear in Scotstoun on Saturday night.

He later added: “I feel ready to move on from the Blade questions. Those questions are for them. They didn’t want to do it, so they should answer that question.”

His comments come after the Marvel head, Kevin Feige, said he felt like a “gigantic loser” for not getting the project off the ground.

The film was at one stage set to be directed by the Mogul Mowgli film-maker Bassam Tariq. Ali and Tariq have since worked together on the revenge thriller Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, which is premiering at this year’s Toronto film festival.

Ali said he “didn’t feel great about the fact that things finished the way that they did” with the Blade reboot. He had provided his voice for the character in a post-credits sequence in 2021’s underperforming Marvel adventure Eternals.

Ali also added on the Blade collapse: “The best way I can answer this question is, when I look at what is for me, is it was either this or that – and I’ll take this. No offence to them. I’ve been doing this professionally for pushing 30 years now, and one thing I’ve learned is that what is for you is for you and what is not is not. For whatever reason, that project is not for me.”

Since winning two best supporting actor Oscars in 2017 and 2019, Ali’s movie roles have included Jurassic World Rebirth and Leave the World Behind as well as providing his voice in the Spider-Verse series. Ali’s voice will soon be heard in much-anticipated stop-motion animated adventure Wildwood alongside Carey Mulligan and Angela Bassett as well as in the delayed third Spider-Verse adventure.

$2m crime novel deal collapses amid questions over AI use

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:45:04 GMT

Agents withdraw Jerry Falade’s hotly anticipated debut after saying they can no longer authenticate ‘how the manuscript evolved’

A high-profile publishing deal for a debut crime novel has collapsed after doubts emerged over whether artificial intelligence played a role in writing it.

The hotly anticipated manuscript Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body, by Jerry Falade, was withdrawn from sale by its agent despite reportedly receiving an offer for more than $2m (£1.5m) from Minotaur, owned by Macmillan US, as part of a 14-way auction. The plan was to publish it in 2028.

An email sent to publishers by Falade’s agents and seen by the Guardian said: “Jerry Falade produced an incredible manuscript that dazzled us and the top publishing professionals around the world. Unfortunately, we are no longer able to authenticate how the manuscript fully evolved from origin to completion.”

It continued: “During the submission process we vetted the manuscript with Jerry for AI and felt trusting in his reassurance that it was written without utilising AI as a resource in the writing or editorial process. We can no longer substantiate that, and we are withdrawing the book.”

The US auction was run by the author’s agent Marc Gerald of Europa Content, according to the Bookseller. In the UK, Sandy Hodgman of Hodgman Literary is said to have secured several six-figure bids through a similarly competitive process. The Guardian has approached both agents for comment.

Gerald told the Bookseller he first read the book in June, and that it was “stunningly good, everyone fell in love with it. It’s a book that appeals to absolutely everyone.”

He said that halfway through the submissions process, an editor raised concerns that the book had signs of potential AI use. Gerald said Europa opted against using AI-detection software to check the manuscript, saying Falade was “clear and credible” in his explanation.

However, after a meeting on 29 July, when “aspects of [Falade’s] story changed”, the agency decided to cut ties, citing the “need to have total faith”.

“We feel terrible for putting this into the universe and the firestorm it has caused,” Gerald added. “The book itself is genius – however it came to be drafted, it’s amazing.”

Falade’s case is the latest in a string of controversies to hit publishing this year, as authors, agents and publishers grapple with how to handle suspected AI use in manuscripts. Earlier this year, Hachette pulled the US release of Mia Ballard’s horror novel Shy Girl after rumours circulated online that the author had relied on AI, something she denies.

In a statement to the Guardian, Falade rejected claims that he had used AI and said the response reflected racial bias in publishing.

He said: “Three Black authors received major publishing deals this year, and all three later had deals cancelled or disrupted following suspicions about AI. There seems to be a troubling assumption that when a Black writer produces work that attracts significant attention, the work could not possibly be their own. Meanwhile, there are popular white writers who have publicly mentioned using AI for their writing processes and they’re still doing fine.”

Falade did not name other authors, but two Black authors in the US – Ballard and HM Wolfe, author of the viral romance Daggermouth – faced allegations of AI use this year. Wolfe also denies she used AI.

Falade said: “In my case, rumours began circulating and, within six hours, I had been dropped by my agency, deals were paused, and press releases were being issued.” He added that AI-detection tools “are widely known to produce false positives”. He said the novel had “passed through first readers, second readers, editors, and acquisitions teams at numerous publishing houses … If the manuscript had shown genuine signs of being generated by AI, it is difficult to believe that every one of those experienced professionals would have failed to notice.”

Daughter of British couple killed in Spanish wildfire rejects claim they ignored order to leave

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:36:26 GMT

Exclusive: Danielle Kirton calls on Ed Miliband to help her get answers about why evacuation order came too late

The bereaved daughter of a British couple who died in a Spanish wildfire is calling on the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, to get answers from Spain’s government about why her parents were not told to evacuate until it was too late.

Severe wildfires have burned across Spain and France since early July, killing people, destroying thousands of homes and forcing more than 300,000 people to flee.

Pete and Fran Gillam, who lived in Bédar in Almería, died in mid-July while fleeing their home as a wildfire tore through the village. They were among 13 people killed in the fires, many of whom died in their cars as they tried to escape.

Danielle Kirton, 42, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, has spent the weeks since her parents died looking for answers. She knows her mother would have followed official advice had she have been given it.

Though the fire alert came at 4.30pm, the evacuation order did not come until more than three hours later. Kirton said this was delivered by a lone police officer, who was “frantically driving from house to house” and Spain’s official emergency alert system, which plays a loud noise on mobile phones and tells people to evacuate, was not used.

“My mother sent me a video at 6.45pm showing the fire a considerable way away from the hill where they live,” Kirton said. “She didn’t sound worried or concerned. I kept in contact with her and she sent me a message saying at 7.53pm that they’d evacuated.”

However, the decision to evacuate was made tragically late. “They stopped at a neighbour’s driveway to shout to a neighbour they needed to evacuate, but then they became trapped as the fire had jumped on both sides of the road.”

There are now other wildfires burning in much of Spain and south-west France, but there have been no civilian casualties so far. In the small village where her parents lived, 13 people died. “It would appear that somewhere within that system there has been a failure. If you look at the subsequent wildfires in Spain, there have been no casualties and the biggest difference is the emergency alert was used in subsequent wildfires,” Kirton said.

She said her mother loved living in Bédar and as a retired headteacher took much joy in organising quiz nights to fundraise for the local school. She had a bag packed and she was ready to evacuate. “She was just waiting to be told what to do,” Kirton said.

Spanish politicians have claimed that those who died ignored instructions. “My parents did not ignore instructions. My parents would have not had an issue with instructions in Spanish,” Kirton said. “My parents heeded advice to shelter in place, until they were then told that they needed to evacuate.

“They took the correct route, and their only route, to the evacuation point. It is a weak and cowardly act to blame victims in the face of tragedy.”

The response from the Foreign Office has been a “slap in the face”, she added. “The help from the consulate has been nonexistent. We got sent a link: ‘What to do when someone dies abroad.’ That is it. It is a slap in the face, to be honest.”

Miliband has been visiting France and Spain to discuss wildfires and the climate crisis with political leaders. Kirton said: “As UK citizens, it is important to ask for his support in asking Spanish authorities to conduct a full and thorough investigation.”

Scientists say the fires have been worsened by the climate crisis, which has intensified the recent heatwaves. Kirton said this makes it more crucial that lessons are learned so no one has to go through what she has.

“It’s vital for planning for the future that we see what exactly were the contributing factors in this case,” she said. “It’s a perfect storm, the weather, the climate, the vegetation, the wind. My parents weren’t concerned before – it isn’t something they felt fearful of, it wasn’t something that happened where they lived.” Kirton has been working every day since her parents died trying to get answers and a substantial response from the Spanish authorities. She said: “My mum and dad would have always spoken up for what’s right and if I can do anything for them it’s that we can ask for the truth and ensure this never happens again to any other families.” The Andalusian government has been contacted for comment.

A Foreign Office spokesperson said that any investigation into the fire response is a matter for the Spanish government: “The foreign secretary has been in regular contact with his Spanish counterpart, including during his visit to Madrid on Wednesday.

“They discussed how the UK could support Spain’s response, ensure British nationals receive the right advice and assistance, and agreed that lessons must be learned as climate change makes these dangerous wildfires more likely.

“Staff at our embassy have been working with the British community in the affected area, collating their questions and concerns and raising them with the Spanish authorities. This work is ongoing.”

The Guardian view on England’s centralised state: Andy Burnham must unbundle it

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:32:06 GMT

Devolution should finance transport, skills and industry, not become a rightwing contest to promise the largest tax giveaway

That England is among the rich world’s most centralised countries underpins Andy Burnham’s critique of the economic history of the past 40 years. Only post-communist Europe deindustrialised as rapidly as Yorkshire and the Midlands did in the 1980s. Centralisation did not close every factory or pit, but left regions without the powers, finance or institutions to cushion the shock or build a resilient, replacement economy. Hence Mr Burnham’s radical and welcome plan to unbundle English government.

There are three facets to his devolution programme. The first are the detailed and concrete proposals contained in a cabinet paper Mr Burnham released on Friday. This appears to be a blueprint to create a decentralised state organised around mayors as the key regional economic actors, while jointly governed pan-regional agencies could emerge, say for transport, energy, investment and industrial systems, that cross mayoral boundaries. Regions without mayors will get a chance to have one – or limit themselves to weaker powers.

The second, outlined in the Guardian and later confirmed by No 10, is that mayors will be able to keep income-tax and business-rate revenues, with the forthcoming budget and spending review deciding on how much. Before entering No 10, Mr Burnham proposed a third pillar: a duty, modelled on Germany’s Basic Law, requiring English regions to pursue equivalent living conditions nationwide.

Following this logic, a mayoral authority would receive a share of tax revenues and benefit when its economy and tax base grow. But the national government would continue redistributing resources so that poorer places can provide comparable services and possess meaningful investment capacity. Without such an equalisation measure, disparities would widen. One thinktank pointed out that if mayors received 2.5% of the 20p basic rate of income tax, London would get £2.3bn in 2026-27 while Hull and East Yorkshire would get £135m.

Ben Houchen, the Tory mayor of Tees Valley, wants to turn devolved income-tax revenues into new powers to offer tax rebates. That mistakes a regional investment settlement for a tax-cutting competition: poorer places would forfeit the cash needed to rebuild transport links as well as skills and industrial capacity. What some rightwingers seek is to turn regional elections into tax-cutting auctions over who can return the most public money. But cash giveaways now would just mean the bill of the underinvestment would land later.

England’s devolution map remains incomplete, but Mr Burnham wants to finish it. New mayors are due in Cumbria, and Cheshire and Warrington, in 2027, followed by ones in southern and eastern regions in 2028. The rest of the country will be asked to choose between mayoral strategic authorities with stronger powers or non-mayoral “foundation” bodies operating with more limited controls.

A new Harvard Kennedy School and King’s College London paper, co-authored by the former Labour minister Ed Balls, argues that Britain’s weak productivity stems from persistent regional divides, with the gap between south-east England and the rest of the nation wider than that separating east and west Germany today. One reason this has not been tackled is that Britain has never had both No 10 and the Treasury committed to regional growth. Now it does. The country may finally discover what happens when the centre pulls in the same direction.

The Guardian view on the Lovell telescope: budget cuts to physics are bad science and worse politics

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:32:01 GMT

Funders have picked a damaging fight with scientists and the public. They should reconsider their plans

The iconic Lovell telescope, housed at the Jodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire, has always expanded our view of the universe – from tracking the Sputnik launch in 1957 to its current contributions to the study of dark matter. It is now threatened with closure after it was announced that government funding will not continue past March 2028. The projected savings are just £2.8m a year.

This is just the latest in a rolling package of cuts from the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) – which disperses government funding to particle, astro and nuclear physics, among other disciplines – aimed at saving about £160m over the next four years. The STFC has insisted that the measures are a result of cost overruns. That may be true, but it is hard not to see this as part of a larger shift in what kind of science the government funds and prioritises, and what areas it allows to wither.

There is no doubt that physics is expensive. From telescopes to synchrotron beams, its instruments are increasingly large-scale and power-hungry. And scientists are not immune to the cost of living crisis. If households are feeling the pinch of electricity costs, just imagine getting the monthly bill for a particle accelerator. However, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), of which the STFC is a subsidiary, has just gone through a revamp of its funding model, one that clearly prioritises economic growth and measureable outcomes. Looking across the programmes cut, which include international collaborations with other telescope arrays and the Cern facility in Switzerland, many scientists believe that long-term, fundamental research is under specific threat.

The UKRI and STFC have not helped the situation by badly misreading the politics. In a session at the House of Lords earlier this month, the UKRI chief, Ian Chapman, seemed surprised by the scientists’ “hyperbolic” reaction, and noted that they “feel that they have been cut” when, in fact, overall physics funding has increased. But scientists have reason to feel slighted when valued ongoing projects and collaborations – rather than future plans – are axed, and when what appear to be relatively small cost savings (the UKRI budget will be £10bn by 2030) fall on their shoulders. There are shades of the departed Starmer government in this saga: the UKRI wants to tell a big story about science funding going up, but instead is mired in a row over a fairly minor sum that has angered scientists and sections of the public. One does not have to be an astronomer to know that optics matter.

The UKRI and STFC are technically arm’s‑length bodies, but it hasn’t escaped notice that the ministers who set its funding priorities, Liz Kendall and Patrick Vallance, are no longer in office, while Andy Burnham has abolished the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. It would seem a good time for the current course to be reconsidered, whether by the funding councils or the new government itself.

There is a conversation to be had about what research we fund with limited resources, and the balance between so-called blue sky projects and those expected to yield commercial returns. But when physicists warn that the UK could lose a “generation of scientists” to these cuts – in one of the few fields in which we can credibly claim to be world-leading – they should be heeded. It’s time to refocus, and look again.

Will Trump be Burnham’s undoing, or the making of him? The answer lies in Europe

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:30:47 GMT

In an increasingly dangerous world, our European neighbours are finding safety in numbers – but Britain is on the outside. The new PM’s task is to change that

There is an orange cloud in the sky. I’m not referring to the wildfires ravaging parts of Europe and East Anglia, though they are connected. I mean the looming pall from across the Atlantic that threatens to spoil the sunny start to the premiership of Andy Burnham – and whose name is Donald Trump.

Burnham’s first 10 days or so in office have gone about as well as he or any of his team could have dared hope. His net approval rating has risen by 17 points, according to one early poll, gaining ground with every category of voter except supporters of Reform UK, though they too like some of what they see. His easy manner, no-notes speech-making and agility on social media have won plaudits, including from a usually sceptical press.

But the new prime minister will know that all this could be upended at a stroke, with a single move by the man in the White House. Keir Starmer watched as the earliest green shoots of economic growth emerged earlier this year, only to be crushed by Trump’s decision to combine with Israel and attack Iran. What can Burnham do to ensure he does not suffer that same fate? As it happens, the answer to that question answers another: what might constitute a Burnham foreign policy that would match the spirit and ethos of the agenda he has set out at home?

So far most of the discussion in this area has concentrated on how the new PM should handle his counterpart in Washington. Some suggest his best bet is to emulate Starmer: swallow your pride, ladle on the flattery, avoid overt confrontation. Maybe tickle Trump’s tummy by promising to drill in the North Sea, even as Suffolk is engulfed in the flames of the climate breakdown. Others say the US president is a bully who only respects strength: therefore, stand up to him, even if that means a row.

All this owes more to the realm of animal psychology than political analysis. Different world leaders have tried both approaches – nice guy and tough guy – and both have failed. And sometimes succeeded. Trump has an attention span measured in seconds; he is erratic and impulse driven; he changes his mind without warning, logic or consistency.

Those at the sharp end have come to understand this, which helps explain the muted reaction to Trump’s announcement late on Thursday of a breakthrough in Gaza. “There is scepticism and cautiousness among Palestinians,” reported Al Jazeera after Trump said Hamas was ready to disarm in return for an Israeli withdrawal from the territory. As anyone who has followed his zigzagging engagement with the Middle East has come to learn, the safest response to any development heralded by the US president is: don’t hold your breath.

Faced with such a man, it’s foolish to imagine a British prime minister can have much impact on American decisions. Even senior US administration officials have been known to admit privately that they have next to no sway over Trump, so why would a British PM fare any better? Brits do have access – I’m told that national security adviser Jonathan Powell is in regular contact with Trump’s personal envoy and golfing buddy Steve Witkoff – but that is not the same as influence.

The remedy, then, is not to hope to change a president who won’t change, but rather to be less exposed to his whims. And that points to a much larger strategy, one that makes sense in terms of both policy and politics – and which just so happens to fit Burnham’s approach to a T.

The prime minister’s opening pitch has been that he will speak to voters candidly, that he will confront the big problems that his predecessors ducked and that he is ready to break from orthodoxies that have held too long. He has already made a start in that vein domestically, with his promise this week to tackle social care. But why not extend it to the international realm?

It would begin with a stark admission that the foundation of postwar UK foreign policy is no longer stable – that we cannot rely on the US as the guarantor of our security. A US president who muses out loud about abandoning Nato, who threatens to seize the territory (Greenland) of a Nato ally (Denmark) and whose support for a country (Ukraine) invaded by an enemy (Russia) is so inconstant, is less a guarantor than a danger. It is clearly reckless to remain in a state of dependence on such a power.

Luckily, there is a group of allies close at hand who have reached that same conclusion and are already acting on it. Our European neighbours are coming together to defend themselves, without relying on Washington. They are borrowing money collectively, which makes it cheaper, and pooling resources, which makes arms spending more efficient. Add the Safe loan programme, funding joint defence procurement to the tune of €150bn (£128bn), to the EU arming of Ukraine, and you can see why Mark Leonard, director of the European Council on Foreign Relations, tells me: “The EU is becoming a security community.”

It is security broadly defined too. Witness joint EU action on energy, to plug the gap previously filled by Russian gas; vaccines during the Covid pandemic; cybersecurity and election interference; the climate crisis and immigration. In an increasingly dangerous world, the Europeans are finding safety in numbers. And we, though they are our nearest neighbours, are on the outside.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

There is an economic dimension to this. Spending your defence budgets closer to home, rather than on US-made hardware, serves pretty well as what Burnham might call a reindustrialisation strategy. The French have long understood that; the Germans increasingly so. Not for nothing has Berlin decided to spend only 8% of its massive €80bn rearmament drive on US weapons. As the EU moves to a “buy European” approach, it will be European industry that benefits – but not us.

The economic dimension goes further, because our security is threatened in that sphere too. As Mark Carney of Canada correctly diagnosed in his Davos speech, globalisation, and the economic interdependence it entails, can easily be turned into a weapon. Trump’s US wields it through the imposition of tariffs, China by controlling access to rare earth metals. The best way for a country to protect itself is to stop being dependent on either of those two titans. The UK’s only shot at such independence is, perhaps paradoxically, to be part of a group large enough to aim for resilience and self-sufficiency – and that means the EU.

It will look politically daring, but that’s only if you adopt the view from Westminster – where Brexit seems untouchable and all anyone can see are red lines. Among the people of Britain, it’s a very different picture. A major survey by the ECFR in June found that Britons now regard Brexit as a “disaster”, with three-quarters wanting a closer relationship with the EU. One striking number: when asked to choose, 63% said they would prioritise the relationship with the EU over the US, with only 19% making the opposite choice. A plurality even favours the creation of that one-time tabloid spectre: a European army with British troops in it. As Leonard puts it: “The waters are much warmer than people realise.”

This, then, is what Burnhamism could look like abroad – a willingness to face the world as it now is, to break from the old, Atlanticist default setting and to pursue a new approach that will make us both militarily and economically more resilient. The answer is no longer to put our trust in a single, unreliable friend – but rather to combine with our nearest neighbours. The new prime minister has so much to do, but he can do almost none of it without challenging a status quo that has done so much damage in a single decade. He will have to undo the folly of 2016 – and look to Europe.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Don’t let Jodrell Bank Observatory become another industrial museum

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:30:45 GMT

Readers respond to reports that the world-famous big dish is facing closure due to spending cuts by UK Research and Innovation

Throughout my long life, Jodrell Bank Observatory has been a source of wonder and pride (Jodrell Bank Observatory facing closure after major funder cuts support, 27 July). Sir Bernard Lovell’s inspirational creation never ceases to awe with its combination of cutting-edge space exploration and heroic engineering structure. A tour of its welcoming visitor centre with my grandchildren confirmed that this sense of awe is being passed on to future generations.

Yes, it would make another fine museum. But here in the north we have quite a few museums of our glorious industrial past. We have only one Jodrell Bank, probing the mysteries of the universe right now. So I’m afraid it is over to my fellow English graduate Andy Burnham to reverse the philistine decision of UK Research and Innovation, reminding him of his poetic hero Philip Larkin’s fear for the possible future of the UK: “Our children will not know it is a different country./ All we can hope to leave them now is money”. Dr Ken SmithMacclesfield, Cheshire

The one thing that Britain can still claim to be a top-division power in is science and technology. From numbers of Nobel laureates, to startups being funded then absorbed by global enterprises, and our universities and research establishments attracting the best minds from all over the world, the evidence is there. When trade delegations travel the world, the selling point is our science and technology. So it seems odd that there is a squeeze of government investment in this area of soft power.

One of the symbols of Britain’s scientific prowess is the big dish at Jodrell Bank. Generations in Britain and around the world have grown up seeing it as the backdrop to space travel and astronomical discoveries. Reducing its funding will draw attention to the reduced circumstances of Britain’s scientific endeavour and a lack of ambition to keep Britain as a world leader. If the government wants to quietly cut spending on scientific research, reducing Jodrell Bank to a museum is not the best route. £2.8m a year seems a small price to pay for keeping an international symbol of Britain’s prowess going. John SommerSaltford, Somerset

I’m dismayed at the news that Jodrell Bank Observatory is under threat. I enjoyed an enlightening day at the visitor centre recently, and was planning a return visit. Could I suggest that the relevant funding body dig out their own telescopes and take a long hard look at the future of British science and those young people looking forward to careers in science, engineering and technology?Peter Baddeley Painswick, Gloucestershire
