The best ice-cream makers in the UK for gelato, soft serve and sorbets – tested

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:22:05 GMT

Our writer spent the hottest weeks of the year churning through the top ice-cream makers, from compressor models to the cult favourite Ninja Creami. Here’s the scoop

Kitchen gadgets top chefs can’t live without

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

I love a scoop or two of the good stuff, even more so when the mercury hits 30C and ice-cream starts feeling less like an indulgence and more like an essential survival tool. This is why owning an ice-cream maker has always made sense to me. I’ve been using the original Ninja Creami for years now, but before that I was spending a small fortune on gelato, fruity sorbets, frozen yoghurt and other such desserts from the frozen aisle.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Some might argue that the best ice-cream makers are a luxury, but if you’re a true dessert devotee, I believe they can earn their keep in no time. A tub of Häagen-Dazs will set you back almost £6 nowadays, which is an expensive habit if you’re getting through a pot a week during the hottest months of the year.

With your own ice-cream machine, you get an endless supply whenever you fancy it, and you can get creative with flavours, tweaking as you go. It’s also ideal if you have allergies or follow a dairy-free diet, as good allergy-friendly ice-cream can be harder to find. Better still, making your own means you can skip the emulsifiers, artificial flavours, sweeteners and stabilisers found in many shop-bought tubs, so it’s a great option if you’re trying to move away from ultra-processed foods.

But with so many options available, where do you start? I’ve taken one for the team – and no doubt my waistline – to test the best ice-cream makers available right now, from trendy soft-serve ice-cream machines to professional-style compressor models.

Best ice-cream maker overallCaso IceCreamer

Best budget ice-cream makerCuisinart Solo Scoops

Best freeze-first ice-cream makerNinja Creami NC300

Best ice-cream maker for small freezersNutribullet Chill

Best soft-serve ice-cream makerGreenPan Frost ice-cream maker and slushie machine

I’ve spent almost a decade researching, testing and reviewing kitchen appliances, which means I’m aware of the very best (and worst) the industry has to offer. I’ve seen appliance trends come and go, and I know what people actually want in their kitchens.

I’m also an avid home cook and dinner party host. When I’m not in my kitchen testing appliances on the clock, I’m still there whipping up feasts for my willing partner and friends.

The research for this article meant making – and eating – a lot of ice-cream and sorbet (someone had to do it). I put 13 machines through their paces with three recipes on each: Felicity Cloake’s perfect vanilla ice-cream, her lemon sorbet and, where the machine allowed, a more basic throw-it-all-in recipe for strawberry ice-cream made with milk, cream, sugar and macerated strawberries. All the machines also came with their own recipe booklet or app, so I also tested one of these, usually a standard vanilla recipe with double cream.

Testing a variety of recipes gave me a sense of how capable and versatile each machine really was, helping to decide whether it’s worthy of taking up precious space on your worktop.

As well as making lots of ice-cream, I put on my technical hat to measure churning speeds, record noise levels using a decibel meter, and assess ice crystal formation, as well as the general taste and texture of the results after some time in the freezer.

As a certified chore hater, I found that ease of assembly and cleaning were just as important. Waiting 24 hours to taste the results of your prep is one thing; spending another hour to disassemble and scrub clean the machine afterwards is quite another.

All ice-cream makers sourced for this article will be donated to charity.

A real surprise standout, this model from the little-known brand Caso turned out to be not only the best compressor ice-cream maker, but also my favourite overall. It may be big and bulky, but that shouldn’t put you off (as long as you have the space).

Why we love itCaso’s IceCreamer was the easiest machine I used, with very little that can actually go wrong. It has a generous two-litre capacity, and as it’s a compressor model, there was no need to prefreeze anything. Caso recommends chilling any mixture beforehand to improve churning times, but that can be as little as an hour – I’m impatient, and I still got great results after about 30 minutes.

I was testing on one of the hottest June days on record, and so I wasn’t expecting miracles when it came to churn times. Impressively, though, the machine produced rich, velvety ice-cream in about 60 minutes using Felicity Cloake’s vanilla recipe. I imagine on a slightly cooler day it would have been even quicker. Unfortunately, the heat did mean my ice-cream began to melt almost instantly once out of the machine, but I managed to get it in the freezer before all the hard work was undone.

Despite this, the ice-cream that initially emerged was well frozen yet buttery smooth and had few ice crystals. After a couple of days in the freezer in an airtight container, it still tasted fantastic. It also made light work of the lemon sorbet recipe in about 40 minutes.

The IceCreamer has post-churn settings that keep the ice-cream at a frozen temperature for up to 60 minutes, or it just churns without freezing. It also comes with an ice-cream scoop and measuring cup. The bowl was easy to clean and, unlike some other machines here, there weren’t any fiddly parts to handle.

It’s a shame that … it’s on the large side – and quite pricey, when not on offer.

Machine type: compressorCapacity: 2l Average churn time: 1hrNoise level: 67dBDimensions: 43 x 28.5 x 28cm (WDH)Wattage: 180WWarranty: two years

Let me temper your expectations here – if you’re spending this little on an ice-cream maker, you’d be silly to expect the world. However, I’m making a case for this mini motor-based machine because it’s so ridiculously simple to use.

Why we love itIf you’re short on counter space or can’t justify the £200+ spend on a more premium machine, this is a great option. For occasional ice-cream indulgers who prefer to make their desserts from scratch – I’m thinking people with allergies and dairy-free dessert fans – the Solo Scoops is a compact, low-risk buy.

The ice-cream maker comes with a small bowl that makes up to 475ml of ice-cream. It needs to be popped in the freezer for at least 24 hours before use, but takes up very little space. You’ll know it’s ready when you can no longer hear the liquid in the walls of the bowl moving around.

Its small size is both a strength and a limitation. Because it relies on the frozen bowl staying cold for as long as possible (which proved a challenge in my furnace-like kitchen), I struggled to achieve the same firm, scoopable texture as the other models here despite using the same vanilla recipe throughout. With a little patience, though, you can get a soft-serve-style ice-cream in about 30 minutes. I got the best results by freezing the bowl for a minimum of 36 hours, chilling the ingredients first, and opting for sorbets over richer, higher-fat ice-creams.

If you’re at all worried about longevity given the price (I was), the good news is that parts are easy to replace or repair. The Solo Scoops’ simple design means there’s less to go wrong, and replacement parts are available through Cuisinart’s website.

It’s a shame that … while it’s not overly loud, the noise it makes is a bit grating.

Machine type: freeze-firstCapacity: 475mlAverage churn time: 30minsNoise level: 66dBDimensions: machine, 25 x 21 x 21cm (WDH); bowl, 15 x 15 x 10cm (WDH) Wattage: 12WWarranty: three years

Ninja’s first iteration of the Creami might be getting on a bit now, with newer models featuring improved designs and new settings, but I’ve owned it for years, and it still produces good results.

Why we love it Ninja’s ice-cream makers are popular for a reason. While some find the brand’s products a little gimmicky (and some are, in my opinion), the Creami stands out because it makes homemade ice-cream genuinely achievable – even for the most reluctant cooks.

Over the years, I’ve used my Creami to create all kinds of frozen desserts, from the brand’s signature strawberry ice-cream, which you’ll find in the accompanying booklet, to gelato-style mixes and even frozen smoothie bowls. Unlike other brands on this list, I really rate Ninja’s recipes, too.

All recipes I tested, including Felicity’s sorbet and frozen vanilla ice-cream, were fully churned in about three minutes – a couple of minutes faster than the Nutribullet Chill below. I also like the Creami’s flat blade, as it allows it to get right to the end of the tub with ease. The compact tubs are also a plus, fitting easily into the freezer without taking up too much space.

I found the Creami easy to clean, and some parts are dishwasher-safe. That’s not to say there aren’t any nooks where mixture can hide, but I haven’t had any problems as long as I’ve cleaned the machine straight away.

The machine comes with two 493ml tubs as standard from SharkNinja, although some retailers offer three, and you can buy more either directly from the manufacturer or at other online retailers. Spare parts are available through the brand’s website, so if anything does go wrong, it’s usually easy to fix at home.

It’s a shame that … it’s quite loud, and it’s unusually tall, so might not fit under some kitchen cabinets.

Machine type: freeze-firstCapacity: 2 x 493ml Average churn time: 3minsNoise level: 81dBDimensions: machine, 40.5 x 16.5 x 27cm (WDH); cup only, 11 x 11 x 10.31cm (WDH)Wattage: 800WWarranty: two years (needs to be registered if bought from a third-party retailer)

Nutribullet’s Ninja Creami-esque machine makes ice-cream, sorbet and frozen yoghurt with minimum fuss after 24 hours of freezing the mixture in the tub. I was won over by its simple design, and much like the Caso, it was an underdog that surprised me in testing.

Why we love itThe Nutribullet Chill isn’t your classic churning ice-cream maker, but it’s easy to use and produced great results with my vanilla ice-cream and lemon sorbet test mixtures. You make and prefreeze your mixture in a compact 470ml tub, then the machine uses a powerful blade to churn it all up from frozen.

The texture isn’t quite the same as a classic compressor machine – it’s less velvety – but for its compact size and ease of use, the trade-off is one I’d be happy to make.

In performance, it’s similar to the Ninja Creami. The vanilla ice-cream and sorbet recipes came out as expected – less smooth than a compressor but still delicious – although I did find that the recipes in Nutribullet’s accompanying booklet and app do need a little tweaking. Using too much fat in your recipe will give you grainy, greasy-tasting results, as the fat from the cream isn’t stable and solidifies. I had better luck swapping out the double cream in Nutribullet’s recipes with a 40:60 split of double and single cream. It also did a great job making vegan ice-cream.

The Nutribullet Chill comes with two 470ml tubs, with extras available to buy. In addition, the blade comes away for easy cleaning, plus replacement parts are available for repairing at home.

It’s a shame that … it’s ear-shatteringly loud: I found myself having to leave the room while noise levels were being measured. Something to bear in mind if you’re noise-sensitive like I am.

Machine type: freeze-firstCapacity: 2 x 470ml Average churn time: 5minsNoise level: 96dBDimensions: machine, 19.6 x 20.5 x 43.1cm (WDH); cup only, 10.5 x 10.5 x 15cm (WDH)Wattage: 500WWarranty: two years if you keep your receipt

Looking for an all-in-one appliance that will keep both kids and adults happy? Then GreenPan – best known for, well, its pans – turns out to make a surprisingly capable ice-cream maker, too.

Why we love it:The GreenPan Frost really impressed in tests. I used it to make a custardy vanilla soft serve using Felicity Cloake’s recipe and a soft-serve “sorbet” – essentially, a lemon slushie. My chilled mixture achieved soft-serve consistency in about 25 minutes, but I did have to tweak the recipe a few times to get it right.

Some research revealed that soft serve works best with an additional stabiliser, such as xanthan gum. I tested this with other batches and found it did indeed help the ice-cream hold its shape better. That said, it’s not essential if you’d rather skip it – you’ll simply get a more traditional soft-serve texture. The GreenPan Frost also has settings for making milkshakes, slushies (of the booze and booze-free variety) and similar treats.

Unfortunately, one of the downsides of this style of machine is cleaning: it was definitely trickier to clean than others on this list. The Frost has a self-cleaning cycle, while its numerous parts can be disassembled for cleaning in the dishwasher – a bonus for convenience and repairability. My advice is to run the clean cycle with two to three rinses of warm water and a bit of washing-up liquid before taking apart the machine.

It’s a shame that … it’s the priciest model on this list.

Machine type: compressor/soft serveCapacity: 1.9l Average churn time: 30-40 minsNoise level: 58dBDimensions: 22.2 x 44.1 x 43.8cm (WDH)Wattage: 150WWarranty: two years

Best for: gelato-style recipes

This is another great classic compressor machine – simple, with gentle churning that’s ideal for gelato. It performed well in tests, with results in about an hour. It’s also easy to clean.

Unlike the Caso IceCreamer, the Lakeland Compressor machine doesn’t allow you to adjust the timing mid-cycle. When I set it to 40 minutes and realised halfway through that my mixture needed longer, I couldn’t simply press the “+” button to add more time – I had to stop and restart the machine instead.

Thankfully, this didn’t affect the quality of the ice-cream – it was still excellent and held its texture well in the freezer. It was just frustrating that I had to use a workaround for something that should have been a simple adjustment.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I found the controls counterintuitive and a pain to use. The Caso IceCreamer offered a slightly better user experience.

Machine type: compressor; capacity: 1.8l; average churn time: 30-40mins; noise level: 58dB; dimensions: 49.8 x 38.6 x 30.4cm (WDH); wattage: 150W; warranty: three years

Best for: families

I had high hopes for this machine: it’s cheaper and easier to clean than the GreenPan, but I found it more difficult to achieve the right ice-cream consistency. It was always just a bit too soft, even after many tweaks to the recipe.

I started with Cuisinart’s own soft-serve recipe from the accompanying booklet, which uses 100% double cream, sugar and vanilla. Unfortunately, the result was less soft serve, more homemade butter. I initially assumed it was my fault, particularly as I’d halved the quantity – but when it happened a second time, I realised something was up.

Swapping to a 60:40 mix of single and double cream fixed this – as it did with other machines – but the whole experience was rather unpleasant. I wouldn’t recommend using your soft-serve maker to churn butter, by the way – it’s not particularly easy to clean.

However, the slushies were amazing, and the standard vanilla recipe I used throughout testing was decent, although it lacked the structure I would have liked for soft serve. While there’s nothing catastrophically wrong with the machine itself, be prepared for a lot of trial and error.

It didn’t make the final cut because … performance wasn’t up there with the GreenPan, although it is slightly more affordable.

Machine type: compressor/soft serve; capacity: 1.6l; average churn time: 30-40mins; noise level: 58dB; dimensions: 16.4 x 41.4 x 41.8cm (WDH); wattage: 150W; warranty: three years at Lakeland

There was a time when you could only get two types of ice-cream maker. The first was a classic freeze-first model, where you needed to prefreeze the coolant-filled bowl for at least 24 hours before starting. The other was a compressor model, using a built-in refrigeration unit that freezes the chilled mixture as it churns, taking up to 60 minutes.

While these two options are still popular today, others have joined the ice-cream-making party. These include soft-serve and slushie machines, which also use a compressor but churn faster to produce softer, Mr Whippy-style ice-cream. Another type is often described as a “frozen dessert maker” (such as the Ninja Creami, Nutribullet Chill, and so on). These machines require you to combine ingredients and prefreeze in a tub, after which the mix is processed from frozen with a sharp blade.

These newer models are more flexible in terms of what you can make, but they require more experimentation to get the best results and are often trickier to clean.

I quickly learned during testing that many of the recipes in the ice-cream makers’ accompanying booklets aren’t very good. Most suggest using double cream exclusively, which doesn’t freeze that well and often creates a greasy, grainy texture when it does.

My advice is to stick to tried-and-tested recipes that use stable, lower-fat ingredients. While you need some fat to achieve that delicious, creamy feel, if it’s too much, it goes the other way.

Compressor machines

You’ll get great results with most recipes – I found sorbet and custard-based ice-creams worked best. Simply chill the mixture, then throw it in. In general, mix-ins aren’t advised while freezing and should instead be added at the end using the “churn-only” setting, which simply spins the paddle.

Freeze-first machinesThese require you to freeze the included bowl for at least 24 hours before making ice-cream (I found 36 hours works best as a minimum), as well as chill your mixture in the fridge separately. With this done, you can churn as usual – but, like compressor models, leave mix-ins until the end.

Soft-serve and slushie machinesThese can be a bit trickier to master, especially if the recipes included with your machine aren’t quite right. For best results, stick to stable, medium-fat recipes (eg not just double cream); otherwise you risk making butter. You can use a chilled mixture straight from the fridge, though – it chills even quicker than a traditional compressor model, so no 24-hour waits.

Blade machinesThese work a bit like freeze-first machines, but instead of freezing the bowl overnight, you freeze the mixture in the tub provided. Again, if it’s too high in fat, your mixture will become grainy, so stick to a custard or single-cream base. You can also freeze certain mix-ins directly within the ice-cream base with these models, as the blade will chop right through them.

Repairability varies. If you want a machine that lasts for years, look for one with easily replaceable parts and a simple design. Models with fewer hidden electronics or that can be disassembled into several pieces for cleaning are generally easier to repair at home or by a local professional. In that light, the Nutribullet Chill and Cuisinart Solo Scoops are two of the most easily repairable machines on this list in terms of the spare parts that are available.

However, spare parts won’t always cover you for issues with electrical components. It’s always worth checking whether the manufacturer of your model offers a repair service. Some have dedicated support pages on their websites where you can buy replacement parts, and of course, don’t overlook warranties when you’re making a buying decision, for valuable peace of mind if anything should go wrong.

‘It’s OK to mess around’: how ‘mop man’ stole the show at Glasgow’s Commonwealth Games

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:21:56 GMT

CJ Miller from West Lothian has delighted global audiences with ‘sheer stupidity’ of his half-time dances

The 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow have already provided plenty of highlights. But fans across the world have been dazzled by one particular breakout star: the “mop man”.

When a cleaner came out at half-time during a netball match to wipe down the court before the restart, everything appeared normal. But as the cleaner swept, and the first bars of Queen’s I Want to Break Free rang out in the venue, he went from sweeping to a standing split.

A full dance routine set to the 1984 hit then followed, much to the surprise and delight of the audience at the OVO Hydro. The crowd watched him do the worm, splits and front handsprings. He has since entertained crowds during breaks in play at a number of other events and clips of his performances have gone viral online.

The man behind the mop is CJ Miller, 25, from Livingston, West Lothian, a trained dancer who was hired by the Games to keep crowds entertained during intermissions.

He considers himself more of an introvert than his cleaning alter ego. “I’m an anxious and paranoid queen,” said Miller. “And I’m so grateful for the turn of events. It’s been a lovely 50 minutes of fame. I wish I’d had a haircut before it happened.”

Miller was initially told he would be part of a flashmob at the Games with other dancers. “Then it was, ‘oh, here’s a mop. Here’s the song.’ It wasn’t until the Tuesday before the Games I found out it was gonna be Boo Boo the Fool here, on his own,” Miller laughed, pointing to himself.

When choreographing the routine, Miller was inspired by “the concept of a volunteer … a cleaner that had been possessed by the music and just exploded.”

But the character soon took on a life – and fanbase – of his own. “People have messaged being like, ‘Thank you for making me smile, I really needed that today.’”

For Miller, the universal charm of his performance comes from “the sheer stupidity, the sheer bonkersness of it all”. “It just made people feel like it’s OK to mess around,” he said. “Sometimes, people need to be reminded to just take a break. Just take a minute to smile at someone else being so bloody ridiculous.”

Miller’s performance was soon picked up by broadcasters and newspapers around the world. There was particular praise for the unexpected chemistry with his dance partner: Doris the mop.

“Phil [Goodlad] from the BBC had named the mop Doris – so I didn’t even name the bloody mop!” said Miller. “He asked me, and I went: ‘The mop is a mop, Phil.’ And he was like: ‘I think it looks like a Doris.’ I went: ‘Brilliant. It’s Doris the mop now, Phil, spectacular.’”

Did he have a name in mind for his other dance partner, the vacuum? “It was a Vax vacuum, so I think the vacuum should be called Vaxtina – like Xtina. You can write that one down.”

Going into the Games, Miller felt nervous about performing in front of a sports crowd for the first time. “Basketball, for me, was a scary one. I was like: ‘I don’t think the basketball crowd are going to want to see my flamboyant ass, giving them a dance to Freddie Mercury. And I was wrong. The basketball crowd were incredible.”

“It was a lesson for me to check my own prejudice,” he said. “It doesn’t excuse the point of view I had of sports fans, and that has been changed now from the immense support I’ve received from the sports fans at the Commonwealth. Thank you for proving me wrong, sports fans.”

Going forward, Miller is soon to join Newcastle College as a dance tutor and continue building his career as a choreographer. But will the world ever see more of mop man?

“I think it would be fun,” said Miller, who has been approached by one company about taking his performance further. “If I were to do it again, let’s get some other professions in there,” said Miller. “Referee, waiter, bloody construction worker. Let’s get inventive with it.”

While mop man’s performances may have come to an end, Miller hopes viewers can be inspired by his character’s self-confidence and sense of whimsy. “Be messy, fail, screw up,” he said. “That’s what makes us human. Get your mop and shake your ass, you know what I mean?”

‘He lived here a long time, so it feels poignant’: Nick Cave thrills Brighton passersby with secret rooftop gig

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:20:52 GMT

Prior to playing huge outdoor show in city’s Preston Park, Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds set up on a record shop balcony – and play to fans visiting from across the world

Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds’ only advertised UK live performance of 2026, a show in Brighton’s Preston Park, arrives with other events across the city attached. The Duke of York’s Picturehouse cinema is hosting a weekend-long Nick Cave takeover, featuring films curated and introduced by the singer-songwriter. There is a pop-up shop replete with exclusive merchandise, and a postbox where physical letters can be sent to The Red Hand Files, the website Cave started in 2018 where he answers fans’ questions on topics ranging from faith and grief to his favourite brand of hair dye (L’Oreal, apparently). Even the announcements at the train station have been changed: arrivals are temporarily greeted by the sound of Nick Cave welcoming them to Brighton.

All these have been well-publicised, but judging by the crowd gathering in Kensington Gardens, a narrow pedestrian road in North Laine – not far from Jubilee Street, the subject of a Cave song – word also seems to have leaked out about a theoretically secret event: a live performance on the roof of Resident Records, which is hosting the two-day Nick Cave pop-up shop.

A substantial group has already assembled, an hour before the performance is scheduled to begin. Some have been tipped off in advance (“My mate told me about it last night, he’s very well connected”). Others simply arrived in order to avail themselves of an exclusive Cave picture disc. (It sold out yesterday and there are already copies on eBay for £60, one disgruntled punter notes, before suggesting that the enterprising soul behind the eBay listing is “a bastard”.) After seeing the musical equipment on the roof, they put two and two together.

By 10.30am, the street is packed. A security guard manages to keep a narrow flow of pedestrians moving through its centre, but no one seems to have considered Snoopers Paradise, the vintage market across the road. The crowd jams its doorways and shoppers can’t get out: “What’s going on?” asks a plaintive voice. “Oh, I can’t stand Nick Cave.”

Said voice is clearly in the minority. The startling thing about the crowd is that it largely isn’t comprised of curious locals: there are people here from Germany, Norway, France, all of whom have flown in specially for the Preston Park gig. There is talk of visitors from the US and east Asia. A couple from Oslo are enjoying what they call “a Nick Cave summer”, following the Bad Seeds around Europe: “Well, we’re going to four shows – he’s playing 32”. The Brighton show has extra appeal, says Lisa, who has travelled down from Edinburgh with her partner because it’s a kind of a hometown gig, although “former adopted hometown” gig would be more accurate. “He lived in Brighton for a long time – he moved when his son died,” she says, referring to Arthur Cave, who fell from a cliff in Ovingdean in 2015. “So it feels quite poignant.”

The distance some people in the crowd have travelled reflects Cave’s ongoing purple patch. The music he has released in the last decade – most notably 2019’s extraordinary mediation on loss, Ghosteen – has been some of the most acclaimed of his career. The harrowing documentary film One More Time With Feeling met with similar acclaim, as did Faith Hope and Carnage, a book containing an astonishingly frank series of interviews with journalist Sean O’Hagan.

Cave has courted controversy over his opposition to the cultural boycott of Israel, although it doesn’t seem to have impacted his popularity. Improbably, the Bad Seeds began playing arena-sized venues at the exact moment their music took a turn towards the abstract, with 2016’s Skeleton Tree, although Lisa suggests the crowds may have been swelled by those only familiar with his most famous songs. “I think there were a lot of Peaky Blinders fans in the audience when he played Glasgow,” she says, “just waiting to hear Red Right Hand.” She wrinkles her noise, irritably. “They were quite chatty during the rest of it.”

By the time Cave and the Bad Seeds arrive, there are people gathered not just on the street but on the roofs of adjacent shops. The set is eclectic – lurching from the apocalyptic clatter of 1985’s Train Long Suffering to a piano-led cover of T Rex’s Cosmic Dancer – and winningly chaotic, as perhaps any performance involving seven musicians and four backing singers on a tiny balcony is wont to be.

Cave occasionally grins at the absurdity of it all (“Fucking Brighton!” he smiles at one point) or issues frantic instructions to his bandmates mid-song, but the really striking thing is how committed his performance is, despite the peculiar circumstances. He hangs precariously over the balcony to conduct the crowd in call-and-response vocals. Singing Henry Lee as a duet with Janet Ramus, he performs it as if wracked by a desire for both the backing vocalist and his wife, Susie, who is watching from an adjacent balcony. Then again, onstage commitment regardless of the circumstances is something of a Cave trademark, as our Norwegian friends enjoying their summer of Nick note. “In Antwerp, the show was in the middle of a heatwave and he played for two and a half hours wearing a three-piece suit.”

It ends with a version of Papa Won’t Leave You, Henry. The police arrive shortly afterwards – one suspects the gig was not officially sanctioned – but the crowd are already dispersing, most of them in the direction of Preston Park. It’s hours before the Bad Seeds are due on stage, but the real lure seems to be the opportunity to outwit the bastards on eBay: a rumour suggests remaining copies of the exclusive picture disc are on sale there, and people scurry off.

Ariana Grande: Petal review – calm, controlled anger at exes, fans and the media

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:12:56 GMT

(Republic) Casting herself as a flower trampled underfoot, the superstar’s eighth album swaps the ​glitz of her Wicked years ​f​or dark blooms of haunted electronics

‘Tell me who’s to blame?” Ariana Grande asks, exasperated, on the title track of her eighth album, Petal. “Is it the people or myself?” As bleary, fuzzed-up drums threaten to drown her out, this shadowy carousel-ride of a song cycles through more questions than answers. Does her success only make her need more of it? Can her new record of No 1 singles stave off heartbreak? Does Grande’s life shape her music, or does her music shape her life?

Moody and muted, Petal is a riposte to the glitz and sparkle of the pop star’s Oscar-nominated turn in Wicked and the theatre kid energy of her last album, 2024’s Eternal Sunshine. She describes this record as one of “unfiltered rage”, and there’s plenty Grande could be angry about: just this week she filed a lawsuit against hackers who allegedly stole and sold numerous unreleased songs.

Intrusive fans are raked over the coals on the icily aloof lead single Hate That I Made You Love Me – a huge global hit since its release in May – while whispery Oh Well casually dispatches “bad guys” (read: exes) to hell. Like I Do opens with panicky gasps, stylised as a vocal exercise, and ruminates on co-dependence with the press – along with a possible dig at years of clickbait headlines pedalling faux concern about her weight: “I’ve got shit to talk, keeps me well fed.”

The album’s central metaphor of a petal on the pavement – something delicate getting trampled underfoot – is mirrored in production that is unusually dark by Grande’s standards. Written and produced by Grande and longtime collaborator Ilya Salmanzadeh, Petal buries her soft, sparkling voice under bass, rattling percussion and a raft of crackling, distorted electronic textures. It sounds lonely: a haunted house of a pop record with Grande’s usual R&B vocal fireworks locked in the basement.

Dread-soaked opener Kiss Me is a crisis of faith, with Grande’s gleaming voice the only light in the dark as she demands, vampirically, for a lover to “bring her to life”. Water drips from the ceiling on Hate That I Made You Love Me, as if her chilly dismissal of her fans’ obsession was recorded in some kind of sewer.

Snatches of shuffling UKG percussion suggest that Kelela’s eerie fusion of club, R&B and alt-rock has replaced Mariah Carey’s glam on Grande’s mood board, but there’s still a shiny, theatrical bent to her new grunge. Sirens wee-woo melodramatically on Never Get Over Me, which threatens another ex over campy, villainous piano. In a similar vein, Big Feelings claims femme fatale status via generically stomping synths and a wide-eyed rendition of a line from Rizzo’s big ballad in Grease: “There are worse things that I could do.”

Through it all, Grande maintains a measured neutrality to her voice. Shelving the powerhouse vocal runs she’s famous for, she leans towards lacy, translucent harmonies and stacked layers (in the vein of her longtime inspiration Imogen Heap), which turn into ghostly cathedrals of sound. The closest we get to an old-school Ariana moment is on interlude Warning Signs, which escalates into a rare outburst: “I wish someone could hear me,” she cries, before the track cuts out.

Petal is an album of quiet, controlled, vetted anger; there’s no rush of blood to the head. Maybe it’s because Grande is rehashing familiar topics – it’s far from the first time she’s dissected fame, romance or self-worth in her music – that she sounds numb to it, tired of treading the same ground. Or maybe it’s because performing anger in public is a new challenge for her. While singing the title track live for the first time this week, she clenched her fists: Anger 101. But as she demanded those answers – from herself, from a sea of screaming fans and phone screens – her voice had real bite.

Hobbies can improve your health – here are four tips for choosing one

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:00:27 GMT

From sea swimming to painting, doctors are ‘prescribing’ hobbies – but you don’t need a doctor’s note to get started

In 2020, the year Amanda lost her mother, husband, job and pre-pandemic normalcy, she was diagnosed with major depressive disorder. “My life was just spiraling down and down and down,” she says.

To help with her symptoms, in addition to an antidepressant prescription, Amanda was given a “social prescription”: a referral to a non-medical, community-based activity, typically involving movement, nature, art or service. Amanda lives near Devon, England, and became curious about sea swimming after reading about its health benefits and watching other women do it at her local beach all year round. When she told this to her mental health nurse, she was prescribed a spot in Chill Therapy, an eight-week course that teaches swimming, floating and breathing techniques to build skill and confidence navigating the open water.

Six years later, Amanda turns to swimming in the sea whenever she feels stressed. “It invigorates me and makes me feel I can cope with anything,” she says. “I can’t do without it, to be honest.” She is now down to the lowest dose of her antidepressant, and has made a ton of friends along the way: “I feel refreshed in body and soul.”

Though research has long linked hobbies involving exercise, arts and nature to a wide range of health benefits, social prescribing now lets people like Amanda participate in them as part of their healthcare, typically covering barriers like cost and transportation. While the practice is more common in the UK, some insurers in the US are starting to participate in social prescribing.

But you don’t need a doctor’s note to get started. We asked experts in the social prescribing field for tips on picking a hobby that will actually improve your health.

When choosing a hobby, think about how you’re feeling now, and how you’d like to feel in the future.

For instance, if you’ve been feeling tired or down, like Amanda, science suggests you should move your body; for example, multiple studies show sea swimming can help reduce depression and depressive symptoms.

On a physiological level, this makes sense: aerobic exercise has been linked with gains in mood-boosting endorphins and serotonin. Additionally, time spent in nature is linked with lower levels of cortisol, a stress hormone.

Feeling distracted? Nature is also good at improving focus. According to the Attention Restoration Theory, nature is uniquely equipped to restore our depleted mental resources by providing “soft fascination”, a state of effortless focus that captures our attention without draining it. This could explain why nature has been shown to improve our executive functioning and concentration.

Creative activities can help with getting through sadness, isolation or pain. “Art is a human experience – it helps folks get out of their loneliness and into a flow state, which can rewire their brain from trauma,” says Holly Jacobson, CEO of Path With Art, a Seattle-based non-profit that offers free arts-based community programming. A new small study found that Path with Art participants experienced statistically significant gains in mental wellbeing and efficacy, and reductions in loneliness. Earlier small studies found that painting can reduce anxiety, and that art-making can reduce cortisol levels after 45 minutes.

Some people can’t see themselves knitting, while others might rule out sports because of injury. Research suggests we are more likely to follow through on an activity if we have intrinsic motivation – the internal drive to do something because we find it genuinely enjoyable or satisfying, rather than an external reward, like losing weight.

That’s what worked for Amanda. Instead of receiving a finger-wagging recommendation to exercise, she says she was intrinsically motivated to go sea swimming. “When I could not go in the sea while waiting for hip replacement for two years, I used to picture myself in the waves with my friends and it always cheered me up,” she says.

To help uncover a patient’s intrinsic motivation, professionals called link workers are tasked with listening to patients and helping them uncover their unique curiosities. Many are trained in motivational interviewing, an evidence-based, person-centered conversational technique that helps people work within their own value system and reasons for change, says Dr Tim Anstiss, a medical doctor who helped to develop the training, which recommends questions like: how might your life change if you joined that group? Who or what gives your life meaning and purpose?

Doing what gives us purpose and meaning is “vital” to our health and wellbeing, agrees Dr Ivory Rose, a California-based occupational therapist and lead within Social Prescribing USA. “Leisure pursuits are a very important part of [our health], but often get forgotten in the face of an illness or busy schedule,” she says, referencing studies that link meaningful activity to greater health.

Rose aims to rebuild this association for clients with questions like: what is something you used to enjoy doing that you haven’t done in a while? What is important to you to be able to do?

after newsletter promotion

Mindfulness is “the very simple process of noticing”, says Dr Ellen Langer, a psychology professor at Harvard University. In her most recent book, The Mindful Body, she explores the wide-ranging benefits of being more mindful, which include improving your memory, creativity and energy, and strengthening your social relationships.

Langer says to start by noticing three new things about something familiar – say, a person, place or object. Every time you notice you are on autopilot, you build “a healthy mindset for uncertainty”, she says. This is important because people who are stressed or in pain often “believe the symptoms they have are going to stay the same or get worse”, and that suffering is constant, Langer says. But according to research, people can feel better when they notice improvements and reflect on why they feel better.

Dr Rachel Zoffness, a pain psychologist teaching at Stanford and the University of California at San Francisco, similarly points to research showing that pain can increase or decrease, depending on where we direct our attention.

In her recent book, Tell Me Where It Hurts, she offers tips for pain relief. She says she sometimes asks patients directly: “Will you tell me about a time you were so absorbed in an activity that you briefly forgot about your pain?”

If you’re not sure what brings you meaning or what captures your attention in adulthood, try reflecting on what brought you joy in childhood. “When we were kids, playing did not relate to a specific goal, but it’s the most natural form of learning,” says Purvi Shah, founder of PlayRx. life, a wellness platform. Shah advises clients to “say ‘yes’ to something new, especially when they are stuck in a rut and problems seem overwhelming”.

Caitlin Marshall, a licensed clinical social worker and co-author of Creative First Aid, agrees. In her work leading creative workshops on activities including beekeeping and watercolor painting, she focuses on helping people who are experiencing psychological distress rediscover a sense of childlike joy. “It’s about learning to help people do what feels good and inspiring to them,” she says.

Encouraging participants to be open-minded helps them to discover new things about themselves. “Some of them will arrive and say: ‘I hate cooking.’ Then those people are the ones that end up loving it,” Marshall says. “It’s hard to be judgmental and curious at the same time.”

Hull funeral director who left bodies to rot in mortuary jailed for 20 years

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 15:46:12 GMT

More than 80 loved ones spoke of horrors of learning about Robert Bush’s crimes, including mother of a miscarried baby

A funeral director has been jailed for 20 years for leaving dozens of bodies – including a miscarried baby – “rotting” in his mortuary and giving bereaved families the wrong ashes.

Robert Bush, the owner of Legacy Independent Funeral Services in Hull, pleaded guilty to 67 offences spanning 12 years and affecting hundreds of families, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial.

After Bush’s sentencing, the government said it planned to crack down on “rogue operators” in the funeral industry, including by developing proposals for formal regulation of the sector.

The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said Bush’s actions “were utterly abhorrent and my thoughts are with all the bereaved families in Hull who have been so badly let down”.

Over a five-day sentencing hearing at Hull crown court, more than 80 victims recounted their horror at learning their loved ones had been left “rotting away” inside his funeral parlour. Many broke down sobbing during their statements.

Sentencing Bush, the judge, Mr Justice Hilliard, said: “The defendant was so preoccupied with his own enrichment that he behaved in a shocking and disgraceful way towards the deceased.

“The awful truth is that anyone whose loved one went through Legacy at any time when it was operating can now have no confidence as to how they were treated or whose ashes they have. Unless, of course, they were one of the 30 bodies recovered in March 2024.

“Culpability is of course high because of the gross breach of trust in respect of people who were vulnerable as they were bereaved.”

Bush, 48, from Otley, West Yorkshire, showed little visible emotion while listening to the statements in the dock, but hung his head lower and lower as the week went on.

Gasps and sobbing could be heard from the public gallery when prosecutors revealed the grim condition of the deceased.

The court heard that bodies had been found uncovered and lying on racks in varying states of decomposition. Damp and mould had spread to the coffins and ash boxes, while dried body fluids and faeces had been left on the floor.

During the search, PC Jason Sutcliffe spotted a brown paper bag on the floor. He initially thought the item inside was a baby bird, before noticing two hospital wristbands wrapped around the waist, identifying the body as the “baby of Jasmine Beverley”.

The baby, Sunny Beverley-Conlin, was miscarried at 18 weeks in May 2022. His parents believed he had been given a funeral and cremated. Instead, Bush had left his remains inside Legacy for almost two years.

Sunny’s mother, Jasmine, sobbed as she faced Bush in court. “I trusted Rob with the most precious and important person in my life,” she said. “The reality I now live with is that my baby boy Sunny has spent more time in your possession than he ever did with his own family.”

In a statement, Sutcliffe described finding Sunny’s remains as “the worst experience of my career” and said it would “never leave my thoughts”.

The ashes presented to Beverley and her family had been “consistent with baby remains in volume but had larger pieces of coarse bones” expected from an adult’s body, according to evidence heard in court.

Some of the ashes presented to Lucy Ness, who lost her child just before 12 weeks, were said to have resembled “animal remains” in terms of size and texture, which prompted cries in the courtroom.

The body of 94-year-old Norman Bridger was recovered at the Legacy premises 323 days after his death. “My lovely dad lay in a cardboard coffin for almost 11 months,” said his daughter Karen King. “It’s beyond belief. I’ll never know why. It feels like he was just forgotten.”

Bush was arrested on 10 March while returning from a holiday in Arizona, US, a £3,000 trip funded by his funeral fraud. Arrest footage showed Humberside and Met police officers escorting a shocked Bush off a plane at Heathrow airport.

Soon after his arrest, Bush told officers: “I fucked it all up, everything, my whole world.”

Police officers found 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes during a search of Legacy premises at Hessle Road in March 2024.

Several families had had the wrong ashes turned into jewellery, and in one instance planned to incorporate some into a tattoo.

David Gorbutt told the court he felt “abused” after learning that Bush had given him a stranger’s ashes rather than those of his late wife, Susan Gorbutt. He had scattered those ashes at the same site as her son’s, as per Susan’s wishes.

“I have had the uncertainty of not knowing who or what I have scattered over the ashes of Susan’s son,” Gorbutt said. “Who was that? One person? More than one?”

The state of Bush’s premises “did not meet industry standards” and represented a “wholly inadequate approach to care for the deceased”, according to evidence from Dr Richard Lloyd, a human anatomy centre manager at the University of Cambridge and Cranfield University. “Bodies were simply abandoned in the Hessle Road mortuary for nature to take its course,” his report stated.

Containers of ashes were “stored in an undignified manner” across the premises, stacked “chaotically on shelves” or left on the floor, where “damp had caused mould to grow on the boxes”. Ash was also found on desk surfaces and, in one room, strewn across the floor. Officers found jewellery that ought to have been returned to families and a large number of photographs that should have been placed inside coffins.

Bush stole money from funeral services intended for 12 separate charities, including Macmillan Cancer Support, Salvation Army and a local hospice. In addition, he sold false funeral plans to 226 people over nearly 12 years, totalling in value £562,117.

In the time he spent defrauding bereaved families, Bush spent more than £42,000 on holidays, including his trip to Arizona, £21,000 on motorcycle racing and £17,400 on home improvements between 2017 and 2024. He spent more than £9,000 on camping expenses in 2022 – the same year he failed to cremate baby Sunny.

Bush’s barrister, Richard Wright KC, said his client wished to apologise to the families and accepted this was “likely to be rejected” by them. Wright added: “He is treated, completely understandably, as a pariah – hated and despised.”

Healey sets budget for late October, promising to ‘spread money and power’ around UK

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 15:43:13 GMT

Chancellor will have to find money for Burnham’s policies while sticking to fiscal rules as borrowing costs rise

Andy Burnham’s government has set a date for a late October budget to “spread money and power” out of Westminster as the new prime minister pushes forward his tax and spending plans.

Announcing an autumn budget for 28 October, the chancellor, John Healey, said Labour would stick to its fiscal rules with its agenda to give businesses and households stability for the future.

Burnham has used his first two weeks in power to make a blitz of policy announcements, including a VAT cut on energy bills, slashing business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues, capping bus fares, and promising to give England’s regional mayors a share of income tax.

Pushing to turn around Labour’s faltering performance in opinion polls under Keir Starmer, the prime minister will however need to spell out how his change in direction is funded in a tricky autumn budget.

The UK government has faced a sharp rise in borrowing costs on global financial markets in recent weeks as the economic fallout from the Iran war hits activity, stokes inflation and adds to the financial pressures for countries around the world.

With elevated levels of annual borrowing and the UK national debt at the highest point since the 1960s, City investors warn that Burnham has limited room for manoeuvre in the public finances. The prime minister has also committed to stick to Labour’s manifesto promises, including ruling out an increase in income tax, national insurance or VAT.

City traders had expressed unease over the potential appointment of Ed Miliband as chancellor and Burnham taking a looser approach to the public finances. While picking Healey for chancellor and pledging to retain Rachel Reeves’s fiscal rules – which require spending to be balanced by receipts – has eased concerns, investors still warn the government faces a delicate balancing act that may lead Burnham to consider tax rises.

In his first weeks in office Burnham had initially suggested he could look at “any flexibility” in the fiscal rules. He has also faced calls to consider a wealth tax and to overhaul property taxes, and has not ruled out tax rises to fund social care.

Approaching the budget, Labour has a raft of policy measures that will require funding details to be spelt out, including Burnham’s cost of living support, devolution plan and billions of pounds of cuts pencilled in by Starmer and Reeves to support a £15bn increase in defence spending over five years.

Healey said Labour was “working fast to restore hope” with the government’s announcements and that he was pushing to “get on with the job” in his first budget as chancellor.

Iran strikes tankers under US escort in Hormuz strait as Trump gathers cabinet to discuss war

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 14:48:53 GMT

Energy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle East

Iran has said it struck two tankers trying to pass through the strait of Hormuz under the escort of the US military as Donald Trump gathered his cabinet to discuss the stalling war and rising prices as midterm elections in the US loom.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Friday that the “non-compliant oil tankers … were struck and brought to a halt, while four other oil tankers quickly changed course and returned to their previous positions”. The military body said the ships had tried to pass through the strait via an “undeclared route” and under US aerial escort.

Iran and the US have said ships should pass through the strait via two competing routes, with Iran bombing ships that take the southern route, close to the coast of Oman, and the US bombing ships that violate its blockade of Iranian ships and ports.

The strait has been almost completely closed to traffic since Iran and the US returned to fighting two weeks ago, sending energy prices soaring. On Thursday, the price of crude oil pushed past $90 a barrel when the US struck Iran in retaliation for its targeting of US bases in Jordan.

Fighting continued on Friday, with the Kuwaiti defence ministry reporting that it had shot down Iranian drones targeting “vital and military facilities” without any casualties.

In Lebanon, the Israeli military carried out a huge detonation overnight near the ancient Beaufort Castle. It said it was targeting Hezbollah tunnels and infrastructure. The explosion was heard across south Lebanon and covered nearby towns in ash, while photos showed the affected area levelled by the force of the blast.

Lebanese officials accused Israel of violating the ceasefire by carrying out the detonation. The Israeli military said it was ensuring the security of its northern residents.

Trump has tried to open the strait of Hormuz by force, but increasingly intense US strikes on Iran have yielded few results. The price of gas and groceries remain high in the US as a result of the energy disruption, complicating Republicans’ chances at the ballot box in November’s midterm elections.

On Friday, Trump brought his cabinet together at the Camp David retreat in Maryland to try to chart a path forward for the war. The White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said at a briefing last week that the cabinet meeting would be “a lot of fun and something different for the cabinet to experience together”.

Top of the agenda will be the Iran war, which Trump promised would last a few weeks but has now dragged on for five months. A Reuters-Ipsos poll this week found that one in three Americans support the war, the lowest polling since the war began.

Support in Congress is also waning, with the US Senate narrowly rejecting a symbolic vote to express disapproval of the war. The war powers resolution asking the president to stop the war failed in a 49-50 vote. Inflation caused by the war is a boon for Democrats, who are hoping to wrest control of the house from the Republicans.

Energy companies have posted record profits as a result of the conflict, with ExxonMobil’s profits doubling and Chevron reporting more than five times its profits in the same time period last year.

Hold the front page! Marilyn Monroe is Dakota Johnson’s ninth cousin three times removed

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 14:37:14 GMT

The vogue for celebrity ancestors can be traced back to Robert Pattinson descending from Dracula and Benedict Cumberbatch being related to just about everyone

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

To mark Marilyn Monroe’s 100th birthday, a short film will premiere at this year’s Venice film festival. Entitled Flesh Impact, the film has been written and directed by Maggie Gyllenhaal, and will star two versions of Monroe. The first, played by Ellen Burstyn, will apparently be “a version of Monroe the world never got to see”, while Dakota Johnson will play Monroe in her pomp.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Ahead of its premiere, a photo of Johnson dolled up as Monroe has been released. And it has to be said that the resemblance is actually pretty good. This could be down to one of two reasons. The first is that Monroe is so iconic that you could slap a wig and a beauty spot on Phil Mitchell and you’d immediately see who he was trying to emulate. Or it could be because Marilyn Monroe and Dakota Johnson are literally related.

No, really. A new press release from MyHeritage has revealed that Marilyn Monroe is Dakota Johnson’s ninth cousin three times removed. According to the release, “their shared ancestry traces back to Richard and Charity Tydings, 17th-century English settlers in Maryland. Marilyn descends from their daughter Pretitia, while Dakota and [her father] Don Johnson descend from her younger sister, Mary.”

This is incredible news indeed. What a scoop, casting one of Marilyn Monroe’s own relatives in a film about Marilyn Monroe. And a close relative, too. Ninth cousins three times removed. Take that, anyone who is only the 12th cousin six times removed of Marilyn Monroe. This is the real deal.

However, if you can believe such a thing, Johnson and Monroe are not the only miraculous relatives in Hollywood. For example, in the 2017 BBC series Gunpowder, Kit Harington played Robert Catesby, the leader of a Catholic group who planned the failed gunpowder plot in 1605. It’s a great, grim character to play – spoiler, he ends with his head on a spike – but the biggest news about the series was the fact that Harington was a descendant of Catesby. The website Famouskin claims that Harington is Catesby’s sixth cousin 11 times removed, although it’s worth pointing out that Harington’s family is so well to do that his 10th great-grandfather was James I – meaning that he is simultaneously related to a failed assassin and the assassin’s intended victim.

Another actor related to royalty is Benedict Cumberbatch. In 2016, Cumberbatch played Richard III in The Hollow Crown, a year after genealogists revealed that the actor was Richard’s second cousin 16 times removed. However, it turns out that Cumberbatch is also related to basically every other character he has ever played.

After appearing in Sherlock, Ancestry revealed that Cumberbatch was the 16th cousin twice removed of Arthur Conan Doyle. When the Alan Turing biopic The Imitation Game was released in 2014, Ancestry went to work again, declaring that Cumberbatch and Turing were 17th cousins, sharing an ancestor in the first Earl of Somerset. You may also remember that Cumberbatch starred in 12 Years a Slave. While not directly related to his character, Cumberbatch’s fifth great-grandfather Abraham was nevertheless an enslaver with a Barbados sugar plantation in his name.

As you can see, Ancestry really comes into its own on matters like this. For example, just one month after Taylor Swift announced her 2024 album The Tortured Poets Department, the website managed to discover that Swift was in fact related to a notoriously tortured poet, being the sixth cousin three times removed of Emily Dickinson. Last year, it was also claimed that Swift was the eighth cousin 11 times removed of King Louis XIV of France. Perhaps this will be a link covered in a future album called The Hubristic Monarchs Department.

But being related to royalty is boring. Being related to something supernatural, on the other hand, is much more fun. And so it came to pass in 2009 that Emma Watson, famous for playing a witch in the Harry Potter films, is actually related to a witch. The news came out of yet another Ancestry deep dive, revealing that Watson’s distant ancestor was Joan Playle, a woman who was convicted of witchcraft in 1592. Although she wasn’t executed for her crimes, Playle was nevertheless excommunicated from the church, although it might be worth pointing out that the evidence for her being a witch essentially begins and ends with the fact that she was unmarried.

Finally, the greatest ancestral link of them all. Shortly before the release of The Twilight Saga: Eclipse, Ancestry managed to work out that Robert Pattinson, who played a vampire in the film, was distantly related to Vlad III, known as Vlad the Impaler or Vlad Dracula. Being a screen vampire who is literally related to Dracula is quite a flex, although it should also be pointed out that other relatives of Vlad include Prince William and Prince Harry, and George W Bush, so hopefully they’ll band together for any further sequels.

A bitter pill: are you wasting your money on supplements?

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 14:00:15 GMT

Will collagen make you look younger? Could magnesium help you sleep better? Or are the benefits overstated? A dietitian reveals which are worth taking

Multivitamins are one of the most commonly used supplements worldwide – but for most people, there isn’t evidence of a huge benefit.

One of the largest trials to date found a small improvement in memory among older adults taking a daily multivitamin. But the difference was tiny, amounting to roughly a quarter of a word in a 20-word recall test. Other outcomes such as mood, immune function and overall wellbeing have generally shown little to no improvement in people who are already meeting their nutritional needs through food.

That doesn’t mean multivitamins are pointless. They may be helpful during life stages with higher nutrient requirements, such as pregnancy, or when intake or absorption is lower. But multivitamins are not standardised, so check with your doctor or dietitian what’s best for you.

Your best return on investment will always come from real food. Aim to include fruits, vegetables, whole grains, beans, nuts, seeds, dairy (or fortified alternatives) and protein-rich foods every day in order to give your body a good blend of the vitamins, minerals, fibre and plant compounds that supplements can’t fully replicate.

Creatine has been getting a lot of hype lately, even though it’s been around for years. It’s a compound that your body naturally produces, though you can also get very small amounts from red meat and fish.

Creatine is stored in your muscles, where it helps provide energy during short bursts of high-intensity exercise. The effects of taking extra creatine are not dramatic, but when combined with training well, eating enough protein and prioritising recovery, it may help you modestly lift heavier weights or sprint better.

Unlike many nutrients, where dietary changes can often achieve similar results to supplementation, there isn’t a practical food-first way to maximise creatine stores.

Collagen is the main structural protein in skin, tendons and connective tissue, and production starts to gradually decline from your mid-20s.

Most collagen supplements come in the form of hydrolysed collagen peptides, meaning the protein has been broken down into smaller fragments that are easier to dissolve and digest. They are typically sold as powders that can be mixed into drinks or foods. Several randomised controlled trials suggest that taking these supplements daily for about three months may lead to small improvements in skin hydration and elasticity, particularly in women in their 40s and 50s.

Collagen supplements are also being studied for tendon and joint health, with some trials suggesting modest improvements. However, these are best seen as a potential edge for very specific groups, such as people with exercise-related joint injuries or those with higher training loads, rather than a magic fix or a replacement for food-first strategies.

Before thinking about supplements, it’s crucial to make sure you are eating enough protein overall, which for most people is about 30g per meal, to provide the amino acids needed for tissue repair and collagen production, including glycine and proline, alongside adequate vitamin C from fruit and vegetables, which is required for collagen synthesis.

Our skin makes vitamin D from sunlight, but in the UK this only really works between late March and early October, when UVB is strong enough. Outside these months, even on bright or warm days, our exposure to the sun is too weak. This is why low vitamin D is more common in winter, and also more likely year-round in people with darker skin, older adults, those who cover their skin, and people who spend most of their time indoors.

There are food sources, but they’re limited and usually not enough on their own, which is why it’s recommended to supplement 10 micrograms (400 IU) daily during autumn and winter. This is mainly for bone health, supporting calcium absorption and reducing the risk of conditions such as rickets and osteomalacia. But more is not better – vitamin D is fat soluble and stored in the body, so avoid very high intakes as these can build up and may cause harm.

Magnesium supplements are getting a lot of attention for improving everything from sleep and muscle cramps to blood pressure and brain health, but the evidence is more underwhelming than the marketing. Most benefits are seen in people with low magnesium intake. This is relevant because the National Diet and Nutrition Survey shows that many people in the UK fall below recommended intakes, largely due to low consumption of nuts, seeds, legumes, whole grains and leafy green vegetables.

These foods, which are naturally high in magnesium, also contain other key nutrients from which we can benefit: fibre, healthy fats, vitamin E, or minerals such as iron.

Meeting your recommended allowance is easier than it might seem. For example, a bowl of porridge with pumpkin seeds or wholewheat pasta with chickpeas and spinach can provide almost half of your daily magnesium needs.

Electrolyte supplements contain minerals such as sodium, chloride and potassium that help regulate fluid balance. They’re often marketed as a daily hydration essential, but for most people this isn’t supported by science.

In reality, our body tightly regulates electrolytes, particularly sodium, which we lose when we sweat. Outside situations involving significant fluid loss, such as long endurance exercise, heavy sweating or illness, most people maintain electrolyte balance through food and simply drinking enough water.

When sweating a lot, sodium and chloride are the main electrolytes we lose, and these can usually be replaced by adding salt to meals or drinks, which is far cheaper than supplements. As a rough guide, during heavy sweating, sodium losses are around the equivalent of 1g to 3g of salt per hour, which is roughly equivalent to between a couple of pinches and half a teaspoon.

In the UK, most people don’t meet the recommendation of at least one portion of oily fish per week, which contains vital omega-3s, including eicosapentaenoic Acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic Acid (DHA), alongside protein, iodine, selenium and vitamin D. Good sources include mackerel, salmon, trout, sardines and anchovies.

We can also get omega-3s from plant sources, known as alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), but this is a less efficient way of meeting our needs, as conversion to EPA and DHA is limited. For people who don’t eat fish, algae-based omega-3 supplements can be a practical alternative. Check the label for adequate levels of EPA and DHA, aiming for about 250-500mg combined.

Ashwagandha is a herbal supplement with a long history in Ayurvedic medicine. The strongest evidence of any effectiveness relates to stress. People taking ashwagandha often report improvements in stress and sleep quality, alongside reductions in cortisol levels of about 10-30%.

But most people in these studies don’t have high cortisol levels to begin with. And because cortisol naturally rises and falls throughout the day and plays an important role in the body, it’s not clear whether lowering it when it’s already within a normal range has any meaningful long-term health benefit.

Before turning to supplements, it’s worth remembering that eating regular meals with enough protein and fibre helps provide steady fuel for the brain and body and supports more stable blood sugar levels, which can help combat energy dips, irritability and sudden pangs of “hanger”.

Fibre supplements can be useful in specific contexts, particularly for symptom management, with psyllium husk having good evidence for both constipation and diarrhoea, and modest improvements in cholesterol levels linked to heart health.

Outside these targeted uses, we tend to benefit more when we get fibre from a wide range of plant foods. Large observational studies, including data from the American Gut Project, have found eating 30 or more different plant foods a week is associated with greater gut microbiome diversity.

This is probably because whole plant foods such as fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds and whole grains provide fibre alongside a range of other compounds, including polyphenols, that aren’t present in isolated supplements. You don’t need to obsess over eating 30, as more research is needed to confirm this number. Just focus on eating as many plants as possible.

Iron is an essential mineral that’s most often low in menstruating women, endurance athletes and people following plant-based diets. It plays a key role in oxygen transport, energy production and cognitive function, so when levels are low, you can feel it.

That said, symptoms such as fatigue can be down to many different factors, so a blood test is essential, as more iron is not better. Higher intakes can cause gastrointestinal side effects such as constipation, nausea and abdominal discomfort, and in rare cases can contribute to iron overload.

Reduce your risk of deficiency by eating red meat, fish and poultry, and plant-based iron found in lentils, beans, tofu and fortified cereals. Iron from plants is less readily absorbed, but smart pairings with vitamin C-rich foods such as red peppers and kiwis can increase absorption by up to 300%. Think beans on toast with tomatoes, or overnight quinoa with strawberries.

Most of your needs over time can be covered by a simple repeating structure: one protein (for maintenance and repair); two different-coloured plants (for micronutrients and fibre); one fibre-rich starchy carb (for energy); two flavour boosters such as herbs and spices (for polyphenols); and one source of fat (for vitamin absorption). This framework helps you quickly sense-check whether a meal is broadly balanced, without needing to track, measure or optimise every detail.

Aim for protein variety across the week by rotating three to five sources – such as eggs, yoghurt or kefir, chicken or turkey, tofu or tempeh, fish, and beans or lentils – in your weekly shop. This also provides a balance of different vitamins, minerals and compounds.

Curate a colourful freezer because frozen fruit, vegetables and herbs are often cheaper, just as nutrient-dense and require zero prep. Think mango chunks stirred into yoghurt, edamame added to salads or rice bowls, raspberries on porridge, spinach blended into sauces, or mixed veg folded into egg fried grains.

Aim to try one new ingredient, recipe or meal combination each week. Small, repeated exposures to different foods is one of the simplest ways to naturally increase diversity in your diet and broaden your intake of micronutrients.

How Not to Take Supplements: A Dietitian’s Guide to Thriving on Real Food by Josie Porter is published by Ebury at £17.99. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Chelsea fined £10m and given suspended transfer ban by FA over agent breaches

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 13:55:58 GMT

Club escape suspended six-point deduction on appeal

Owners admitted secret payments by previous regime

Chelsea have been fined £10m by the FA and served with a suspended transfer ban for multiple violations of transfer rules during the Roman Abramovich era.

The sanction reflects a similar punishment handed to the Blues by the Premier League earlier this year after the club were found to have used unlicensed agents and sought to obscure the nature of their transfer dealings between 2009 and 2022. Deals involving Chelsea legends Samuel Eto’o, Eden Hazard and Willian were among those found to have breached the rules. The commission originally handed down a stronger sanction that would have given Chelsea a suspended six-point deduction, but it was overturned after an appeal by the club.

The offences were self-reported by Chelsea when new ownership entered Stamford Bridge in 2022 and the disciplinary panel praised the club for their actions and cooperation through the hearing. Chelsea, who are also operating under a settlement agreement with Uefa, said they had “worked openly and transparently with all regulators” and were “pleased to confirm that this brings all regulatory proceedings against the club to a close”.

Written reasons published by the FA show the independent commission took a very dim view of the Abramovich-era administration, saying their rule-breaking showed “a shameful and arrogant disregard for the rules of the game … which has done so much to bring the game of football in general, and the name of CFC into disrepute”. They also said, however, that there were aspects of the case brought by the FA that caused them “particular concern”.

While praising the FA’s cooperation on the case, the commission criticised the governing body for both failing to charge individuals related to the misdemeanours and for requesting that a sporting sanction should not be applied as punishment. After a submission by the Premier League, which also argued against a sporting sanction, Chelsea appealed against the commission’s original sanction and the six-point deduction was replaced with a suspended two-window ban on registering new players. While the commission had originally argued Chelsea had sought and gained a sporting advantage from their actions, the appeal board found that there was insufficient evidence to show that any advantage had actually been achieved.

“Chelsea’s lawyers performed a masterclass in non-adversarial diplomacy with both the FA and the Premier League,” said Stefan Borson, a football finance expert who is head of sport at the law firm McCarthy Denning.

“Even where the FA’s independent panel disagreed with the position presented by the FA and Chelsea, it still found a way to discount a 15-point deduction starting point down to a six-point suspended penalty. Ultimately, even that was appealed away, leaving Chelsea to pay a final meagre fine out of its retained escrow from Abramovich’s proceeds.”

Chelsea winger Mykhailo Mudryk can return to playing immediately after the Football Association and the World Anti-Doping Agency “resolved his appeal” against a ban for failing a doping test.

The Ukrainian was suspended for four years after failing a drug test which revealed the presence of a low concentration of meldonium, a prohibited substance, in 2024. Mudryk filed an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport while changes to Wada procedures in the interim mean that had his failed test produced the same result now, charges would not have been brought.

The FA said: “Changes have been made … which, while not retroactive, mean that if Mr Mudryk’s sample was collected today, the concentration of meldonium in the sample would not have been reported and no anti-doping rule violations [ADRVs] would have resulted. Further to that development and to other circumstances of the case, the FA and Mr Mudryk have now – with the agreement of Wada – resolved the appeal proceedings.

“As a part of the agreement, Mr Mudryk accepted that he had committed the ADRVs charged and acceded to a period of ineligibility equal to the time served at the date of the agreement. Mr Mudryk is no longer ineligible and may return to competition with immediate effect.” PA Media

The Premier League and the FA had been examining tens of millions of pounds in secret payments made by offshore companies that were owned by Abramovich. Details of the transactions were uncovered as part of Cyprus Confidential, an investigation by the Guardian and international media partners, based on a leak of data from Cypriot financial services firms that the Russian oligarch used to manage his vast fortunes.

Deals revealed by the leak included apparent off-book payments to Hazard’s agent and an associate of the title-winning manager Antonio Conte.

Documents published as part of the finding offer a rare insight into the inner workings of Chelsea’s transfer policy during the tenure of Abramovich. They refer to internal conversations at Chelsea about the purchase of Willian in 2013, a deal agreed at the last minute, after the Brazilian had apparently been set to join London rivals Tottenham. According to the documents, an unnamed senior figure at Chelsea felt that to lose Willian was “not good” and that to lose him to Tottenham was “adding insult to injury”.

In its argument, the FA said the unnamed individual may have “loved the power associated with having a bottomless pocket when it came to acquiring players of great quality and/or with great potential, but to seek to suggest that there was no intention to obtain a sporting advantage is stretching our credulity beyond reasonable limits”.

The rulings published by the FA also reveal for the first time that BlueCo, the consortium that bought Chelsea from Abramovich, reached a multi-million pound settlement with HM Revenue & Customs relating to transactions dating back to 2011. The size of the settlement is redacted in the FA’s case against Chelsea but the appeal board’s decision indicated that the club repaid at least £1.35m.

The FA said that the entirety of Chelsea’s £10m fine will be invested into grassroots football.

Andy Burnham calls on Infantino to resign over ‘outrageous’ World Cup plans

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 13:30:13 GMT

UK prime minister is the first head of a major nation to call on the under-pressure Fifa president to step down

Andy Burnham has called on the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, to resign over his “outrageous” plans to sell a stake in the World Cup.

Infantino faces growing pressure over his proposals, which triggered a backlash among football bodies and prompted the resignation on Friday of a key adviser.

Asked about the Fifa proposals during a visit to a community centre in Sheffield on Friday, the prime minister said: “My view is strengthening – this was an outrageous suggestion. The idea that it could even be brought forward, in my view, shows that the Fifa [president] is the wrong man to lead the organisation.”

When Burnham was told the Fifa president was sticking to his plans despite a furious backlash from Uefa and other membership bodies, the prime minister said: “Oh wow. Have they actually done that? Oh wow.”

The intervention makes Burnham the first leader of a major country to call on Infantino to step down.

Under Fifa’s plan, the world football body would create an investment vehicle holding commercial rights related to the World Cup and sell a portion of it to investors for $4.2bn (£3.1bn).

Fifa is facing calls for an urgent review of its governance after insisting the planned World Cup sell-off will continue despite the threat of a boycott from all 55 European nations.

Carlos Cordeiro, one of Infantino’s senior advisers, resigned on Thursday over what he called “a bad deal for football”.
