“I cannot stand by while Fifa considers selling a stake in the World Cup,” Cordeiro said in his resignation statement. “I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for Fifa’s member associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game.”

Cordeiro worked for Fifa since 2021 as a senior adviser to Infantino. He also operated as a senior adviser to the White House taskforce on this summer’s World Cup.

Burnham, a lifelong Everton fan, previously said: “Let me say this very directly. Football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine.

“The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone’s to sell. Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.”

Drifting SpaceX rocket heading for accidental collision with moon

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 13:05:10 GMT

Scientists and sky gazers will watch intently as rocket’s upper stage slams into lunar surface on Wednesday

A drifting SpaceX rocket is on a collision course with the moon after launching a pair of lunar landers more than a year ago.

The rocket’s upper stage will unintentionally slam into the moon on Wednesday, carving out a crater and sending up a plume of dust and rubble that scientists – and sky gazers – are eager to observe.

Space tracking expert Bill Gray predicts an impact of 5,400mph (8,700km/h) – seven times the speed of sound – near Einstein Crater on the moon’s sunlit western limb. With the action unfolding in the wee hours of the morning for the US, the eastern portions of the US and Canada, and much of South America, should have the best views.

While scientists are not too concerned about this particular piece of space junk, it highlights the growing threat as more and more items cram into orbit.

“Things are getting crowded up there,” said Gray, who plans to view the aftermath from New Brunswick, Canada.

It was never SpaceX’s intent to hit the moon. But space experts said the crash could have been avoided if the upper stage had been nudged into orbit around the sun.

It will be the second dead rocket known to crash into the moon accidentally. A Chinese rocket segment dug out a pair of craters on the lunar far side in 2022.

The new smashup will occur on the moon’s near side, packing the equivalent energy of three tons of TNT explosives.

The impact flash, lasting less than a second, will probably be too dim to see from Earth, according to experts. But the stream of ejected material could stretch for several miles into space and remain visible to telescopes for tens of minutes.

“Gravity on the moon is low and there is no wind to blow the dust away,” said Los Alamos national laboratory’s Benjamin Fernando, who is encouraging observations by professionals and amateurs alike.

“Part of the reason for our interest in this event is to figure out how much of a hazard debris impacts pose to future astronauts,” he added in an email.

Fernando anticipates an impact crater nearly 90ft across and 16ft deep (27 meters across and 5 meters deep), too small to see from Earth but visible to spacecraft.

Nasa’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and South Korea’s Danuri lunar orbiter will gather before-and-after shots of the crash scene.

A World Cup with no participants – it could be Gianni Infantino’s boldest move yet

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 12:44:21 GMT

You’ve got to admire the Fifa president’s chutzpah in trying to flog off football’s greatest prize. If only Uefa wasn’t being so pesky about it all

Imagine a plan so distasteful that even the Americans and a Middle Eastern nepo-royal football boss can’t be doing with it. Such is the status of Fifa president Gianni Infantino’s scheme to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors. More historically, perhaps, the 55 nations that make up Uefa have reacted to this horror show by voting unanimously to boycott Fifa tournaments, including World Cups, if Infantino presses ahead. That would mean Spain and Portugal boycotting their own men’s World Cup next time around, which you’d think – not to call it too soon – would come off as slightly bad vibes.

A testing moment, then, for the haunted cue-ball. Again. Can it really already be time to turn to Infantino once more, even after he appeared in this spot only on Tuesday, after his 15-page Instagram crash-out about his haters? Yes. Yes, I’m afraid it can. Demanding the federations of the world sell off the World Cup to some fund led by Donald Trump’s son-in-law’s brother will regrettably draw attention to you in ways that will prove difficult to control. As indicated, the Fifa president’s plan has contrived to appear vulgar to the North American confederation, Concacaf, as well as the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).

Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, the Bahraini royal who leads the AFC, has issued a statement, declaring that “the AFC is deeply concerned that Fifa’s unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football, which are based on solidarity, cooperation and transparency”. He went on to call for “the highest standards of ethics and good governance”. And certainly, it’s always a pleasure to take an ethics lesson from a guy like this. A number of human rights organisations claim that during the Arab spring, Salman busied himself with identifying dissident players and other athletes, many of whom were imprisoned and tortured. (He denies this.) Yet even he simply cannot force himself through Infantino’s latest show of full-spectrum amorality.

It’s hard to escape the sense of gathering momentum against not only Infantino’s plan but the man himself, even from federations he has showered with disproportionate amounts of development cash over the years. A hotly defensive new statement declaring that “Nobody is selling football” emanated overnight from Fifa, which, to repeat, is proposing literally selling stakes in football to private investors.

It’s a testing moment, too, for one of the most extravagant pieces of corporate bullshit of our entire era – the post-binfire promise: “We will learn from this.” And so to the involvement of JP Morgan in Infantino’s scheme. Five years ago, JP Morgan ended up apologising to fans after its part in the imploded plan to create a breakaway European Super League. Back then, it said: “We clearly misjudged how this deal would be viewed by the wider football community and how it might affect them in the future.” Then, it was time to deploy the mother lode: “We will learn from this.” Will you though? JP Morgan evidently regards time as a great healer, because it is once again the bank at the centre of the firestorm, having been working with Fifa to raise $4.2bn with the new commercial vehicle.

At time of writing, Infantino was still insisting that he was pressing ahead with the scheme despite Uefa’s boycott pledge, which is certainly bold, given he would be trying to sell stakes in a tournament in which most of the best sides would not be playing. One intervention that has yet to materialise is any comment on the idea from Trump. The US president has, of course, been quite taken up over the past few days with his Middle East peace manoeuvres, crediting his “historic” agreement to disarm Hamas and other militant groups in Gaza to the machinations of his Board of Peace – a body whose inauguration, you might recall, Infantino showily attended. Perhaps the most excruciatingly on-brand move for the Fifa president now would be to post a 15-page Insta meltdown about how he was way more concerned with the slightly more important matter of Middle East peace as brought about by his special friend, than about trifling matters such as flogging the World Cup to private equity. Certainly wouldn’t put it past him.

But it is hard not to conclude that it is too much time with his special friend that has caused Infantino to overplay his hand in precisely the way he has. Maybe the real Trump derangement syndrome is the betas who suck up to the alpha in the apparent belief they will somehow osmotically absorb his unique characteristics and political gifts, and then themselves get away with the sort of stuff that only he has historically been able to pull. It’s personality cult as cargo cult.

We see it in Nigel Farage, a man who threw a byelection to which no one turned up, and is now having to chomp his way through a long hot summer of wasting time and money. And we see it in Infantino, a man who has spent the past year or two getting as up close and personal as possible with Trump, and presumably concluded that the US president’s ability to defy various laws of politics had rubbed magically off on him. But that isn’t how it has worked at all, as he is now finding out, presumably to his own bemusement. The first rule of politics, famously, is to learn how to count – and Infantino’s failure to do so now suggests his own days are numbered.

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 12:00:13 GMT

She lit up screens as Sex Education’s steamy sci-fi writer, wowed Streep in the West End and now she’s starring in the return of TV’s feelgood footie hit. The star talks about pretending to be sporty – and why she’s a total cheese string

By the time its third season came to an end in 2023, Ted Lasso was a Big Deal. The cosy comedy about an indefatigably positive American football coach gee-whizzing his way into the hearts of a London football team had won 13 Emmys and racked up more than 25bn minutes of viewing.

Contributing exactly zero minutes to this staggering stat was Tanya Reynolds, who joins the series in its fourth season as Ted’s assistant coach, Alice.

“I don’t know where I was!” she tells me with a helpless shrug as we chat. “I mean, I am a bit of a hermit. I do sort of live under a rock, so it’s not surprising I missed it.” She had heard of it, she assures me, and accepted the invitation to audition because it was “so unlike anything I’ve done before. I just was like: ‘Football coach. Mad. Yeah, OK.’” A week after sending her tape and thinking nothing more of it “because I didn’t think it was very good”, Tanya had a Zoom with the show’s co-creator, writer and titular star, Jason Sudeikis, who offered her the part on the spot. She swiftly watched all three seasons and realised “I really want to be part of this world”.

She’s speaking from her north London home on a Monday morning – every hermit’s favourite time to meet a prying journalist who is snooping at your background (I spot candles, books – Tanya recommends her favourites on Instagram – and a huge painting of sunflowers, which she swings her camera towards so I can get a better look). In a sleeveless red top, her hair in a scrunchy, Reynolds is blissfully free of media-training gloss – her answers are peppered with pauses and rephrasings (or perhaps they’re just a result of her being a “nervous person”). She is also warm, never far from a face-splitting laugh and, like all self-respecting Brits, mocks herself routinely and expertly.

As we settle, amid apologies about her whirring washing machine (“I’m hoping it chills out. You know when it goes mental?”), I ask about Meryl Streep and Martin Short coming to see 1536, the play she is starring in when we speak, with Margot Robbie as co-producer.

“We’d known they were coming for weeks. We actually graffitied it backstage: MERYL STREEP IS COMING ON THE TENTH!” she says. “We all stood on the stage, lined up like …” she does her best impression of an old-timey family portrait, “and couldn’t speak. But they were so kind … We all cried. Meryl cried. It was lovely.”

She adds that “Margot’s input has been huge … It’s so wonderful that someone with that amount of power is championing really important work, new work.” And how beautiful is she in real life, on a scale of one to obscene? Reynolds laughs. “She’s like a painting that’s come to life.”

1536 is the latest entry on Reynolds’s impressive theatrical CV, which also includes playing Masha in The Seagull last year opposite Cate Blanchett, and being nominated for an Olivier award in 2024 for her performance in A Mirror at the Almeida. But many will still know her best for her breakout role in Netflix’s Sex Education as Lily Iglehart – the space-bun sporting, cosplaying teen writer of alien erotica (The Trial of Glenoxi: Fucklord of the Universe being one of her efforts). The show proved a hotbed for young talent, with Ncuti Gatwa and Aimee Lou Wood among the cast. “I remember feeling in my very first days: ‘I am in the presence of superstars,’” says Reynolds.

She has since become a TV fixture, starring in Netflix’s bubonic plague romp The Decameron, in which she stole the show as wild maid turned “noblewoman” Licisca, and the BBC’s The Other Bennet Sister, where she played a deliciously disdainful Caroline Bingley (please Google the primrose-eating scene). There have been films, too, including Alice Lowe’s era-hopping comedy Timestalker.

Encouraged by Lowe, Reynolds wrote her own film, Dog Person, which she will direct (“I’m definitely terrified, for sure”) and star in, alongside Hugh Bonneville and James Norton. “Hopefully” shooting this year, it follows a thirtysomething woman, exhausted by life’s pressures, who “discovers this desire to be a dog”. (As if by magic, her own dog, a shaggy rescue called Borage, pads in at this point, after a trip to the vet).

Born in Hemel Hempstead into “not a theatrical family at all” (her Italian dad was a builder and her mum a sign painter – both were “quite quiet and quite shy”), Reynolds decided, aged four “or maybe six”, to be an actor. Where did that come from?

“I don’t. Know,” she enunciates. “I was always showing off and I remember my mum saying: ‘You’re brilliant at acting,’ and something in my brain was like: ‘Oh, I’ll do that.’ My parents, even though they we were not even adjacent to that world … never made it seem like it would be hard.” She was the first person in her family to go to university before winning a fully funded scholarship to the Oxford School of Drama – the only way she could afford to go.

Given that she “never had a backup plan”, what does she think about the decline of drama in schools? “It’s crazy to me that drama’s even on the chopping block of the curriculum,” she says. “That breaks my heart … The drama department was always my safe space. It’s so upsetting to me that there are kids that may not be able to explore that side of themselves because of government cuts. What is happening? It’s absolutely mad.”

If there is a through-line in Reynolds’s career, it is refreshingly complex characters – flawed, forthright, spiky, violent. Playing Licisca, she says, helped her find her “feral” side. “It’s always been there but it never comes out – unless in a medieval costume!”

Coach Alice is another complicated proposition. She glowers through much of my allotted four episodes, eyeing Ted’s proffered high fives as if she might catch rabies, or worse, fun. But there are glimmers of an unfurling. “I was quite scared at the thought of playing someone tough. The thought of me being tough is hilarious. Because I am a cheese string,” she laughs. “[But] she’s almost performing at the beginning … Particularly in fields that have been historically male-dominant, I think women can often feel they have to present as the opposite to what is typically regarded as feminine. Alice is trying to be this sturdy, unemotional, humourless machine. But what the show is so good at is showing that, beneath any exterior, no matter how tough or spiky, there’s complexity and depth and tenderness.”

Indeed, the show is still a wholesome delight: reliably funny, big on cockle-warming, and this season with a great dollop of female empowerment thanks to its new storyline, in which Ted coaches Richmond’s women’s team. It is also a welcome break from the incessant violence against women on our screens, and indeed in all art forms. I mention last month’s revelation that nine out of 10 bestselling novels in the UK feature a murdered woman. “Yes!” shouts Reynolds, head in hands in exasperation.

“A big part of why I loved Ted Lasso so much was that it’s exactly the kind of TV I want to watch right now,” she says. “Personally, and maybe this is because of my own slightly nervous, anxious disposition …” a pause, “or maybe it’s because I’m just fucking exhausted, like so many women out there are just exhausted of ... yeah,” she trails off, rubbing her eyes wearily. “But I can’t watch things that are violent, and especially violent towards women. I just can’t,” she concludes.

“1536,” she adds, “is basically a play about how history is repeating itself [and asking] how far have we moved on from that time that a king [Henry VIII] decided to start changing the laws so he could kill his wives.” A gallows laugh. “Take us out of our huge dresses and put us in jeans, and you could have the same script, essentially.” She adds: “Ted Lasso is very different but its whole thing is about optimism and positivity and … communicating with each other. That’s the kind of telly I’m craving.”

Others who have been craving Ted will be pleased to see many of the original cast returning. In fact, outside of the footballers, Reynolds is the only new lead. How was her first day on set?

“I was so nervous. And they write as they go, so it wasn’t like we had 10 scripts in advance. By the time I started, I had read two,” she says. “They know where they would like to go but they’re also so open to collaboration and they write for the actors, so everything’s getting built as you’re going.”

A lot of her scenes were with “genius improvisers” Sudeikis and Brendan Hunt (the co-creator and writer who plays Coach Beard). “So much of the improv was just them being hilarious, and me trying not to laugh. The whole shoot felt like an exercise in ‘Don’t laugh. Just don’t laugh.’”

They also helped Reynolds find her footballing feet. “Like a lot of people, I definitely have gotten into women’s football in the last couple of years but I had to up the ante getting this [job].” Despite watching “more football than I’ve probably ever watched”, the match scenes proved tricky. “They filmed the coaches separately, so we’re not actually watching any football. The lads would improv and shout things out. I just was like ‘Er, kick! Go on, um, kick the ball!’ I had to constantly ask Brendan and Jason: ‘What’s a good football-coachy thing to say?’”

The release of Ted Lasso will no doubt catapult Reynolds to a new level of stardom. But despite being “obnoxiously sure of [herself]” at primary school, she has been dogged by imposter syndrome throughout her career. Surely it’s getting better with all her successes, I ask?

“To be honest, I think it’s maybe getting worse!” she laughs a ‘what you gonna do?’ laugh. “It gets worse every year. The way I’m dealing with it currently is to take every job as it comes, do my best with it, and then afterwards I don’t watch anything. I just think: ‘I’m just gonna keep going until they tell me I can’t.’”

Ted Lasso is on Apple TV from 5 August.

‘Change is happening! I can cut off my hair and misbehave’: Vicky Krieps on rage, rebellion, and rejecting Hollywood

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 12:00:13 GMT

After her star turn in Phantom Thread, everyone expected a move to Tinseltown – but the actor embraced indie European films instead. It’s because of a lifelong instinct to be bold, she says

Back when she was a rising actor, Vicky Krieps had her fill of people telling her what not to do. When she got pregnant in her 20s, she was advised not to have the baby as it would derail her career, but she did it anyway. When, after playing a fashion designer’s muse in Paul Thomas Anderson’s Phantom Thread, she went back to making low-budget French films, she was, she says, “actually laughed at. It just seemed absurd to these people that I would turn my back on Hollywood and invest so much energy and passion in something that wasn’t giving me money.”

Yet Krieps’s determination to forge her own path has reaped rewards. For the last decade she has had one foot in the Hollywood mainstream, appearing in Fede Álvarez’s The Girl in the Spider’s Web and M Night Shyamalan’s Old, while keeping the other firmly in independent cinema where she has freedom to experiment. Krieps also does her utmost to avoid the pantomime of red-carpet events. On the occasions she does make an appearance, she will stick out her tongue or give photographers the finger. “I always smile when I’m doing it. But I’m telling them: ‘Guys, this is really ridiculous and the shouting is a bit much. Just talk nicely to me.’”

It comes as no surprise to learn that Krieps, 42, who was born and raised in Luxembourg and speaks four languages, has declined to make the obligatory move to Los Angeles. For the past 15 years, she has lived in Berlin – though, when we speak over video call, she is in Greece, which she regularly visits since marrying her husband, the Greek film production assistant Lazaros Gounaridis, last year. (They met on the set of the 2023 film Hot Milk.)

Sporting a pixie cut and a crisp white shirt, Krieps is open, thoughtful and speaks with unusual seriousness and candour about her job which, for her, is all-consuming. “Sometimes I feel less like an actor and more like a scientist who is experimenting on my own body,” she says.

This immersive approach can take a toll. Two weeks after wrapping her forthcoming film Love Me Tender, in which she plays a woman who loses custody of her young son, Krieps began feeling “really bad in my body. I was lying on my bed, and I couldn’t move my arms and my neck. I thought I had a serious disease.” She saw doctors and had an MRI, and found everything was fine but the pain itself was real. “I think I had assembled so much psychological pain that it became physical. You know the saying ‘My heart is aching’? I feel that in my whole chest.”

Directed by Anna Cazenave Cambet and based on the autobiographical novel by Constance Debré, Love Me Tender challenges the unfair expectations foisted upon mothers. Krieps plays Clémence, who has given up a well-paid legal career to write books. After separating amicably from her husband, Laurent, she gives away most of her belongings, immerses herself in the club scene and explores her sexuality. When she eventually tells Laurent that she is dating women, he appears to accept it. But afterwards, he makes dark allegations about her and questions her mental stability in a bid to secure sole custody of their eight-year-old son, Paul.

“Laurent,” says Krieps, “is an example of when the male ego starts to rage because it is hurting and doesn’t understand what is happening. He’s thinking: ‘Why am I not included in this? Why did this train leave without me?’” When “there is no real dialogue between men and women, men like this can become mean, sour and self-righteous”.

As their case creaks through the courts, Clémence is denied permission to see Paul. When they finally meet after nearly 18 months apart, it’s for an hour every fortnight under supervision. Those meetings, where Clémence must hold in her grief and keep it together for her son, are devastating. The tension of those scenes, Krieps realised, “caused me to hit a wall. But it was good for me to learn that the next time I work on something like this I will need to look after myself and take longer breaks while filming.”

Krieps has spent much of her career playing women trying to break out of the boxes that others have put them in. In Phantom Thread, she is Alma, a serving maid who is expected to remain meek in front of Daniel Day-Lewis’s dictatorial dressmaker but instead stands her ground and answers back. In 2022’s terrific Corsage, she is Elisabeth, Empress of Austria, celebrated in the 19th century for her beauty and her tiny waist (made tinier by ruthless corsetry), who rebels against her tightly controlled existence. In Emily Atef’s More Than Ever, she is a terminally ill woman fighting for the right to live out her days on her own terms.

“I talked to Charlotte Rampling about this after we worked on the Jim Jarmusch movie Father Mother Sister Brother,” Krieps reflects. “We realised what we have in common is that we are constantly drawn to exploring the edge of a [character], the place where it starts to hurt. I think I take this to every part.”

Where possible, Krieps tries to work with female directors – or rather, she clarifies, directors who preside over “feminine sets. I’ve worked with men where the set was not masculine and there was no male ego. And there are female directors who unfortunately operate with a male ego. A lot of film sets are run like the military and are very hierarchy-driven. It’s incredibly loud and it’s about pushing. But take a director like [Corsage’s] Marie Kreutzer: her set is extremely quiet and calm. No one is shouting. And the positive side to that is when you create silence, you start hearing each other.”

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

Picking apart societal roles and rejecting authority is in Krieps’s blood. Her grandfather was in the resistance during the second world war and survived internment at Dachau. He later became a socialist politician in Luxembourg and successfully mounted a campaign to abolish the death penalty. “Knowing that someone so close almost lost his life to fight for humanity, this is something you can’t forget,” reflects Krieps. Meanwhile, her mother “is just a crazy hippy, in the best way, and raised me to question everything: how do I know this is what they say it is? I think this made me dare to be brave and risk my livelihood.”

That daring surfaced when a teenage Krieps attended her school graduation ceremony and thanked her teachers for giving her “proof that I know how to learn off by heart, that I know how to copy and how to shut my mouth”. The incident made the papers in Luxembourg. It is also evident in her habit of tweaking the words and actions of her characters mid-scene. In Corsage, she launched herself out of a window in frustration at her onscreen husband (she emerged unscathed; the scene was filmed on the ground floor). The moment was not in the script but nonetheless made the final cut, with Krieps’s character sustaining a fracture from the fall. “These things are not premeditated but sometimes you just feel something that feels like the truth, and it wants to come out,” Krieps says.

True to her straddling of popular and arthouse entertainment, this autumn Krieps can be seen in Ryan Murphy’s series Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story playing the Borden family’s maid Bridget Sullivan. She has also just finished work on Emma Doucet, a film by the French director Élise Girard about a single mother who falls in love with the French prime minister and which, she says, is “close to a poem. It’s very nouvelle vague.”

Krieps acknowledges that her questing spirit and single-mindedness as an actor wouldn’t have been possible even 20 years ago. “You wouldn’t have a woman who’s allowed to do all these different movies, and not give a fuck, cut off her hair and generally misbehave. The fact that I exist shows me change is happening and is possible.”

Love Me Tender is in UK and Irish cinemas from 7 August.

Digested week: As wildfires rage, should I buy a helicopter or marry a guy with a bunker?

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 11:47:11 GMT

Plus, train toilet roulette, an astonishingly stoic hiker and the tradwife paradox

As I read the headlines about Europe on fire, and imagine – or is it true? – I can smell smoke from the Suffolk wildfire encroaching on a nuclear power facility a county away from me, I’m remembering the wisdom of a friend who told me years ago that she wasn’t aiming to buy a house but a helicopter. “Because,” said Sarah, gesturing around us, “it’s going to be no good trying to get across flood waters or dusty plains or great drifts of virus-ridden corpses. You’re going to need to go up.”

However. I have noticed a trend emerging among the true oracles, the true bellwethers of society – our lady film stars. The likes of Reese Witherspoon, Nicole Kidman and Jennifer Garner are all taking up not with fellow stars but financiers – usually tech financiers – who are the very richest of the rich. And you know what this means. It means they do not have just helicopter money (even a lady film star has helicopter money) – they have bunker money.

The parameters have subtly shifted. The dream is not lifelong luxury in a mansion or two. It is survival in subterranean safety with whoever can fund it. I now have to decide between buying a helicopter or marrying a bunkerman. I hope I haven’t left it too late.

The sex toy retailer Pulse & Cocktails has taken over Little Chef. This is an unhappy sentence. But it is, alas, true. Or rather, it is true that Pulse & Cocktails has taken over the service station chain’s former venues to allow its customers more privacy.

I have many questions. One: have drivers to Kettering never heard of the internet? Two: is selling roadside gimp masks really more profitable than hash browns and American-style pancakes? Am I so detached from the national appetite? And, most importantly, three: what is going on with this name? Pulse & Cocktails? It’s terrible. Rhythmically awful and in its evocations, worse. “Pulse” suggests checking for one and unless this is a terrifically niche roadside sex shop (and again, I would point you to the financial viability issue with which we are already struggling in an interwebbed world), is not a fabulously sexy opener. And “cocktails” is meh.

Or it suggests you are throwing one in the face of the unresponsive body upon which you, for reasons best known to yourself, have designs. Or am I missing a pun? There should surely be a pun here. And no, the first syllable of “cocktails” is not enough. Answers, of a semantic nature only, on a postcard to the usual address please.

Train drivers are considering strike action over a lack of loo facilities. Now look. Up the working man and all that, but let’s extend that.

I am travelling by train a lot at the moment and I think it’s time customers got a turn. What is the equivalent of customers striking until we get not just working toilets but – and this is a vital detail – guaranteed working toilets?

As someone who needs to wee about every 12 minutes, each time I step on to a train, I also step into a vortex of anxiety and unknowns. And do you know what anxiety isn’t good for? Yes, exactly.

We can’t withhold our journeys – we need to get to places. We can’t withhold our fares because we’d get very arrested and still not get to our places. I’m on the verge of suggesting just protest-weeing where you sit if there isn’t a working convenience conveniently close by, but I think I’m edging too near niche Little Chef territory again, so we’ll stop here.

A hiker in Montana’s Beartooth Mountains made a 10-mile, six-hour descent after being impaled through the chest by his walking pole, rather than call out the medical rescue team. “I’m pretty confident this is outside my chest wall,” 32-year-old David Cifaldi told the two friends he was crossing the Froze-to-Death Plateau (no, really) with on the way to Granite Peak of the 44in metal stick piercing his torso.

Now, Cifaldi is a nurse but “I’m pretty confident this 44in metal stick that entered under my left arm and came out of my back isn’t going to move and kill me so let’s tra-la-la down this ice-covered mountain to save everyone’s time and resources” is still a ballsy move. If this guy’s got bunker money too, I think he could be The One.

This week I have spent a lovely afternoon playing with and kissing the delectable face off a friend’s baby, picked nearly seven homegrown tomatoes from my garden and defrosted the fridge. Am I … Am I a tradwife now? On the one hand, I have quite enjoyed myself. On the other, I don’t believe in God, am too short for prairie dresses, and when I bake I kill people.

Tradwives obsess me. The convolutions of the thought processes involved. Celebrating traditional domesticity while monetising every moment of it in the most modern way possible. Doting on a brood of children who are being raised the old-fashioned way while being paraded on the internet.

Selling a vision of effortless ease and fulfilment while keeping a schedule that periodically puts you in bed with exhaustion (as the leader of the tradwife pack Hannah Neeleman once mentioned).

Ostentatiously deferring to your husband while building an empire that rests entirely on your work, talents and looks and would disappear overnight without you. Amazing. Women – not for the first time, I feel we really need to get together and talk about a few things.

Release schedule: when to wee and when to wait during this summer’s biggest movies

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 11:00:13 GMT

With run-times hitting three hours, you will probably need to take a bathroom break during this season’s blockbusters. Here’s a handy guide for your urination calculations

‘An intermission is a must’: why Greek cinemas are adding a loo break to The Odyssey

You will almost certainly need to urinate during Christopher Nolan’s epic. Do not make the same mistake I did, and sneak off after the big cyclops setpiece. You might assume that the plot will relax after this, but you will be wrong. If your cinema’s toilet is as far from the screen as my cinema’s, you will end up missing most of the Trojan Horse section. Much better would be to cling on until after the horse, because then you’ll only miss the Laestrygonians. These are the giants depicted on the film’s poster but you pretty much get the gist of the scene from the poster anyway.

This feels bizarre to say, but do not go to the toilet at any point during the first half of this movie, because it is somehow the most lovingly observed tribute to the early days of Hollywood in recent years. It almost exclusively deals with the bumpy transition from silent films to talkies, with such carefully observed tenderness that it is genuinely quite moving. If you think that sounds a lot like Damien Chazelle’s Babylon, then you would be right (including the elephant). However, since that film didn’t have minions in it and this film does, this is better. Anyway, this element burns out after about an hour, at which point you can wee at will.

Plenty of choices here, depending on why you went to see the film in the first place. If you want to find yourself emotionally engaged with the heart of the film, then get up and go to the toilet whenever the army of Buzz Lightyears arrive on the screen. Until close to the very end, these scenes are just superfluous fan service that have no bearing whatsoever on the plot. However, if you went purely because you love superfluous fan service, then you should probably get up and go as soon as Jessie unearths the lunchbox full of Emily’s memories, you heartless monster.

Look, Backrooms derives a lot of its power from the sustained eeriness of its tone – which is to say that the film essentially bores you into terror. As such, any trip to the toilet has the potential to ruin the effect. But needs must, so perhaps try to go about halfway through when Renate Reinsve enters the shop. You’ll miss a long scene of her wandering around. If you’re invested in the film, the scene serves to ratchet the tension even higher. If you’re busting for the toilet, though, it will feel so endless that you’ll convince yourself that the film is punishing you for having a bladder.

At two-and-a-half hours, Disclosure Day feels a little longer than it needs to be, and this will go double if you managed to slurp down an entire large Sprite before the trailers finished. I checked the trusty RunPee app for this, and I am in broad agreement that the best time to go involves some counterintuitive thinking. A little over halfway through, there is an action sequence where Emily Blunt’s car gets pushed on to some train tracks. What follows is a long and not particularly interesting sequence, the likes of which you will have seen many times before.

I don’t know if you’ve ever taken a 98-minute pee, but nothing in this film is good or memorable, so why not try? Heck, you may as well walk all the way back home and use your own toilet. You literally won’t miss anything.

Will Burnham fix our barbaric prisons – or cave to rightwing populism? The answer is a tragedy

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 10:22:23 GMT

England and Wales’s prisons are overcrowded, drug-infested and barbaric. Labour has halted a once-in-a-generation effort to change that sorry state

Andy Burnham’s “pausing” of the Starmer government’s prisoner release scheme and the resignation of its architect, James Timpson, are disasters. They indicate a Downing Street that puts populism ahead of policy. England and Wales’s prisons are a total disgrace. Timpson was the first justice minister in 15 years prepared to handle them. Now he has gone. Although he said it had been an “honour” to serve in the government, it is reasonable to assume he resigned in disgust.

In August 2024, the prison population in England and Wales hit a record high. The following March, a savage report from the public accounts committee warned that prisons, already full to bursting, could not cope with such numbers and would overflow by the start of 2026.

The early release of 16,000 prisoners in the last three months of 2024 eased pressure on the system, but now another crisis is forecast for this November. Under Timpson’s law passed in January, a surge in electronic tagging was being frantically prepared for another bout of early releases in September. But pressure from probation unions, parliamentary opponents and victim groups, backed by the rightwing press, has persuaded Burnham to call a halt. Chaos beckons.

Victims of crime may deserve sympathy and support, but they should not dictate justice policy. Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, should not do anything but apologise for her party in government reducing prisons to their current state.

The facts cannot be repeated too often. England and Wales’s penal policy is the most backward in western Europe. They imprison roughly twice the proportion of the population as Germany, and three times as many as Italy and Spain. Prisoner numbers in England and Wales have doubled in 30 years.

In 2024, a quarter of prisoners in England and Wales were having to share cells designed for one person. Two-thirds were estimated to spend most of their days in their cells with little to occupy them, fuelling reports from prisoners of mental health problems and self-harm. In the 21st century, this is indefensibly primitive.

Prisoners are some of the nation’s most assiduous consumers of drugs. About 40% of prisoners in England and Wales say it is easy to access drugs while inside, cells are simply awash in illegal substances. As for training and rehabilitation to prepare for release, curbed budgets and staff shortages have seen them collapsing.

Half of short-term prisoners reoffend as a result. Rehabilitation – the one sure way to cut reoffending – is a farce. Community sentences such as Timpson’s favoured intensive supervision courts offer an alternative but are still in their infancy.

As for England and Wales’s fixation with incarcerating women, in December 2024, a quarter of those in prison were on remand, awaiting what might not have been imprisonment at all. Most need help, not separation from their families and loved ones, with many said to be victims of worse crimes than they commit. The Prison Reform Trust has pleaded for sentences to take account of family stability, but to no effect. Even Reform UK’s Colin Sutton, the new police and crime commissioner for Norfolk, has said most women in custody should be released.

To allow prisons policy to be led by public opinion is absurd. It should be led by evidence of what works. Many non-violent prisoners will be drug and alcohol addicts chronically in need of effective treatment in the community. There are also the kind of prisoners I used to visit prisons in the London area. They are victims of family or personal breakdown, poverty, homelessness or sheer misfortune. Above all they needed hostels and help.

Nothing more infuriates the pro-prisons lobby than mention of Norway. The reason is that Norway’s prisons work. In the 1990s, the country suffered a dire 70% recidivism rate. It examined evidence and opted for drastic reform. This tied new “correction centres” to local communities, relating rehabilitation to local jobs and family ties. Prisoners were treated with dignity. Reoffending plummeted and Norway’s prison population has been drastically reduced.

The late Ann Widdecombe, a former Tory prisons minister, boldly went to Norway in 2020 with a television crew to see what she called The World’s Most Luxurious Prison. She called it a holiday camp. She admitted it “worked” but was appalled at the absence of what she regarded as penal retribution. Loss of liberty was combined with a total lack of humiliation.

Nothing more typified the British approach to social policy than Widdecombe’s reaction. Foreigners must be wrong, even if she could not explain why. To her, as to many of her compatriots, the survival of our Dickensian prisons embodied justice. Their harshness was an appropriate response to crime. Even if they did not “work”, they must be right.

A liberal society must be able to look abroad, examine evidence and be open to reform. Even in the prison-loving US, states from Texas to Oregon and North Dakota have visited Norway and are professing to learn from it. They know it makes no sense to imprison but not rehabilitate.

Our justice policy is crippled by changes of leadership. Catherine McKinnell, appointed as Timpson’s replacement, is the 13th prison minister in the past decade – a ludicrous number, as if it was a hobby rather than a job. Policy is left at the mercy of rightwing sentiment, fed by victims groups and the press. They are now joined by the prime minister. Beware the autumn.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

My family is coming apart – so it’s time for one last video game session

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 09:00:10 GMT

I wanted our last family games night to be the best fun we’ve ever had. Maybe we should have stuck with Mario Kart …

It is the end of an era for the Diamond family. For 20 years, there have been five of us living together. It has not been easy. Militant vegan daughters, sons who have inherited Scottish tempers, and a youngest child who attracts trouble like an industrial magnet, have meant our house has been conflict-laden at times. Throw in the fact that we are beset with all manner of mental health bobbins and chronic illnesses that resulted in two of our three kids almost dying in hospitals and you get a family that is combustible – but extremely close.

Through it all, we had games. They always brought us back together. Not just us all hunkering over Super Mario Kart like some kind of UN-mandated family therapy, but the conversations that happen when any of us spy another playing something new. Games are a cultural touchstone that helped us crack through the veneer of disagreements and distrust and remind us that we have more things in common than we sometimes feel.

But now we are moving out of the house we have shared for years. My wife has to go back to the UK for family reasons, #1 Child is moving in with her boyfriend and youngest child is moving in with a friend. This leaves the Son and I – we are moving into an apartment for the next few months, which Charlie is already dubbing the bro-tel. (I am filled with equal parts excitement and dread about this.)

So I wanted one last family games night to remind us of simpler times before we all go our separate ways. I wanted it to be the best fun we have ever had. I wanted … Quiplash!

Quiplash is one of the most important games in the history of our family, because I view it as the game that trained my kids to be funny. Seeing them all become fairly high-level comedy beings has been the greatest thrill of my life as a dad.

It’s a simple “fill in the blanks or answer the question with something funny to get the most votes” game, the beauty of it being you can play using mobile phones as controllers and five people can play. That’s why I have it as a go-to. Getting any family together to do anything is like herding particularly wilful sheep, and when was the last time you saw a shepherd try that while hunting for 10 working batteries for gaming controllers? Exactly.

It’s not just the genuinely funny answers that get votes: there is also a lot of love for old family running gags, most of which are at my expense, usually my baldness or my rigidity with rules.

However, while I am impressed by my grownup kids’ quick-thinking quippery, I am still appalled by some of their spelling. So for our final game, I introduce a rule that you can only vote for answers spelt correctly. This rule is not just ignored but aggressively mocked with answers that are part punchline and part Welsh street name.

I am in last place because they can tell which answers are from me. So, I start deliberately entering badly spelt answers to confuse them, so they give up trying to play the game seriously and while I am writing quality punchlines such as “God said ‘wrong door’” (you had to be there), I am faced with answers from them such as “pee pee poo poo”.

And then the rows break out. My two youngest kids work at the same trendy bar/restaurant, and they have issues with each other. One suggested a role for the other there that they are not happy about, so they declare they never want to work in the same place together again. Impressively, during the argument, my son still manages to answer “skittle flavour that just missed the cut” with “narly Netenyahu nectarine”. Which almost got my vote until I noticed that neither Netanyahu nor gnarly are spelt like that.

Sign up to Pushing Buttons

after newsletter promotion

The row escalates. Wife and #1 Child have reverted to doomscrolling on their phones instead. No one wants to play. It’s all falling apart. Not just this desperate attempt at one final family gaming session, but the family itself. In one week, our matriarch, the most important one of us, will be on the other side of the Atlantic. In a couple of months, #1 Child could be the only one still actually living on this side of it.

Memories start flooding back: the summer I spent playing Super Mario Sunshine with #1 Child when she was five. Evading guard dogs in the snow with my son on Call of Duty: Modern Warfare when he wasn’t much older. Seeing my youngest child fall in love with Kirby. The years of Mario Kart, Mortal Kombat and Just Dance. The conversations. The debates. The windups. There is such joy in those moments but now they are spilling through my fingers like water.

I think of all the times in recent years when one of the kids has asked me if I want to play a game with them. And I’ve been “too busy”. I wish I had all those moments back to create more memories.

My wife, ever the peacemaker of the family, declares the next day that we will have one more go at this the night before she goes back to Blighty. That prospect seems as good as it gets right now.

New solar panels in Great Britain at 15-year high as fossil fuel costs soar

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 09:00:09 GMT

Boom in solar farms and home installations in first half of 2026 began shortly after start of US-Israel war against Iran

Great Britain has recorded more new solar power installations in the first half of this year than in any six-month period since 2011, as households turn to rooftop panels to help cut their energy bills.

An analysis of the government’s official figures shows that Great Britain added 142,536 solar installations in the first six months of the year, putting it on track to top last year’s record solar additions.

The government data, which includes large ground-mounted solar farms and rooftop panels, showed that the half-year solar boom is second only to the record 167,316 installations recorded in the second half of 2011, when the first large-scale solar farm was built in Cornwall on the site of a disused tin mine.

Most of the new solar installations recorded in the government’s official figures are on household rooftops, although these smaller solar systems make up slightly less than a third of the country’s total solar power capacity.

More households have fitted solar panels to their rooftops in recent years, hoping to cut their energy bills by generating their own low-cost electricity as fossil fuels have caused bills to rocket, according to energy companies.

The government’s data shows that more households are taking up grants to replace their gas boilers with low-carbon heating alternatives. The total number of applications for the boiler upgrade scheme reached 4,512 last month, up by 21% compared with June last year.

Heat pumps are expected to be in higher demand in the months ahead after the government raised its grant funding by 20% last week, from £7,500 to £9,000, to help cover the costs of replacing fossil fuel heating. Andy Burnham has also cut VAT on electricity bills from October, which makes running a heat pump cheaper.

E. ON Next, which is expected to become the UK’s biggest energy retailer, said it has recorded a 151% rise in the number of homes installing solar panels in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year.

“More and more households are realising just how much they can save by generating and storing their own energy,” said Phil Gilbert, a director at E. ON Next. Some of its customers have saved up to £600 a year on their annual energy bill when signed on to its solar and battery tariff, he said.

“People want to engage with their energy use, take control of their bills and rely less on the grid – and solar gives them a practical way to do that,” Gilbert added.

Octopus Energy, which is currently Great Britain’s biggest energy supplier, also noted a sharp increase in solar panel sales within weeks of the Middle East conflict causing oil and gas prices to soar. The supplier said sales increased by more than 54% in March compared with the month before. In total there are more than 2m solar installations across Great Britain.

The 1.4 megawatt (MW) Wheal Jane solar farm is now easily dwarfed by newer projects, including the 373MW Cleve Hill project in Kent, which became Britain’s largest working solar development when it reached full power last summer, and the 800MW Springwell solar farm in Lincolnshire, which is expected to begin generating in 2029.

By the end of August UK bill payers living in flats or rented properties will be able to join the millions of people across Europe using “balcony solar panels” to lower their bills, according to legislation passed this month.

‘Extremely scary findings’ show climate crisis is supercharging Europe’s wildfire weather

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 07:00:07 GMT

Latest study says global heating has made hot, dry and windy conditions in Spain at least 20 times more likely

The extreme heat and drought stoking huge wildfires in Spain and France were made far more likely by the climate crisis, a scientific analysis has found.

Global heating made hot, dry and windy weather at least 20 times more likely in Spain and twice as likely in France, experts from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) consortium calculated. The finding is the latest to pin the blame for the continent’s sweltering and deadly summer firmly on the heating caused by the burning of oil, gas and coal.

The intense heatwave at the end of June, which is estimated to have killed 20,000 people, could not have happened without the extra heat trapped by carbon pollution, a previous WWA study showed. Another found that the climate crisis-driven heat was “sucking soils dry” as extreme drought spread across Europe.

Searing heat and parched land led to very high “daily severity ratings”, the metric that was used in the new analysis and which measures how severe a wildfire will be if ignited. Studies of the 2025 wildfires also found they were supercharged by the climate crisis.

This year’s wildfires in western Europe have been made worse by a wet winter and spring, which boosted the growth of vegetation, which then dried out and provided fuel for the fires – so-called whiplash conditions. Global heating is making winters wetter and summers drier and hotter in Europe.

Dr Clair Barnes, a research associate at Imperial College London and part of the WWA study team, said: “We’ve seen repeatedly how climate change increases hot, dry, flammable conditions that are extremely conducive to wildfires.

“What’s unique about [the July fires in Spain and France] is that it’s still early in the season – and with another heatwave looming, these findings are extremely scary. What we’re seeing is a clear sign of the escalating impacts of [human-caused] warming.”

Julie Arrighi, the director of programmes at Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, said: “What we are seeing now in Spain and France goes well beyond what we would expect from past events.”

The wildfires have released huge plumes of toxic smoke. Dr Augustin Colette, at the French National Institute for Industrial Environment and Risks, said: “The smoke increased particulate [pollution] peak levels up to 20 times above what is considered ‘fair air quality’, and extremely poor air quality was felt up to 400 km away from the fires.” About 1.5 million people a year are estimated to have their lives shortened by wildfire smoke.

Severe wildfires have burned across Spain and France since early July, killing people, destroying thousands of homes, and forcing more than 300,000 people to flee. The WWA analysis assessed the seven-day period with the highest daily severity ratings (DSR) for each country. The scientists used weather records and established statistical methods to estimate how much more likely a week of extremely high DSR is in today’s heated world compared with in the world before mass fossil-fuel burning raised the global temperature by 1.4C (2.5F).

Big wildfires have also broken out in the UK and Greece, where three firefighters lost their lives.

The UN’s climate chief, Simon Stiell, said: “These European megafires show how fast climate-driven extreme heat and dry landscapes can turn wildfires into devastating national disasters.

“Humanity continuing to burn colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas is making these conditions more dangerous, and these megafires more deadly and destructive,” he said. “But the solutions are equally clear: all countries must move faster from fossil fuels to renewables and protect people from worsening climate impacts, from wildfires, to megastorms and floods, to droughts hitting food production.”

The Burnham bounce is eclipsing the Green surge – and Zack Polanski’s radical hope is being tested

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 07:00:07 GMT

The new PM is enjoying a honeymoon period but, longer-term, the Greens have the freedom to say whatever Labour won’t

Cackling happily into their pints, the two most powerful men in the country scoff their way through a selection of pub snacks.

Pork scratchings or scampi fries? Or maybe old-school peanuts? It’s hardly the toughest choice currently facing Andy Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, so some may find this week’s made-to-go-viral Instagram reel of them gleefully ranking crisps a bit silly. (I’m writing this, laptop balanced on my knee, beside a hospital bed; right now I couldn’t care less whether the chancellor likes bacon fries.) But I do care, intensely, about a government that is promising once-in-a-generation reform of care for elderly people winning the public’s confidence for long enough to actually carry out that promise, and weirdly in 2026 that means chomping crisps on camera to establish your bona fides with people who’d scroll straight past conventional political content.

Pulling off this kind of freewheeling, seemingly casual content actually takes surprising skill, as the compulsively online Green leader, Zack Polanski – until now the reigning king of leftwing British TikTok – has just inadvertently demonstrated. On Wednesday, the police cleared Polanski of any wrongdoing over reposting a picture of a man in a T-shirt emblazoned with a guillotine and the words, “We’re only making plans for Nigel”. (Polanski says it was among a bunch of images he uploaded without looking properly first, and he deleted it as soon as he realised.) An innocent mistake but a sloppy one, coming days after the alleged murder of the Reform spokeswoman Ann Widdecombe; the kind he can no longer afford to make too often.

The unexpected resurgence of hope, joy and radical energy in the Labour party over the last week and a half poses an unmistakable threat to the leader who until now has had a virtual monopoly on those things. Hardened Green voters – those for whom Burnham’s “business-friendly socialism” will never be socialist enough, or who see the new prime minister’s support for more drilling in the North Sea as environmental vandalism – are going nowhere. But newcomers who migrated to the Greens because they felt Keir Starmer’s government had lost its moral compass, or become too relentlessly miserable, are now squarely in Burnham’s sights. Interestingly, the More in Common poll this week, which put Labour back in the lead for the first time since last March, found that “Burnham bounce” coming if anything more at the Greens’ expense than Reform’s.

When the new prime minister apologises for the way his predecessor approached the Gaza war, or condemns what he calls 40 failed years of neoliberalism, he’s signalling that it’s safe for those lost Labour voters to come home. When he’s messing about on Instagram, he’s reaching out to younger people unused to seeing Labour politicians doing anything interesting on Green-dominated feeds. And when he holds cross-party talks on fixing social care without either Polanski or Farage, then intentionally or not, he is sending a message about who he takes seriously. Polanski, whose partner works in palliative care, has spoken movingly about the issue. But it was only the Lib Dems and the Tories, Downing Street says, who actually wrote to the prime minister expressing interest in his call for a non-partisan approach to this difficult issue.

It would be ridiculous, of course, to think this Labour honeymoon can last. Keir Starmer was popular, right up until his first spending cut. The Green surge may be receding for the moment but it’s only five months since they left Labour for dust in the Gorton and Denton byelection, and it would be a surprise if they don’t at least improve on their 2024 performance in this week’s Manchester mayoral elections.

Yet something has clearly shifted. As recently as early May, 22% of Britons thought Polanski would be a better prime minister than Starmer, according to YouGov. But only 9% now prefer him to Burnham. The guillotine T-shirt affair, meanwhile, was merely the latest in a string of mistakes – from Polanski’s failure to register to vote in May’s local elections, to confusion over whether he paid enough council tax while living on a houseboat in London, to a spate of antisemitism allegations involving Green candidates at the local elections – that together raise questions about Polanski’s readiness for the remorseless scrutiny that wannabe main parties of the left inevitably face.

The Greens’ defence is to argue that only they can offer a “full fat” socialist revolution, not some watered down Burnhamite version. If he won’t impose rent controls or new property taxes – both ideas circulating around the sprawling Burnham camp that have died an unceremonious death since he entered Downing Street – then they will. Unconstrained by the realities of government, their freedom to say whatever Labour won’t could easily become a powerful weapon again given time and the inevitable disappointments of office, though it’s unclear how much time Burnham intends to give them. (He has publicly ruled out a snap election, but the current strategy – a blitzkrieg of exciting but vague announcements, starving Reform and the Greens of political oxygen but without giving them much to fight him on – wouldn’t half be good preparation for one.)

But for the next few weeks at least, it’s Burnham on whom the fickle political sun shines: Burnham who has the priceless opportunity to actually do something about what ails the country, rather than simply talk – however fluently or winningly – about it. Political careers, as he should know, are notoriously short these days. He should make the most of every moment while it lasts.

Think our basic rights are safe? In the age of oligarchs and corporate lobbying, think again

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 05:00:04 GMT

The global assault on our freedoms is coming ever closer to home. Just look at the sinister prosecution of UK lawyer Rajiv Menon

No more resistance in the US. The era of human rights is over, and dissent is once more forbidden. This is what certain billionaires and their concierges want, and this is the model they’re also seeking to project across the world. If we fail to resist, if our new prime minister is as weak and suggestible as the last one, this is what we will get. In fact, we are halfway there already.

Why? Because successive governments in the UK have succumbed to a global campaign to cancel our fundamental freedoms, a campaign led by oligarchs and corporations, the media they own and the junktanks they fund. A campaign that has become definitional for the second Trump presidency.

At a global summit convened by the US government earlier this month, the Trump administration officials Marco Rubio, Stephen Miller and Scott Bessent explained that they were redirecting counterterrorism efforts away from Islamic jihadism and towards “the political left”. Most of the examples they cited to justify this shift were more than 30 years old. Several times they had to dig down to the 1970s to find a sufficiently menacing threat. You could hear the barrel being scraped.

Without producing a shred of evidence, Rubio, the secretary of state, claimed that the Cuban government is “inextricably linked to the far-left groups and movements across and beyond the west”. The following week, his department sought to justify this claim with a report containing a long list of leftwing legislators, journalists and activists that attempted to link them to Cuba in ways that ranged from the tenuous to the hilarious. This is a well-honed tactic, used prolifically by the Nazis among others: they claimed dissenters, by definition, were part of an international communist conspiracy. They insisted, as Rubio did, that “it is time to crush this evil for ever”.

That wasn’t the only crude reminder. Miller, Donald Trump’s deputy chief of staff, maintained that when you see antifascist protests, “not one of the people that is demonstrating looks like a normal person. Not one looks normal. They’re all deformed in some way – in their appearance, in their dress, in their mannerism … their outer appearance becomes a manifestation of their inner hatred.” I’m just surprised he didn’t say “untermenschen”. The US government, by contrast, promotes “normal, healthy, ordered living”.

But what hit me even harder was Miller’s attack on “jury nullification”: jurors acquitting people who, he said, were “obviously guilty”. Shutting down this possibility has been an aim of illiberal governments and conservative judges around the world. We saw it in the UK in the prosecution of Trudi Warner and others for holding signs that state an ancient principle in English law: “Jurors have an absolute right to acquit a defendant according to their conscience.”

We see it in the astonishing prosecution, being pursued at the moment, of Rajiv Menon KC, who reminded jurors of this right at the trial of the Palestine Action campaigners he was defending. He became, as a result, the first lawyer in English history to be charged with contempt of court for a closing speech. If convicted, he faces up to two years’ imprisonment and will be struck off. Prosecuting lawyers for defending their dissident clients is more or less the definition of authoritarianism.

We also saw it in the assault Keir Starmer launched on jury trials as a whole, greatly curtailing, without any coherent justification, our strongest defence against injustice.

Starmer was a weak man, without a clear vision of his own, who was rolled by any powerful state or corporate lobby. He was no match for a well-funded and highly effective international campaign. A network of groups such as the American Legislative Exchange Council, funded by corporations and billionaires, has been producing “model legislation”. The groups test these laws in sympathetic jurisdictions. If they are found to work, they then press for their adoption elsewhere. The result is a sustained assault on our rights to protest, to political equality and to a habitable planet.

The globalisation of this attack on our fundamental rights is a key conservative aim. As capital operates everywhere, so should its ability to crush our objections. The long series of vicious anti-protest laws in the UK is an outcome of sustained lobbying by junktanks, the media and other governments. The result is a country that now keeps hundreds of political prisoners, a country in which you can get six months in jail for marching slowly down the street.

These oppressive laws have culminated – so far – in an act of parliament passed in April that enables the police to shut down any protest they deem to have a “cumulative” impact on the community. The only protests that have ever succeeded are those with a cumulative impact. Protest is acceptable as long as it’s useless. Let the people have their say, but only if we can’t hear them.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

The new laws have been accompanied by that age-old trick, traditionally associated with fascist regimes, of smearing leftwing dissidents as terrorists. As the rights group Liberty has pointed out, the definition of terrorism here has greatly expanded, to incorporate tactics formerly regarded as civil protest. This is what enabled Starmer’s government to ban Palestine Action.

The judge who referred Menon for contempt, Mr Justice Johnson, was also the first – at the same trial – to use the extraordinary powers quietly inserted by the Conservatives into the Sentencing Act 2020. These enable someone tried for one crime to be sentenced for another. The four Palestine Action protesters were convicted of ordinary crimes. But, without informing the jury, Johnson marked the case as having a “terrorist connection”. He then sentenced them for terrorist offences, which means much more prison time.

Already, his example has been followed by another judge: a different group of pro-Palestine protesters, who sprayed red paint and broke some windows of a branch of Barclays Bank, are about to be sentenced as terrorists, though neither they nor the jurors were told of this possibility during their trial for criminal damage. This means, of course, that they were unable to defend themselves against this far more serious charge.

Nothing is safe from the billionaire assault on humanity. None of our rights, however ancient and familiar, are impregnable. Fight for them now or lose them, perhaps for ever.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

After teargas, protests and legal strife, Turkey has a new opposition party. Is this the man who can defeat Erdoğan?

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 04:00:03 GMT

Under Özgür Özel, the CHP became Turkey’s most popular party. Now his Yeni (New) movement is growing fast

In May this year, police in Ankara stormed the headquarters of the Republican People’s party (CHP), the oldest political party in Turkey. Officers used teargas to enforce a controversial appeal court decision that reinstated the CHP’s 77-year-old former leader Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu – seen as less of a threat to the ruling Justice and Development party (AKP). CHP members aligned with Kılıçdaroğlu’s successor, Özgür Özel, placed furniture at the building’s entrance, creating a barrier to prevent police from entering. It didn’t work. Hours later, party members loyal to Özel were physically removed from the premises.

Entering the offices of Turkey’s leading opposition party in such a fashion was a spectacular act with historic consequences. Last Friday, Özel and 90 CHP deputies resigned from their party and declared the founding of the New (Yeni) party. The CHP had served as Turkey’s main opposition since 2002. But not any longer: with the exodus of members to the New party, the CHP is reduced to just 44 legislators in the 600-seat parliament, its third smallest party out of seven.

Over the past week, Turkey’s new main opposition, with its 91 legislators, enjoyed strong winds in its sails. Throughout Turkish political history, those who have suffered legal injustices have gone on to benefit from them at the ballot box. In 1999, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan himself spent four months in prison. Four years later, he was prime minister. If managed well, the ousting of Özel from the CHP will probably boost the popularity of Turkey’s progressives overall.

But what of the CHP itself? This is the party Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded in 1923, which played a crucial role in establishing the modern republic of Turkey. In the past 18 months, it has witnessed a stunning reversal of fortunes.

At Turkey’s nationwide local elections in March 2024, the CHP was Turkey’s most popular political party. Özel’s leadership engineered that success: the CHP won 37.8% of the vote, beating Erdoğan’s AKP on 35.4%. This was the first national election since the AKP’s establishment in 2001 in which it wasn’t the largest party – a decisive moment in Turkish politics and one with worrying implications for Erdoğan in the run-up to 2028’s presidential elections. The CHP victory, on a platform of municipal socialism, has raised the profile of a generation of young, charismatic leftwing mayors who, like Zohran Mamdani in New York, won office in Turkey’s wealthiest and most populous cities: Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir.

Their proximity to power must have raised concerns among the country’s ruling elites, who have profited from an economic order that prioritises the construction, defence and tourism industries. Three weeks after he announced his candidacy for the presidential elections, in March last year, Istanbul’s CHP mayor, Ekrem İmamoğlu, was removed from office. He has been accused of 142 offences, including accepting bribes, unlawfully obtaining personal data, racketeering, leading a criminal organisation, interfering with public tenders and aiding the outlawed Kurdistan Workers’ party (PKK). His charges could lead to 2,430 years behind bars, and it looks extremely unlikely that he will be able to run for president in 2028. Writing in this newspaper from jail last September, İmamoğlu claimed Erdoğan was “weaponising the courts against the democratic opposition”. (The government has denied putting pressure on the courts to prosecute CHP mayors.)

Since İmamoğlu’s arrest, a different CHP city or district mayor has been arrested almost every month. One after another, politicians have been sent to jail or threatened with prosecution. Several detained CHP mayors have since been released, including İnan Güney, the suspended mayor of Istanbul’s touristic hub, Beyoğlu.

Over time these developments led to apathy among opposition supporters: for months, it felt almost impossible to keep up with CHP’s legal troubles, which dominated the Turkish media.

When İmamoğlu was arrested in March 2025, it triggered nationwide protests, the largest in Turkey in more than a decade. But since then, court cases against the CHP have largely been met with silence. In April, I went to follow İmamoğlu’s case in a courtroom in Silivri, 83km (52 miles) away from Istanbul’s city centre; I saw no supporters inside or outside the courtroom. The cab driver who took me to the court that day said he wished to see the CHP mayor of Silivri in jail next. While holidaying on Büyükada island off the coast of Istanbul two months later, I heard of the Silivri mayor’s arrest. By the end of June, Büyükada’s CHP mayor had been jailed too.

After his reinstatement as party leader, Kılıçdaroğlu implied, in a public statement, that those CHP mayors could indeed be guilty. Likening the CHP to a tree, he said: “The shade of this mighty tree can never, ever be a refuge for the forbidden and the polluted. When necessary, it knows how to purify itself and conduct its inner accounting.” Kılıçdaroğlu’s call for purification has led to fury among opposition supporters, protests and an exodus of party members.

Despite the excitement over Özel’s New party, it faces challenges: it lacks CHP’s resources, personnel, history and financial support from Turkey’s treasury. Breakaway parties have often suffered defeat in Turkish politics: the Good party, established in 2017 by disgruntled Turkish nationalists, has little support among the electorate. The Future party and the Democracy and Progress party (DEVA), founded by former AKP leaders in 2019 and 2020, fared poorly in elections, failing to distinguish themselves from the AKP.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

The CHP is a similar colossus, with an unsurpassable brand name in Turkish politics. It is the Republic of Turkey’s founding party, the party of Atatürk, and its history carries a lot of weight.

Özel has defined the New party as “social democrat”, and the party programme acknowledges Turkey’s different religions, ethnicities and languages. It also references gender and sexual orientation, terms that have become taboo in Turkey in recent years. The New party embraces full membership of the EU and promises to increase Turkey’s role at the Council of Europe and Nato.

If Özel can position his party as not just another splinter party but the new CHP, that would be an attractive proposition. A century ago, the CHP implemented a flurry of social, cultural and political reforms across Turkey, from the abolition of the caliphate to significant advancements in women’s rights. In the 1960s and 1970s it found support from students, the underprivileged and the marginalised with its leftist turn.

The New party should promise an equally bold and progressive agenda. That way it won’t just emerge as the victor of the 2028 elections but will be in a position to truly transform Turkey.

Kaya Genç is a novelist and essayist from Istanbul, and the author of The Lion and the Nightingale: A Journey Through Modern Turkey
