OpinionGuest Essay

Credit... Lydia Roberts

Supported by

By Catherine Shannon

Ms. Shannon is a writer of essays, fiction and a newsletter on Substack.

Everything is strange. We work from home. We socialize online. Our private lives are increasingly public. People pretend to be brands; brands pretend to be people. We optimize our bodies until they break. And the more we know, the less secure we feel.

In this inverted world, we seek to understand what is real and what is true. To know the truth of ourselves, we begin at what feels like a natural place: the mirror. We wish to see ourselves as others do, and modern life gives us countless opportunities.

We are constantly confronted with our own image, whether we like it or not: on our phones, front-facing videos, selfies, public spaces (the communal mirrors in Aritzia’s dressing rooms come painfully to mind), our social media profiles, Zoom calls, FaceTime, Ring doorbells. But we can forget that mirrors both duplicate reality and reverse it. None show you exactly as you are. Everything is strange.

The historian Christopher Lasch wrote that “for the narcissist, the world is a mirror.” Almost 50 years later, this remains a tidy diagnosis, but it doesn’t quite capture the extent of the spiritual crisis that we’re now facing. I believe the room of mirrors that constantly surrounds us conjures something unsettling, something dark. It is a spiritual trap in which the imagined displaces the real: We choose a fantasy of ourselves over the reality of others. And that trap is baited and facilitated by technology.

To see what I mean, we need only to imagine our online behavior in real life, without the platforms that blur the boundaries of what’s acceptable.

Picture yourself at a cocktail party — one you’re dreading, one for work. A colleague approaches you. Beside him, there is a large mirror, and as you converse with him and answer his invasive personal questions, you do not look at his face. Instead, you look at yourself, at your own reflection. You watch yourself talk and laugh, you see the face you pull when he asks if you’re going to have another kid soon. You monitor your reflection, correct your posture, exaggerate your “I’m listening” face. In person, this would be utterly bizarre. People would probably ask if you need to sit down. But this is what we do, all day long, on Zoom.

Or imagine a so-called skinfluencer taking us through a haul of her summer favorites — but without her phone. For six minutes straight, she stares into her own eager eyes, in the bathroom mirror, speaking to her reflection. She taps the products, murmuring about — I don’t know — the benefits of snail mucin. You would call the police. Or at least whoever is casting the new Ari Aster movie.

There is something eerie about being both the speaker and the watcher, performing one’s own identity for oneself, rather than simply living it. When we take on the roles of actor, audience and critic all at once, it’s going to cause some psychic strain.

Historically, we humans have had very little access to our own image, as much as we’ve always wanted it. The copper and bronze mirrors of ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome — cultures obsessed with beauty — were luxury objects produced for the wealthy. During the Renaissance, commissioned oil portraits were for the aristocracy and were notoriously unreliable. Any fan of Tudor history has heard the tale of Anne of Cleves catfishing King Henry VIII with a portrait so inaccurate that he claimed he could not bring himself to consummate the marriage.

Mirrors were not common household objects until the mid-1800s, and then came still images of ourselves, moving images of ourselves and the pervasive smartphone camera that combines all three, while also making these images accessible anywhere, by anyone. For most of our ancestors and almost all of human history, we were not gazing into our own eyes, and we certainly weren’t watching ourselves on a loop on Instagram Stories, boomeranging Bellinis at a bachelorette brunch.

Let’s be honest: I shouldn’t know what I look like taking out the trash. But I do, because my Google Home security camera recently alerted me that there was a “Person Seen — Back Camera.” “Person” is a generous term for what I saw, which was a beleaguered, ghostly figure, greasy hair pulled back, hunched over a bag of trash like an old witch.

We are recorded constantly: in public, by the government, by private companies trying to sell us things, even by strangers. I shudder when I think about all the incidental pictures of myself that live on strangers’ phones. In my own personal horror film, there I am, eating a bagel, and some 17-year-old tourist zooms in on my pixelated face, screenshots it, and sends it to the family group chat — “this woman’s face lol” — and I become the inside joke that defines that New York City holiday for years to come.

It’s curious, especially given how little we looked at ourselves in the past, and how rare and imperfect mirrors were for thousands of years, that traditional wisdom teaches us to be wary of the act of regarding the self. The three major American faiths — the Abrahamic religions of Judaism, Christianity and Islam — all warn against the dangers of mirrors, vanity, pride and excessive concern with the self.

Mirrors are covered during shiva, the Jewish seven-day mourning period, both to encourage contemplation of the relationship between God and man and to discourage vanity and self-concern. The Book of Proverbs teaches that pride is spiritually deleterious: “Pride goes before ruin, / Arrogance, before failure.”

Many Christians believe pride is not only a sin, but the original one, and the worst of them. It is demonic, “the complete anti-God state of mind,” as C. S. Lewis wrote in “Mere Christianity.” Pride is a turning away from God, and an exultation of oneself. The mirror is a symbol of pride and vanity, but it also symbolizes our incomplete, earthly knowledge. As the Apostle Paul wrote about God in his first letter to the Corinthians: “For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face.”

Islamic prophetic tradition (hadith) discourages the depiction of living beings in religious contexts. In Islamic mysticism, however, a smudged mirror is a metaphor for the human soul. It is only when the ego is annihilated, and the surface is polished clean, that the divine becomes visible. The Quran is also explicit about pride and social vanity: “Do not turn your nose up to people, nor walk pridefully upon the earth.”

The message is clear: Self-obsession is spiritually dangerous, and we need to keep our guard up. In all three faiths, the mirror is a poor, incomplete way of seeing. It is covered, dark and smudged. It does not reveal God, truth or even ourselves as we are. It is only through private contemplation, face-to-face encounters and an inner spiritual transformation that we come to know truth.

If only it were that easy. Like Narcissus, we are easily seduced by our own reflections, by our imagined, idealized selves. Every day, we are encouraged in this self-seduction. But seducing oneself is frankly not how seduction should work.

Mainstream psychology, and nearly every feature of modern life, puts a strong emphasis on the healthy ego. It’s a comforting, whole-wheat kind of idea, an essential part of any balanced personality. We all know we can have too little self-love, too little self-care. By all means, put yourself first, set the boundaries, don the moisturizing face mask. The opposite message, that there is such a thing as too much self-love or self-concern, is not widely circulated on TikTok. But obviously everything has its limits.

What happens when the limits are off? Bad things, I’m sorry to say. Frightful things. The reflected self is rarely reassuring for long. Across cultures, mirrors have been used by soothsayers, sorcerers and witches for scrying, divination and attempts to peer beyond the visible world. In folklore and occult practice, the mirror is not merely reflective but permeable — a portal where something might appear, or someone may return.

Even the postmodernists have their own warnings. In 1967, Michel Foucault darkly described the mirror as a kind of threshold, a mix between a fantasy world, a utopia and some weird other place on the margins — which he called a “heterotopia.” The mirror is one such strange place because we discover our presence and our absence at the same time. “I see myself there where I am not,” he wrote, “in an unreal, virtual space that opens up behind the surface.”

Some other heterotopias, according to Foucault, include the honeymoon trip, psychiatric hospitals, vacation villages, prisons, the theater, the cinema, museums, libraries, brothels and the cemetery. In these settings, the normal order of things breaks down and certain truths are exposed. Each of these places could serve as an apt metaphor for the screens, monitors and social media applications that relentlessly reflect us back to ourselves. This technology is a mirror, but it is also a museum, a theater, a prison.

Inhabiting this mirrored, dual realm, this doubled existence, doesn’t feel natural. It doesn’t even feel neutral. Something is off, and when something is off, Freud has probably attempted to explain it. He called this “the uncanny,” a concept that by its very nature resists a clean definition, though if you’ve seen a David Lynch movie, you’ve experienced it firsthand.

Castration complexes and womb fantasies aside, Freud does a pretty good job: The uncanny, according to his 1919 essay by the same title, “is that class of the terrifying which leads back to something long known to us, once very familiar.” It is easy for something new or unknown to frighten us, but the feeling of uncanniness relies on its being known to us in some way.

The uncanny is a dark twist on the familiar. It emerges when the boundary between imagination and reality begins to blur, when hidden mechanisms seem to be at work beneath the surface and when something appears alive that should not be. (Or vice versa, in the case of influencers, who can have that dead, sharklike look in their eyes.) It is marked by repetition, by a sense of something fateful and inescapable. Freud noted that the uncanny is often and easily produced when a symbol begins to take on the full force of the thing it represents. It is difficult to imagine a more precise description of life online.

The psychological effects of prolonged self-viewing are uncanny, indeed. A 2010 study from the University of Urbino in Italy found that when healthy young adults gazed at their own faces in a mirror under low light, the results were immediate and disturbing. Participants reported seeing huge deformations of their own faces, an unknown person, even fantastical and monstrous beings. Some saw an animal face, such as that of a cat, pig or lion. Some saw their parents. All experienced a form of dissociation. Some subjects felt that the other face in the mirror was the one watching them.

Closely tied to mirrors and the uncanny is the idea of the double, or doppelgänger, a theme long explored in literature and film, from Dostoevsky’s novella “The Double” to Jordan Peele’s horror movie “Us.” In German and Eastern European folklore, the doppelgänger is an omen, a usurper, the shadow self, and a sign that identity is unstable. The self is split, haunted, mimicked and stalked by its own likeness.

Today, we treat our own image — both in the mirror and online — as something psychologically protective: a way of stabilizing our identity, managing our reputations and securing a coherent sense of self.

But all of this suggests the opposite possibility: The more we try to stabilize ourselves through repetition, doubling, self-observation and — I’ll say it — posting to the grid, the more uncanny and fragile we become. A preoccupation with the stable self produces instability. These days, we don’t approach our doubles with caution; we invite them, and go so far as to curate them.

It’s like an inverted version of “The Picture of Dorian Gray.” In the novel by Oscar Wilde, Dorian keeps his beautiful public image, while his portrait bears his inner corruption and ugliness. Under modern image culture, we attempt the reverse operation: We present a perfect digital double at the cost to our real selves, who are left to absorb the discomfort and tension between the two. If you post the good picture, it hardly matters that you feel sad inside.

The situation is worse than vanity, darker than narcissism. The mirrors all around us, especially the technological ones, divide us against ourselves — and this is destabilizing, even dangerous. As more and more of our lives take place in a virtual realm, and we increasingly identify with the fantasies of our digital doppelgängers, we begin to dehumanize ourselves, and when we do this, it is undoubtedly easier to dehumanize others.

One small way this happens every day: the general disappearance of manners. In New York City, I often encounter someone walking on the sidewalk toward me, head down in their phone, until they sense the presence of another thing coming upon them, which in this case is me, a human being. This unbearable game of chicken might have something to do with how we’ve been conditioned to view one another: as things, not people. We see other people as obstacles to what we want, on sidewalks and elsewhere. Or as things we can use to get us the things we want. So much of technology treats us as things to be manipulated, “users” to be used. We grow accustomed to this, internalize it and return that treatment to those around us.

When we look at ourselves, we are seeking something. We want to be known, seen and understood. But we are looking in the wrong place. The mirror shows us our own self-critical and self-exalting gaze — the gaze of pride, pleasure and ego. This fantasy is powerful, even mesmerizing, but unreliable. When we look solely at ourselves, we fail to encounter anything that resists us; there are no contradictions, no interruptions. We need the honest gaze: the gaze of others and the gaze toward others. To see ourselves clearly, we don’t use mirrors. We use relationships.

Before I had a child, I was under the impression that I was a very patient person. I thought I would wipe scrambled egg off the floor without any frustration, read “Owl Babies” for the umpteenth time without growing exhausted of Sarah, Percy, Bill and their unnamed Owl Mother. But my beautiful son has exposed my inadequacies with alarming clarity. (I’m working on it.) In our loving relationships with others, we are drawn out of ourselves and into the world.

Mirrors encourage us to choose the fantasies of ourselves over the realities of others. It’s best we look away.

Loved the thinking here. Yes uncanny. Every day I walk my old ghost face dog through the park and see the tourists come and go taking pictures for their feeds. And the thing I notice is they hold up the phone and make a big smile and then the phone is lowered and the smile vanishes and they stare at the picture as if disappointed.

Beautiful observations here. This line reveals much about what I believe you are trying to say, “To see ourselves clearly, we don’t use mirrors. We use relationships.” If we are introspective, we can observe both the inadequacies and beauty of others and search within ourselves to see if they exist in us. This requires thought and meditation, not looking at the physical self.

Catherine Shannon is a writer of essays, fiction and a newsletter on Substack. Lydia Roberts is an artist and photographer based in the South of France.

Trump Blames Minnesota, Not Iran, for Cyberattack, Despite Initial Investigation

The New York Times July 31, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump claimed without evidence that Minnesota’s Democratic government was “behind” a cyberattack on the state’s own water systems. Investigators believe Iran is likely responsible.

By Chris Cameron

Reporting from Washington

President Trump on Friday disputed that Iran was behind a cyberattack on dozens of municipal water systems in Minnesota, as U. S. and state investigators have said is most likely the case, instead blaming the state and its Democratic governor, Tim Walz, without evidence.

Mr. Walz dismissed the accusation in a social media post soon after.

The New York Times reported Thursday that U. S. and Minnesota state officials believed Iran was likely responsible for the cyberattacks on water systems. The F. B. I. said late Thursday the hackers had targeted water facilities in at least seven states.

Mr. Trump dismissed that assessment in a freewheeling cabinet meeting on Friday, saying: “I don’t think so. I think Minnesota is behind it,” adding, “I think the governor’s behind it. I don’t think there was an Iranian cyberattack.”

The president’s baseless claim, contradicted by investigators’ statements that other states had been targeted and their water systems were “degraded” by the attack, appeared aimed at downplaying the threat of the increasingly unpopular war with Iran inside America’s borders. Mr. Trump instead shifted blame to Mr. Walz, Kamala Harris’s running mate in 2024, and his state government, continuing a pattern of trying to punish Minnesota and its Democratic leadership, particularly over the issue of immigration.

“Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too,” Mr. Walz said on social media, adding, “This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there’s no plan to win a war with Iran.”

Officials had cautioned in their preliminary assessments that they had not definitively determined that Iran was responsible for the attack and that their conclusions could change as the authorities collected more data — though on Friday some federal and state officials familiar with the matter said nothing had surfaced to challenge the prevailing view. The hacking spree, if confirmed to be the handiwork of Tehran, would amount to one of the most significant cyberattacks of the war and one of the most serious efforts to compromise U. S. water systems on record.

The officials also warned that the hackers could be attempting to pose as being based in Iran in an effort to ratchet up tensions between the two countries, though former intelligence officials said such a situation was unlikely.

Katie Rogers and Dustin Volz contributed reporting.

Chris Cameron is a Times reporter covering Washington, focusing on breaking news and the Trump administration.

U. S. Raises Threat of Steep Water Cuts in Lower Colorado River Basin

The New York Times July 31, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A federal plan would impose drastic water cuts on Arizona, California and Nevada in dry years over the next decade. A legal battle could follow.

By Scott Dance

Reporting from Washington

Communities and farms across Arizona, Nevada and California face potentially drastic cuts in the water they can use from the Colorado River over the next decade under a plan the Trump administration published on Friday.

The proposal is meant to try to break a logjam among the seven states that rely on the Colorado and comes as rising temperatures and decades of drought and water overuse have overwhelmed a river system that feeds major cities and important farmland.

The proposal raises the potential for complex legal battles that could play out for years. The administration’s move is significant in that it inserts the federal government into a deep crisis affecting the American West and lays bare the challenge of bringing water consumption in line with an increasingly sparse supply.

Across much of the region, access to water is spawning bitter disputes that pit farming communities against cities and states against neighboring states as soaring demand has clashed with decades of overuse. Rising temperatures and drought exacerbated by climate change have also intensified the conflict. The fight over the Colorado has international implications as well, as some parts of northern Mexico also depend upon its water.

In laying out its approach to the crisis, the Trump administration has heightened a thorny legal and practical question of who should shoulder the burden of a shrinking Colorado River.

Its plan suggests that the answer would be the Sun Belt communities along the lower portions of the river basin — cities like Phoenix, Las Vegas and Los Angeles — and not the upstream Mountain West. The federal government’s main tool to control water supply on the Colorado is its ability to limit flows through the Hoover Dam, which straddles Arizona and Nevada and creates Lake Mead, and Glen Canyon Dam, which impounds Lake Powell along the Utah-Arizona border.

The question of how to most equitably balance the sacrifices made by Mountain States and Sun Belt communities has been one of the most difficult sticking points in years of fighting. It has prevented agreement in a rapidly growing region of the country. A solution needs to address not just changes to home landscaping or lawn-watering limits, but also the vast fields of water-guzzling alfalfa and soy, a growing data-center industry and the supply of much of the nation’s produce.

The Trump proposal alarmed Arizona officials on Friday.

“Phoenix has spent decades planning for a moment like this and is prepared to use less Colorado River water, but it is wrong to lay a disproportionate share of the burden on Arizona,” Mayor Kate Gallego of Phoenix said in a statement.

But the proposal was short on important specifics, including plans for water use over the next two years or detailed amounts of water it would allow to flow under varying river conditions.

And it appeared to leave room for the states to find their own way to share in the pain of increasing water scarcity, said Jennifer Pitt, the Colorado River program director for the National Audubon Society.

“Only time will tell if that is possible,” Ms. Pitt said.

So far, it has not. With decades-old rules governing water use set to expire at the end of this year, the Trump administration stepped in and said it would decide.

The plan, released by the Interior Department, does not force mandatory cuts to water use on what are collectively known as the upper-basin states — Colorado, Utah, Wyoming and New Mexico.

The booming Phoenix area could find its water supply severely reduced in the driest years under the plan, because Arizona holds some of the lowest-priority rights in a river system where many water rights were determined a century and a half ago. Arizona officials have signaled they are preparing to fight for their water in court, a step that could send Colorado River conflicts on an unpredictable path to the U. S. Supreme Court.

Tom Buschatzke, Arizona’s chief negotiator on Colorado River issues, said the plan could have “draconian impacts” on that state and its economy, at the same time upper-basin states would not be required to use any less water.

“It’s unacceptable,” Mr. Buschatzke said.

Even without some details, the Interior Department’s plan provided states more clarity on what could be coming in the years ahead, said Sarah Porter, director of the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University.

“It is an agency statement of what it believes it’s empowered to do,” Ms. Porter said. “It’s not necessarily the last word.”

Though the plan, known as an environmental-impact statement, is final, more steps remain to govern how much water will actually flow to communities. The Interior Department’s Bureau of Reclamation, which oversees water resource management in the West, is expected to release more details in the coming days and weeks.

The bureau’s officials have also said they would scrap the plans if states can agree on a different solution.

Across the region, two decades of drought have reduced winter snowpack, which creates the majority of the river’s flow. At the same time, warming temperatures caused by climate change have increased water losses from evaporation.

The basin faced an October deadline to have a new water use plan in place. Its implementation fell to the Bureau of Reclamation, after years of negotiations among the river basin states failed.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the plan released on Friday “provides the flexibility to respond to changing hydrologic conditions.” He said the Interior Department had “a responsibility to ensure the Colorado River system remains reliable and resilient for the millions of Americans, communities and industries that depend on it.”

The Colorado not only supplies drinking water to tens of millions of people but also provides irrigation to 5.5 million acres of farms. Mexico also receives a share of the Colorado’s water, and negotiations between the country and the United States are separately ongoing. About two dozen native tribes also have rights to the river’s water.

The rules laid out on Friday call for a wide range of potential water releases — including reductions by more than half in the driest years — from Lake Powell, the nation’s second-largest reservoir and the dividing point between the upper and lower basins. Arizona, California and Nevada, the lower basin states, depend heavily on steady releases from the reservoir, and from Lake Mead farther downstream, for municipal water and farm irrigation.

The smallest reservoir releases under the plan would be low enough to potentially lead to legal action by the lower basin states citing the Colorado River Compact, an interstate agreement made in 1922 that is central to river operations. The threat of such a lawsuit has loomed over discussions among states as the river’s flow has dwindled.

Officials from those states had already offered to make significant water use cuts in the coming years. The Bureau of Reclamation’s plan goes even further in requiring potential reductions over the next 10 years.

The plan includes opportunities for the bureau to reconsider water use rules every two years over the next decade, and for states to renegotiate with one another. That stipulation was designed to create opportunity for consensus, but state officials have warned it may raise tensions across the river basin.

Water supply estimates and forecasts have only grown more grim as basin states and Reclamation officials have searched for a long-term solution over the past nine months. Water storage in Lakes Powell and Mead has plummeted to its lowest level since 1957, when Glen Canyon Dam, which impounds Lake Powell, was still under construction, according to an analysis published this month.

By March, Lake Powell is forecast to reach a critical low. Its surface is expected to fall below the threshold to generate hydropower at Glen Canyon Dam, according to a federal analysis released this month.

Scott Dance is a Times reporter who covers how climate change and extreme weather are transforming society.

What Caused the Surge in Ceuta?

The New York Times July 31, 2026

Migrant Surge Into Spanish Territory

Advertisement

Supported by

Speculation has focused on lax Moroccan policing, attractive Spanish immigration policies and misinformation from human traffickers. In reality, experts said, it’s too early to know.

By Jonathan Wolfe

When tens of thousands of migrants began crossing on Thursday into Spanish territory in Africa, leading to chaotic scenes and political infighting across Europe, there was one major question that sparked wildly different explanations. How did this happen?

Among the theories:

The European far right joined the White House in accusing Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, of inspiring the crossings with his migrant-friendly policies.

Mr. Sánchez blamed human-trafficking networks for misleading migrants about the ease with which they could remain on Spanish territory.

Migrants said in interviews that the Moroccan authorities had encouraged their crossing.

In reality, said Krzysztof Borowski, a spokesman for the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, “It’s too early to give a real account of why this surge happened, or how it moved so fast.”

Here’s why the surge prompted such speculation.

Usually, Moroccan officials make it hard for migrants to get close to Ceuta, the Spanish exclave that neighbors Morocco. This week, several migrants said in interviews, police officers waved them through, allowing them to overwhelm Spain’s border fence with relative ease.

That has led to suggestions that Morocco was seeking to pressure Spain for political reasons. Perhaps, analysts said, Morocco wanted to deter Spain from strengthening ties with Algeria, Morocco’s neighbor and rival. Mr. Sánchez visited Algeria in July, weeks after his foreign minister made a similar trip and spoke of importing more Algerian gas.

“For me, that plays a fairly central role,” said Lorenzo Gabrielli, a senior researcher at Pompeu Fabra University in Barcelona who researches migration in Ceuta. “It is impossible for nearly 50,000 people to cross the border between Morocco and Spain in a single day without Morocco having a hand in it,” he added.

He said it recalled an episode in 2021, when more than 10,000 people came over the border in two days, and said it was part of a cycle that Morocco uses to exert pressure on Spain.

The Moroccan government did not respond to requests for comments and had not made any public statement on the mass crossings by Friday evening.

Moroccan analysts said the government may not have been behind the huge numbers of arrivals. They said that was partly because it would not have wanted to endanger the country’s Throne Day celebrations, which are taking place near Ceuta, and are aimed at highlighting the country’s economic achievements.

“It would therefore be inconsistent to send contradictory signals by encouraging a migration crisis that could undermine this message,” said Said Saddiki, a professor of international relations at Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University, in Fez, Morocco.

Mr. Saddiki also did not see a link between the recent events and the improvement in relationship between Spain and Algeria, which “does not, on the available evidence, provide sufficient motive for such a high-risk move,” he said.

Mr. Sánchez has developed an image as a pro-immigration liberal and a leading opponent of the Trump administration’s hard line against migrants. He made global headlines this year by allowing more than a million migrants living illegally in Spain to apply to formalize their status.

According to Mr. Sánchez’s right-wing opponents, that move enticed the migrants who crossed Ceuta’s border this week. “By regularizing hundreds of thousands of illegal immigrants, the socialist prime minister of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, has opened the doors of Europe,” wrote Jordan Bardella, a far-right leader in France.

Mr. Sánchez has dismissed such claims, noting that illegal migration to Spain had been lower in recent years than in Italy and Greece. He instead blamed human traffickers for spreading misinterpretations of a recent ruling by Spanish judges, who last month placed restrictions on when the Spanish authorities can expel migrants who attempt to swim by sea to Spain’s territories in Africa.

Some Moroccans said Mr. Sánchez may have been right. “All of this was triggered by messages circulating on social media about the Spanish Constitutional Court’s decision, which created a pull factor,” said Abdullah Abaakil, a left-wing political leader in Morocco.

Smuggling networks exploited that “within days,” said Rachid El Houdaigui, a research fellow at the Policy Center for the New South, a think tank in Morocco.

Aida Alami and Jason Horowitz contributed reporting.

Jonathan Wolfe is a Times reporter based in London, covering breaking news.

Trump to Appeal Judge’s Ruling Denouncing I. R. S. Suit as Exercise in Self-Dealing

The New York Times July 31, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

It was the latest sign that the president was doubling down on his fight for aspects of a deal that brings him vast benefits, even though they have jeopardized the confirmation of his pick for attorney general.

By Alan Feuer and Andrew Duehren

Lawyers for President Trump said on Friday they would appeal a recent order from a judge casting doubt on the legitimacy of a $1.8 billion fund and extraordinary personal tax protections that emerged from a deal to drop his lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service.

The notice of appeal, filed in Federal District Court in Miami, was the latest sign that Mr. Trump was willing to pursue his fight for the fund and the tax provision even though they have badly damaged his relations with Senate Republicans and jeopardized the confirmation of his pick for attorney general, Todd Blanche.

The move came at a moment of simmering tension between the White House and two Republican senators — John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — who have repeatedly vowed that they will not confirm Mr. Blanche unless he makes changes to the tax deal benefiting Mr. Trump and provides written assurances that the $1.8 billion fund to compensate his allies is dead once and for all.

On Thursday, Mr. Trump threw a wrench into the protracted negotiations between the senators and the Justice Department, threatening to withdraw Mr. Blanche’s name rather than give any ground to the demands by Mr. Cornyn and Mr. Tillis, who are not returning to Congress next year.

In a social media post on Friday, the president reiterated his support for the so-called anti-weaponization fund in particular, writing that the people it was intended to benefit — potentially including rioters who stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 — still deserved restitution.

“Perhaps there has never been a group of people treated so badly in our Nation’s history,” he wrote. “They are suffering still, many ruined, and I felt that they should be given compensation for what has been done to them.”

The ruling by Judge Kathleen M. Williams, issued two weeks ago, was a repudiation of the secretive deal that ended Mr. Trump’s suit against the I. R. S., which originally demanded at least $10 billion in damages. The judge effectively accused the president and top officials at the Justice Department, including Mr. Blanche, of seeking to manipulate the court system to lend a veneer of validity to the backroom negotiations that had led to the creation of the fund and a sweeping provision to protect Mr. Trump, his family and his businesses from past tax inquiries.

Judge Williams issued her order at the request of 35 former federal judges who urged her to scrutinize the settlement of the suit as an act of fraud. A lawyer for the former judges, Norman L. Eisen, the chairman of Democracy Defenders Action, said the plan to appeal the decision proved that the concerns by Mr. Cornyn and Mr. Tillis were well-founded and that the president was still trying to keep the fund and the tax protections in place.

“This is the hill Trump has chosen to die on,” Mr. Eisen said.

The appeal would seek to lift Judge William’s finding that the underlying lawsuit — which accused the I. R. S. of failing to stop Mr. Trump’s tax returns from being leaked to the news media — was itself an improper exercise in self-dealing, given that he had brought the claim against a federal agency that he controlled.

If successful, it would also have a more practical effect: rolling back the judge’s efforts to seek disciplinary actions against Mr. Trump’s personal lawyers and Mr. Blanche and other department officials.

While Judge Williams described the deal in scathing terms, she acknowledged that she could not necessarily stop Mr. Blanche from establishing the $1.8 billion fund or giving the president immunity from audits.

“Whether executive branch actors can privately agree to give themselves and their former clients blanket immunities and billions of dollars in tax monies for legally undefined grievances was never an issue advanced to this court,” she wrote in her order.

Instead, it has been political pushback on Capitol Hill that has shaped the fate of the fund and audit deal. The fund was immediately politically toxic, even among Republicans, and Mr. Blanche has said that it is dead, though he has not formally put that commitment in writing.

The I. R. S. protections for the president and his family initially seemed to fly under the political radar for Republicans, until Mr. Cornyn and Mr. Tillis protested advancing Mr. Blanche’s nomination over the issue.

Mr. Cornyn and Mr. Tillis have both demanded that Mr. Blanche pare back the audit provision so that it only applies to Mr. Trump, two of his sons and the Trump Organization, rather than a potentially large pool of affiliates of the family. Mr. Cornyn also wants Mr. Blanche to include a provision making clear that Mr. Trump’s future tax return could still be audited.

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

Andrew Duehren covers tax policy for The Times from Washington.

Coast Guard Vows to Protect Crews From Brain Injuries Caused by Rough Seas

The New York Times July 31, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The head of the Coast Guard said “decisive action” would be taken so the injuries would be recognized, treated and prevented.

By Dave Philipps

The head of the U. S. Coast Guard told all personnel on Thursday that slamming through rough seas was causing brain injuries to small-boat crews and vowed to take what he called “decisive action” to prevent, recognize and treat the injuries, which have often gone undiagnosed.

“Our crews operate in a dangerous and unforgiving maritime environment. The demands of our missions are immense,” Admiral Kevin Lunday, the commandant of the Coast Guard, wrote in an email sent to the whole force. “We owe it to you to protect your long-term health from the damage caused by relentless wave pounding.”

The email was sent just hours after The New York Times published an article detailing how rescue boat crews working in crashing surf are exposed to thousands of impacts that cause a whiplash motion and seem to cause brain injuries, even if crew members never hit their heads or feel concussed.

After years of exposure, many crew members suffer from headaches, memory lapses, cognitive problems, anxiety attacks, mood swings and a list of other ailments that can be symptomatic of brain injuries. But for years, the root cause went unrecognized, by both crew members and the Coast Guard, because the symptoms often look like normal reactions to traumatic stress.

Many crew members were diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder but were never assessed for a physical brain injury.

The Times report detailed how some elite lifeboat drivers — known as surfmen — fall apart in perplexing and sometimes violent ways. It followed the efforts of one high school student, Kayleigh Bonner, who sought to understand why her father, after years of growing increasingly erratic, had died suddenly by suicide.

For a senior project, she surveyed more than 70 surfmen and found widespread signs of undiagnosed brain injuries. Her research became the foundation of the article in The Times.

On Friday she said she hoped the Coast Guard would follow through in making necessary changes to ensure the safety of crews.

“I’m grateful the research and article have had this much influence,” she said. “Seeing people who feel less alone in their struggle, validated in their experience, or have clues to what they may also be dealing with is amazing and made all of the hard work and pain in sharing our story worth it.”

Admiral Lunday told the force that the Coast Guard will begin a servicewide brain health initiative that will train crews on how to recognize brain injuries and encourage members to report symptoms of potential injuries. He said the service will also work with civilian medical experts and other military branches that are dealing with similar issues to create new monitoring protocols and treatment standards for its medical providers.

The Coast Guard partnered with civilian researchers in June to place sensors on some of its small boats to measure impacts. The data could eventually give insight into what levels of wave slamming are dangerous and who is at risk.

The Coast Guard has more than 40,000 active-duty members who do rescue missions as well as law enforcement and drug interdiction. The forcewide message acknowledged that personnel may also be at risk of unseen brain injuries from the blast wave exposure of repeatedly firing weapons, or from being close to explosions.

As part of the initiative, the admiral said the Coast Guard would work to encourage personnel to come forward and report injuries.

“Taking care of your brain health is an operational necessity and a matter of readiness,” he said. “We need leaders at every level to ensure our people are aware of potential brain injury symptoms, get medical attention without hesitation or fear of stigma, and receive proper medical care.”

Dave Philipps writes about war, the military and veterans and covers The Pentagon for The Times.

Amid Talk of a Party Switch, Fetterman Vows ‘Never’

The New York Times July 31, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

congressional memo

Changing one’s affiliation is rare in the Senate, but it can have big consequences. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania says he is staying put as a Democrat.

By Carl Hulse

Reporting from the Capitol

An evenly divided Senate. A senator disillusioned with the direction of his own party. A sudden party switch that shifts Senate control, sending shock waves through the institution and American politics itself.

That scenario unfolded in 2001, when then-Senator Jim Jeffords of Vermont stunned his fellow Republicans by bolting from the party to become an independent. He then aligned with Democrats, briefly handing them the Senate majority early in the first term of George W. Bush.

Now, with the possibility of a razor-thin Senate majority looming again after November’s midterm elections, the focus is already on the prospect of party-switchers upending the Senate equilibrium, with the most attention focused on Senator John Fetterman, Democrat of Pennsylvania.

Mr. Fetterman, a Senate nonconformist right down to the hoodie-and-shorts uniform he often wears instead of a suit, has taken harsh aim at elements of his own party, broken with his caucus, avoided party gatherings, developed deep friendships across the aisle and even set up a joint fund-raising committee with his Republican Senate colleague from their home state of Pennsylvania.

He recently published an op-ed chastising his fellow Democrats for having tried to gut the filibuster a few years ago. And he has said that if his party officially turns against Israel, as some of its most progressive voices are urging, it would be a “red line” that would prompt him to leave.

Does all this activity signal that he intends to flee the Democratic Party, pulling the rug out from under Democrats if they manage to net the four seats that would give them the majority next January?

“Never,” Mr. Fetterman said in an interview, declaring that he has no intention of switching. “I’m not being cute. I vote 90-something percent with Democrats.”

That doesn’t mean that Mr. Fetterman is at all pleased with the trajectory of his party, which has shifted starkly away from decades of unequivocal support for Israel, and whose loudest voices are promoting proposals for reshaping government that many mainstream Democrats find extreme.

“These people aren’t Democrats,” Mr. Fetterman said. “We can have different views on certain things, but would you want to abolish the border, abolish prison, abolish the presidency, abolish the Senate? That’s just full-on communism.”

Despite his deep-blue Democratic voting record, Mr. Fetterman, who suffered a stroke during his drive in 2022 but returned to the campaign trail and won, has fueled discussion of a party switch because of his biting critique of some aspects of Democratic politics, not to mention his obvious disdain for some of the formalities and traditions of the Senate.

He also has plenty of friends on the Republican side of the aisle who would like nothing more than to win a new convert, and, regardless of how real the prospect of a Fetterman defection is, enjoy any discussion that highlights Democratic divisions. His unique new joint fund-raising committee with Senator David McCormick, the Pennsylvania Republican, has only fueled the chatter.

Republicans have certainly left the door wide open, along with a big welcome mat, though Senator John Thune, the South Dakota Republican and majority leader, said he hasn’t discussed the matter recently with Mr. Fetterman.

“I have had conversations with him in the past, as have many of my colleagues, about the challenges he faces in his caucus,” Mr. Thune said. “There are many of us who I think would welcome the opportunity to have him join the Republican conference. But, you know, ultimately that’s a decision that’s left up to him.”

Senate Democrats watched two members leave their ranks following the 2022 election, as Arizona’s Kyrsten Sinema announced she was an independent the month following the election, and Joe Manchin III of West Virginia became an independent two years later.

Both centrist senators were visibly frustrated with Democratic politics, broke from the party to prevent a weakening of the filibuster sought by their colleagues, and tried to push the caucus to the right on some issues. They remained aligned with Democrats in order to keep their majority committee membership status, but neither ultimately sought re-election in 2024.

Mr. Manchin said that his party had shifted in a way that made it untenable for him to remain a Democrat.

“I just came to a realization that they had moved into an area and I couldn’t move them back,” said Mr. Manchin, who said he also felt penalized for working with Republicans. “I like both sides and I wanted to be able to talk to my friends on both sides without being a threat to anybody.”

While Mr. Fetterman has broken with the party on some issues, such as the spending fights and efforts to rein in President Trump’s conduct of the war with Iran, he hasn’t yet been the legislative obstacle that Ms. Sinema and Mr. Manchin could sometimes be. And though some Democrats say they don’t know him well, they do see him as one of their own, and appear to be going out of their way not to make him feel shunned, as some previous party-switchers had.

“The people in our caucus very much like him and respect him,” Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, said, noting Mr. Fetterman’s backing of most Democratic initiatives. “And we’re a big-tent party; we can have a lot of different views in that party.”

Mr. Fetterman isn’t the only senator who comes up in discussions about switching parties. Senator Lisa Murkowski, Republican of Alaska, has mused about taking the leap in the past, and come under harsh attack from President Trump over the years. After losing a primary re-election bid in 2010 to a G. O. P. challenger on her right, she held on to her seat as a write-in candidate, cementing her reputation for having an independent streak. But she has kept her Republican affiliation, despite expressing the view that the party was moving away from her.

The outcome of the midterm election could be the factor determining any defections. If the Senate ended up tied 50-50, as it did in 2001 and 2021, Republicans would remain the majority party by virtue of Vice President JD Vance’s tiebreaking power. A four-seat Senate pickup would put Democrats in charge, but a switch by Mr. Fetterman would restore Republicans to power. Conversely, a 50-50 Senate followed by a Republican switch would empower Democrats.

The switch by Mr. Jeffords of Vermont 25 years ago was an explosive moment in the Senate. It came after the senator, who chaired the health and education committee, concluded that the Bush administration and conservative Republicans were shortchanging special education and students with disabilities.

Republicans recaptured the majority in the 2002 midterm elections following the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks.

Mr. Fetterman appears to be in a far different frame of mind.

“I would say to John, he has to be the person he is,” Mr. Manchin said, noting that his decision would carry major political implications for both Mr. Fetterman and the Senate. “He believes a little bit in both sides. He has strong convictions to the progressive side, which is where he comes from.”

In an essay in The Washington Post in May, Mr. Fetterman wrote that he would be a “terrible Republican.” In other interviews, he has also insisted he has no intention of switching. But the speculation persists and is likely to continue despite his denials.

In the interview, he suggested that any future change of heart on the matter would be worthy of an exclusive story in this newspaper.

“Like, if I ever decide to change, and I won’t, I will seek you out and give that to you,” Mr. Fetterman said.

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.

Ukraine’s Strike on Iranian Ship Shows How Two Wars Could Spiral

The New York Times July 31, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

Iran sent military aid to Russia for its war against Ukraine. Now the question is whether that conflict and the U. S.-Israeli war against Iran are converging.

By Edward Wong

Edward Wong, a diplomatic correspondent based in Washington, reported from Manila, where he covered the visit of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Ukraine and Iran, two nations at war with nuclear powers, tiptoed dangerously close to conflict with each other in recent days, when Ukraine struck an Iranian commercial cargo ship in the Caspian Sea.

The attack killed an Iranian civilian sailor. Ukraine said the ship was transporting military equipment to Russia. Iran considered retaliating, but diplomats defused the crisis through a phone call.

For analysts observing the two wars closely, it was only a matter of time before violence escalated between Ukraine and Iran. The questions now confronting governments around the globe are whether the wars are converging, and when the next flashpoint might be.

If the conflicts merge more directly, the result could be cataclysmic, with multiple nations, including the United States and Russia, taking part in open warfare spanning Eurasia and the Middle East.

Both wars have already drawn in myriad countries. With American and European support, Ukraine has been defending itself against a full-scale invasion by Russia since 2022, while Iran and North Korea have sent weapons and even troops to assist the army of President Vladimir V. Putin.

In February, Iran was plunged into a full-scale war, too, when the United States and Israel attacked. By one count, at least 17 nations — including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Lebanon and Iraq — have been involved.

“In reality, the two conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have been intertwined from the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022,” said Alina Polyakova, the president of the Center for European Policy Analysis, a research group in Washington that advocates strong U. S. support for Ukraine.

Russia and Iran have a long partnership, and both have been on the same side of recent wars, including the civil war in Syria. So it was perhaps unsurprising that Iran gave weapons aid to Russia soon after Mr. Putin’s military invaded Ukraine.

Iran sent drones and drone trainers to work with the Russian military in Crimea, the peninsula that Russia seized from Ukraine in 2014. The symbiosis is evident in the full-circle nature of that partnership: Russia improved the Iranian drones, began mass-producing them and is now sending the new versions to Iran to use against the United States and Israel.

The U. S. government has also said Iran provided ballistic missiles to Russia.

In the war in the Middle East, Russia has provided Iran with intelligence collected by satellites on U. S. military assets in the region. U. S. officials say recent Iranian attacks on American troops and military sites have been more accurate and deadlier. A strike late this month killed three U. S. service members in Jordan.

When asked by a reporter last week whether Russia and China were giving targeting information to Iran, Secretary of State Marco Rubio avoided answering, except to say that nothing China had done “has in any way changed the trajectory” of the war. He did not mention Russia.

William B. Taylor, a U. S. ambassador to Ukraine in the Bush and Obama administrations and the head of the embassy in Kyiv during the first Trump administration, said the wars “overlap but have not merged.”

“Ukraine is singularly focused on defeating the Russian invasion — an existential threat to the nation — by any and all means possible,” he said. That includes using military means to cut off support other nations are providing Russia.

“Ukraine is not seeking conflict with Iran but is bound to act to cut support to Russia from wherever it originates,” Mr. Taylor said.

It was unclear whether another such attack could occur again.

Ukraine’s ambassador to Washington, Olha Stefanishyna, said at a briefing on Thursday organized by The Christian Science Monitor that it is not the government’s policy to try to connect the two wars. The recent attack on the Iranian ship, she said, had been “unintentional.”

Drone and counterdrone innovation has been central to the war in Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said in March that he was sending more than 200 military experts to the Middle East to help countries there defend themselves against Iranian drones.

Mr. Zelensky has tried to make the case that the two wars have some common elements. On Saturday, he said Ukraine was ready to share intelligence with Western allies that showed Russia was providing Iran with satellite information on Gulf Arab nations and U. S. military bases in the region.

Soon after the war in Ukraine began, Mr. Zelensky sought aid from Israel. But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel has maintained a neutral stance on the war, taking care not to jeopardize his relationship with Mr. Putin. Last year, the Israelis sent a refurbished Patriot air defense missile system to Ukraine, but only after the Biden administration secured a pledge from Israel.

Mr. Zelensky and Mr. Netanyahu shook hands and spoke on Tuesday at the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham in Washington. It was the first time they had met in person in nearly three years. Both went to the White House for separate talks with President Trump.

Some analysts who have been critical of American wars, including the one in Iran, have warned that the Trump administration needs to be wary of how both Mr. Zelensky and Mr. Netanyahu might seek to deepen American involvement in the conflicts.

“Trump should be on guard as Zelensky and Netanyahu arrive, hats in hands, to Washington,” Andrew Day, a senior editor for The American Conservative, wrote this week. “Both will push for greater U. S. military assistance, and both will frame their demands as serving American interests.”

Trita Parsi, the co-founder of the Quincy Institute, which is critical of American foreign policy that relies on military aggression, wrote that Mr. Zelensky could achieve a “strategic breakthrough” with the “dangerous gambit” of trying to persuade Washington that the two wars are intertwined.

However, other analysts say the United States should strengthen its commitments to Ukraine and Israel in order to stand more firmly against a loose anti-American coalition that they argue includes Russia, China, Iran and North Korea.

That line of thought spans the political spectrum in Washington and is rooted in traditional foreign policy, but gained momentum late in the Biden administration.

The most powerful variable in the backdrops of the conflicts is China, the only country capable of challenging American global supremacy.

Ms. Polyakova, the advocate of U. S. support for the Ukrainian military, said that “behind much of this is, of course, China, which has been the key enabler of Russia’s war in Ukraine.” China is also the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, and U. S. officials say Chinese companies have been planning to send shoulder-fired missiles known as MANPADS to Iran.

Edward Wong reports on global affairs, U. S. foreign policy and the State Department for The Times.

A Fledgling Food Reviewer’s Battle With Cyclospora

The New York Times July 31, 2026

Cyclospora Cases

Advertisement

Supported by

Christina Hart, 29, started posting reviews on social media in May. Less than two months later, a stomach illness forced her to stop.

By Madaleine Rubin

Moments before posting her first food review on social media in May, Christina Hart was sitting in her red pickup truck, in a carwash parking lot, and “crying out to God,” she said.

“That was my breaking point,” said Ms. Hart, 29, of the Nashville area, who had recently lost her job and has two young children, including a daughter with severe autism whose care can be “all-consuming,” she said.

To raise her spirits, she filmed herself rating two items from a coffee shop in Hendersonville, Tenn.: a sausage-biscuit sandwich (six out of 10; “really dry,” she said) and a matcha lemonade (10 out of 10). Overnight, the video racked up thousands of views.

Since then, Ms. Hart has reviewed Cuban sandwiches, coffee, cookies and more around the Nashville suburbs and has gained about 20,000 followers across social media platforms, she said. She has used her videos to raise money for a struggling local business.

“It’s pretty much gave me hope,” she said through tears. “For having a way to take care of my kids.”

But this July, her fledgling career stopped as fast as it started. Ms. Hart became one of thousands around the country debilitated by cyclosporiasis, an intestinal illness caused by a microscopic parasite hidden among heads of lettuce, stalks of broccoli, crates of berries and more.

Suddenly, she could not leave her house, she said. “I’m so sorry,” she told restaurant and coffee shop owners. “I can’t get off the toilet.”

On July 14, in lieu of her weekly food reviews, she posted a selfie from bed on Facebook. “Well,” she told her followers after a doctor’s appointment, “#Cyclospora has officially entered the chat.”

The cyclospora parasite, spread through food or water contaminated with human feces, infects the intestines and can cause cramping, diarrhea and fatigue. Though infections are common, the U. S. is currently in the midst of its largest-ever breakout, with more than 18,000 cases confirmed or under investigation across 45 states.

Many have been linked to shredded lettuce that Taylor Farms supplied to Taco Bell, but the parasite also clings to fresh produce. Raspberries — which Ms. Hart said she often ate in the morning — are a common carrier.

“I wasn’t ever in a million years thinking I had a darn parasite,” said Ms. Hart, who initially assumed she had food poisoning and was unsure how she got the parasite. Tracing cyclosporiasis is difficult because it can incubate inside someone for up to 14 days before producing symptoms.

Ms. Hart said she lost 17 pounds in less than four weeks.

While that’s a high figure, “a significant illness can cause significant weight loss,” said Dr. Stephen Feagins, medical director of the public health department of Hamilton County, Ohio, where several cases of the parasite have been reported. Much of that weight could be fluids, he added.

Eventually, Ms. Hart reached a “state of delirium,” she said. How could she be a food reviewer without eating any food?

“I’ve done so many things in my life that have failed,” Ms. Hart said. “It just makes you question: Is this what I’m supposed to do? Am I imagining it? Was this a sign that I’m supposed to stop?”

But posting about the illness brought her videos more attention than ever. People sent messages of support, encouraging her to keep uploading reviews. Others shared their own experiences with the parasite.

“This whole cyclospora thing — I thought it was actually a curse, but it ended up being a blessing,” she said, adding that she was upgrading her video equipment and hoped to one day expand her reviews beyond Tennessee.

“If poop is what lands me there,” she said, “I guess that’s what lands me there.”

The Douglas DC-3 was mass-produced during World War II. Today, one of the few still remaining transports passengers in Colombia’s jungle.

Credit...

Supported by

By Max Bearak

Visuals by Federico Rios

We were cruising at eight thousand feet, low enough to make out individual trees in the rainforest below, when a towering wall of midafternoon cumulus arose before us.

There was no way around it — it was many miles wide — and no way over it because we were in an 84-year-old Douglas DC-3, arguably the most legendary plane ever mass-produced yet one without a pressurized cabin, which limited how high we could fly.

As the plane and the storm closed in on each other, Captain Joaquín Mosquera slid his window shut. When traversing clear skies, he hangs his elbow out of it as if he were driving an old pickup truck down a dirt road. That’s how riding in a DC-3 feels, too: like being pulled by a tractor through the sky.

This exact plane — one of only 16,000-or-so that were made — was the last operating a scheduled passenger service. As soon as I heard about it while on assignment in Colombia, I knew that I’d do whatever it took to get on board — both as a journalist and as an aviation geek.

The remaining few DC-3s mostly operate either as tourist novelty flights or in remote areas like the Canadian tundra, where they transport cargo only. But this one, operated by Aerolíneas del Llano — Plains Airlines — delivers passengers throughout far-flung corners of Colombia’s savannas and jungle.

I couldn’t help but wonder about the world in which this octogenarian plane still served as transport for people: Who were they — and did they feel any of the excitement I did about the DC-3?

Weeks later, standing in the cockpit behind Capt. Mosquera, finally passing through the dark curtain of clouds, the plane suddenly catapulted hundreds of feet heavenward, thrown aloft by the thermal updraft drawing moisture from the jungle and billowing it, and all of us, toward the stratosphere.

My heart swelled. This felt like what I live for. Behind me, other passengers, sitting shoulder to shoulder, clutched the bench below them.

The first time I saw a DC-3 was in Beira, Mozambique in 2019. It belonged to Samaritan’s Purse, an evangelical group delivering food to people made homeless by Cyclone Idai, the aftermath of which I was reporting on. Many of those people were in incredibly remote areas, but the DC-3 could take off and land on makeshift landing strips or even barren fields while laden with 7,000 pounds of cargo — double as much as a Cessna Grand Caravan.

That combination made it advantageous in this and other humanitarian situations. It is also what made them a decisive factor in the Allied victory in World War II, when the vast majority were produced. DC-3s ferried troops and airdropped supplies throughout the war, from Belgium to Burma.

That the DC-3 still flies eight decades after its heyday also speaks to its durability. This is the kind of plane that can be put back together when its nose gets dented or a hard landing rips off a wheel. The one used by Aerolíneas del Llano crash-landed in 1973, seventeen years before I was born. According to an article in El Tiempo, a Colombian newspaper, the passengers were unscathed. The plane was hammered, literally, back into flying condition. Even now, the safety kit hanging in the cockpit consists only of an ax, a machete and a straw hat stained with engine oil.

I discovered the plane because one day I was absently checking an app I’m mildly addicted to, FlightRadar24, which shows real-time flight tracking information on a map. I tapped my finger on a plane flying in a sparsely populated part of the country and, to my surprise, it was a DC-3.

A couple of weeks later, I took a shared taxi from Bogotá through the Andes Mountains to the airline’s dimly lit office in Villavicencio, the largest city on Colombia’s llanos. I paid in cash and got a handwritten boarding pass.

If you’re a fisherman, you might pay for a flight in salted fish. Farmers have used cacao as currency. It’s no big hassle to the airline’s owners — they resell the goods at the wholesale market in Villavicencio.

As dawn broke on what would be the first of three days I spent flying in the DC-3, Leonardo Rivera, whose family contracts the plane for weekly flights to secluded communities in the Amazon, leaned against burlap sacks of dried fish.

“Bagre apuy, bagre tigre, cachama,” he said, listing kinds of riverfish. “As good as money.”

The passengers were mostly people who are Indigenous to Colombia’s plains and rainforest or tradespeople who’ve settled in those frontier areas. Many from both groups spoke about the “settlement” of the region still being underway, usually as a good thing. Many villages don’t have doctors or any government services beyond ramshackle schools. Very few can be reached over land.

A typical landing strip in Colombia’s vast eastern regions is made of dirt and can be as short as 350 meters. Or, put differently, seven and a half times shorter than the shortest runway at New York’s J. F. K.

Germán Romero, who flew DC-3s in Colombia for 47 years before retiring in 2023, recalled transporting not just medicine, but iceboxes, mattresses and the outboard motors that locals affixed to their wooden canoes.

“The jungle has been settled piece by piece,” he said. “For many years, that has mostly been by the occasional barge and the DC-3s.”

It took very little time to realize that what had been a nerdy novelty for me was a necessity for people in the country’s remotest communities.

As we rattled down the runway, Francy Mosquera, no relation to the captain, covered her ears with her hands and closed her eyes.

“I’m terrified of this,” she said. But she had little choice.

Ms. Mosquera, 36, was a teacher from the city who had been reassigned by the government to a newly built school in an Indigenous community called Pueblo Nuevo, an hour upriver from Barrancominas. In this town, our flight would make its first stop. It would have taken her at least three days to get there by boat.

She carried little, no more than a backpack and a small, black duffel. She knew no one in the area. When I bade her farewell on the dirt landing strip in Barrancominas, she looked paralyzed.

“Well, here we are,” she said, looking at the smattering of buildings and the muddy Guaviare River. “I haven’t the faintest idea where I’m going.”

We had more stops to make, and the afternoon clouds were getting tall and dark. The captain beckoned back the passengers who milled about, stretching their legs. They clambered in and squeezed onto the long bench in the plane’s hold, which can fit, at most, 19 average-sized people on it. Across from them, tied down with ropes, was an assortment of cargo, some typical, some unusual, but all indicative of the plane’s role in that slow but ongoing “settlement.”

There was a box of Starlink internet receivers. There was tin sheeting. There were two female mannequins with enormous butts. And there were three marble chairs addressed to Monsignor Joselito Carreño Quiñones.

When we tracked him down in the town of Inírida, where he is a vicar, he explained why he had spent a couple thousand dollars of his church’s savings to fly out the heavy chairs.

“It is a way to convey the beauty of God’s creation to our growing parish,” he said. “You don’t have to paint it. It expresses its own God-given beauty.”

As we rolled for takeoff, the plane hadn’t even reached 100 miles per hour when it began to levitate, clearing the trees just in time.

When the DC-3 was introduced in 1936 by Douglas, an American company, it immediately revolutionized air travel. Aboard it, one could get from New York to Los Angeles in just 18 hours — with only three stops — fast enough to convince many people to trade railways for airways. That kicked off the commercial aviation era we have lived in ever since. By 1939, 90 percent of all flights worldwide were on DC-3s.

Several hundred entered passenger service, but ten thousand more were made for the war, which began shortly after their debut. Most were put together in California by the famous Rosie the Riveters, women who joined the war effort on industrial assembly lines. Nearly 5,000 were produced in 1944 alone. The then-U. S.-allied Soviets, who had been granted a U. S. government license to build their own variant of the DC-3, built 5,000 more.

“I can feel that this plane was made by women,” Capt. Mosquera said one day during a short stopover in Barrancominas. He flashed a characteristic grin; he has a flirtatious energy in much of what he does. “I cannot be brusque with this plane. It requires you to treat it softly,” he said.

All planes are machines with switches and buttons and levers, but the DC-3 is from an era before autopilot, and flying it requires constant attention and finessing of various dials, the occasional pulling of latches and the monitoring of many this-and-that-o-meters.

According to the Air Force Research Agency, Aerolíneas del Llano’s aircraft began its life with the U. S. Air Force on April 17, 1942. After the war, a U. S. government agency called the Reconstruction Finance Corporation sold thousands of DC-3s into commercial service.

Vast fleets ended up in developing countries with only the barest infrastructure. According to Alexandre Avrane, who runs AeroTransport Data Bank, the world’s most extensive collection of aircraft history, the plane first went to the Texas-based Lone Star Air Cargo, then Brazil, and finally to Colombia.

At the time, most people thought that DC-3s would be replaced by the more advanced planes rapidly becoming available, like Douglas’s DC-6 or the Boeing 307 Stratoliner, which had pressurized cabins and could fly over the weather, reducing turbulence.

American Airlines retired its last DC-3 in 1949. An article in the Times from that year said that while the DC-3 had been “one of the greatest passenger planes ever built,” it would soon be “as obsolete as the fringed surrey.” (A fringed surrey being a horse-drawn passenger carriage with a frilly canopy.)

But what will finally extinguish the run of this last passenger DC-3, however, isn’t a better plane, or a lack of spare parts, or even another crash, but insurance agents who don’t seem to feel any of the plane’s romance. Aerolíneas del Llano is fighting with its current insurers as they continue to inch their rate upward toward the bounds of affordability.

For now, though, the people of Colombia’s llanos rely on the DC-3 to make modern life a little less distant. On my second day of flying, someone was expecting the plane to deliver a birthday cake. Someone else awaited a bottle of Buchanan’s Deluxe whiskey.

The cargo hold was stuffed. That day, a sampling of what it contained included 10 boxes each with 100 live baby chicks (all chirping excitedly), dozens of grown hens, two cockfighting roosters, iron rods, and sacks of potatoes and onions. Passengers were returning from doctor’s appointments, or essential errands like cashing pension checks at the bank in Villavicencio.

While I stood on the tarmac in the dawn’s calm, I had thought all the cargo for the day was in order — a tableau of rural miscellany on a dilapidated trolley — and then a van from a funeral parlor pulled up.

Its driver opened the back door and carried out a coffin wrapped in black plastic. It was about a foot and a half long.

Capt. Mosquera tilted his head knowingly. “We see that a lot,” he said.

Nicodemus León, a two-year-old from a community called Siare, had fallen severely ill and been brought to Villavicencio weeks earlier but didn’t survive.

When we landed in Barrancominas, we expected to find baby Nicodemus’s mother waiting, but she was still on her way from Siare, eight hours away by boat. Siare has no cell reception, internet or any other reliable means of long-distance communication.

We left the coffin on a tarp on the airstrip, next to boxes of dried goods, and flew on.

At our next stop, a red-dirt outpost called Cumaribo, we picked up a severely ill 20-month-old and her mother, and I felt as if I were seeing Nico’s story play out, just at an earlier stage.

Ana Gabriela Martínez, 22, and Cloe were leaving their Indigenous reserve for the first time. Over the roar of the DC-3’s engines, Ms. Martínez explained that every time Cloe cried, she fainted. To reliably resuscitate her, she could press on Cloe’s right side and lift her right arm. Doctors who visited the reserve recently had told her that Cloe had been born with a heart murmur and that an operation in Villavicencio might be the only way to save her.

Capt. Mosquera flew low and steady with the windows open, letting the humid air rush through the plane.

Simón Posada contributed reporting.

Like some of you, perhaps, I’m really into planes. When I chanced upon an 84-year-old plane still in service while using an aviation app, I was intrigued. But when I learned it was the last of its kind flying scheduled passenger routes, I knew I had to get on it.

Max Bearak is a correspondent for The Times focusing on breaking and international news.
