Justice Dept.’s Case Against Minnesota Protesters Hits Hurdles as Missteps Mount

The New York Times July 31, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The problems plaguing the case have not only hurt the government’s chances, lawyers say, but have also undermined the bonds of trust that prosecutors have traditionally enjoyed in court.

By Alan Feuer and Ernesto Londoño

The Trump administration came out swinging in January after a group of activists in Minnesota, accompanied by camera-toting journalists, held a demonstration at a St. Paul church to protest President Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown in the state.

Officials cast the incident as part of a larger narrative of left-wing protesters being out of control at a fraught political moment — just days after a Minneapolis woman, Renee Good, had been killed in her car by an immigration agent. The authorities moved swiftly, arresting several people who had been inside the church. Among them was Don Lemon, the former CNN anchor who had long run afoul of Mr. Trump.

Harmeet K. Dhillon, who runs the Justice Department’s civil rights division, which helped to bring the charges, set the tone for the administration’s moves by trumpeting the case with a brash remark. “We’re going to pursue this to the ends of the earth,” she said.

Six months later, however, the case, which is unfolding in Federal District Court in St. Paul, has been plagued by an array of prosecutorial missteps. Defense lawyers have accused the government of rushing to bring headline-grabbing charges, and the judges overseeing the proceeding have, from its outset, been voicing their concerns.

In May, for instance, it was revealed that one judge undertook the highly unusual step of rejecting a raft of search warrants after finding they would be unlikely to turn up evidence that crimes had been committed. Last week, another judge made an even more unusual move: He demanded to see some grand jury transcripts in an effort to determine whether prosecutors had acted improperly when securing the indictment.

At the same time, the defense has said investigators botched their efforts to search Mr. Lemon’s cellphone, issuing a warrant in Minnesota even though the phone was seized in California. Lawyers have also accused the prosecution of bypassing its problems with securing warrants by issuing administrative subpoenas typically used in customs enforcement cases, not criminal proceedings, to obtain information from some of the defendants.

All of this, the lawyers claim, has damaged the government’s case and had a broader impact, undermining the bonds of trust — known in legal circles as the presumption of regularity — that prosecutors have traditionally enjoyed in court.

“It is clear to me that in this case, the government in many respects, candidly, has gone off the rails,” Matthew Ebert, a defense lawyer who served as a federal prosecutor until late last year, told a judge last week.

“We’re talking about a growing confluence of conduct,” Mr. Ebert added, “which ultimately, Your Honor, I think goes to the fact that the presumption of regularity has eroded, if not evaporated.”

Prosecutors have adamantly denied such accusations, claiming that whatever errors they have made — and they have admitted making some — were purely accidental. A Justice Department official played down the troubles, saying that the case was moving forward in a normal way with the defendants challenging the charges.

Still, in a signal that prosecutors are somewhat concerned about bringing the case to trial, they have offered plea deals to 29 of the nearly 40 people facing indictment. Under the proposed agreement, defendants would plead guilty to a single misdemeanor charge and avoid any prison time, according to a draft shared with The New York Times.

So far, however, none of the defendants have agreed to take the deal, according to defense lawyers.

The U. S. attorney’s office declined to comment on the plea deals.

The case in St. Paul is only the latest prosecution arising from Mr. Trump’s nationwide immigration sweeps to face significant problems. Over and over, in cities like Chicago and Los Angeles, the Justice Department has followed the same pattern: It has loudly announced indictments, often tarring defendants as radicals or terrorists, then watched as cases have run aground because of a lack of evidence or prosecutorial errors.

An investigation by The Times found that hundreds of officer assault cases stemming from immigration raids have unraveled as juries have acquitted, judges have thrown out charges or prosecutors have themselves withdrawn indictments.

From the start, the case against Mr. Lemon and his co-defendants struggled to get off the ground, not least because of the uncomfortable way in which it lumped together activists engaged in political protest and journalists who covered them. Three sets of judges — including some on a federal appeals court — refused to go along with the government’s initial attempt to seek criminal complaints against Mr. Lemon and other journalists — including the reporter, Georgia Fort — after finding there was simply no evidence they had committed crimes.

Some career federal prosecutors in Minnesota were alarmed by the anomalous investigative steps that set the case in motion and by the pointed remarks administration officials made about the defendants. The protest happened days after several experienced prosecutors resigned over the Justice Department’s handling of Ms. Good’s shooting.

Lauren Roso, a career prosecutor assigned to work on the case in its early days, said it led her to quit what had been a dream job.

“The Cities Church protest case gave me significant pause,” Ms. Roso said, disclosing for the first time the reason she resigned. “I was uncomfortable with the pace and manner in which the case was proceeding, and those concerns played a role in my decision to leave the U. S. attorney’s office.”

In the end, prosecutors persuaded grand jurors in St. Paul to return an indictment charging the two journalists and seven other people with a conspiracy to violate the Face Act, a law that forbids using threats of force to intimidate or interfere with people seeking reproductive health services or trying to participate in a service at a house of worship. A subsequent indictment expanded the case to include another 30 people, most of them demonstrators who joined the protest at Cities Church on Jan. 18.

But the case ran into trouble almost immediately as the White House posted a digitally altered image of the lead defendant — Nekima Levy Armstrong, a local civil rights lawyer — appearing to sob as she was being arrested. Weeks later, prosecutors dropped the charges against one of the new defendants, Heather Danae Lewis, in what appeared to be a case of mistaken identity.

Overall, prosecutors have vigorously defended their indictment. In recent court papers, they said they intended to prove the charges by showing, among other things, that Mr. Lemon and Ms. Fort attended a meeting where activists organized the protest at the church where one of the pastors also works as a senior official with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The prosecutors also say that they have a large amount of video footage of the “disruptive protest operation” and that one churchgoer injured her elbow when she fled from the building. Moreover, another of the church’s pastors, Jonathan Parnell, has testified to the grand jury that he felt “threatened and crowded” by both the activists and the journalists.

Lawyers for Mr. Lemon and Ms. Fort have scoffed at such assertions, arguing that their clients, unlike the actual protesters, never shouted anti-ICE slogans during the demonstration and got close to Mr. Parnell and his congregants only to do their jobs.

At the court hearing last week, most of the discussion focused on Ms. Fort, a St. Paul native who has covered the extensive protests against ICE in Minnesota as well as the killings of Ms. Good and another demonstrator, Alex Pretti. The government has already acknowledged that in some of the rejected search warrants, investigators falsely claimed that Ms. Fort shouted things like “ICE Out!” during the church protest and used her camera as a “weapon to intimidate, threaten and scare the congregants.”

Her lawyer, Mr. Ebert, asked Magistrate Judge Douglas L. Micko to scrutinize the grand jury proceedings to be certain that the same false statements had not been used to secure the indictment against her. By the end of the hearing, Judge Micko agreed to do so, saying there was some evidence that prosecutors may have “misinstructed” the panel.

Typically, a case like this would be overseen by prosecutors from the U. S. attorney’s office in Minnesota, but as with other politically sensitive cases, the proceeding in St. Paul has largely been run by lawyers based in Washington. One of them was new enough to the case — and to Minnesota — that during last week’s hearing he mispronounced the name of a veteran judge in the district, Patrick J. Schiltz.

In a sign of local discomfort with the case, three defense lawyers formerly served in the office that is prosecuting the defendants. At the hearing, one of them, Mr. Ebert, immediately accused the prosecution of unfairly going after his client, Ms. Fort, and her co-defendants.

“We have a situation where the government unfortunately charged the case first and then tried to investigate it later,” he told Judge Micko. “And the consequences of that are playing out in unfortunate real time.”

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

Ernesto Londoño is a Times reporter based in Minnesota, covering news in the Midwest and drug use and counternarcotics policy. He welcomes tips and can be reached at elondono.81 on Signal.

Connections Coach

Wilson, whose 2017 translation of Homer’s Greek classic influenced the director Christopher Nolan, panned his screenplay for the movie version in an essay for The London Review of Books.

Emily Wilson holding her written translation of Homer’s “The Odyssey.”Credit... Lauren Chineme/W. W. Norton & Company

Supported by

By Neil Vigdor

As Christopher Nolan’s epic “The Odyssey” closes in on $1 billion in ticket sales at the box office, one of the leading translators of the Homeric tale eviscerated the summer blockbuster as a grandiose and superficial movie that strays from classical interpretations.

The scholar, Emily Wilson, weighing in on Mr. Nolan’s big-screen adaptation in The London Review of Books, said she would have been “ashamed to have written any part of this script.”

Her 4,000-plus-word takedown of this year’s most-talked-about movie appeared to temporarily crash The LRB’s website and fueled a debate over balancing commercial success with literary authenticity.

Here’s what to know about the controversy:

In 2017, Wilson became the first woman to translate “The Odyssey” from ancient Greek into English, an interpretation widely celebrated in academia and the literary world as comprehensive, modern in sensibilities and faithful to Homer’s nearly 3,000-year-old poem.

The project took several years to complete for Wilson, 54, who has published four books on ancient literature, including a 2023 translation of “The Iliad,” another epic poem by Homer.

In her translation of “The Odyssey,” which was published by W. W. Norton & Company, Wilson departed from the masculine framing used by her male predecessors. She has said on several occasions that the decision has subjected her to online harassment and misogyny from men and far-right figures who object to her translation.

While promoting his blockbuster movie, Nolan mentioned Wilson’s translation of “The Odyssey” as one of his influences.

Wilson is department chairwoman of Classical studies at the University of Pennsylvania and was recognized as a 2019 MacArthur fellow for “bringing classical literature to new audiences in works that convey ancient texts’ relevance to our time.” She has a bachelor’s degree in Classical literature and philosophy from Oxford, a Master of Philosophy in English literature from Oxford and a Ph. D. in Classics and comparative literature from Yale.

Five days before the movie “The Odyssey” had its premiere, Wilson, appearing on a July 12 episode of “The Daily,” the podcast of The New York Times, said she was “pumped” to see how the tale played out on the big screen.

“I mean, it’s going to be exciting that so many people who may have thought, Oh, ancient literature is boring, or it’s not for me, or it’s too inaccessible, are then going to realize, actually, this is a really compelling story,” Wilson said. “And some proportion of the people who go to the movie will then turn back to the original poem, which I think is great. I love that.”

Asked about purists potentially taking exception to Nolan’s artistic choices, Wilson said it would not be the first time that Homeric poems were adapted for performance.

“I think it’s totally fine and valid for a director to explore his own vision,” she said of Nolan.

But after she saw the movie, the floodgates of criticism opened: Wilson wrote that Nolan’s adaptation lacked many of the elements that made the poem great.

“It has nothing convincing to say about time, memory, history, war, or about the relationship between one warrior’s glorious return and the lives of his family, adversaries, comrades, friends and neighbours,” she wrote. “It lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth. Its narrative structure is gimmicky. The writing is abysmal.”

Wilson argued that the movie embraced style over substance.

“It’s a family-friendly audiovisual spectacle, like an elaborate Fourth of July fireworks display — and with about the same level of narrative and emotional depth,” she wrote.

Nolan’s casting choices also drew criticism from Wilson.

“Most of the non-white actors — Zendaya, Lupita Nyong’o, Himesh Patel, Corey Antonio Hawkins, Travis Scott — play versions of the Black best friend, whose only role in the drama is to provide aid to the white protagonist,” she wrote.

On Wednesday Wilson expressed regret on Bluesky over how she had presented that criticism.

“In this piece, I regret the paragraph about the uses of the POC actors — who are all great, but IMO under-utilized (and why couldn’t Himesh Patel be Odysseus instead?),” she wrote. “I still think the film largely wastes its strong cast, but I framed it badly.”

Nolan, whose “Oppenheimer” won seven Academy Awards in 2024, including for best picture and best director, has not responded publicly to Wilson’s scathing review.

Among those who have pushed back against Wilson’s criticism and in Nolan’s defense are the novelist Joyce Carol Oates, a retired professor of the humanities at Princeton and a National Book Award winner.

“Yes, her tone of dismissal & haughty superiority strike a sour note,” Oates wrote on X. “Rather than disagreeing with interpretations of Homer in a collegial manner, this person, who has benefited enormously from Nolan’s film, speaks in the crude language of MAGA folks attacking someone with ideas that differ from hers.”

Oates said she would have expected a translator, whose role she described as having subjectivity, to be more tolerant.

In an online commentary for Slate, Theo Nash, who has published on the textual history of “The Odyssey,” accused Wilson of using “baffling arguments” to “flay” Nolan’s latest movie.

The article was titled: “I’m a Classicist. Were Emily Wilson and I Watching the Same Odyssey Movie?”

Nash said Nolan was entitled to artistic interpretation.

“Wilson is naturally at her best when discussing the poem itself: This is a work to which she has dedicated years of her life, and she knows it intimately,” Nash wrote. “But too often she simply criticizes Nolan for deviating from it, as if the filmmaker’s choices were not also an act of interpretation. The close attention to the text that informs Wilson’s translation is lacking in her reading of the movie, and the idea that Nolan might have something new to say about ‘The Odyssey’ is denied.”

Daniel Mendelsohn, a professor of humanities at Bard College whose own translation of “The Odyssey” was published last year by the University of Chicago Press, wrote in The New York Review that the most authentic thing about the movie was its “densely braided narrative,” while the “tormented hero sounds like the heroes of Christopher Nolan movies.”

“Whatever his lifelong fascination with the epic, Nolan has merely remade Homer’s hero in his own image, just as he has imposed on Odysseus’s adventures values utterly foreign to Homer,” Mendelsohn wrote.

Neil Vigdor covers breaking news for The Times, with a focus on politics.

In the Surf

The New York Times July 31, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

By Sam Sifton

I am the host of The Morning.

President Trump said his “Board of Peace” had reached a disarmament deal in Gaza. “For the first time, Hamas officially has committed to an actionable plan for relinquishing all its weapons, which will be followed by Israeli withdrawal from Gaza,” the board said. Neither side commented publicly.

We have more news below. I’m going to start with the United States Coast Guard.

Dave Philipps, who covers the United States military and veterans for The Times, has spent the past few years focused on the brain injuries suffered by members of elite and specialized units. He’s written about artillery crews who repeatedly fire high-powered cannons and about SEALs who do the same with shoulder-fired rockets. He’s written about what happens to the brains of fighter pilots who catapult from aircraft carriers, and to those of fast-boat crews who pound across the ocean.

And now he’s turned his attention to the crews of Coast Guard rescue boats, who work and train in heavy, crashing seas in order to save lives. They’re called surfmen, and their work is among the most challenging and dangerous jobs in the service.

It is work that comes at a cost, Dave reports. They take a beating from the ocean. Many veteran surfmen experience headaches, memory lapses, anxiety attacks, nightmares, mood swings and cognitive problems that can be symptoms of brain injuries.

“A 20-foot wave breaking on you is like being in a car crash,” a surfman named Aaron Harris told him. “If you are out training in big surf, that’s like 20 car accidents a day.” Harris was on the boats for 22 years, before retiring in 2024.

The surfmen are alone, Dave discovered. The Coast Guard has no regular testing protocol for brain injuries. It delivers no formal briefings on the dangers of pounding waves. The website it maintains on brain injuries is more than 10 years old. Dave found that many of the links that appear under a heading reading “Where to get help” are inactive.

The surfmen suffer, and their families suffer, and the results can be fatal.

Dave’s story explores the life and death of a surfman named Brett Bonner, who saved hundreds of lives during his 21 years driving rescue boats. Bonner developed post-traumatic stress disorder during his service, and his life unraveled after he retired in 2022. Here’s Dave:

He struggled to make decisions. Even ordering at a drive-through was overwhelming. He grew paranoid. He was sure his father-in-law, who lived next door, was out to get him and punched him over a minor disagreement about new closet doors.

In February 2025, Bonner shot himself. His wife and four children saw it happen. He left no note.

Bonner’s eldest child, Kayleigh, is now 18. After her father’s death, she did something remarkable. Seeking some understanding of what had happened to her dad, and whether it had anything to do with his work in the unrelenting surf, she decided to send questionnaires to as many surfmen as she could locate. Her survey asked 36 questions about their time in the service and their health during and after it.

Nearly 80 active and retired surfmen responded, and a vast majority reported symptoms similar to her father’s. They had headaches. Sleeplessness. Their memories were shot. Anxiety stalked them. Their moods swung, hard. Some were getting worse.

“My brain has started to fail me. I feel it, I see it,” one responder in his early 50s wrote. “It is difficult to do things that used to be natural to me.”

“It has been a struggle for me to keep my life together,” another in his mid-40s wrote.

Kayleigh wrote up the results of her study as a senior-year high school research project. It earned an A. (I’d have gone A+.) Dave reports that she plans to share her findings with the Coast Guard.

Yesterday I reached out to Dave to ask him what to make of his reporting. Not just about the Coast Guard surfmen, but also about the Navy pilots and boat skippers and SEALS and Army mortar soldiers and all those who’ve been exposed, repeatedly, to concussive blasts in service to the nation, and who’ve been left with injured brains.

Here’s what he told me:

I think the big takeaway is that these injuries are preventable. There never needs to be another story like Brett Bonner’s, even if we will always need Coast Guard crews to brave rough waters. On these motor lifeboats, most of the damaging exposure occurs during training, not in emergencies. The same is true in the rest of the military. That is both infuriating and a stroke of good luck, because training is a controlled environment. We can change it to limit damage.

If anything is going to change, though, the first step is recognizing that there is a problem. That has been tricky because these types of brain injuries develop slowly and often resemble other mental health problems. For decades the military has been stuck in a cycle where it doesn’t see these injuries as a problem, and therefore isn’t on the lookout for them.

I hope the reporting The Times has done can break that cycle.

Please read the complete article here. I’ve only scratched its surface. (Not a subscriber? Not a problem. The click is free.)

Spain mobilized its military after thousands of migrants crossed — some swimming — to Ceuta, a Spanish-governed peninsula on Morocco’s coast.

Climate change is an important factor in Europe’s wildfires. So is the continent’s shift away from farming, experts say.

A wildfire on the Greek island of Crete has forced thousands of people to flee and killed two firefighters, the latest in a series of blazes that have charred Europe this summer.

Russia pounded Ukrainian cities with a barrage of missiles and drones that killed at least eight people. With the attacks, Russia set a record for the country’s ballistic missile attacks in a single month.

During the assault, a Russian missile crashed in Poland. The episode raised the possibility of a confrontation with NATO.

An appeals court is still considering the legality of President Trump’s White House ballroom project. Yet construction is racing ahead, as these photos show.

The Trump administration exempted natural diamonds from its latest batch of tariffs, after negotiations and a gift to Trump of a ring encrusted with 321 diamonds from a trade group in Belgium.

Trump says he may temporarily withdraw his nomination of Todd Blanche to be attorney general. Two Republicans have threatened to block Blanche’s confirmation.

Elon Musk says that he plans to spend at least $100 million on the midterm elections to help Republicans.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he supported reparations for some Black New Yorkers but said it was too early to commit to direct cash payments.

Texas parents are suing to remove Ten Commandments posters from classrooms.

Anthropic revealed that its artificial intelligence systems broke into computers at three outside organizations, heightening fears about the technology’s safety.

U. S. economic growth slowed in the last quarter, pulled down by the higher prices and supply chain disruptions caused by the war in Iran.

The father of a teenager who killed four people at a Georgia high school was sentenced to 15 years in prison over his son’s attack. The son was sentenced to life earlier this week.

Maggie Haberman spoke to Ezra Klein about DOGE, Iran and her new book with Jonathan Swan on Trump’s second term, “Regime Change.”

Vivek Ramaswamy could be the Republican Party’s future. But first he has to win, Lydia Polgreen writes.

— That is how many hours it could take to fly nonstop between Sydney and London when Qantas launches a new flight next year, aboard specially manufactured Airbus jets. The route would become the world’s longest commercial flight.

FIFA announced plans to allow private investment in its tournaments. In response, European nations threatened to boycott the World Cup.

But if you happen to run in tuna-fishing circles and someone gives you a fat loin off a fish caught earlier that morning? Use that instead and experience nirvana.

What You Need to Know About Installing Plug-In Solar Panels

The New York Times July 31, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

You can now buy panels that plug into electrical outlets, but there are some important safety issues to consider when picking and installing a system.

By Ivan Penn and Claire Brown

So you want to cut your electric bill and are eyeing the solar panels that can plug into any outlet in a home to produce your own power?

You may want to wait for a little while.

None of the systems available in the United States have yet received a crucial certification that deems them safe to use in single-family homes, condominiums and apartments. Experts who set safety standards expect to certify some panels soon.

“We really do love the idea of empowering consumers,” said Kenneth Boyce, vice president of engineering at UL Solutions, a company that tests, validates and sets standards for various products. “We’re really focused on keeping people safe.”

Plug-in or so-called balcony-solar systems have become popular in Germany in recent years. Ten American states have passed legislation making them legal, and many others are considering measures that would allow consumers to buy and install them.

Cost and simplicity have driven much of the excitement over the plug-in solar systems. Typically, homeowners do not need to hire installers to connect these solar panels, as they would for conventional rooftop systems that, in the United States, can cost as much as $36,000.

Plug-in systems can be as cheap as a few hundred dollars and typically top out at roughly $2,000.

You want to look for products that carry the “UL 3700” certification. It indicates that the product has been tested and meets the safety criteria set by UL Solutions.

Some systems produce so little electricity — under 400 watts — that they do not pose a safety risk, their makers claim.

But the prongs on larger systems could deliver a momentary shock risk after they are disconnected from the outlet. The UL 3700 standard requires the prongs to be “touch safe,” prompting some developer to encase them in plastic, similar to those found on electric vehicle chargers. Others have created equipment like protective sleeves.

Another potential problem has to do with home circuit breakers. Typically, a household circuit operates on a breaker based on how much electrical current an appliance requires.

When circuits are overloaded, breakers can trip to prevent fires and damage to the electrical equipment.

A plug-in solar system that lacks UL 3700 certification could mask how much electrical current is flowing on a particular circuit because the panels are supplying electricity. In that case, a breaker might not detect that the circuit is being overloaded by other appliances on the same circuit.

“The holy grail is to wait and make sure it is listed to UL 3700 certification,” said Bernadette Del Chiaro, a senior vice president at the Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit organization focused on health and safety. “It puts all the onus on the manufacturers to put in safety devices.”

Some products may claim to be UL certified or UL compliant because certain components of the system, such as inverters, meet existing or draft standards. However, UL Solutions has said it expects its certification to apply to entire systems, not just individual parts. Other organizations also certify these products, but certifications from UL Solutions tend to be coveted by industry players.

Theoretically, yes. A major selling point for these systems is that they are no more difficult to set up than a television or a Wi-Fi router. They are designed to be lightweight and renter friendly.

But some state lawmakers have considered mandating that qualified electricians install the systems. And the final UL 3700 safety certification may require an electrician’s help to install a special electrical outlet for plugging the panels into.

The panels are generally about the size of a window, and can be hung on balconies or placed in backyards — anywhere outdoors with six hours or more of full sun. South-facing areas are ideal because they tend to get the most sun.

If you rent your home, check your state’s law to see if there are any requirements about notifying your landlord. Vermont, for example, requires tenants to give their landlords 10 days’ notice before installing plug-in solar.

Ivan Penn is a reporter based in Los Angeles and covers the energy industry. His work has included reporting on clean energy, failures in the electric grid and the economics of utility services.

Claire Brown covers climate change for The Times and writes for the Climate Forward newsletter.

Plug-In Solar Panels Are Starting to Sprout in U. S. Backyards

The New York Times July 31, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Ten U. S. states have legalized systems that can be plugged into standard wall outlets. The technology typically does not require permits or electricians.

By Ivan Penn and Claire Brown

Ivan Penn reported from Los Angeles, and Claire Brown from New York.

After watching a YouTube video about solar panels that can be plugged into a regular electrical outlet, Melani Jackson plopped four panels in the backyard of her Salt Lake City home.

In the six months since, she has lowered her electricity bill by about $77 in total. While that’s not a large sum, she is happy to have banked those savings, which required little effort on her part.

“I just really appreciated the idea of being able to do something to cut even just a few dollars off my energy bill plus just become a little bit more environmentally friendly,” Ms. Jackson, 35, said.

Millions of Americans worried about rising energy costs might soon follow in her footsteps as states start allowing homeowners and renters to plug in solar panels on balconies, in backyards and other places. Plug-in systems are much smaller and cheaper than rooftop build-outs — some costing just a few hundred dollars a panel. Permits are not required in the states that allow their use, and people can often install them on their own.

Utah became the first state to legalize plug-in solar systems last year. Nine others, including New Jersey, Virginia and Colorado, have joined it, and lawmakers in California, Massachusetts, New York, Pennsylvania and several other states are considering doing so.

Colorado enacted one of the broadest plug-in solar laws this year. The sponsor of the bill, State Representative Lesley Smith, a Democrat, said she had first seen the technology during a trip to Germany, which has pioneered its use. When she discussed plug-in solar systems at a town hall, she said, “everyone started clapping.”

Home solar panels have, of course, been around for many years. But conventional rooftop systems can cost as much as $36,000, and in many American cities and towns it can take months to obtain the required permits. Such systems have also lost financial appeal in recent years because states, at the urging of electric utility companies, have reduced the bill credits that homeowners can earn from the excess electricity their panels send to the grid.

Plug-in systems get around many of the hassles of conventional rooftop solar. But despite the enthusiasm for the technology, no plug-in solar system has yet been certified as safe to use in the United States. States that have passed laws allowing the systems to be sold require them to be certified by organizations like UL Solutions, a company that tests, validates and sets standards for various products.

The result is a gap growing between enthusiasm for plug-in solar and the availability of a product that has been proven safe.

UL Solutions soon expects to certify at least one of the plug-in solar systems for use in the United States, said Kenneth Boyce, the company’s vice president of engineering. He warned that people should avoid uncertified products, because they could cause electrical shocks or damage electrical equipment and start fires.

For now, some Americans are exploiting a murky certification landscape and shopping online for plug-in systems for their homes, condominiums and apartments.

In the San Francisco Bay Area, Alex Ottoboni, who lives in a condominium, bought two panels even though he knew that California had not yet passed a plug-in solar law. Hanging from his balcony, the panels generate enough electricity to save him $5 to $7 a month on a bill that typically runs about $400 but has reached as high as $680 in winter.

“I don’t like having to be reliant on my utility,” said Mr. Ottoboni, 32, who works in software. He added that his electricity service was not reliable and “just getting more expensive every year.”

The average residential electricity rate in the United States in April was up 7 percent from a year earlier, according to the Energy Information Administration. But rates have been steadily rising for several years, and most industry experts expect costs to continue increasing. Utility companies are spending to upgrade their systems to keep up with electricity demand from data centers and to make up for maintenance that was deferred over the past several decades.

Energy experts say power bills this summer could rise as much as 10.5 percent. The National Energy Assistance Directors Association, which represents state governments in securing federal money, warned last month that one in six U. S. households had fallen behind on its electric bills this year.

A handful of companies have begun catering to people like Mr. Ottoboni and Ms. Jackson.

Bright Saver, a California nonprofit group, recently began selling plug-in solar kits at cost, meaning the organization makes no profit on the sales. Its goal is to expand access to solar systems and push other companies to drive down their prices. Its two-panel, 360-watt system is roughly big enough to power a refrigerator and sells for $414.17.

Those systems are too small to pose any safety risks, said Cora Stryker, a co-founder of the organization. Even so, the laws in Maine, New York and Vermont require certification of those systems because of the more stringent policies in those states.

“We know people want these — they want them now,” Ms. Stryker said. “Electricity prices are skyrocketing, and people are really worried about climate change.”

EcoFlow and Craftstrom sell larger systems for $1,300 to $2,600. EcoFlow ships to addresses in Utah and Maryland, which have passed laws allowing plug-in solar, and Craftstrom sells to all 50 states, capitalizing on certification standards. Both companies have said they plan to seek full certification from UL Solutions.

Stephan Scherer, founder and chief executive of Craftstrom, said sales had increased 50 percent in the past year as state lawmakers passed legislation for plug-in solar systems. The company is on track to sell thousands of units a year, he said.

Plug-in solar systems route the direct current generated by one or a few panels to an inverter, which converts it to alternating current. The inverter, in turn, is plugged into a wall socket through which it transmits energy to appliances, lightbulbs or anything else that is using electricity.

Germany first allowed residents to install plug-in solar in October 2024. Some 800,000 people registered their systems in the first three months, and buyers can now pick them up at IKEA in that country. But the American electrical system is different enough from Germany’s that panels sold there cannot be used here.

Utility executives in the United States have expressed concerns that electricity produced by the systems might feed back into the power grid, posing a danger to linemen working on power lines that they believed were not carrying electricity.

Pedro J. Pizarro, president and chief executive of Edison International, the parent company of the utility Southern California Edison, said that he supported the idea of the plug-in solar technology but that his company opposed legislation introduced in the California Legislature to legalize such systems. He said the bill did not go far enough in protecting utility workers.

“It has to be safe, not only for consumers but for our workers,” Mr. Pizarro said. “It shouldn’t receive unfair subsidies. Beyond that, though, we’re all for it.”

But companies that sell plug-in systems argue that safety risks are minimal or nonexistent. Mr. Scherer of Craftstrom said his company’s systems would not shock electrical workers because they shut off automatically within one second of a power disruption or grid outage.

Mr. Boyce of UL Solutions said his company would certify panels only if they did not pose a risk to consumers or utility workers.

Backers of plug-in solar technology say that the safety issues will soon be resolved and that more states ought to legalize it to help people with rising energy costs.

“Politicians all over the country are wringing their hands, wanting to do something about energy affordability,” said Bernadette Del Chiaro, a senior vice president at the Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit organization focused on health and safety. “Here is an immediate answer.”

Ivan Penn is a reporter based in Los Angeles and covers the energy industry. His work has included reporting on clean energy, failures in the electric grid and the economics of utility services.

Claire Brown covers climate change for The Times and writes for the Climate Forward newsletter.

It Looks Like Nothing Can Dent MAGA’s Support for ICE

Wired July 29, 2026

On Tuesday, the day after hundreds of thousands of Haitian migrants effectively lost their temporary protected status that allowed them to live and work in the US, Republican pundit Steve Bannon wasted little time in demanding their instant removal.

“I was under the assumption that when they pulled TPS and their eligibility for that program ended … they were going to be boarding planes or buses today … today, this morning at dawn to go back to Haiti,” said Bannon, a longtime ally of President Donald Trump, on his War Room podcast on Tuesday. “Why are they not out of the country?”

Mike Davis, a conservative political strategist agreed with Bannon: “The solution is to get these people the hell out of our country as fast as possible, and that includes these Haitians.”

White nationalist Nick Fuentes, who has been a vocal critic of Trump’s deportation policies because he doesn’t find them extreme enough, called Haitians “the worst of the worst” and “very low IQ people” on his Rumble show Tuesday night.

In a Telegram channel run by the Proud Boys of Columbus, one member posted a clip of the song “I’m Walking on Sunshine” alongside the news about the revoking of temporary protected status. “They gotta go back,” the member wrote.

It’s been a while since shock-and-awe tactics from Immigration and Customs Enforcement first gained national notoriety. For months, figures like former Border Patrol leader Greg Bovino terrorized cities like Minneapolis and Chicago. But since replacing former Department of Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem with Markwayne Mullin—derisively referred to by Bannon as the “Kung fu plumber”—ICE’s operations have shrunk into the shadows, though the agency’s deportation and arrest numbers have remained astronomical.

In recent weeks, things are boiling over again.

Earlier this month, an ICE agent shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas. Araujo had lived in the country for 35 years, had three children, and owned his own business. Just days later, another ICE agent killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine. Both men were shot while in their vehicles. ICE, as WIRED has revealed, is also tracking its critics online, using data brokers to “identify unaccompanied minors,” and working to prevent state health inspectors from reviewing its network of detention centers. On Tuesday, The New York Times reported that the Trump administration was now targeting immigrants at airports whose visas have expired, or are in a transition status, arresting spouses of American citizens.

Even so, Steve Bannon and the other Republican pundits aren’t alone: Support for ICE among Trump’s most loyal supporters remains incredibly high, with 74 percent of people who identify as MAGA Republicans professing confidence in ICE, according to a YouGov poll published last week. The same poll shows that 80 percent of MAGA Republicans oppose abolishing ICE.

The YouGov findings were backed up by another poll published last week by the Public Religion Research Institute , which found that three-quarters of Republicans had a positive view of ICE, would be in favor of more funding for the agency, and disagreed that ICE was making communities less safe. The poll also found that 73 percent of Republicans are in support of internment camps to hold “immigrants who are in the country illegally” until they can be deported.

The YouGov poll also found that just 51 percent of Republicans had, in the week of the shootings, read, seen, or heard anything about immigrants being shot and killed by ICE agents. What they may have seen however is Trump’s Truth Social post around the same time. In the post, Trump appeared to overrule an internal ICE memo telling agents to suspend vehicle stops, after a furious response from his MAGA base. He also told his supporters that ICE was “loved and respected in America.”

Much of his base thinks that deportations are actually not happening fast enough. ICE is on track to deport 458,000 individuals this year according to its own data, a colossal figure that still falls well short of the 1 million deportations Trump promised shortly after his inauguration. (This, in the words of border czar Tom Homan, is what the administration calls “deportation-maxxing.”)

Americans have been caught in the dragnet as well, as ICE’s actions have resulted in widespread civil rights violations, according to a report published this month by the American Civil Liberties Union, which found that across eight states, ICE agents targeted 155 US citizens, 32 of whom were children, during the first year of Trump’s second term. Previous research from UC Berkeley found that half of all the people ICE has arrested had no criminal records, despite the administration claiming to be deporting the “worst of the worst.” Federal agents have shot and killed four people, including two US citizens.

On the other hand, the majority of Americans believe ICE has used too much force, according to YouGov, and as a result have little or no confidence in the agency. Almost half of Americans believe it's time for ICE to be abolished.

What these polls show is that while America as a whole is rejecting Trump’s immigration policies, his base is almost completely supportive. And rather than distancing themselves from ICE’s actions, Republicans seem to be leaning in again, even spending more money and running more ads about immigration than Democrats, NPR reported last week.

With just months left before the midterms offer voters a chance to have their say on these policies, Republicans are gambling that their base doesn’t actually want ICE going anywhere. In November, the country will see if they’re right.

Which of Dyson’s 2026 Stick Vacuums Is Worth the Upgrade?

Wired July 29, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Dyson's vacuum lineup has a whole new look these days, but that doesn't necessarily make it easier to decide if you're looking to buy one.

The Dyson V16 Piston Animal ($980), V10 Konical ($500), and V8 Cyclone ($400) arrived to change up Dyson's cordless vacuum options. The older V15 Detect ($650) and Gen5Detect ($800) are also still available and great vacuums, which raises the question: Should you upgrade? Which Dyson model is worth the cash with so many options (and widely ranging price points) to choose from?

I tested all five of these vacuums against each other in a series of tests to see which ones stood out among the pack. The two overall winners? The Gen5Detect was the number one winner, with the V16 Piston Animal right behind it, and the V10 Konical coming up third even though it's a much cheaper option. Read on to find out which model did best in each test, what the stats look like for each Dyson vacuum, and how I scored the final results.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Amazon

Amazon

Dyson

Dyson's naming convention is fun, and the numbers usually represent which models are more powerful or offer better accessories, but not always. Most of its vacuums have the V name, which, to my best guess, simply stands for “vacuum.” The numbers aren't always in order of release and usually reflect a vacuum's power level and capabilities. The V10 and V8 have the same power level but different heads, for example, while the V16 is more powerful than the V15. But not all vacuums are named the same; the Gen5Detect has a different name entirely, and falls in between the V15 and V16 when it comes to suction power and price tag.

Here's a quick chart to understand the power levels and compatible accessories that differentiate each vacuum from the other. You might also spot things like “Plus” or “Total” when you're shopping for a Dyson vacuum, and that usually reflects the attachments included with the vacuum.

This gives you a pretty easy look at what you're getting for each model. As the models increase in number (both in the name and in the price tag), the vacuum usually gains more accessories or cleaner heads, more air watts of suction power, and sometimes the option to add the Submarine wet cleaner head on for an additional price, or future compatibility with Dyson's Auto-empty Dok station that's coming out soon.

The Digital Motorbar and All Floor Cones cleaner heads are both compatible with soft and hard floors, which is why sometimes it's the only head included. More expensive Dyson models will also include the Fluffy Optic cleaner head, which is designed specifically for hard floors and has an illuminated light to help you spot dust and debris. The All Floor Cones cleaner head includes a light too, so you're able to get that feature on both the V16 and V10 without switching heads.

Here are the tests I ran for each vacuum, and which ones did best—and worst.

The V10 Konical and the sand obstacle.

After one pass of the V10, only a few thin lines remained of sand, the best results of these five vacuums on this rug.

BEST: V10 Konical ($500)

WORST: V8 Cyclone ($400)

I tested all five Dyson models on a small black rug onto which I poured fine, white sand to see how well it was vacuumed up. The best was the V10 Konical, followed by the V15 Detect. Both left a small trail of sand behind in different spots, which makes sense since they have different head designs, but the V10's trail was smaller than the V15's, with a small line in the middle compared to the larger trail the V15 had on its right side.

The V8, meanwhile, stalled entirely when I tried to use it on the rug and couldn't vacuum up sand whatsoever. It weirdly seemed to have an issue with the thin rug, even though equally or more powerful vacuums were able to vacuum on it.

Both Gen5Detect and V16 Piston Animal were able to vacuum on the thin rug, but the stronger suction also kept trying to take the rug with it, giving both mixed results and leaving a lot of sand behind on each pass. I retested both of these on a thicker rug in case the suction level wasn't a match for the thin rug, and both did much better, but the Gen5Detect did the best, getting every bit of sand in one swoop. The V16 got most of its sand, but pushed some sand into a little pile in front of itself.

The Gen5Detect and the Cheerios obstacle.

After one pass of the Gen5Detect, it only missed Cheerios that were out of its cleaner head range and didn't send any pieces flying.

BEST: Gen5Detect ($800)

WORST: None

When I last did a cereal test, I used a cornflake-style cereal. This time I switched to the cereal I know many parents like myself are much more likely to have all over the floors: Cheerios. I crushed up several in my hand and dropped those along with full Cheerios onto my thicker living room rug. Overall, every Dyson did a good job cleaning this up on the first pass.

The results on this one had pretty minimal differences for these models. The V8, V10, and V15 Detect all usually got the Cheerios and pieces on the first run, sending one to three pieces flying while it did so, but not so far away you wouldn't get to vacuum them up. The Gen5Detect sent nothing flying, though, so it pulls slightly ahead. The V16 sent only a single tiny piece flying forward. But it was right behind the Gen5Detect out of these Dyson models.

The V16 Piston Animal and the litter obstacle.

After one pass of the V16, the only litter left behind was out of the cleaner head range. It did create a thin pile of litter in front of itself as it went, which was vacuumed before moving the head back to the start point to check if any litter had been missed.

BEST: Gen5Detect ($800)

WORST: V8 Cyclone ($400)

Next, I tested these vacuums against a thing I vacuum the most off my vinyl plank floors: cat litter. For this test, since it was on a hard surface instead of a rug, I switched the vacuums' heads to the Fluffy Optic cleaner head when available. That's only on the V15, V16, and Gen5Detect, so those heads changed while the other two models still used the Digital Motorbar (V8) or the All Floor Cones (V10) heads they came with.

It's no surprise that the two standouts both had a Fluffy Optic head. The Gen5Detect left the cleanest floor behind, with not a spec of litter dust to be found from the vacuum's illuminated light after a single pass. The V16 Piston Animal mostly did well, leaving no litter behind, but it did push a small amount of litter in front of itself, similar to the sand test. This only happened in a pass of extremely thick litter, so more day-to-day litter cleanup shouldn't have this issue. Still, the Gen5Detect pulls slightly ahead once again.

The V15 is right behind these two, but left a little dust behind that I could see with the Fluffy Optic's headlight (though no large pieces, and it looked just as clean to the naked eye). Meanwhile, the V10 Konical did fine enough, but needed two passes to get all the debris. The V8 landed last after it pulled a similar move when vacuuming sand and simply pushed the litter into a pile in front of itself, so I then had to move the vacuum on top of and around to vacuum it up, and it took a few passes to do so.

The V16 Piston Animal in handheld mode with the All Floor Cones Sense cleaner head attached.

The V16 Piston Animal without the cleaner head and only the built-in crevice tool on the handheld motor.

BEST: V16 Piston Animal ($980) and Gen5Detect ($800)

WORST: V15 Detect ($650)

Dyson's vacuums function nicely as a handheld vacuum, no matter the model. I tested all five models on my carpeted stairs, and I'd recommend any one of them if that's a big use in your household. The V16 and Gen5Detect pull ahead for me because you can really feel the higher suction at work when you're in handheld mode, and both vacuums showed serious results afterward of dustbins filled with new hair and dust. Especially as a cat owner and a parent of a small child, the carpeted stairs around my house have a lot of debris worked into them. Plus, both of these vacuums have built-in crevice tools you can use in handheld mode, but the V16's will always stay attached, while you need to remove the Gen5's to attach the head directly to the handheld motor.

The V15 also did a fine job, but it felt like it was gliding over my stairs rather than locking into the carpet like the other Dyson vacuums. Even the V8 and V10 with lower power levels felt more suctioned into my carpet than the V15 did for me during my handheld stair testing. Both those cheaper models fell into the runner-up range for me with this test.

The Gen5Detect on my rug.

BEST: Gen5Detect ($800) and V10 Konical ($500)

WORST: V15 Detect ($650)

Originally, I tested an early release version of the V16 Piston Animal that had some clogging issues on carpet. But after getting a current release model, the V16 did much better overall. Both the V16 and the Gen5Detect did an impressive job on my carpets and rugs, and pulled an impressive amount of cat hair and dust out of my recently vacuumed carpets. These both have different heads, but the powerful suction really comes into play on carpet more than anywhere else, especially if you have pets.

Meanwhile, the V10 Konical has the All Floor Cones cleaner head that glided nicely on carpet. The V10's head was a little easier to push around than the Digital Motorbar head (which both the V8 and V15 have) on rugs. The V8 Cyclone took the most effort to push around on my rug, but moved much better on carpet.

The V15 Detect was similar, but unlike the rest of these vacuums, it has a trigger button instead of a power button. That means you have to keep that engaged the entire time when doing a longer vacuuming session. The rest of these vacuums have a power button you click instead, so I don't love the trigger for longer vacuuming sessions. If you're a big vacuumer or have a home with a large amount of carpet, you're going to want a power button, and likely one of the higher-suction vacuums.

(L to R) V10 Konical, Gen5Detect, and V16 Piston Animal.

The results, as you can tell above, are a little murky. The higher-suction vacuums usually took home the prize in most categories, but the V10 Konical was a surprisingly solid all-around performer. To find my winner, I put all of my tests and Dyson models into a chart and scored them on a 1 to 4 point scale, allowing 4 points if the vacuum did the best, 1 if the worst, and a 2 or 3 depending on how middle-of-the-road the results were. One vacuum had a nice lead with a near-perfect score of 19 points.

Dyson

Amazon

Wayfair

The biggest standout from these tests was the Gen5Detect. It came out of these tests with a near-perfect score after the five rounds of testing. It does a great job with its level of powerful suction, and it transitions well between most kinds of debris. As a pet owner, I especially like it for carpet, since the 280 air watts do a great job pulling out hair and pet dander from deep in the carpet. I've actually filled up this vacuum's debris tank before after vacuuming only a few days before with a weaker option.

It's one of the most expensive for a reason, and comes with more attachments than any other model. I do find myself regularly grabbing the Fluffy Optic head for vacuuming my hard floors, which cover many square feet of my home. If you're looking to really splurge on the best vacuum, this is still the one to get.

The only downside is compatibility with Dyson's bigger attachments, namely a mop head or docking station. It doesn't have a Submarine option like the V16 or V15, and Dyson's Auto-empty Dok won't work with this model. But if you aren't worried about add-ons, this is the vacuum to buy. It's had better sales since the launch of the new models, too.

Dyson

Amazon

Amazon (Submarine)

Dyson

Dyson (Submarine)

The V16 Piston Animal's powerful 315 air watts of suction did pretty well on almost every test. My only issue with this vacuum compared to the Gen5Detect is that it was more likely to push small debris (in my tests, both sand and litter) into a pile in front of itself if you were vacuuming a large spill. Gen5Detect did better all around, but the V16 Piston Animal stayed close behind that hiccup.

It's a powerful all-around vacuum with some nice design upgrades to make it a little easier to use. This newer model has a release below the vacuum motor to release the cleaner head without having to bend down, and built-in crevice tools to both the handheld motor and the long wand that makes up the middle of the device. There's also a compressor to help push dust out of the dustbin, and it'll be compatible with Dyson's upcoming self-emptying docking station. There's also a Submarine version ($1,100) so you can use this vacuum as a mop, too.

It has some nice quality-of-life upgrades, but it's really expensive. I'd recommend it if you know you also want to invest in the mop head and docking station; otherwise, just get the Gen5Detect.

Dyson

Dyson

Best Buy

One of the best overall performers is nearly half the price of my winners. The Dyson V10 Konical never once scored in last place, and was especially comfortable to use on carpets and rugs with the new cleaner head design. It did much better than the more expensive and powerful Gen5Detect and V15 Detect when vacuuming up sand, and I found it more comfortable to push around than the Digital Motorbar head on the V15 and V8 when it came to vacuuming a low-pile rug.

It didn't do as well on hard floors, but it didn't do poorly, either. This cheaper model comes with just the single head, but if you don't want to spend the better part of a grand, I'd rather only have this head than the Digital Motorbar head. The All Floor Cones cleaner head also has a built-in light, which you won't get on cheaper or older models. Plus, it'll be compatible with the self-emptying docking station Dyson has coming out soon. For the price point, it's a fantastic buy.

V10 Konical with the Auto-emptying Dok.

BEST: V16 Piston Animal Submarine ($1,100) and V10 Konical with Auto-empty Dok ($650)

WORST: V8 Cyclone ($400) and Gen5Detect ($800)

I'm putting this section after the testing because if you're just looking for a good vacuum, this might not be relevant for you. But there are some interesting upgrades with certain Dyson models you might want to consider, which might sway you toward a certain model over the testing aspects—like if you want a stick vacuum that can work with a self-emptying docking station, or one that can double as a mop. Not all of Dyson's vacuums can do these things, but some of them can—and one can do both.

Both the V16 Piston Animal and the V15 Detect have a Submarine variant (that retail for $1,100 and $750, respectively) that will give you the Submarine head along with the rest of the vacuum accessories. They have slightly different designs, but both are a wet roller head that stores both clean and dirty water while being powered by the motor in the rest of the vacuum. Former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So loved the Submarine version of the V15, and I've been really impressed by the V16's version as well.

If you hate emptying your cordless vacuum, there's an add-on for that, too. You can buy the V10 Konical now with Dyson's new Auto-emptying Dok that can hold up to 60 days of debris. It's a great add-on I've tried with other vacuums like Shark and Tineco and loved because it keeps my vacuum charged and upright, and it stores accessories as well. Dyson has mentioned launching one of these for the V16 in the future, but I'm not sure when that could come to fruition.

If I were to assign points based on these, the V16 Piston Animal ties with the Gen5Detect after getting its add-on while the Gen5Detect has none since it has neither of these additions, and once its own docking station arrives it would pull into first. The V10 Konical remains close behind. It's up to you whether these add-ons make it worth buying, or if you want to choose the models that actually performed best for what you need vacuumed most.

The FCC Is Coming for Robot Vacuums. How Soon Will It Be a Problem?

Wired July 30, 2026

This week, the US Federal Communications Commission banned the import of foreign-made advanced mobile robots. Humanoid and quadruped robots are specifically named, indicating the true target is robotic versions of people and animals, but something else happens to be an “advanced mobile robot”: robot vacuums.

So what does this ban mean? Though it's effective immediately, nothing changes for now. Robot vacuums won't get removed from the market, and your current robot vacuum won't stop working. The ban will instead stop new models from getting FCC approval to be sold in the United States. The vacuums available now won't be affected, but new models likely won't make it to the US if they're manufactured outside the country. And, unfortunately, a lot of great robot vacuum brands aren't based in the States.

Here's everything to know about what will happen next.

The FCC updated its Covered List this week to include foreign-made advanced mobile robots, which include robot vacuums. The Covered List, which comes from Section 2 of the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019, is a “list of communications equipment and services that are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.”

It may feel like overkill for just a robot vacuum, but the definition of an advanced robotic device from the National Security Determination, an interagency body of the Executive Branch, clearly includes them. That definition includes the following highlights:

The National Security Determination said that connected vehicles, vehicles on rail lines, aircraft, and unmanned underwater vehicles are not included in the ban, along with stationary robots. But foreign-made robot vacuums, along with similar robots like robotic pool cleaners and automated lawn mowers, look to be on the chopping block.

The announcement comes after the FCC labeled all of these devices a security risk, since, according to the National Security Determination, “the networked capabilities of advanced robotic systems create extensive vulnerabilities and vectors for attacks that can manipulate the data and physical operation of the advanced robotic system.”

The concern is primarily with the cameras and sensors built into these devices—some even have microphones built into the base station for voice commands. It is a security risk to bring any device into your home that has a camera and the ability to connect to the internet—especially if your Wi-Fi isn't secure. But it's interesting to see the ban stop at robot vacuums and not, say, smart speakers or devices with always-on cameras. The FCC documentation actually lists live cameras as an example, as well as an example of a humanoid robot being hacked, but no example for robot vacuums.

For the most part, it looks like robot vacuums just got unlucky. They're using the same sensors as other robots but aren't streaming live feeds of their surroundings. They do map your home, but that map isn't useful for anything besides knowing where the couch is and which rooms have carpet or hard floors. I wouldn't call these the most dangerous device with a camera in my home by any means, but it seems the government disagrees. This is not the only thing that's been banned lately, either—in May, the FCC also banned foreign-made routers, so we might continue to see bans for various household technology products roll out as the year goes on.

For now, you can shop robot vacuums (and other, similar automated home cleaning robots) as you normally would. FCC approval has already been given to all the robots on the market, so we can expect changes to take place in the future rather than immediately.

I reached out to the makers of my top robot vacuum picks, Shark and Eufy, along with popular robot makers Dreame and Roborock. Shark and Dreame didn't respond, and Roborock declined to comment. Eufy replied with the following statement:

“We are aware of the FCC’s recent update. Based on our current understanding, the new rule does not affect the continued availability, use, or support of products we currently sell in the United States. Those products remain available and will continue to receive updates and customer support.”

So don't worry about getting rid of your robot vacuum if you already have one you love. If you're in the market for a new model, I'd recommend shopping the newest models from brands that could be affected, like Dreame and Eufy, in case future models are blocked from arriving in the States.

It will also be interesting to see which companies avoid the ban—Shark is based in the US, for example, but it's unclear where the company's robot manufacturing is located. Matic is another US-based brand that could potentially evade the ban. But the buying options will be much, much more limited as time goes on.

The ban is disappointing news with IFA Berlin starting September 4, where we often see new robot vacuums announced. I'm not sure anything we'll see there this year will reach the US. A reduced market also isn't good for consumers—having fewer options never helps a category and might ultimately raise prices on less powerful vacuums because of limited supply. Only time will tell what the fallout will be.

A Leaked Memo Ties Cyberattacks on Minnesota Water Utilities to Iran

Wired July 30, 2026

Since the US launched its war against Iran in late February, the country’s hackers have struck back with retaliatory intrusions that have ranged from paralyzing medical supplies company Stryker to breaching the personal email of FBI director Kash Patel. Now, after an unprecedented wave of disruptive cyberattacks hit water utilities in Minnesota, a memo circulated within the water industry ties those attacks to Iran, too, in the widest and most disruptive strike yet inflicted by the country’s hackers against the US since the war began.

A communication obtained by WIRED on Thursday and sent to members of the Water Information Sharing and Analysis Center, or WaterISAC, an industry group for water utilities to share cybersecurity information, links to Iran a series of cyberattacks that targeted dozens of Minnesota water and wastewater utilities.

The WaterISAC note states that the Minnesota Fusion Center, a state-level intelligence-sharing entity, issued an alert “regarding ongoing malicious cyber activity impacting public drinking water systems across Minnesota” and adds that the fusion center has found that those attacks were “aligned” with a hacking campaign first described in April by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) as having been carried out by “Iran-affiliated” hackers. (Both the WaterISAC and Minnesota Fusion Center reports were marked as unclassified but “for official use only.”)

Confirmation of Iran’s responsibility for hacking the water utilities represents a kind of state-sponsored targeting of civilian infrastructure that has rarely been seen outside of Russia’s war against Ukraine, says Joe Slowik, a former Los Alamos National Labs cybersecurity researcher working on contract for the Department of Energy. “Now we have documented disruption and even modification of safety and protection parameters in critical infrastructure,” Slowik says. “Seeing this sort of tradecraft expand to Iran, and seeing it across multiple sites, it should really be making people concerned right now.”

Slowik adds that there’s no reason to believe that the attacks would stop with the incidents in Minnesota. “There are plenty of other sites that have the same targeted technology,” he says. “There’s plenty of areas for this to still be executed by an adversary that has shown a willingness to do so.”

A new CISA advisory related to the attacks released Thursday warns that “these threat actors are targeting water entities of all sizes” and warns utilities to disconnect PLCs from the internet, password-protect access with strong passwords, and “allow-list” only trusted devices to connect to them.

Earlier this week, Minnesota state officials revealed that more than 30 municipal water and wastewater systems had been targeted in hacker breaches that had in some cases disabled telecommunications between the industrial control system technologies and water utility equipment. In at least one municipality, the 1,700-person city of Braham, the hacking reportedly led to a brief outage of the city’s water plant, though there’s not yet evidence of any resulting water shortages or a threat to the safety of Minnesota’s water supply. The latest CISA advisory notes that the attacks have, however, “resulted in boil-water notices”—suggesting fears of water contamination— and “sustained manual operations.”

In the days since that wave of incidents became public, Iran has emerged as the leading suspect behind the attacks, despite the lack of any official confirmation of the country’s involvement or any statement from an Iranian hacker group claiming responsibility. In a report published Monday, cybersecurity firm Tenable wrote that signs suggested CyberAv3ngers, an Iranian hacker group tied to the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps, may be responsible for the water utility breaches, noting that “the operational pattern is consistent with” the group or hacking groups associated with it. Separately, The New York Times reported Thursday that US and state officials and others familiar with the hacking incidents had concluded the Minnesota attacks were “likely” carried out by Iranian state-sponsored hackers, but without naming a specific group.

In its report on the Minnesota water cyberattacks, Tenable pointed to an advisory from CISA that was initially released in April but was updated last week, warning that Iran-linked actors were targeting programmable logic controllers (PLCs) used for automation and coordination in critical infrastructure to cause “operational disruption and financial loss.” That advisory specifically pointed the finger at an “Iranian-affiliated” hacker group and noted that CyberAv3ngers specifically had carried out similar targeting of PLCs.

The updated advisory, however, still doesn’t mention the Minnesota attacks—only the timing of its update on July 22 suggests a connection to the more recent hacking of the state’s water utilities. The WaterISAC memo is the first official document to explicitly draw that connection, tying the attack to Iran.

The WaterISAC memo states that, according to the Minnesota Fusion Center, the hackers who targeted the water utilities compromised remotely accessible PLCs, just as in the earlier hacking campaign described by CISA, “with the likely desired impact to cause loss of system pressure and potential contamination of the water supply.” The memo adds that the facilities “were able to mitigate further compromise, but the full impact is still being assessed.”

WaterISAC’s director of infrastructure cyber defense, Jennifer Lyn Walker, wrote in a statement that the organization had not provided the leaked memo to WIRED, nor did it “assess attribution at any time.”

“WaterISAC always maintains information sharing protocols and safeguards information shared by our members, partners and the broader information sharing community,” Walker wrote.

In the wake of the cyberattacks earlier this week, Minnesota officials said that all drinking water is still safe, and statements from multiple targeted municipalities emphasized that failsafes had protected the systems. “While the incident affected certain automated controls, established contingency procedures were immediately implemented, allowing Public Works staff to maintain normal water and wastewater operations,” South St. Paul officials wrote in a statement.

The CISA advisory that was updated last week, which specifically cited water and wastewater systems operators as part of the “intended audience” of its warning, noted that the attackers were exfiltrating and manipulating the project files that govern automated industrial systems. The alert, which issued with a consortium of US federal agencies including the FBI, the National Security Agency, Cyber Command, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Department of Energy, originally warned in April that likely Iranian hackers were tampering with PLCs to change information on the displays of industrial control systems, which can in some scenarios cause system disruption, damage, or dangerous conditions for utilities. “In a few cases, this activity has resulted in operational disruption and financial loss,” the advisory reads.

That advisory also notes that similar activity, including the targeting of PLCs, was carried out by CyberAv3ngers. That group first emerged in a hacking campaign in late 2023, after Hamas’ October 7 attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza that followed. In that first wave of cyberattacks, CyberAv3ngers targeted devices sold by industrial control systems firm Unitronics, which are typically used in water and wastewater facilities, setting devices to read “Gaza” and display an image of the CyberAv3ngers logo. While the attacks appeared to be mere vandalism, cybersecurity firms that tracked the attacks such as Dragos and Claroty told WIRED that the hackers had in fact rewritten the Unitronics’ devices’ code, leading to disruption of water-related services from Israel to Ireland to a US facility in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

Even after the US State Department offered a $10 million bounty for information about the group and the US Treasury sanctioned six IRGC officials alleged to be linked to it, CyberAv3ngers’ attacks continued to escalate. According to Dragos, it went on to breach a US oil and gas company in 2024 and then to carry out a widespread hacking campaign infecting industrial control and internet-of-things devices with a piece of malware known as IOControl.

Whether CyberAv3ngers is behind the cyberattacks on the Minnesota water utilities remains far from clear. In an interview with WIRED, Yhonatan Harari, a researcher at the cybersecurity firm Claroty, said the company had found other evidence that the attacks might have been carried out by Handala, a distinct hacker group that claimed responsibility for the Stryker cyberattack in March, the breach of Kash Patel’s email later the same month, and numerous other disruptive hacking incidents.

Despite that uncertainty, Harari says that all signs point to Iran as the culprit. “We’re not sure yet if it’s CyberAv3ngers or Handala,” Harari says, “but in a very high likelihood we can say it’s Iranian actors.”

The string of attacks on the Minnesota utilities does, however, closely fit the modus operandi of CyberAv3ngers, which has established itself as a rare state-sponsored hacker group that has shown its willingness to not only target but also sabotage industrial control systems—and water in particular.

“They definitely have the capability; they have the intent,” Dragos cybersecurity researcher Kyle O’Meara told WIRED about CyberAv3ngers last year. “They have the interest in learning how to shut things off and potentially cause harm.”

Additional reporting by Lily Hay Newman.

Updated 7/31/2026 at 10:05 am EDT: Added comment from WaterISAC.
